================================================================================
  ABOUT THIS DOCUMENT
================================================================================
  This is the GOLD-STANDARD Docker learning guide — a single source of truth
  for content, structure, visual language and quality bar. It takes a complete
  beginner from zero → production-competent → DCA-ready, WITHOUT ever needing
  official docs, blogs, books or videos again.

  MISSION — every concept is taught once, in depth, and demonstrated on ONE
  real application (easypj/jobpost) so knowledge compounds instead of
  resetting each chapter. Reference appendices (A–I) are exhaustive against
  the official Docker documentation so this guide can stand in for it.

  INTENDED AUDIENCE
  -----------------
    • Primary ... newcomers taking an application from a laptop to a
                  production-grade container pipeline (no prior Docker
                  assumed).
    • Secondary . practitioners wanting one deep, DCA-AND-production
                  reference for day-to-day container work.

  SCOPE
  -----
    IN  ... 100% of the Docker Certified Associate (DCA) domains (see Section
            6), PLUS production depth: CI/CD, security scanning, Swarm,
            observability, incident response, cost tuning, and the Docker →
            Kubernetes bridge.
    OUT ... deep Kubernetes administration (the companion CKA guide) and deep
            security specialism (the companion CKS guide) are referenced
            where useful (marked [KUBERNETES GUIDE]) but are not the focus.

  CONVENTIONS
  -----------
    Difficulty and content types use a fixed symbol system — see SECTION 1
    (Symbol & Icon Legend) and SECTION 2 (Visual Component Catalog). Reading
    guidance is in SECTION 0. The running project is SECTION 5; the DCA
    certification audit is SECTION 6; the roadmap is SECTION 7; the master
    TOC closes the front matter.


================================================================================
  SECTION 0 — HOW TO READ THIS GUIDE  (the design philosophy)
================================================================================

    THE 5 PROMISES OF THIS GUIDE
    ────────────────────────────
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  1. ZERO-ASSUMPTION       Every term is defined the first time it      │
    │                           appears. No "you should already know X."     │
    │  2. SHOW, DON'T TELL       Never 3 paragraphs in a row without a        │
    │                           diagram, table, card, or code block.         │
    │  3. ONE REAL PROJECT       Every concept is demonstrated on easypj/     │
    │                           jobpost — the SAME app, start to finish.     │
    │  4. DCA + PRODUCTION       Each topic builds toward the certification   │
    │                           AND the production skill it represents.      │
    │  5. SELF-CONTAINED         Reference appendices included so you never   │
    │                           need to leave this document.                 │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    THE LEARNER'S LADDER  (how difficulty is signposted)
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
       🟢 BEGINNER      Concepts, vocabulary, "what & why"
       🟡 INTERMEDIATE  Hands-on, Dockerfiles, Compose, "how"
       🔴 ADVANCED      Internals, security, HA, "what if it breaks"
       🎯 DCA TOPIC     Directly graded on the Docker Certified Associate exam
       🏢 PRODUCTION    Real-world operations the exam doesn't test
       🧪 LAB           A hands-on, verification-ended practice task

    PREREQUISITES & YOUR TOOLKIT  (what you need before Chapter 1)
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  💻 Basic terminal / command-line familiarity                        │
    │  🐍 Any programming literacy (examples use Python/Django — easypj)    │
    │  💾 A computer with 4 GB+ RAM (8 GB+ recommended for Part 9's         │
    │     Docker → Kubernetes bridge and Part 10's Swarm labs)              │
    │  🌐 Internet access — to pull images (Appendix I lists supplementary  │
    │     resources, though this guide is designed to be self-sufficient)   │
    │  🧰 Tools (installed in Ch 3): Docker Desktop or Docker Engine +       │
    │     Docker Compose plugin                                             │
    │  ⏱️ Budget ~40-60 hours; Appendix (Section 6.7) has a study-plan       │
    │     pointer for DCA candidates.                                       │

    LEARNING PATH OVERVIEW
    ──────────────────────
    [ROADMAP ILLUSTRATION: 11-Part journey from Docker novice to production-ready]

    Prerequisites:
      • Basic terminal / command line familiarity
      • A computer with 4 GB+ RAM

    How to Use This Guide:

      • Every concept includes easypj/jobpost real examples

      • Lab questions at the end of each chapter (minimum 10)
      • [INTERACTIVE PROGRESS TRACKER BAR]

    HOW EVERY TOPIC TEACHES — THE 5-RAIL METHOD
    ────────────────────────────────────────────
    Every numbered topic (N.M) in this guide is built on the same five rails,
    in the same order. The HTML build must render all five — no rail skipped.

      🎯 GOAL      One sentence: what you will be able to DO after this topic.
      🧠 CONCEPT   Dual explanation, always as a pair:
                   [TECH]    — the technically precise version: exact terms,
                               real component names, correct mechanics.
                   [ANALOGY] — the human version: a picture from everyday life.
                   BOTH versions must point at the SAME illustration. The
                   illustration is the bridge between them — never decoration.
      🔬 EXAMPLE   The concept applied to easypj/jobpost (our Django job board:
                   models Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, User). Real
                   commands, real files, real output — never pseudo-code.
      🧪 PRACTICE  A hands-on drill the reader performs, ending with a
                   verification step: "how do you KNOW it worked?"
      📊 SUMMARY   2-4 lines compressing the topic + one ⚠️ gotcha to remember.

    [DIAGRAM:flow — The 5-Rail Method]
    ┌─────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌──────────┐
    │ 🎯 GOAL │─▶│ 🧠 CONCEPT       │─▶│🔬 EXAMPLE│─▶│🧪 PRACTICE│─▶│📊 SUMMARY│
    │ why     │  │ [TECH]+[ANALOGY] │  │ easypj/  │  │ do it +   │  │ compress │
    │ bother? │  │ one illustration │  │ jobpost  │  │ verify it │  │ + gotcha │
    └─────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └──────────┘  └───────────┘  └──────────┘

    Chapter discipline:
      • Every chapter opens with WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS — the problem it
        solves and what breaks if you skip it.
      • Every part opens with a THINK box: What runs where? What talks to
        what? What breaks first?
      • Kubernetes-deep topics are never skipped silently — they are marked
        [KUBERNETES GUIDE] and handed off to the Kubernetes guide.
      • The 80/20 rule governs depth: the 20% of features that solve 80% of
        real problems get diagrams, labs and drills; the rest gets a table.

    THE PER-CHAPTER SCAFFOLD  (fixed anatomy of every chapter — see SECTION 3)
    and THE PER-PART SCAFFOLD (fixed anatomy of every part — see SECTION 4)
    wrap the 5-Rail topics above in a consistent open/close structure so every
    chapter and part is self-contained and revision-ready.

    Every icon below carries a FIXED meaning across the whole guide so your

    NAVIGATION & STATUS
    ┌───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  🎯       │ DCA exam topic (graded competency)                        │
    │  🏢       │ Beyond-the-exam / production knowledge                    │
    │  🧪       │ Hands-on lab / practice task                              │
    │  ⏱️       │ Time budget note                                          │
    │  🟢 🟡 🔴 │ Beginner / Intermediate / Advanced difficulty             │
    └───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    TEACHING CUES
    ┌───────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  💡       │ Key insight / "aha" moment                                │
    │  🧠       │ Mental model / analogy                                    │
    │  📖       │ Definition of a term (Key Term box)                       │
    │  🔧       │ Under the Hood (internals / how it really works)          │
    │  ⚠️       │ Gotcha / common mistake / trap                            │
    │  ⚡       │ Speed tip (imperative shortcut, muscle-memory command)    │
    │  🔑       │ Must-remember command / fact                              │
    │  ✅ ❌     │ Do / Don't · Correct / Wrong · Pass / Fail               │
    │  🧭       │ Decision guide ("which one do I use?")                    │
    │  🩺       │ Troubleshooting / diagnosis flow                          │
    └───────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    VISUAL LANGUAGE — SYMBOLS & DIAGRAM TYPES
    ──────────────────────────────────────────
    One symbol = one meaning, across all 11 parts:

      🐳 Docker Engine/daemon    📝 Dockerfile         📦 Image
      ▶️ Running container       🗄️ Registry           🎼 Compose
      🌐 Network                 💾 Volume/storage     🔐 Security
      🐝 Swarm                   ☸️ Kubernetes         🚀 CI/CD
      ⚡ Command to memorize     ⚠️ Gotcha/trap        💡 Key insight
      🔧 Under the hood          🧪 Practice/lab       🎯 Goal/exam target

    Diagram directives — what the HTML build must render (NO placeholders):
      [DIAGRAM:architecture]  boxes & arrows: components and where they run
      [DIAGRAM:flow]          left→right sequence of steps or data
      [DIAGRAM:state]         lifecycle state machine with transitions
      [DIAGRAM:layers]        stacked layers (image layers, security onion)
      [DIAGRAM:decision]      decision tree — "which one do I use, when?"
      [DIAGRAM:timeline]      evolution over time
      [TABLE]                 comparison / reference table
      [CARDS]                 grid of concept cards
      [TERMINAL]              annotated real session ($ command + output)
      [CODE]                  complete runnable file — never fragments
      [CHECKLIST]             actionable checklist
      [LAB]                   hands-on exercise: steps + verification


================================================================================
  SECTION 2 — THE VISUAL COMPONENT CATALOG  (the art direction)
================================================================================
    These are the building blocks used to render content. The rule:
    "NEVER a wall of text." Every subsection must contain >=1 of these.
    Each entry = [WHAT it is] + [WHEN to use it] + an ASCII mock to follow.

    2.1  CONCEPT CARD GRID          — 2-4 cards, icon + title + 1-line idea.
         WHEN: introduce a set of sibling concepts (e.g. 4 volume types).
         [ 📦 Image ][ ▶️ Container ][ 🗄️ Registry ][ 🎼 Compose ]

    2.2  ANATOMY CALLOUT            — label every field of a command/file.
         WHEN: first time a command or file format is shown.
         docker  run   -d   -p 8000:8000   easypj:v1
         └cmd─┘ └verb┘ └flag┘ └──ports───┘ └──image──┘

    2.3  COMPARISON TABLE          — side-by-side feature matrix.
         WHEN: "X vs Y" decisions (bind mount vs volume, CMD vs ENTRYPOINT).

    2.4  DECISION TREE 🧭          — branching "which one do I use?" guide.
         WHEN: choosing among options (volume vs bind vs tmpfs).

    2.5  SEQUENCE / FLOW DIAGRAM   — numbered steps with arrows (left->right
         or top->down). WHEN: a process over time (build, push, pull, run).

    2.6  ARCHITECTURE DIAGRAM      — boxed components + connections + legend.
         WHEN: showing how parts of the system relate spatially.

    2.7  MENTAL-MODEL / ANALOGY 🧠 — relate Docker to everyday life.
         WHEN: a concept is abstract (layers = transparent sheets stacked).

    2.8  COMMAND CHEAT-CARD 🔑     — grouped, copy-paste commands with notes.
         WHEN: end of every chapter ("most-used commands to remember").

    2.9  ANNOTATED FILE SKELETON   — minimal Dockerfile/compose.yaml, every
         line commented. WHEN: teaching the shape of a file; also used
         inside lab answers.

    2.10 UNDER THE HOOD 🔧         — deep-dive (daemon internals, storage
         drivers, network namespaces). WHEN: once per chapter.

    2.11 GOTCHA BOX ⚠️            — the trap + why it happens + the fix.
         WHEN: a place learners reliably fail (detached HEAD-style layer
         cache misses, port conflicts, volume permission errors).

    2.12 SPEED TIP ⚡             — a muscle-memory shortcut beats typing
         the long form. WHEN: an alias or flag combo saves real time.

    2.13 PRODUCTION OPS 🏢        — "in a real job you would..." scenario.
         WHEN: connecting a tested skill to actual container operations.

    2.14 TROUBLESHOOTING FLOW 🩺  — symptom -> checks -> cause -> fix tree.
         WHEN: any failure mode (container exits 137, port already allocated).

    2.15 BEFORE / AFTER SPLIT     — "without Docker" vs "with Docker" panel.
         WHEN: motivating why a feature exists.

    2.16 LIFECYCLE PILLS          — state badges joined by arrows
         (Created -> Running -> Paused -> Exited). WHEN: object states.

    2.17 STAT / PROGRESS BARS     — image-size deltas, exam-domain %.
         WHEN: quantitative emphasis.

    2.18 RELATIONSHIP / MIND MAP  — central node with labeled spokes.
         WHEN: "how everything connects" (object relationship map).

    2.19 KEY TAKEAWAYS BANNER     — ✅ bullet recap + 🎯 DCA relevance +
         🔑 commands. WHEN: end of every chapter AND every part.

    2.20 VISUAL SUMMARY           — one big picture that re-tells the whole
         chapter/part in a single diagram. WHEN: closing every chapter/part.
         (RULE: every diagram-only block also carries a short prose summary
         — we never give a diagram without its text recap.)

    2.21 PRACTICE DRILL 🧪        — short timed checklist task (do-it-now).
         WHEN: mid/after a chapter, before the formal lab questions.

    2.22 LAB Q&A CARD 🧪          — practice question + Answer + Explanation
         (with diagram/table where useful). WHEN: 10+ per chapter, end.

    2.23 DCA-TOPIC BADGE 🎯       — inline tag marking graded competencies.

    2.24 KEY TERM / GLOSSARY POP 📖 — bold term + tight definition box.


================================================================================
  SECTION 3 — THE PER-CHAPTER SCAFFOLD  (fixed anatomy of EVERY chapter)
================================================================================
    Every chapter is assembled from these blocks IN THIS ORDER:

      [A] CHAPTER HEADER      Title + difficulty meta (🟢/🟡/🔴, ⏱️ est time,
                              🎯 DCA domain if applicable) — the META line.
      [B] WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS   The problem it solves and what breaks if
                              you skip it — framed on easypj.
      [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES "after this chapter you can" — action bullets.
      [D] DCA RELEVANCE       Which exact DCA domain(s) this maps to (or
                              "not graded, but assumed by X" where relevant).
      [E] SECTION-MAP DIAGRAM A single diagram showing how all sections of
                              THIS chapter relate (the "you are here" map).
      [F] CONCEPT SECTIONS    The numbered sections (x.1, x.2, ...), each
                              following the 5-Rail Method (Section 0):
                                🎯 GOAL · 🧠 CONCEPT ([TECH]+[ANALOGY]) ·
                                🔬 EXAMPLE (easypj) · 🧪 PRACTICE · 📊 SUMMARY
      [G] UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 / DEEPER   One internals deep-dive for the chapter.
      [H] KEY TAKEAWAYS 🔑   ✅ recap + 🎯 DCA relevance.
      [I] GOTCHAS ⚠️         The top traps for this chapter, listed.
      [J] SPEED TIPS ⚡      Muscle-memory shortcuts / aliases.
      [K] COMMANDS TO REMEMBER 🔑  Cheat-card of must-know commands.
      [L] PRACTICE DRILL 🧪  A short, timed do-it-now checklist.
      [M] LAB QUESTIONS 🧪   >=10 practice Q&A. EACH has: Question, Answer
                              (commands/steps), Explanation (the WHY) + at
                              least one diagram/table where useful.
      [N] VISUAL SUMMARY      One closing big-picture diagram + prose recap.


================================================================================
  SECTION 4 — THE PER-PART SCAFFOLD  (fixed anatomy of EVERY part)
================================================================================
      [A] PART COVER          Title, difficulty band, chapter range, "what
                              you'll build" line.
      [B] PART INTRO          What this part is, why it exists, what it
                              unlocks — framed on the easypj journey.
      [C] "HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT" DIAGRAM   A map showing each chapter in the
                              part and the dependency/flow between them.
      [D] SECTION SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION  (placed BEFORE the chapters) — a
                              concise summary of the whole part and HOW it is
                              implemented end-to-end on easypj.
      [E] CHAPTERS            (each following the Section 3 scaffold)
      [F] PART KEY TAKEAWAYS  ✅ + 🎯 + 🔑 across the whole part.
      [G] PART VISUAL SUMMARY One diagram tying the whole part together.


================================================================================
  SECTION 5 — THE RUNNING PROJECT: easypj / jobpost
================================================================================
    Everything in this guide is taught on ONE real application so concepts
    compound instead of resetting each chapter.

    5.1  WHAT IT IS
         📖 easypj   = the Django PROJECT (the deployable unit / repo root).
         📖 jobpost  = the Django APP inside it (a job-board: post & browse
                       jobs, skills, employers, locations).
         Stack: Python 3.13, Django 5.2.5, PostgreSQL (never SQLite/MySQL —
         easypj is containerized from the start, so there is no "dev SQLite,
         prod Postgres" split; the same database runs in every environment).

    5.2  THE DATA MODEL  (real models from jobpost/models.py)
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  User (django.contrib.auth)                                    │
         │     │ 1─1                                                       │
         │     ▼                                                          │
         │  Author(company, designation)                                  │
         │     │ 1─many (jobpost)                                          │
         │     ▼                                                          │
         │  JobPost(title, description, salary, type, slug, expiry, date) │
         │     ▲ 1─1            ▲ many─many                                │
         │     │                │                                         │
         │  Location(...)     Skills(name)                                │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    5.3  THE CONTAINERIZATION STORY  (the through-line)
         🐳 Build:  Dockerfile → multi-stage build → small gunicorn image
                    easypj:vN (Part 3).
         🎼 Compose: django + postgres + nginx (+ redis) wired together for
                    local dev and small production (Part 4).
         🌐 Ship:   image pushed to a registry, versioned and promoted
                    across environments (Part 8).
         ☸️ Bridge: the SAME image runs unmodified under Kubernetes once a
                    single host stops being enough (Part 9).
         📖 Why PostgreSQL from day one? A containerized app should behave
            the same in dev and prod — SQLite's single-file model does not
            survive multi-container or multi-host deployment, so this guide
            never introduces it. PostgreSQL runs in its own container from
            Chapter 9 onward.

    5.4  TARGET ARCHITECTURE  (what we build by the end)
         ┌─────────────────────── easypj production stack ─────────────────┐
         │  🌐 nginx (reverse proxy, :80)                                    │
         │              │                                                    │
         │       🎼 Compose network: easypj-net                              │
         │        ┌─────┼───────────────┐                                   │
         │     📦 django   📦 celery-worker (optional)                       │
         │        │  env via .env / secrets                                 │
         │        ▼                                                          │
         │     🐘 postgres  ── 💾 named volume (postgres_data)               │
         │                                                                   │
         │  🔐 Docker Scout scanning  🐝 Swarm/K8s for scale  🚀 CI builds   │
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    5.5  WHERE THE PROJECT APPEARS (mapping)  — every part advances easypj:
         P1 understand it · P2 run it by hand · P3 build its image ·
         P4 compose its full stack · P5 network it · P6 give it storage ·
         P7 secure it · P8 ship it (CI/CD) · P9 bridge it to Kubernetes ·
         P10 orchestrate/certify it · P11 operate it in production.


================================================================================
  SECTION 6 — DOCKER CERTIFIED ASSOCIATE (DCA) AT A GLANCE  &  DOMAIN MAP
================================================================================

    6.1  THE FACTS  (verified against the official Mirantis DCA exam page)
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Duration: 90 minutes   Format: 13 multiple-choice + 42       │
         │  discrete-option multiple-choice (DOMC) questions              │
         │  Cost: $199 / €200   Delivery: remotely proctored              │
         │  Prereq: 6-12 months of Docker experience recommended          │
         │  Validity: 2 years   Passing score: not published by Docker/  │
         │  Mirantis (subject to change without notice)                   │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         📖 Administration note: the DCA program is administered by
         Mirantis (Docker's training partner), not Docker, Inc. directly.

    6.2  DOMAIN WEIGHTS  (per the official DCA Exam Preparation Guide)
         🎯 Orchestration ............................ 25%  ██████████
         📦 Image Creation, Management & Registry .... 20%  ████████
         🔧 Installation & Configuration .............. 15%  ██████
         🌐 Networking ................................ 15%  ██████
         🔐 Security ................................... 15%  ██████
         💾 Storage & Volumes .......................... 10%  ████

    6.3  DOMAIN -> CHAPTER MAP  (so nothing is missed)
         ORCHESTRATION (25%)
           • Swarm init, join, node management ......... Ch 28
           • Service create/scale/update/rollback ....... Ch 28
           • Stack deploy from Compose files ............ Ch 28, 29
           • Compose fundamentals & multi-container apps  Ch 10-12
         IMAGE CREATION, MANAGEMENT & REGISTRY (20%)
           • Dockerfile instructions & best practices ... Ch 4, 8
           • docker build / buildx, multi-stage builds .. Ch 5, 8
           • Image tagging, versioning, promotion ........ Ch 23
           • Registries (Docker Hub, ECR/GCR/ACR, mirrors) Ch 2, 7
         INSTALLATION & CONFIGURATION (15%)
           • Docker Desktop / Engine installation ........ Ch 3
           • Daemon configuration, storage drivers ....... Ch 3, 18
           • Swarm cluster installation ................... Ch 28
         NETWORKING (15%)
           • Bridge, host, overlay, macvlan networks ..... Ch 13, 15
           • Container DNS & service discovery ........... Ch 13, 14
           • Port publishing & the CNM model .............. Ch 13
         SECURITY (15%)
           • Image scanning (Docker Scout) ................ Ch 21
           • Least-privilege, non-root, capabilities ...... Ch 19, 20
           • Secrets management ........................... Ch 20
         STORAGE & VOLUMES (10%)
           • Volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs .............. Ch 16, 17
           • Storage drivers ............................... Ch 18
           • Backup/restore patterns for volumes .......... Ch 17

    6.4  DCA DOMAIN COVERAGE AUDIT               ✅ 6/6 DOMAINS COVERED
         Every official DCA domain -> where it is taught AND drilled in
         this guide. ✓ = concept + commands + >=1 lab question.
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────┬──┐
    │ DOMAIN                                    │ Weight │ Chapter   │  │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼───────────┼──┤
    │ Orchestration                              │ 25%    │ 10-12, 28 │✓ │
    │ Image Creation, Management & Registry      │ 20%    │ 2,4,5,7,8,│✓ │
    │                                             │        │ 23        │  │
    │ Installation & Configuration                │ 15%    │ 3, 18, 28 │✓ │
    │ Networking                                  │ 15%    │ 13-15     │✓ │
    │ Security                                    │ 15%    │ 19-21     │✓ │
    │ Storage & Volumes                           │ 10%    │ 16-18     │✓ │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴───────────┴──┘
         RESULT: 6/6 graded domains covered (concept + hands-on + labs).
         The "+beyond" depth — CI/CD (P8), the Kubernetes bridge (P9), Swarm
         production ops (P10), and observability/incident response/cost
         tuning/AI workloads (P11) — exceeds the DCA syllabus so you never
         need external docs.

    6.5  DCA vs CKA vs CKS  (the container/orchestration cert ladder)
         ┌────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────┐
         │            │ DCA (this)   │ CKA          │ CKS              │
         │ Focus      │ containerize │ run/operate  │ secure/harden    │
         │ Owns       │ THE IMAGE    │ THE CLUSTER  │ THE ATTACK SURF. │
         │ Prereq     │ none         │ none         │ CKA required     │
         │ Analogy    │ 📦 pack the  │ 🏗️ build the │ 🛡️ guard the     │
         │            │   crate      │   house      │   house          │
         └────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────┘

    6.6  EXAM-DAY SETUP — MUSCLE-MEMORY SHORTCUTS
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Commands worth typing until they're automatic:               │
         │                                                                │
         │  docker ps -a --format '{{.Names}}: {{.Status}}'              │
         │  docker system df                                             │
         │  docker compose logs -f <service>                             │
         │  docker inspect <id> --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'           │
         │  docker network ls / docker volume ls                         │
         │                                                                │
         │  ⏱️ Muscle memory on `docker ps`, `logs`, `inspect` and       │
         │  `exec` saves real minutes under any time pressure.           │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    6.7  STUDY PLAN & PRACTICE POINTERS
         This guide's Appendix H holds 100+ DCA-style practice questions.
         A suggested 4-week study cadence: Week 1 = Parts 1-3 (concepts,
         hands-on, images); Week 2 = Parts 4-6 (Compose, networking,
         storage); Week 3 = Parts 7-8 (security, CI/CD); Week 4 = Parts
         9-11 (Kubernetes bridge, Swarm/certification, production ops) +
         Appendix H practice questions + weak-domain review using Section
         6.4's coverage table.

    Swarm orchestration and certification prep, then production mastery —

    🔄 The Container Revolution — Why Docker Changed Everything
       - Before Docker: "Works on my machine" syndrome
       - After Docker: Consistent environments everywhere
       - The shipping container analogy: standardized, stackable, portable

         [TIMELINE: Evolution of Software Deployment]
         ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐

PART 1: DOCKER CONCEPTS — THE BIG PICTURE                              🟢
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    THINK BEFORE PART 1:
      What runs where?    → everything on YOUR laptop — one host, one daemon.
      What talks to what? → docker CLI → REST API → dockerd → containerd → runc.
      What breaks first?  → your mental model: a container is NOT a small VM.

    [PART 1 INTRO]
    Every easypj deploy starts the same way: it runs perfectly on your laptop,
    then something breaks the moment it leaves — a missing psycopg2 wheel, a
    Python patch version nobody pinned, a package that quietly upgraded on the
    server. Part 1 exists to kill that gap for good. By the last page of
    Chapter 3 you will have gone from "I type docker commands and hope" to a
    working mental model AND a working Docker Desktop/Engine install with your
    first container running on it.

    This is the ONLY part of the guide that writes no Dockerfile and builds no
    easypj image — that starts in Part 2. Part 1's job is narrower and more
    important: get the vocabulary (image, container, registry, layer, tag) and
    the architecture (client → daemon → containerd → runc) so solid that every
    later command reads as a sentence, not an incantation.

    🧠 ANALOGY. Picture moving apartments. Without Docker you carry everything
    loose — boxes of dishes, a mattress strapped to a car roof, a lamp riding
    on your lap — and something always breaks or gets left behind (that is
    "works on my machine"). Docker is the moving company that packs your
    ENTIRE apartment into one sealed, labeled shipping container: the same box
    goes on the same truck onto the same ship no matter what continent it
    lands on, and nothing shifts in transit. Part 1 is you learning what the
    container is made of (Ch1), what you call its parts (Ch2), and how to
    actually rent your first one (Ch3) — before Part 2 teaches you to pack it
    yourself.

    [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 1 map]
    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Ch1 THE PROBLEM ─────▶ Ch2 THE NOUNS ─────▶ Ch3 THE HANDS-ON         │
    │  why Docker exists,      image, container,     install Docker, run   │
    │  container vs VM,        registry, layer,      your first container, │
    │  the daemon chain        tag — the vocabulary  the CLI's grammar     │
    │       │                        │                       │             │
    │       └────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┘             │
    │                                ▼                                     │
    │              You can now READ every command Part 2 types             │
    │              before you have typed a single one yourself.            │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    Read the map as a sentence: Chapter 1 tells you WHY containers exist and
    what makes them different from a VM, Chapter 2 hands you the FIVE NOUNS
    every command manipulates, and Chapter 3 puts a terminal in your hands so
    those nouns stop being theory. Each chapter assumes the one before it —
    do not skip ahead to Ch3 without Ch1-2's model in place first.

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE — where do I start?
    ┌───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┐
    │ If you...                          │ Then...                          │
    ├───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
    │ have never touched containers      │ start at 1.1, read every diagram │
    │ used Docker but never read the docs│ skim Ch1, study Ch2 (vocabulary) │
    │ are coming from VMs                │ go straight to 1.3, then Ch2     │
    │ just need Desktop/Engine running   │ jump to Ch3, backfill Ch1-2 later│
    └───────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘

    WITHOUT vs WITH DOCKER — why any of this exists
    ┌────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
    │  WITHOUT Docker                     │  WITH Docker                    │
    ├────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
    │  easypj needs Python 3.11 + Django  │  easypj + its ENTIRE userspace  │
    │  5.2 + psycopg2 installed by hand   │  ship as one immutable image    │
    │  New hire loses a day installing    │  New hire: docker compose up    │
    │  Postgres, exact package versions   │  (30 seconds — Part 4)          │
    │  Staging ≠ prod ≠ laptop — drift    │  Same image runs on all three   │
    │  3 AM fix = SSH in and hope         │  3 AM fix = redeploy the image  │
    │  "It worked yesterday" — undebuggable│ Image = versioned, immutable   │
    │                                      │  snapshot — yesterday = today  │
    └────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
    CAPTION: Docker does not make easypj smarter — it makes easypj
    REPRODUCIBLE. You stop asking "what's installed on this machine?" and
    start shipping the machine's entire relevant userspace with the app.

    [PART 1 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION — read before the chapters]
    By the end of Part 1 you will not have written a single Dockerfile — that
    is Part 2. What you WILL have: a Docker Desktop or Engine install that
    reports healthy, a `hello-world` container run start-to-finish, and enough
    vocabulary to read `docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000
    easypj:v1` and explain every token in it. Implementation thread: no
    easypj code has moved yet — you are installing the platform that Part 2
    will hand easypj to.

        $ docker version              →  client AND server both answer
        $ docker run --rm hello-world →  pull (if needed) → create → run
                  │
                  ▼
        You now own: a working daemon, the 4 Docker objects (image,
        container, network, volume), and the CLI grammar to read ANY
        docker command on sight.
    CAPTION: this install-and-verify loop is the one you will repeat on
    every new machine for the rest of your Docker life — Part 1 makes it
    boring, which is exactly the goal.

Chapter 1: What is Docker? (The Container Revolution)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: You cannot debug, secure, or optimize what you
    cannot picture. This chapter builds the mental model — the problem Docker
    kills, the architecture that does the killing, and the vocabulary every
    later chapter assumes. Problem solved here: "I can type docker commands,
    but I have no idea what is actually happening."

    [A] META: 🟢 Beginner · ⏱️ ~2h · not a graded DCA domain by itself, but
        the Image Creation, Management & Registry domain (20%) — and every
        domain after it — assumes this exact mental model.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
         ✅ Name the three environment problems Docker eliminates and point
            at exactly where each one bites easypj (1.1).
         ✅ Give the one-sentence definitions of Docker, image, and
            container, and separate Docker Inc./Docker the technology/
            docker the CLI (1.2).
         ✅ Explain why containers share the host kernel while VMs don't —
            and defend the one case where a VM still wins (1.3).
         ✅ Trace one `docker run` end-to-end through the client → dockerd
            → containerd → shim → runc chain (1.4).

    1.1  The Problem Docker Solves
         - "Works on my machine" — the universal developer frustration
         - Dependency hell: Python 3.8 vs 3.11, Django 4.2 vs 5.2
         - Inconsistent environments: dev ≠ staging ≠ production
         - Real-world: easypj runs on your laptop but crashes on the server

         [THE "WORKS ON MY MACHINE" PROBLEM — Illustrated]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                  🖥️  THE DEPENDENCY NIGHTMARE                              │
         │                                                                          │
         │   Developer Laptop              Staging Server            Production      │
         │   ┌────────────────┐          ┌────────────────┐       ┌──────────────┐  │
         │   │ Python 3.11 ✅ │          │ Python 3.8  ❌  │       │ Python 3.9   │  │
         │   │ Django 5.2  ✅ │          │ Django 4.2  ❌  │       │ Django 4.2   │  │
         │   │ psycopg2  ✅  │          │ psycopg2  ✅   │       │ psycopg2 ❌  │  │
         │   │ Node.js  ✅   │          │ Node.js  ❌    │       │ Node.js  ✅  │  │
         │   │ ───────────── │          │ ─────────────  │       │ ───────────  │  │
         │   │ App WORKS! 😊 │          │ App BROKEN! 😡 │       │ App BROKEN!  │  │
         │   └────────────────┘          └────────────────┘       └──────────────┘  │
         │                                                                          │
         │   "BUT IT WORKS ON MY MACHINE!!!" — Every Developer Ever                 │
         │                                                                          │
         │   SOLUTION: 🐳 Docker packages Python 3.11 + Django 5.2 + ALL deps      │
         │   into ONE portable container that runs IDENTICALLY everywhere!          │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [PAIN POINT CARDS — 3 Scenarios Without Docker]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  😰 Scenario 1: New Developer Onboarding                                 │
         │  Without Docker: Install Python, Django, PostgreSQL, Redis, configure    │
         │  virtualenv, set env vars... (2+ hours)                                   │
         │  WITH Docker: docker compose up (30 seconds)                             │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  🔥 Scenario 2: Production Emergency at 3 AM                             │
         │  Without Docker: SSH into server, find the right config, restart         │
         │  process manually, pray dependency versions match...                     │
         │  WITH Docker: docker pull easypj:v2 && docker compose up -d              │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  📦 Scenario 3: "It worked yesterday, what changed?"                     │
         │  Without Docker: System update changed Python version, pip packages      │
         │  drifting over time. Impossible to reproduce exact environment.          │
         │  WITH Docker: Image is immutable snapshot. Yesterday's image = today's.  │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Name the three environment problems Docker eliminates and
            point at exactly where each one bites easypj.
         [TECH] The root cause is environment drift: unpinned interpreter
            versions, diverging system libraries, and OS packages that mutate
            over time. Docker removes drift by shipping the entire userspace
            (interpreter + libraries + app code + config) as one immutable,
            versioned artifact — the image.
         [ANALOGY] Moving house with loose boxes vs one sealed shipping crate:
            loose boxes (pip installs, apt packages, env vars) get lost or
            crushed in transit; the sealed crate arrives exactly as packed.
            The DEPENDENCY NIGHTMARE diagram above IS the loose-boxes move —
            three machines, three different piles.
         🔬 easypj: laptop has Python 3.11 + Django 5.2; staging has 3.8 →
            `python manage.py runserver` dies on syntax it has never seen.
            One easypj image ends that entire class of bug permanently.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: Write down every single thing easypj needs to run
            (interpreter, pip packages, OS libraries, env vars, ports). That
            list is exactly what a container freezes. Verify: could a teammate
            rebuild your machine from the list alone? If not — that gap is
            where "works on my machine" lives.
         📊 SUMMARY: Docker packages the app + its full userspace into one
            immutable unit that runs identically everywhere.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Docker does NOT package the kernel — that still comes
            from the host (see 1.3). "Identical everywhere" means userspace.

    1.2  What is Docker? (The Simple Answer)
         - Docker = a platform for building, shipping, and running containers
         - Container = lightweight, standalone, executable package of software
         - The shipping container analogy in detail
         - Docker Inc. (company) vs Docker (technology) vs docker (CLI tool)

         [THE SHIPPING CONTAINER ANALOGY]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │             🚢 PHYSICAL SHIPPING  =  🐳 SOFTWARE CONTAINERS                │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ┌─────────────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────┐               │
         │  │  📦 Standard Container│          │  🐳 Docker Image     │               │
         │  │  Same size, shape,   │          │  Same format, runs   │               │
         │  │  fits on any ship,   │          │  on any OS, any      │               │
         │  │  truck, or train     │          │  cloud, any server   │               │
         │  └─────────┬───────────┘          └─────────┬───────────┘               │
         │            │                                │                            │
         │            ▼                                ▼                            │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐                │
         │  │  🏗️ Standardized, Stackable, Portable, Isolated      │                │
         │  │  What's INSIDE doesn't matter to the transport!      │                │
         │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘                │
         │                                                                          │
         │  Analogy: Just like a shipping container can carry cars, TVs, or        │
         │  furniture — and any ship/truck/train can carry any container —          │
         │  Docker containers can run Python, Node.js, Go, or Java apps            │
         │  on ANY machine that has Docker installed. 🌍                           │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Give the one-sentence definition of Docker and of a
            container, and separate the three things people call "Docker".
         [TECH] Docker is a container platform: a daemon (dockerd) exposing a
            REST API that builds OCI images and runs them as isolated Linux
            processes using kernel namespaces and cgroups. A container is a
            process with a private view of the OS — not a machine.
         [ANALOGY] The shipping container diagram above: transport companies
            stopped caring what is INSIDE the box once every box got the same
            corners and the same locks. Ships/trucks/trains = laptop/server/
            cloud; the standardized corners = the OCI image format.
         💡 Definitions to keep (exam-grade):
            • Image     = read-only, layered filesystem snapshot + metadata.
            • Container = a running (or stopped) instance of an image with
                          one writable layer on top.
            • Docker    = the platform that builds, ships and runs them.
         🔬 easypj: `docker run easypj:v1` starts gunicorn inside an isolated
            process — same laptop, but easypj believes it owns the machine.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: Say out loud, without notes: "an image is ___, a
            container is ___". Verify against 2.1's class↔object diagram.
         📊 SUMMARY: Build once → ship anywhere → run identically; container
            = isolated process, image = its frozen blueprint.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Docker Inc. (company) ≠ Docker (technology) ≠ docker
            (the CLI binary) — job interviews test exactly this sloppiness.

    1.3  Containers vs Virtual Machines — The Critical Difference
         - VMs: Each has its own OS kernel (heavy, GBs, minutes to boot)
         - Containers: Share host OS kernel (lightweight, MBs, seconds to start)
         - Side-by-side architecture diagram
         - Resource comparison table (CPU, RAM, Disk, Boot time, Density)

         [SIDE-BY-SIDE ARCHITECTURE: VM vs CONTAINER]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
         │        VIRTUAL MACHINES           │  │           CONTAINERS               │
         │                                   │  │                                   │
         │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ │  │  ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ ┌─────┐ │
         │  │App A│ │App B│ │App C│ │App D│ │  │  │App A│ │App B│ │App C│ │App D│ │
         │  └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ │  │  └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ └──┬──┘ │
         │     │       │       │       │    │  │     │       │       │       │    │
         │  ┌──┴───────┴───────┴───────┴──┐ │  │  ┌──┴───────┴───────┴───────┴──┐ │
         │  │  Guest OS (Full Kernel)     │ │  │  │     Docker Engine           │ │
         │  │  ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐       │ │  │  └─────────────────────────────┘ │
         │  │  │Bin/Lib│ │Bin/Lib│       │ │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │
         │  │  └───────┘ └───────┘       │ │  │  │     Host OS (Shared Kernel)  │ │
         │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │  └─────────────────────────────┘ │
         │  ┌────────────────────────────┐ │  │  ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │
         │  │      Hypervisor            │ │  │  │     Hardware / Cloud         │ │
         │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │  └─────────────────────────────┘ │
         │  ┌────────────────────────────┐ │  │                                   │
         │  │    Host OS                 │ │  │  ❌ NO hypervisor needed          │
         │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │  ❌ NO guest OS per app            │
         │  ┌────────────────────────────┐ │  │  ✅ Shared kernel = lightweight   │
         │  │    Hardware / Cloud        │ │  │                                   │
         │  └────────────────────────────┘ │  │                                   │
         └───────────────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────────────────┘

         [STAT COMPARISON TABLE — VMs vs Containers]
         | Metric        | Virtual Machine      | Docker Container      | Winner     |
         | Startup Time  | 30-90 seconds        | 1-3 seconds           | 🐳 x30     |
         | Memory Usage  | 1-2 GB per VM        | ~50 MB per container  | 🐳 x20-40  |
         | Disk Space    | 10-40 GB per VM      | ~100 MB per image     | 🐳 x100+   |
         | CPU Overhead  | Significant (hyperv.)| Near-native           | 🐳         |
         | Density       | ~10 VMs per host     | 100s per host         | 🐳 x10+    |
         | Isolation     | Full OS isolation    | Process-level (weaker)| VM         |
         | Portability   | Hypervisor-dependent | Runs anywhere Docker  | 🐳         |

         🎯 GOAL: Draw the VM vs container stack from memory and defend the
            one case where a VM still wins.
         [TECH] A VM virtualizes hardware — a hypervisor boots a full guest
            kernel per VM. A container virtualizes the OS — all containers
            are ordinary processes scheduled by the ONE host kernel, isolated
            by namespaces (what you can SEE) and cgroups (what you can USE).
         [ANALOGY] Houses vs apartments: every house (VM) pours its own
            foundation and plumbing (guest OS); apartments (containers) share
            the building's foundation (host kernel) — cheaper, faster to move
            into, but a foundation problem touches every apartment at once.
            Both readings map onto the side-by-side diagram above.
         [DIAGRAM:decision — VM or Container?]
            Need a different KERNEL/OS (Windows app on Linux host)? ──▶ VM
            Hard multi-tenant isolation for untrusted code?          ──▶ VM
            Same-kernel app, fast start, high density?               ──▶ 🐳
            CI jobs, microservices, dev environments?                ──▶ 🐳
         🔬 easypj: one 4 GB laptop cannot run easypj + PostgreSQL + Redis +
            Nginx as four VMs (needs 16 GB+). As four containers: ~300 MB.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: Using the stat table above, compute how many
            easypj containers fit inside the RAM overhead of ONE idle VM.
            Verify: ~1.5 GB VM overhead ÷ ~50 MB per container ≈ 30 free
            containers before the VM has run any app code at all.
         📊 SUMMARY: VMs isolate with hardware + guest kernels; containers
            isolate with one shared kernel — lighter, faster, denser.
            ⚠️ Gotcha (exam favorite): you cannot run a Windows container on
            a Linux host — kernels must match. Docker Desktop only "does it"
            by hiding a Linux VM under the hood.

    1.4  Docker Architecture — How It All Fits Together
         - Docker Client (docker CLI) — what you type commands into
         - Docker Daemon (dockerd) — the background service that does the work
         - Docker Registry — where images are stored (Docker Hub, ECR, etc.)
         - Docker Objects — Images, Containers, Networks, Volumes

         [DOCKER ARCHITECTURE — CLIENT-DAEMON-REGISTRY]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                      🐳 DOCKER ARCHITECTURE                               │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │
         │  │    Docker CLI        │          │        DOCKER HOST                │ │
         │  │    (Client)          │  REST    │                                  │ │
         │  │                      │  API     │  ┌────────────────────────────┐  │ │
         │  │  $ docker run       │─────────▶│  │      dockerd (Daemon)      │  │ │
         │  │  $ docker build     │ over     │  │                            │  │ │
         │  │  $ docker push      │ Unix     │  │  ┌──────────────────────┐  │  │ │
         │  │  $ docker compose   │ Socket   │  │  │    containerd         │  │  │ │
         │  │       ▲             │          │  │  │    (container runtime)│  │  │ │
         │  │       │             │          │  │  └──────────┬───────────┘  │  │ │
         │  │       │             │          │  │             │              │  │ │
         │  └───────┼─────────────┘          │  │      ┌──────┴──────┐       │  │ │
         │          │                        │  │      │    runc     │       │  │ │
         │          │                        │  │      │ (OCI runtime)│       │  │ │
         │     Docker Desktop                │  │      └──────┬──────┘       │  │ │
         │     (GUI + CLI +                   │  │             │              │  │ │
         │      Daemon bundle)               │  │      ┌──────┴──────┐       │  │ │
         │                                   │  │      │  Containers │       │  │ │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐          │  │      │  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ │       │  │ │
         │  │   🗄️ Registry        │          │  │      │  │C1│ │C2│ │       │  │ │
         │  │   Docker Hub         │◀─────────│──┼──────│  └──┘ └──┘ │       │  │ │
         │  │   ECR / GCR / ACR   │ pull/push│  │      └────────────┘       │  │ │
         │  │   ghcr.io            │          │  │                          │  │ │
         │  └──────────────────────┘          │  │  Images: easypj:v1       │  │ │
         │                                   │  │  Networks: bridge, host   │  │ │
         │                                   │  │  Volumes: /var/lib/docker │  │ │
         │                                   │  └────────────────────────────┘  │ │
         │                                   └──────────────────────────────────┘ │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [DAEMON INTERNALS — containerd → runc → OCI Runtime]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                     🔧 DOCKER DAEMON INTERNALS                            │
         │                                                                          │
         │  dockerd ───▶ containerd ───▶ containerd-shim ───▶ runc ───▶ Container  │
         │  (API,       (Image mgmt,     (Handles stdio,     (OCI      (Your app)   │
         │   Build,      Pull/Push,      exit signals,       runtime,              │
         │   Network)    Lifecycle)      keeps container     creates               │
         │                               alive after         namespaces)            │
         │                               dockerd restart)                           │
         │                                                                          │
         │  Key: dockerd manages HIGH-LEVEL stuff (API, build, networking)          │
         │        containerd manages MID-LEVEL (image pull/push, container lifecycle)│
         │        runc does the LOW-LEVEL (creates namespaces, cgroups, starts proc)│
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Trace one `docker run` end-to-end through every box in the
            architecture diagram above — no box skipped.
         [TECH] Request path: docker CLI → REST API over the Unix socket
            (/var/run/docker.sock) → dockerd (API, build, networking) →
            containerd (image + container lifecycle, over gRPC) →
            containerd-shim (per-container babysitter) → runc (creates
            namespaces + cgroups, execs your process, then exits).
         [ANALOGY] A restaurant: you (CLI) give the waiter (dockerd) an
            order; the waiter passes it to the kitchen manager (containerd),
            who calls in a food runner (shim) to babysit the table so
            service continues even if the waiter changes shift (daemon
            restart) — the runner then hands the order to the line cook
            (runc), who actually makes the dish. Same boxes, same arrows,
            in the DAEMON INTERNALS diagram above.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — one docker run, numbered ①-⑦]
            ① $ docker run easypj:v1        ② image present? pull if not
            ③ POST /containers/create       ④ containerd creates task
            ⑤ shim spawns                   ⑥ runc builds namespaces/cgroups
            ⑦ gunicorn becomes PID 1 inside the container
         [TABLE: The 4 Docker objects — object | what it is | easypj example]
            Image     | read-only template          | easypj:v1
            Container | running instance            | easypj-web
            Network   | virtual LAN for containers  | easypj_default
            Volume    | persistent named storage    | pgdata
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `docker version` and split the output into
            Client vs Server halves; then `ls -l /var/run/docker.sock`.
            Verify: you can name which architecture box answered each half.
         📊 SUMMARY: the CLI is just an API client; dockerd delegates to
            containerd → shim → runc; the registry stores what they run.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: because the SHIM parents the container, restarting
            dockerd does not kill running containers (with live-restore on —
            see 2.7).

    1.5  The Docker Ecosystem
         - Docker Engine (core)
         - Docker Compose (multi-container)
         - Docker Swarm (native orchestration)
         - Docker Hub (public registry)
         - Docker Desktop (GUI for Mac/Windows)
         - Docker Scout (vulnerability scanning)
         - Docker Buildx (advanced builds)
         - Docker Build Cloud (remote builds)

         [DOCKER ECOSYSTEM ORBIT DIAGRAM]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                     🌍 THE DOCKER ECOSYSTEM                               │
         │                                                                          │
         │                         ┌──────────────┐                                 │
         │                         │  🖥️ Docker   │                                 │
         │                    ┌────│   Desktop    │────┐                            │
         │                    │    │ (GUI + CLI)  │    │                            │
         │                    │    └──────────────┘    │                            │
         │                    ▼                        ▼                            │
         │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────┐           │
         │  │ 🎼Compose │  │                            │  │ 🐝 Swarm │           │
         │  │ Multi-    │  │      🐳 DOCKER ENGINE       │  │ Native   │           │
         │  │ Container │  │      (dockerd + containerd) │  │ Cluster  │           │
         │  │ Local Dev │  │                            │  │ Orch.    │           │
         │  └──────────┘  └────────────┬───────────────┬─┘  └──────────┘           │
         │                             │               │                            │
         │                    ┌────────┴──────┐  ┌─────┴────────┐                  │
         │                    ▼               ▼  ▼              ▼                  │
         │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────┐            │
         │  │ 🏗️Buildx│  │ 🗄️Hub    │  │ 🔍Scout  │  │ ☁️Build Cloud│            │
         │  │ Advanced │  │ Registry │  │ Vuln.    │  │ Remote       │            │
         │  │ Builder  │  │ + Teams  │  │ Scanner  │  │ Builds       │            │
         │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────────┘            │
         │                                                                          │
         │  TOOL BELT: docker init | docker extension | docker context | docker sbom │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: For any task, pick the right ecosystem tool in one step.
         [TECH] The ecosystem is one engine (dockerd + containerd) with
            satellite tools attached three different ways: Compose and
            Buildx ship as CLI plugins (`docker compose`, `docker buildx`),
            Swarm is compiled straight into dockerd with nothing to
            install, and Scout, Hub, and Build Cloud are hosted services
            the CLI talks to over the network.

         [TABLE: Which tool, when — task | tool | one-liner]
            Run my app locally            | Engine + CLI 🐳 | docker run
            Multi-container dev stack     | Compose 🎼      | docker compose up
            Build faster / multi-arch     | Buildx 🏗️       | docker buildx build
            Store + share images          | Hub/registry 🗄️ | docker push
            Find CVEs before production   | Scout 🔍        | docker scout quickview
            Cluster without Kubernetes    | Swarm 🐝        | docker swarm init
            GUI + batteries on a laptop   | Desktop 🖥️      | (install once)
         [ANALOGY] The orbit diagram above: Docker Engine is the phone;
            Compose, Scout, Buildx, Swarm are apps installed around it. You
            never need every app — but you must know the phone.
         🔬 easypj: `docker compose up` starts easypj + PostgreSQL together
            from one file; `docker scout quickview easypj:v1` lists CVEs in
            that exact image before it ever reaches production.

         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: match blind: "team needs the same 5-service
            stack" / "image has 120 CVEs" / "build for ARM Mac AND AMD64
            server". Verify: Compose, Scout, Buildx — straight off the table.
         📊 SUMMARY: one engine, satellite tools — pick per job, not per hype.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Swarm is built INTO the engine (nothing to install);
            Compose v2 is a CLI plugin — `docker compose`, not the old
            `docker-compose` binary.

    1.6  Docker Editions & Installation Overview
         - Docker Desktop (Mac, Windows, Linux — recommended for beginners)
         - Docker Engine (Linux server — production)
         - Docker CE vs EE (Community vs Enterprise)
         - System requirements
         - Quick install commands per OS

         [TABLE: Docker Editions Compared]
         | Feature              | Docker Desktop    | Docker Engine (CE) | Docker EE/Mirantis |
         | Target               | Dev machines      | Servers            | Enterprise         |
         | GUI Dashboard        | ✅ Yes            | ❌ No              | ❌ No              |
         | Windows/Mac support  | ✅ Yes            | ❌ Linux only      | ❌ Linux only      |
         | Kubernetes built-in  | ✅ Yes            | ❌ No              | ❌ No              |
         | WSL2 integration     | ✅ Yes            | N/A                | N/A                |
         | Production-grade     | ⚠️ Not recommended| ✅ Yes            | ✅ Yes             |
         | License              | Free (personal)   | Free (Apache 2.0)  | Paid               |
         | Security scanning    | ✅ Scout included | Optional           | Advanced           |

         🎯 GOAL: Choose the right edition for laptop vs server and verify a
            fresh install in under a minute.
         [TECH] Desktop wraps Engine inside a lightweight Linux VM (WSL2 on
            Windows, Virtualization.framework on macOS) — that hidden VM is
            how Linux containers run on non-Linux machines. Servers run bare
            Engine (CE) as a systemd service; EE/Mirantis adds support/FIPS.
         [ANALOGY] Editions are subscription tiers on one product, not
            different engines: Desktop is the premium plan with every
            extra bundled in (GUI dashboard, built-in Kubernetes, WSL2) —
            built for one device, not a fleet; Engine (CE) is the free
            self-hosted tier with nothing extra; EE adds a paid support
            contract for regulated fleets.

         [TERMINAL: 60-second install verification]
            $ docker version              # Client AND Server = daemon is up
            $ docker info                 # storage driver, cgroups, runtimes
            $ docker run --rm hello-world # full pull→create→run→exit path
         🔬 easypj: on a laptop, Desktop's GUI gets easypj + Postgres
            running in minutes; the server hosting easypj in production
            only ever installs Engine (CE) — no GUI, no Kubernetes toggle
            left on by accident.

         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the three commands above on your machine.
            Verify: hello-world prints its message; `docker ps -a` stays
            empty because --rm cleaned up (drop --rm and look again).
         📊 SUMMARY: Desktop = dev convenience with a VM inside; Engine (CE)
            = what production actually runs.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Docker Desktop is NOT for production — and beyond a
            company size, Desktop needs a paid license; Engine never does.

         - easypj example: All 5 use cases applied

    1.8  Docker Terminology Cheat Sheet
         [TABLE: 25+ Docker terms defined — Image, Container, Dockerfile, Layer,
          Tag, Registry, Volume, Network, Compose, Swarm, etc.]


         - Terms are grouped, not alphabetical: BUILD terms (Dockerfile, layer,
           build context, .dockerignore, multi-stage) | RUN terms (container,
           ENTRYPOINT/CMD, restart policy) | SHIP terms (registry, tag, digest,
           manifest) | PLUMBING terms (daemon, containerd, runc, OCI, overlay2,
           namespace, cgroup)
         🎯 GOAL: Sort any of the 25+ terms in the table into its BUILD/
            RUN/SHIP/PLUMBING family without hesitating.
         [TECH] The table groups terms by WHERE they act in the pipeline,
            not alphabetically: BUILD-time (Dockerfile, layer,
            .dockerignore), RUN-time (container, ENTRYPOINT/CMD, restart
            policy), SHIP-time (registry, tag, digest, manifest), and
            PLUMBING (daemon, containerd, runc, OCI, overlay2, namespace,
            cgroup) — the same four buckets this guide uses everywhere
            else.
         [ANALOGY] A bicycle factory floor: BUILD is the welding station
            assembling the frame (Dockerfile, layers, .dockerignore); RUN
            is the test-track ride once it's finished (container,
            ENTRYPOINT/CMD, restart policy); SHIP is the export paperwork
            stapled to the crate (registry, tag, digest, manifest);
            PLUMBING is the conveyor belts and robotic arms between
            stations nobody names (daemon, containerd, runc, overlay2,
            namespace, cgroup).
         🔬 easypj: a `Dockerfile` (BUILD) builds `easypj:v1` (SHIP tag),
            started as a running `container` (RUN) whose process is
            actually created by `runc` under `containerd` (PLUMBING)
            beneath dockerd.

         💡 Study trick: every term must attach to ONE diagram you have seen
            in this chapter — a term you cannot place on a picture is a term
            you do not own yet.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: cover the definition column and score yourself
            /25; anything below 20, reread the section printed next to it.
         📊 SUMMARY: this vocabulary is the API of the rest of the guide.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: image ≠ container is the #1 beginner confusion — when
            in doubt, return to the class↔object analogy (2.1).

    1.9  Containers Beyond Docker — OCI Standards & the Runtime Landscape
         - OCI (Open Container Initiative): image-spec + runtime-spec + distribution-spec
         - Docker images ARE OCI images — they run on any OCI-compliant runtime
         - The landscape: Docker | Podman (daemonless) | containerd (K8s) | CRI-O
         - Why it matters: Kubernetes removed the Docker SHIM, not Docker images
         🎯 GOAL: Explain why "Kubernetes dropped Docker" scared everyone and
            changed almost nothing.
         [TECH] OCI defines three specs: how an image is packaged
            (image-spec), how a container is started from it (runtime-spec),
            and how images move between registries (distribution-spec).
            `docker build` produces OCI artifacts; containerd + runc consume
            them — with or without dockerd in the picture. Kubernetes talks
            to containerd directly through CRI.
         [ANALOGY] OCI is the DVD standard; Docker is one brand of DVD
            player. Kubernetes swapped players (dockershim → containerd) —
            every movie (image) still plays exactly the same.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — who implements which OCI spec]
            image-spec:    docker build │ buildah │ kaniko
            runtime-spec:  runc │ crun │ gVisor │ Kata Containers
            consumers:     dockerd │ Podman │ containerd ◀── Kubernetes (CRI)
         🔬 easypj: the `easypj:v1` image built with `docker build` is an
            OCI image — it runs unmodified under Podman or a Kubernetes
            node's containerd, no dockerd required, the day this guide
            reaches Part 9.

         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker info | grep -i runtime` — name the OCI
            runtime your engine uses right now. Verify: it says runc.
         📊 SUMMARY: learn Docker, inherit the whole OCI world — images you
            build here run under Kubernetes untouched. [KUBERNETES GUIDE]
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "K8s removed Docker support" = removed dockershim;
            Docker-BUILT images were never affected, only the runtime path.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — namespaces + cgroups: what actually isolates a container
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        A container has NO virtualization hardware underneath it — it is an
        ordinary host process wrapped in kernel primitives:
          • NAMESPACES control what the process can SEE — each type
            virtualizes one resource: PID (its own process tree, PID 1
            inside), NET (its own interfaces/routes/ports), MNT (its own
            filesystem view), UTS (its own hostname), IPC (its own shared
            memory/semaphores). These five are created for every container
            by default. A sixth type, USER (remapping container UID/GID to
            an unprivileged host range), is NOT on by default — root inside
            a container IS root on the host unless the daemon is explicitly
            configured with userns-remap (Part 7, 20.3).
          • CGROUPS (control groups) control what the process can USE — CPU
            shares/quota, memory limits, block I/O, PID count. A container
            hitting its cgroup memory limit is OOM-killed by the KERNEL,
            not by Docker.
        runc's entire job (1.4) is calling the kernel syscalls that create
        these namespaces and attach these cgroups, then exec-ing your
        process inside them — after that, runc exits and the shim babysits.

        [NAMESPACES + CGROUPS — what isolates one easypj container]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  HOST KERNEL (one, shared by every container)                    │
        │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
        │  │  easypj-web container                                       │ │
        │  │  NAMESPACES (what it SEES): PID·NET·MNT·UTS·IPC (USER: opt-in)│ │
        │  │  CGROUPS   (what it CAN USE): --memory 512m · --cpus 1.5    │ │
        │  │  PID 1 inside: gunicorn (easypj.wsgi)                       │ │
        │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
        │  Other containers on the SAME host get their OWN namespaces —   │
        │  none can see each other's processes or files by default.       │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ⚠️ Namespaces are NOT a hard security boundary the way a hypervisor
        is — a kernel exploit can cross them. That gap is exactly why
        Part 7 exists (userns-remap, seccomp, capabilities).

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🔑 Docker solves environment drift by shipping the whole userspace
           (interpreter + libraries + code) as one immutable image.
        🔑 Image = read-only blueprint; container = running instance with
           one writable layer on top (class vs object).
        🔑 Containers share the ONE host kernel via namespaces (what you
           see) and cgroups (what you can use) — no hypervisor, no guest OS.
        🔑 A `docker run` travels CLI → REST API → dockerd → containerd →
           shim → runc; the shim is why containers survive a daemon restart
           (live-restore, see 2.7).
        🔑 The ecosystem is one engine with satellite tools bolted on three
           ways: CLI plugins (Compose, Buildx), compiled-in (Swarm), or
           hosted services (Hub, Scout, Build Cloud).
        🔑 Desktop wraps Engine in a VM for laptops; production servers run
           bare Engine (CE) — Desktop is never a production runtime.
        🔑 Docker images are OCI images — they run unmodified under Podman
           or a Kubernetes node's containerd; "K8s removed Docker" only
           removed the dockershim glue.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚠️ "Docker packages the kernel too" is false — the kernel always
           comes from the host (1.3); "identical everywhere" means userspace
           only.
        ⚠️ Windows containers need a Windows kernel, Linux containers need a
           Linux kernel — Docker Desktop only "does both" by hiding a Linux
           VM underneath.
        ⚠️ `:latest` is just a tag NAME, not a freshness guarantee — and
           Docker Desktop is a dev tool, never a production runtime.
        ⚠️ Deleting a container deletes its writable layer — anything not
           saved elsewhere (a volume, a registry push) is gone for good.
        ⚠️ "Kubernetes dropped Docker" means it dropped the dockershim CRI
           glue, not Docker-built images — those still run fine.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚡ `docker version` before anything else — if Client answers but
           Server doesn't, connectivity is the problem, not the daemon.
        ⚡ `docker info | grep -i runtime` any time you need to prove which
           OCI runtime (almost always runc) sits under this engine.
        ⚡ Read an image reference right to left when confused: TAG, then
           REPOSITORY, then NAMESPACE, then REGISTRY — defaults fill every
           gap.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 COMMANDS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        docker version                # client AND server — daemon reachability
        docker info                   # runtime, storage driver, cgroup version
        docker run --rm hello-world   # full pull→create→run→exit path, self-clean
        docker ps                     # running containers only
        docker ps -a                  # every container, including exited
        docker images --digests       # local images with their immutable digest
        docker manifest inspect <img> # which platforms an image tag covers
        docker system df              # disk used by images/containers/volumes

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 DRILL
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🧪 In 5 minutes, sketch the 1.4 architecture diagram from memory —
        label CLI, dockerd, containerd, shim, runc, and the registry — then
