    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 1)
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Q1. What is "dependency hell," and where exactly does it bite
            easypj?
            → Environment drift: unpinned interpreter versions and libraries
              that differ between machines. easypj's laptop has Python 3.11
              + Django 5.2; staging has 3.8 → `python manage.py runserver`
              dies on syntax it has never seen. Docker ends this by shipping
              the interpreter + libraries + code as one frozen artifact.

        Q2. Define image and container in one sentence each, and say what
            `docker run` adds.
            → Image = a read-only, layered filesystem template (the class).
              Container = a running or stopped instance of that image (the
              object). `docker run` adds ONE writable layer on top and
              starts a process inside it.
                 easypj:v1.0 (image) ──docker run──▶ easypj-web (container)

        Q3. Why are containers lighter than VMs, and what's the ONE case a
            VM still wins?
            → Containers share the host's ONE kernel (isolated by
              namespaces + cgroups); VMs boot a full guest kernel each via a
              hypervisor. A VM wins when you need a DIFFERENT kernel/OS than
              the host (e.g. a Windows app on a Linux host) or hard
              multi-tenant isolation for untrusted code.
              | Metric   | VM            | Container      |
              | Startup  | 30-90s        | 1-3s           |
              | Memory   | 1-2 GB        | ~50 MB         |
              | Isolation| full OS       | process-level  |

        Q4. Using ~1.5 GB of idle VM overhead and ~50 MB per container, how
            many easypj containers fit in the RAM ONE idle VM wastes before
            running any app code?
            → 1.5 GB ÷ 50 MB ≈ 30 containers — pure overhead, before a
              single line of easypj has executed.

        Q5. Trace the dockerd → containerd → shim → runc chain for one
            `docker run easypj:v1`.
            → dockerd (API, build, networking) hands the request to
              containerd (image + container lifecycle, over gRPC), which
              spawns a containerd-shim (per-container babysitter, keeps the
              container alive even if dockerd restarts), which calls runc
              (creates namespaces + cgroups, execs the process, then exits).
                 dockerd ▶ containerd ▶ shim ▶ runc ▶ gunicorn (PID 1)

        Q6. What role does a registry play, and what travels over the wire
            on push?
            → A registry stores image layers + manifests for distribution
              (Docker Hub, ECR, GCR, ACR, Harbor...). A push uploads only
              the layers the registry doesn't already hold — content-
              addressed dedup — then the manifest.

        Q7. Match the job to the tool: "team needs the same 5-service dev
            stack," "image has 120 CVEs," "build for ARM Mac AND AMD64
            server."
            → Compose 🎼 (multi-container dev stack), Scout 🔍 (CVE
              scanning), Buildx 🏗️ (multi-platform builds).

        Q8. You `docker rm` a running easypj container that was never given
            a volume. What data survives, and why?
            → Nothing written inside the container survives. A container's
              writable layer holds all its runtime changes (per 1.2's
              image/container split); deleting the container deletes that
              layer. Only data written to a mounted volume (outside the
              container's own filesystem) would survive — the reason Part 6
              exists.

        Q9. What do the three OCI specs each define, and who commonly
            implements them?
            → image-spec (how an image is packaged: docker build, buildah,
              kaniko), runtime-spec (how a container starts from it: runc,
              crun, gVisor, Kata), distribution-spec (how images move
              between registries). Consumers include dockerd, Podman, and
              containerd (used directly by Kubernetes via CRI).

        Q10. Sort these terms into BUILD / RUN / SHIP / PLUMBING: Dockerfile,
             container, registry, containerd, tag, ENTRYPOINT, digest,
             namespace.
             → | BUILD      | RUN         | SHIP     | PLUMBING   |
               | Dockerfile | container   | registry | containerd |
               |            | ENTRYPOINT  | tag      | namespace  |
               |            |             | digest   |            |
               The buckets are grouped by WHERE each term acts in the
               pipeline, not alphabetically — the same four families this
               whole guide uses.

    (1.1), Docker packaging the full userspace into an image/container pair
    is the cure (1.2), sharing one kernel instead of many is WHY the cure is
    cheap (1.3), the client-to-runc chain is HOW a single `docker run` turns
    an image into a live process (1.4), the ecosystem and editions are WHERE
    you get that engine depending on laptop or server (1.5-1.6), and OCI is
    the guarantee that everything you just built travels — untouched — into
    every chapter after this one, including the day this guide reaches
    Kubernetes.

    [E] SECTION MAP (you are here):

         & versioning → 2.6 manifests & multi-arch → 2.7 daemon.json.

    2.1  Docker Images — The Blueprint
         - What is a Docker image? (read-only template)
         - Image = class (blueprint) | Container = object (running instance)
         - Image naming: repository:tag (e.g., easypj:v1.0, python:3.11-slim)
         - Official images vs community images
         - Image digests (SHA256) for immutability

         [IMAGE vs CONTAINER — CLASS vs OBJECT ANALOGY]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │            📦 IMAGE (Blueprint)  →  ▶️  CONTAINER (Running Instance)       │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐        │
         │  │  Class in Python:       │         │  Object in Python:       │        │
         │  │  class Car:             │         │  my_car = Car()          │        │
         │  │      wheels = 4         │ create  │  my_car.wheels → 4       │        │
         │  │      color = "red"      │────────▶│  my_car.start()          │        │
         │  └─────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘        │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐        │
         │  │  Docker Image:          │         │  Docker Container:       │        │
         │  │  easypj:v1.0            │ docker  │  docker run easypj:v1.0  │        │
         │  │  (read-only layers)     │  run    │  (read-write layer on    │        │
         │  │  stored on disk         │────────▶│   top, running process)  │        │
         │  └─────────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────────┘        │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [DOCKER IMAGE LAYER CAKE — easypj Layers Visualized]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Layer 6 (R/W): Container Writable Layer      │  ← Container-only
         │  (logs, temp files, runtime changes)          │     (ephemeral!)
         ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Layer 5: CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:app"] │  ← Startup command
         │  (≈ 0 bytes — just metadata)                 │     (read-only)
         ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Layer 4: COPY . /app/                        │  ← Your code!
         │  (models.py, views.py, urls.py, settings.py)  │     (~500 KB)
         ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Layer 3: RUN pip install --no-cache-dir      │  ← Dependencies
         │  -r requirements.txt                          │     (~80 MB)
         │  (Django 5.2, gunicorn, psycopg2, etc.)      │
         ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Layer 2: COPY requirements.txt .             │  ← Deps list
         │  (≈ 200 bytes)                    ▲ CACHED!   │     (tiny)
         ├───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │  Layer 1: FROM python:3.11-slim               │  ← Base image
         │  (Debian 12 + Python 3.11, ~150 MB)           │     (never changes)
         └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         
         💡 KEY INSIGHT: Layers 1-5 are READ-ONLY and SHARED across containers.
         Layer 6 (writable) is unique per container and DELETED when container removed.

         🎯 GOAL: Read any image reference (registry/repo:tag@digest) and say
            exactly what each part pins down.
         [TECH] Full form: REGISTRY[:PORT]/NAMESPACE/REPOSITORY:TAG@DIGEST.
            Every omission has a default: registry→docker.io, namespace→
            library, tag→latest. A tag is a movable pointer; a digest
            (sha256:…) is content-addressed and immutable — same digest ⇒
            byte-identical image, forever.
         [ANALOGY] Class vs object (the diagram above): the image is the
            class definition frozen on disk; every `docker run` news-up one
            more object. Tag = a sticky note on the class; digest = its DNA.
         🔬 easypj: docker.io/you/easypj:v1.0 is convenient;
            ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:… is what production should pin.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker pull python:3.11-slim`, then
            `docker images --digests`. Verify: you can point at repository,
            tag, digest and IMAGE ID and state how they differ.
         📊 SUMMARY: image = read-only layered template; a full reference is
            registry/repo:tag@digest, with defaults filling the gaps.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `:latest` is only a tag NAME — nothing guarantees it
            is newest, and it silently changes underneath you.

    2.2  Docker Containers — The Running Instance
         - What is a container? (runnable instance of an image)
         - Container lifecycle: created → running → paused → stopped → deleted
         - Container isolation: Process, Network, Filesystem, IPC
         - Container is ephemeral by design (cattle, not pets)

         [CONTAINER LIFECYCLE STATE MACHINE]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                     🔄 CONTAINER LIFECYCLE                                │
         │                                                                          │
         │                              docker create                               │
         │                          ┌───────────────────┐                          │
         │                          ▼                   │                          │
         │  ┌─────────┐     ┌─────────────┐     ┌─────────────┐                    │
         │  │  📦      │     │  ▶️ CREATED  │     │  ▶️ RUNNING  │                    │
         │  │ Image   │────▶│             │────▶│             │                    │
         │  │         │     │ (on disk,   │     │ (process     │                    │
         │  │(blueprint)│    │  not started)│     │  active)    │                    │
         │  └─────────┘     └──────┬──────┘     └──┬──┬──┬───┘                    │
         │                        │               │  │  │                          │
         │                        │ docker start  │  │  │ docker stop (SIGTERM)    │
         │                        └───────────────┘  │  └──────────────┐           │
         │                                           │                 │           │
         │                                    docker │ pause    docker  │ kill      │
         │                                           │          │      │           │
         │                                           ▼          ▼      ▼           │
         │                                     ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌─────────┐  │
         │                                     │ ⏸️     │ │ ⏹️      │ │ 💀      │  │
         │                                     │PAUSED  │ │STOPPED │ │ DELETED │  │
         │                                     │(frozen)│ │(exited)│ │ (gone)  │  │
         │                                     └────┬───┘ └───┬────┘ └─────────┘  │
         │                                          │        │                     │
         │                               docker unpause  docker start              │
         │                                          │        │                     │
         │                                          ▼        ▼                     │
         │                                     ┌────────────────┐                 │
         │                                     │  ▶️ RUNNING     │                 │
         │                                     └────────────────┘                 │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Walk the lifecycle state machine above and name the command
            AND the signal behind every arrow.
         [TECH] stop = SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after --time (default 10 s) —
            graceful. kill = SIGKILL immediately. pause = cgroup freezer; the
            process never even sees a signal. The exit code stays on the
            stopped container (`docker ps -a`); 137 = 128+9 = SIGKILLed.
         [ANALOGY] stop is "please save your work and leave the building";
            kill is cutting the power; pause is stopping time in the room.
         🔬 easypj: `docker stop easypj-web` lets gunicorn finish in-flight
            job-post requests; `docker kill` drops them mid-response.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run nginx, then stop / start / pause / unpause /
            kill it, watching `docker ps -a` STATUS after each move.
            Verify: Exited (0) after stop, Exited (137) after kill.
         📊 SUMMARY: created→running→{paused|stopped|deleted}; stop is
            polite (SIGTERM), kill is not (SIGKILL).
            ⚠️ Gotcha: deleting a container deletes its writable layer —
            anything not on a volume is gone forever (Part 6 exists for this).

    2.3  Docker Registries — The Storage
         - What is a registry? (image storage and distribution)
         - Docker Hub: The default public registry
         - Private registries: ECR, GCR, ACR, GitHub Container Registry
         - Self-hosted: Docker Registry, Harbor, GitLab Container Registry
         - Registry authentication (docker login)

         [REGISTRY PUSH/PULL FLOW]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                     🗄️ DOCKER REGISTRY WORKFLOW                           │
         │                                                                          │
         │   DEVELOPER LAPTOP                      🗄️ REGISTRY                      │
         │   ┌────────────────┐                ┌────────────────────┐              │
         │   │ docker build   │   docker push  │  Docker Hub / ECR  │              │
         │   │ -t easypj:v1 . │──────────────▶│  ┌──────────────┐  │              │
         │   │                │                │  │ easypj       │  │              │
         │   │ ┌────────────┐ │                │  │  ├─ v1.0     │  │              │
         │   │ │ easypj:v1  │ │                │  │  ├─ v1.1     │  │              │
         │   │ │ (local)    │ │   docker pull  │  │  ├─ v2.0     │  │              │
         │   │ └────────────┘ │◀───────────────│  │  └─ latest   │  │              │
         │   └────────────────┘                │  └──────────────┘  │              │
         │                                     │  ┌──────────────┐  │              │
         │   CI/CD SERVER                       │  │ python       │  │              │
         │   ┌────────────────┐    docker pull  │  │  ├─ 3.11-slim│  │              │
         │   │ GitHub Actions │◀───────────────│  │  ├─ 3.12-slim│  │              │
         │   │ pulls + tests  │                │  │  └─ alpine    │  │              │
         │   └────────────────┘                │  └──────────────┘  │              │
         │                                     └────────────────────┘              │
         │                                                                          │
         │   REGISTRY AUTH: docker login -u username -p password registry.io        │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [REGISTRY COMPARISON TABLE]
         | Registry              | Type    | Pricing         | Best For              |
         | Docker Hub            | Public  | Free (1 private)| Public images, OSS    |
         | Amazon ECR            | Cloud   | Pay per GB      | AWS workloads          |
         | Google GCR/Artifact   | Cloud   | Pay per GB      | GCP workloads          |
         | Azure ACR             | Cloud   | Pay per SKU     | Azure workloads        |
         | GitHub Container Reg. | Public  | Free (public)   | GitHub CI/CD           |
         | Harbor                | Self-Host| Free OSS       | Enterprise, air-gapped |
         | GitLab Container Reg. | Built-in| Free (per repo) | GitLab CI/CD           |

         🎯 GOAL: Push an image to a private registry and explain what
            actually moved over the wire.
         [TECH] A push uploads only the layers the registry does not already
            hold (content-addressed dedup), then the manifest. `docker login`
            stores a token in ~/.docker/config.json (or a credential helper).
         [ANALOGY] Registry = GitHub for images: Hub is public GitHub;
            ECR/GCR/ACR are the company's private server; push/pull =
            git push/pull — and unchanged layers, like unchanged files, are
            never re-uploaded. That is the dedup shown in the flow above.
         🔬 easypj: docker tag easypj:v1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 &&
            docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 — the python:3.11-slim base
            layers are almost certainly on the registry already.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: push easypj:v1 twice in a row. Verify: the second
            push prints "Layer already exists" for every single layer.
         📊 SUMMARY: registries store layers + manifests; auth via docker
            login; only missing layers travel.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the image NAME decides the destination — you cannot
            push easypj:v1 to ghcr.io without re-tagging it
            ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 first.

    2.4  Image Layers — The Secret to Docker's Speed
         - How layers work: each instruction in Dockerfile = one layer
         - Copy-on-Write (CoW) filesystem
         - Layer caching: why order matters in Dockerfile
         - Union filesystem (Overlay2, aufs, etc.)
         - Practical: easypj image layers visualized

         [LAYER CACHING STRATEGY VISUALIZED]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │               🏎️ LAYER CACHING — WHY ORDER MATTERS                        │
         │                                                                          │
         │  BAD ORDER (cache useless after code change):                            │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
         │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
         │  │ COPY . /app/             │ ❌ REBUILT (code changed!)       │         │
         │  │ COPY requirements.txt .  │ ❌ REBUILT (previous layer       │         │
         │  │ RUN pip install -r req.. │ ❌ REBUILT  changed!)            │         │
         │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
         │                                                                          │
         │  GOOD ORDER (only changed layers rebuilt):                               │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐         │
         │  │ FROM python:3.11-slim    │ ✅ CACHED (never changes)        │         │
         │  │ COPY requirements.txt .  │ ✅ CACHED (same requirements)    │         │
         │  │ RUN pip install -r req.. │ ✅ CACHED (same install)         │         │
         │  │ COPY . /app/             │ ❌ REBUILT (only code changed!) │         │
         │  └──────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘         │
         │                                                                          │
         │  RESULT: Good order = 3 layers cached (fast!), Bad order = 3 rebuilt     │
         │  For easypj: Good build = ~3 seconds (only code changed)                 │
         │              Bad build = ~45 seconds (pip install reruns)                │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CACHING STRATEGY — What Changes → What Gets Rebuilt]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  📋 CACHE INVALIDATION RULE: If layer N changes → layers N, N+1, N+2... │
         │  ALL rebuild! (Docker doesn't know if later layers depend on earlier.)   │
         │                                                                          │
         │  OUR STRATEGY FOR easypj:                                                │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
         │  │ Layer 1: FROM python:3.11-slim       ← Only rebuild if upgrading│    │
         │  │ Layer 2: COPY requirements.txt .      ← Only rebuild if deps change│  │
         │  │ Layer 3: RUN pip install              ← Only rebuild if deps change│  │
         │  │ Layer 4: COPY . /app/                 ← Rebuilds on ANY code change│ │
         │  │ Layer 5: CMD ["gunicorn", ...]       ← Almost never rebuilds    │    │
         │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
         │  💡 99% of your changes are in Layer 4 (code).                            │
         │     Only 3 layers get cache checked, 1 gets rebuilt. 🚀                  │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Predict which layers rebuild when you change one line of
            code — BEFORE running the build.
         [TECH] Every layer is a content-addressed diff. Cache rule: a layer
            is reused iff its parent chain is identical AND its instruction +
            inputs (file checksums for COPY/ADD) are unchanged. The first
            miss invalidates every layer after it — no exceptions.
         [ANALOGY] Back to 2.1's layer cake: you cannot swap a middle
            layer without re-baking every layer above it — frosting
            included. The BAD/GOOD ORDER boxes above are that cake
            baked two different ways — same layers, different rebuild
            cost depending which one you frosted last.
         🔬 easypj: editing models.py touches only the COPY . . layer →
            ~3-second rebuild. Editing requirements.txt melts the pip layer →
            ~45-second rebuild. That asymmetry IS the caching strategy.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build easypj twice, then `touch` one .py file and
            rebuild. Verify: early steps print CACHED; only COPY . . and
            later steps re-run.
         📊 SUMMARY: layers = cached diffs; order the Dockerfile from
            rarely-changing to always-changing.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a lone `RUN apt-get update` layer caches a stale
            package index forever — always chain `update && install && clean`
            in ONE layer.

    2.5  Tags and Versioning
         - What are tags? (human-readable labels for image versions)
         - Semantic versioning: easypj:v1.2.3
         - latest tag: convenience and danger
         - Multi-tagging: same image, multiple tags
         - Tagging strategies: git SHA, semantic, date-based
         [TABLE: Tagging strategy comparison]

         [TABLE: Tagging strategies — drawn]
         | Strategy | Example              | Pro                | Con                     |
         | Semantic | easypj:1.4.2         | human meaning      | manual discipline       |
         | Git SHA  | easypj:a1b2c3d       | exact provenance   | unreadable to humans    |
         | Date     | easypj:2026-07-02    | sortable           | says nothing of content |
         | Env alias| easypj:staging       | simple promotion   | mutable — it MOVES      |
         | Combined | easypj:1.4.2-a1b2c3d | best of both       | long                    |
         🎯 GOAL: Design easypj's tag scheme so any running container can be
            traced back to one exact commit.
         [TECH] Tags are mutable pointers in the registry database; nothing
            stops :v1 from being force-pushed onto different bytes tomorrow.
            Only the digest is immutable — CI should always record it.
         [ANALOGY] Tag = the name plate on an office door; digest = the
            occupant's fingerprint. People swap offices; fingerprints don't.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: tag one build as 1.0.0 AND latest AND its git
            SHA, then `docker images | grep easypj`. Verify: one IMAGE ID,
            three tags, zero extra disk used.
         📊 SUMMARY: tag for humans, digest for truth; never deploy prod from
            :latest.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: pulling a newer :latest does NOT update running
            containers — they keep the image they were created from.

    2.6  Docker Manifest and Multi-Architecture Images
         - What is a manifest? (image metadata)
         - Multi-arch images: one tag, multiple platforms (linux/amd64, linux/arm64)
         - docker manifest inspect
         - Buildx for multi-platform builds
         [DIAGRAM: One image tag → multiple platform-specific images]


         [DIAGRAM:architecture — one tag, many platforms]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │             $ docker pull easypj:v1                       │
         │                        │                                  │
         │              ┌─────────▼─────────┐                        │
         │              │   MANIFEST LIST   │  ("fat manifest")      │
         │              │   easypj:v1       │                        │
         │              └─────┬───────┬─────┘                        │
         │        linux/amd64 │       │ linux/arm64                  │
         │            ┌───────▼──┐ ┌──▼───────┐                      │
         │            │ manifest │ │ manifest │                      │
         │            │ + layers │ │ + layers │                      │
         │            └──────────┘ └──────────┘                      │
         │   Your CPU architecture decides which one downloads.      │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         🎯 GOAL: Explain why the same `docker pull` works on an ARM MacBook
            and on an AMD64 server.
         [TECH] A manifest list maps platform → per-architecture manifest;
            the client sends its os/arch pair and receives the matching
            manifest, then that manifest's layers. `docker manifest inspect`
            shows the whole map.
         [ANALOGY] One book title, many translations: you ask the shop for
            "easypj v1" and are handed the edition in YOUR language — the
            title on the cover never changes.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker manifest inspect python:3.11-slim` and
            count the platforms. Verify: amd64 and arm64 are both listed.
         [TABLE: single-arch vs multi-arch build/push workflow — drawn]
         | step     | single-arch               | multi-arch (buildx)      |
         | builder  | default builder           | buildx create --use      |
         | build    | docker build -t easypj:v1 | --platform amd64,arm64   |
         | push     | docker push easypj:v1     | push flag: --push        |
         | registry | 1 manifest, 1 platform    | manifest list + N imgs   |
         | ARM pull | risk: exec format error   | correct arch auto-picked |
         | audit    | docker image inspect      | docker manifest inspect  |
         💡 Buildx builds non-native platforms via QEMU emulation,
            registered automatically by Docker Desktop — an arm64 layer
            built on an amd64 CI runner is a REAL image, just noticeably
            slower to produce than a native build.

         📊 SUMMARY: one tag → manifest list → per-arch image; Buildx (5.5)
            is how you PRODUCE these yourself.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: build on an ARM Mac without --platform and the AMD64
            server greets you with "exec format error".

    2.7  Docker Daemon Configuration — daemon.json Deep Dive
         - Location: /etc/docker/daemon.json (Linux) | Desktop → Settings → Docker Engine
         - Apply: sudo systemctl restart docker — invalid JSON = daemon won't start
         - Keys that matter: log-driver/log-opts, storage-driver, registry-mirrors,
           insecure-registries, default-address-pools, live-restore, userns-remap, icc
         🎯 GOAL: Add log rotation + live-restore to a fresh engine without
            taking running containers down — and know why both belong on
            every production host.
         [TECH] dockerd parses daemon.json once at startup; a key set BOTH as
            a CLI flag and in the file is a fatal conflict, not a merge.
            live-restore:true lets containers survive daemon restarts because
            the containerd-shim, not dockerd, parents them (see 1.4).
         [ANALOGY] daemon.json is the building's house rules: every tenant
            (container) inherits them, changing the rules requires a building
            meeting (daemon restart) — and live-restore is the clause letting
            tenants stay home during the meeting.
         [CODE: complete production daemon.json]
            {
              "log-driver": "json-file",
              "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" },
              "live-restore": true,
              "storage-driver": "overlay2",
              "default-address-pools": [ { "base": "172.80.0.0/16", "size": 24 } ]
            }
         [TABLE: 10 daemon.json keys — key | what it does | when you need it;
            include userns-remap (container root ≠ host root), icc:false
            (inter-container comms off, Part 7), registry-mirrors (CI and
            air-gapped pulls), data-root (relocate /var/lib/docker),
            insecure-registries (lab-only HTTP registries)]
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: apply the file above, start a long-running nginx,
            restart the daemon, then `docker info | grep -A2 "Logging
            Driver"`. Verify: json-file with your limits AND nginx never
            stopped running — that is live-restore, proven.
         📊 SUMMARY: one JSON file sets every container's defaults on this
            host; log rotation + live-restore are non-negotiable in prod.
            ⚠️ Gotcha (exam + real life): unbounded json-file logs are the #1
            silent disk-filler on real Docker hosts.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — overlay2: how layers become ONE filesystem
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Docker's default storage driver, overlay2, stacks read-only image
        layers and one writable container layer into a SINGLE merged view
        using the kernel's OverlayFS:
          • lowerdir = the read-only image layers (the "layer cake" from
            2.1), stacked, never written to again.
          • upperdir = the container's one writable layer — every new or
            changed file the running process creates lands here.
          • workdir  = OverlayFS-internal scratch space.
          • merged   = the single view the container's process actually
            sees — reads fall through top-to-bottom to the first layer that
            has the file; writes always go to upperdir.
        Changing a file that exists in a lower (read-only) layer triggers
        COPY-ON-WRITE: the file is copied UP into upperdir first, then
        modified there — the original lower-layer bytes are untouched,
        which is exactly why many containers can share the same image
        layers on disk simultaneously.

        [OVERLAY2 — one easypj container's merged view]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  upperdir  (writable) │ logs/, /tmp/*  ← new files land HERE      │
        ├───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  lowerdir  (RO, top)  │ COPY . /app/         (your code)          │
        │  lowerdir  (RO)       │ RUN pip install...   (dependencies)       │
        │  lowerdir  (RO, base) │ FROM python:3.11-slim                     │
        ├───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┤
        │  merged    = what the container's process sees as "/"            │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ⚠️ `docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}' <container>` prints
        the real lowerdir/upperdir/merged paths on the host — useful the
        day you need to prove where a "missing" file actually went.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🔑 A full image reference is registry/namespace/repo:tag@digest —
           every omitted part defaults (docker.io/library/…:latest); only
           the digest is immutable.
        🔑 Container lifecycle: created → running → {paused|stopped|
           deleted}; stop = SIGTERM (graceful), kill = SIGKILL (immediate),
           pause = cgroup freezer (no signal at all).
        🔑 A push/pull only moves layers the far side doesn't already
           have — content-addressed dedup, just like git.
        🔑 Cache rule: a layer reuses only if EVERY layer before it matched
           too — one early change invalidates everything after it, so
           order Dockerfiles rarely-changing before always-changing.
        🔑 Tags are mutable pointers (a name plate); digests are immutable
           (a fingerprint) — never deploy production from `:latest`.
        🔑 A manifest list ("fat manifest") maps one tag to per-architecture
           images; Buildx is how you produce multi-arch images yourself.
        🔑 daemon.json sets host-wide defaults (log rotation, live-restore,
           storage driver); live-restore works because the shim, not
           dockerd, parents running containers.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚠️ `:latest` is a name, not a freshness guarantee — pulling a newer
           `:latest` never updates containers already running from the old
           one.
        ⚠️ Deleting a container deletes its writable (upperdir) layer —
           anything not on a volume or pushed to a registry is gone for
           good.
        ⚠️ A lone `RUN apt-get update` caches a stale package index
           forever — always chain `update && install && clean` in ONE
           layer.
        ⚠️ Building multi-arch without `--platform` on an ARM Mac ships an
           image that greets an AMD64 server with "exec format error."
        ⚠️ A daemon.json key ALSO passed as a CLI flag to dockerd is a
           fatal conflict, not a merge — dockerd refuses to start.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚡ Order Dockerfiles rarely-changing → always-changing (base image,
           deps, code) so `docker build` reuses cache by default, not luck.
        ⚡ Multi-tag every build (semantic + git SHA) in one `docker build`
           — one IMAGE ID, several handles, zero extra disk.
        ⚡ `docker manifest inspect <image>` proves which platforms a tag
           actually covers before someone's ARM pull fails.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 COMMANDS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        docker images --digests              # local images + immutable digest
        docker pull / docker push <image>    # move layers to/from a registry
        docker tag easypj:v1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1   # re-point before pushing
        docker manifest inspect <img>        # every platform a tag covers
        docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}' <c>  # real overlay2 paths
        docker system df                     # disk used by images/containers
        docker login <registry>              # store registry credentials

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 DRILL
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🧪 Build easypj once, `touch` one .py file, rebuild, and circle every
        line that prints CACHED — then edit requirements.txt and rebuild
        again, circling every line that does NOT print CACHED. If your two
        circles don't match 2.4's GOOD ORDER table, your Dockerfile order
        is inverted.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 2)
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Q1. Define image and container in one sentence each, and say
            exactly what's added when you `docker run` one into the other.
            → Image = read-only layered template; container = a running
              instance with one writable layer added on top. `docker run`
              is the "new" that turns the class into an object.

        Q2. Decompose `ghcr.io/you/easypj:1.2.3@sha256:abc123...` into its
            parts, and give the defaults if you had just written `easypj`.
            → | Part      | Value              | Default if omitted |
              | Registry  | ghcr.io            | docker.io           |
              | Namespace | you                | library              |
              | Repository| easypj             | (required)           |
              | Tag       | 1.2.3              | latest               |
              | Digest    | sha256:abc123...   | (none — mutable tag) |

        Q3. Fill in the lifecycle table: command → signal → resulting
            state, for stop, kill, and pause.
            → | Command      | Signal          | Resulting state |
              | docker stop  | SIGTERM→SIGKILL | Exited (0 or 143)|
              | docker kill  | SIGKILL         | Exited (137)     |
              | docker pause | cgroup freezer  | Paused (frozen)  |

        Q4. You push easypj:v1 to ghcr.io, then push it again unchanged.
            What happens the second time, and why?
            → Every layer prints "Layer already exists" — push is content-
              addressed, so identical layers are never re-uploaded, only
              the manifest is confirmed.

        Q5. Why does `docker push easypj:v1` fail against ghcr.io without
            re-tagging first?
            → The image NAME decides the destination registry. `easypj:v1`
              implicitly means `docker.io/library/easypj:v1`; you must
              `docker tag easypj:v1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1` before pushing
              there.

        Q6. Given `FROM python:3.11-slim` → `COPY . /app/` → `COPY
            requirements.txt .` → `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`
            (bad order), predict what rebuilds after editing one .py file,
            versus editing requirements.txt.
            → Editing a .py file invalidates COPY . /app/ AND every layer
              after it (including the pip install!) because it comes
              first in this bad order — a ~45s rebuild for a 1-line code
              change. In the GOOD order (deps copied/installed before
              code), the same edit would only rebuild the final COPY layer
              (~3s).

        Q7. Design a tag scheme for easypj so any running container traces
            back to one exact commit.
            → Combined tagging: `easypj:1.4.2-a1b2c3d` (semantic version +
              git SHA in one tag) — human-readable AND exactly traceable;
              also multi-tag with `:latest` or `:staging` as a convenience
              alias, never as the deploy-of-record.

        Q8. What does `docker manifest inspect` show, and why does the
            same `docker pull` work on an ARM Mac and an AMD64 server?
            → It shows the manifest list ("fat manifest") mapping one tag
              to several per-architecture manifests + layers. The client
              sends its os/arch pair and the registry serves the matching
              one automatically.
                 easypj:v1 ──▶ MANIFEST LIST ──▶ {linux/amd64, linux/arm64}
                                                   your CPU picks one

        Q9. Write the two daemon.json keys that guarantee running
            containers survive a daemon restart AND that logs never grow
            unbounded — and explain the mechanism for each.
            → `"live-restore": true` — containers are parented by the
              containerd-shim, not dockerd, so a daemon restart doesn't
              kill them. `"log-opts": {"max-size":"10m","max-file":"3"}`
              under `"log-driver":"json-file"` caps and rotates logs so
              json-file never silently fills the disk.

        Q10. A container without a volume is deleted. What is lost, and
             which chapter component is directly responsible?
             → Everything written to the container's writable (upperdir)
               layer is lost — deleting the container deletes that layer
               (2.2's lifecycle + this chapter's overlay2 internals). Only
               data on a mounted volume, or already pushed to a registry
               as a new image layer, survives.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — "Chapter 2, the five nouns"
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  📦 IMAGE (2.1)        registry/repo:tag@digest — read-only layers  │
    │         │ docker run                                                │
    │         ▼                                                           │
    │  ▶️ CONTAINER (2.2)    created→running→{paused|stopped|deleted}    │
    │         │ docker push/pull                                          │
    │         ▼                                                           │
    │  🗄️ REGISTRY (2.3)     Hub/ECR/GCR/ACR/Harbor — only missing layers│
    │                          travel                                     │
    │         ▲ built from                                                │
    │  🍰 LAYERS (2.4)       cached diffs, order = rebuild cost           │
    │         │ named by                                                  │
    │  🏷️ TAGS (2.5)         mutable name │ 🧬 digest = immutable         │
    │         │ fans out via                                              │
    │  📐 MANIFEST (2.6)     one tag → per-arch images (amd64, arm64...)  │
    │         │ all governed by                                           │
    │  ⚙️ daemon.json (2.7)  log rotation, live-restore, storage driver   │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    .vs-prose — Chapter 2 in one line: an IMAGE is a read-only, digest-
    addressed template stored in a REGISTRY; `docker run` turns it into a
    CONTAINER with its own writable LAYER; the image itself is built from
    cached LAYERS whose order decides rebuild cost; humans find images by
    mutable TAGS while machines pin the immutable digest; a MANIFEST list
    lets one tag serve many CPU architectures; and daemon.json is the one
    file deciding how every container on this host logs, survives a
    restart, and stores its files on disk.

         🎯 GOAL: Get a healthy Docker Desktop and prove it with one command.
         [TECH] Desktop = a managed Linux VM (WSL2 backend on Windows,
            Virtualization.framework on macOS) + the engine inside it + GUI +
            bundled Compose/Buildx/Scout. Containers never run "on Windows" —

            Verify: the message prints, and Settings shows the WSL2 backend

         📊 SUMMARY: Desktop = dev bundle wrapped around a hidden Linux VM.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "Docker is eating my RAM" is usually the WSL2 VM's
            appetite — tune it in .wslconfig, not in Docker.

    3.2  Installing Docker Engine on Linux
         - Ubuntu/Debian installation
         - CentOS/RHEL installation
         - Post-installation steps (docker group, start on boot)
         - Verifying installation: docker version, docker info
         [CODE BLOCKS: Exact terminal commands for each OS]

         🎯 GOAL: Install the engine on a fresh Ubuntu box and run docker as
            a non-root user.
         [TECH] The apt repo installs docker-ce + docker-ce-cli + containerd
            + the buildx/compose plugins; systemd starts dockerd; the docker
            group owns the socket — membership is root-equivalent power
            (Part 7 explains why that matters).
         [ANALOGY] Wiring a building straight into the power grid: the
            apt repo is the utility crew wiring the service; the systemd
            unit is the meter that keeps current flowing after they
            leave; and `docker group` membership is a key to the breaker
            panel — anyone holding it can cut power to (or root) anything
            on the box, which is exactly the danger Part 7 walks back.

         [TERMINAL: the 4 lines that matter]
            $ curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sh      # convenience script
            $ sudo usermod -aG docker $USER && newgrp docker
            $ docker version
            $ docker run --rm hello-world
         🔬 easypj: once these 4 lines finish, `docker run -d -p
            8000:8000 easypj:v1` on this VM behaves identically to the
            same command on a laptop running Docker Desktop — same
            engine underneath either way.

         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: do it on any free-tier cloud VM. Verify:
            hello-world runs WITHOUT sudo.
         📊 SUMMARY: repo → service → group → verify; four lines, done.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: skipping the group re-login is the #1 cause of
            "permission denied on /var/run/docker.sock".

    3.3  Your First Docker Command — Hello World
         - docker run hello-world (the "Hello World" of Docker)
         - Step-by-step breakdown of what happens:
           1. Docker Client sends command to Daemon
           2. Daemon checks local images (not found)
           3. Daemon pulls hello-world from Docker Hub
           4. Daemon creates a new container from the image
           5. Container runs, prints message, exits

         [FLOWCHART: docker run hello-world — 5 Steps Visualized]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │              ⚡ docker run hello-world — WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS              │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ┌─────────┐      ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐                │
         │  │ You type │      │              │      │              │                │
         │  │ $ docker │──1──▶│  dockerd     │──2──▶│ Local Image  │                │
         │  │ run hello│      │  (Daemon)    │      │ Cache        │                │
         │  │ -world   │      │              │◀─────│ "hello-world"│                │
         │  └─────────┘      └──────┬───────┘      │ NOT FOUND!   │                │
         │                         │              └──────────────┘                │
         │                         │ 3. Pull image                                 │
         │                         ▼                                               │
         │                  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐                │
         │                  │  🗄️ Docker   │─────▶│ Local Image  │                │
         │                  │  Hub         │      │ Cache        │                │
         │                  │  hello-world │      │ hello-world  │                │
         │                  │  (tiny: ~13KB)│      │ (cached now!)│                │
         │                  └──────────────┘      └──────┬───────┘                │
         │                                               │ 4. Create container     │
         │                                               ▼                         │
         │                  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐                │
         │                  │ 5. Container │◀─────│  dockerd     │                │
         │                  │ Runs +       │      │  Creates     │                │
         │                  │ Prints:      │      │  Container   │                │
         │                  │ "Hello from  │      │  from Image  │                │
         │                  │  Docker!"    │      │              │                │
         │                  │ Then EXITS   │      └──────────────┘                │
         │                  └──────────────┘                                       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Narrate all 5 steps of the flowchart above from memory the
            next time any image "just works".
         [TECH] Not found locally → pull from registry → create container
            (new writable layer + namespaces) → start process → process exits
            → container remains on disk, STATUS Exited (0).
         [ANALOGY] Ordering a pizza you don't have in the freezer: delivery
            (pull) happens once; every later run is just reheating (local
            image cache).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker run hello-world` twice. Verify: the
            second run shows NO "Pulling from library/hello-world" lines —
            you just proved the image cache exists.
         📊 SUMMARY: run = (pull if absent) + create + start.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: hello-world exits instantly BY DESIGN — a stopped
            container is not an error; it is a finished process.

    3.4  Running easypj in Docker — First Contact
         - Pull Python base image: docker pull python:3.11-slim
         - Run interactively: docker run -it python:3.11-slim bash
         - Inside the container: ls, python --version, exit
         - Understanding -it flags (-i interactive, -t TTY)
         - docker ps vs docker ps -a (running vs all containers)
         [TERMINAL: Full session capture with annotations]

         [TERMINAL: first contact, annotated — drawn]
            $ docker pull python:3.11-slim           # fetch the base image
            $ docker run -it python:3.11-slim bash   # -i keep stdin, -t give TTY
            root@9f2c1a7b3e4d:/# python --version    #   Python 3.11.x — inside!
            root@9f2c1a7b3e4d:/# ls /                #   a whole Debian userland
            root@9f2c1a7b3e4d:/# exit                # PID 1 ends → container stops
            $ docker ps                              # empty — nothing running
            $ docker ps -a                           # the exited shell is HERE
         🎯 GOAL: Enter a container, look around, leave — and know where the
            container went afterwards.
         [TECH] `-i` keeps STDIN open even without an attached terminal;
            `-t` allocates a pseudo-TTY so the shell prompt renders
            correctly. Together they turn `docker run` into an
            interactive session where bash becomes PID 1 inside the
            container — and PID 1 exiting (`exit`) stops the whole
            container, not just the shell.

         [ANALOGY] -it is scuba gear: -i is the air hose (stdin stays
            connected), -t is the mask (a terminal you can see through).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: repeat the session with --rm added. Verify:
            after exit, `docker ps -a` shows nothing — cleanup on exit.
         📊 SUMMARY: -it = interactive TTY; exit kills PID 1; the corpse
            stays visible in ps -a unless --rm.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: easypj's code is NOT in this container — a base image
            is an empty stage; COPYing the app in is Chapter 4's job.

    3.5  Essential docker run Flags
         - --name: Give your container a name
         - -d: Detached mode (run in background)
         - -p: Port mapping (host:container)
         - -e: Environment variables
         - -v: Volume mounting
         - --rm: Auto-remove on exit
         - --restart: Restart policy
         [TABLE: 15+ docker run flags with examples]

         [TABLE: the 12 flags you will actually use — flag | meaning | easypj example]
            --name     | stable handle          | --name easypj-web
            -d         | detach (background)    | -d easypj:v1
            -p         | host:container port    | -p 8000:8000
            -e         | one env var            | -e DEBUG=False
            --env-file | many env vars          | --env-file .env
            -v         | volume / bind mount    | -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
            --rm       | auto-delete on exit    | --rm easypj:v1 python manage.py test
            --restart  | restart policy         | --restart unless-stopped
            --network  | attach to a network    | --network easypj-backend
            --memory   | RAM cap                | --memory 512m
            --cpus     | CPU cap                | --cpus 1.5
            -w         | working directory      | -w /app
         🎯 GOAL: Compose a correct docker run for easypj from memory —
            named, detached, port-mapped, env-fed, restartable.
         [TECH] The 12 flags in the table above split into four jobs:
            identity & lifecycle (--name, -d, --rm, --restart), networking
            (-p, --network), configuration (-e, --env-file), and resource/
            filesystem control (-v, --memory, --cpus, -w). Flag ORDER
            before the image name is free; the image name marks the
            boundary — anything after it is the container's command, not
            a docker option.
         [ANALOGY] Prepping a race car before it leaves the pit: --name
            paints the car's number on the door, -p assigns which lane it
            exits onto, -e/--env-file load the fuel-mixture settings
            before the engine starts, -v wires it to a spare-parts bin it
            can reach mid-race, and --restart is the standing order to
            push it back onto the track if it stalls.
         ⚡ docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 --env-file .env
            --restart unless-stopped easypj:v1
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: type the ⚡ line from memory, then break it on
            purpose (-p 8000 alone; image name before the flags). Verify:
            you can read both error messages and explain each.
         [DIAGRAM:decision — dev run vs prod run: which flags fire?]
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │        docker run easypj — dev laptop, or prod server?         │
         ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ DEV (laptop, iterate fast)                                     │
         │   -v $PWD:/app     live code, no rebuild needed                │
         │   --rm  -it        throwaway container, live tracebacks        │
         │   (skip --restart & --memory — you control the lifecycle)      │
         │                                                                │
         │   $ docker run --rm -it -v $PWD:/app -p 8000:8000 \            │
         │       easypj:v1 python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000        │
         ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ PROD (server, stays up unattended)                             │
         │   --restart unless-stopped   survives crash & reboot           │
         │   --env-file .env            secrets in, never bare -e         │
         │   --memory 512m --cpus 1.5   caps the noisy neighbor           │
         │                                                                │
         │   $ docker run -d --name easypj-web \                          │
         │       --restart unless-stopped --env-file .env \               │
         │       --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1          │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         💡 --rm and --restart are mutually exclusive at the CLI level:
            `docker run --rm --restart unless-stopped ...` fails instantly
            with "conflicting options: --restart and --rm" — Docker itself
            enforces the dev/prod split drawn above.

         💡 The table above is the 12 daily-driver flags; the official
            docker run surface has ~50+ documented flags (health checks,
            cgroups, GPUs, ulimits, security options, and more). See
            Appendix A.11 for the complete official flag reference.

         📊 SUMMARY: 12 flags cover 95% of daily docker run usage.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: everything AFTER the image name is the container's
            COMMAND, not a docker flag — position is grammar, not style.

    3.6  Docker CLI Structure & Help System
         - docker <command> <subcommand> [options] [arguments]
         - docker --help, docker <command> --help
         - Tab completion setup
         - Common command patterns

         [DOCKER CLI — COMMAND ANATOMY]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                        🔤 DOCKER CLI STRUCTURE                             │
         │                                                                          │
         │   docker [GLOBAL_OPTIONS] COMMAND [SUBCOMMAND] [OPTIONS] [ARGUMENTS]     │
         │   ────── ──────────────── ─────── ──────────── ──────── ──────────        │
         │     │          │             │         │           │          │           │
         │     │          │             │         │           │          └─ Targets │
         │     │          │             │         │           │             (images, │
         │     │          │             │         │           │            containers│
         │     │          │             │         │           └─ Flags      names...)│
         │     │          │             │         │              -p, -d, -e,         │
         │     │          │             │         │              --name, -v,         │
         │     │          │             │         │              --rm, --restart     │
         │     │          │             │         └─ Subcommand                     │
         │     │          │             │            (run, ls, rm, start,           │
         │     │          │             │             stop, build, push...)         │
         │     │          │             └─ Management Group                          │
         │     │          │                container, image, volume,                │
         │     │          │                network, system, compose,                │
         │     │          │                swarm, stack, secret, config...          │
         │     │          └─ Global Flags                                           │
         │     │             --help, --version, --config, --context,                │
         │     │             --log-level, --tls, --host (rarely used)               │
         │     └─ The Docker CLI binary itself                                      │
         │                                                                          │
         │  EXAMPLES:                                                                │
         │  docker container run -d -p 8000:8000 --name easypj easypj:v1            │
         │  docker image ls --filter "reference=easypj*"                            │
         │  docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d                              │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Predict what any docker command does from its shape alone —
            management group + subcommand + flags + target.
         [TECH] Modern CLI grammar: docker <group> <verb> [flags] [target].
            Legacy shortcuts (docker ps, docker images) are aliases for
            docker container ls / docker image ls — same code path.
         [ANALOGY] The anatomy diagram above is sentence grammar: group =
            subject, verb = verb, flags = adverbs, target = object. Commands
            stop being memorization the day you parse them as grammar.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: without running them, translate: docker network
            ls / docker volume rm pgdata / docker image prune -a. Verify
            with --help: every guess matched.
         📊 SUMMARY: groups make the CLI guessable — learn the grammar, not
            300 commands.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: --help works at EVERY level (docker --help, docker
            image --help, docker image ls --help) — the fastest docs you
            own, exam included.

    3.7  When docker Commands Fail — Reading Error Messages
         - The five errors every beginner hits in week one, decoded
         - permission denied on docker.sock → not in docker group (see 3.2)
         - Cannot connect to the Docker daemon → daemon not running
         - port is already allocated → host port taken: change -p or free it
         - No such container → name typo, or it was --rm'd / never started
         - exec format error → wrong CPU architecture image (see 2.6)
         [TABLE: error string | real meaning | first command to run]
         🎯 GOAL: Turn the five most common error strings into 10-second
            fixes instead of 30-minute searches.
         [TECH] docker errors have two sources: the CLIENT (bad grammar,
            unknown flag — fails before any API call) and the DAEMON (API
            errors: conflicts, missing objects, kernel refusals). Knowing
            which side failed halves your search space instantly.
         [ANALOGY] Client errors = the waiter rejects your order (you
            misread the menu); daemon errors = the kitchen reports a problem
            (out of stock, oven busy). You complain to different people.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: cause all five errors on purpose (stop the
            daemon, double-book a port, typo a name…). Verify: for each, you
            can say client-side or daemon-side BEFORE reading the fix.
         📊 SUMMARY: read the error's SOURCE first, the string second —
            docker errors are short, precise, and never random.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "port is already allocated" usually means a FORGOTTEN
            CONTAINER owns it — docker ps first, lsof second.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — what `-p 8000:8000` and `--restart` actually do
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Publishing a port is not "opening a port on the container" — it is
        dockerd programming the HOST's own packet filter. On Linux, every
        `-p hostPort:containerPort` adds a DNAT rule to the `DOCKER` chain
        in iptables/nftables: a packet hitting the host's hostPort is
        rewritten to the container's private IP:containerPort on the
        bridge network, before it ever reaches the container's own
        namespace. (Desktop hides an extra hop: host → WSL2/VM → the same
        iptables rule → container.)

        `--restart` is not a kernel feature either — dockerd itself watches
        every container's exit event and decides whether to recreate it,
        purely from the policy string you passed:
          • no              → never restart (default)
          • on-failure[:N]  → restart only on non-zero exit, up to N times
          • unless-stopped  → always restart, EXCEPT after an explicit
                              `docker stop` (survives daemon/host reboot)
          • always          → restarts even after an explicit stop, on
                              reboot

        [PORT PUBLISHING — one packet's path]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  client :80 ──▶ host eth0:8000 ──▶ iptables DNAT (DOCKER chain)   │
        │                                          │                        │
        │                                          ▼                        │
        │                docker0 bridge ──▶ easypj-web (172.17.0.x:8000)   │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ⚠️ This is why a host firewall that blocks the DOCKER chain
        silently breaks every published port — the container is fine, the
        RULE never fired.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🔑 Desktop = Engine wrapped in a managed Linux VM (WSL2 on Windows,
           Virtualization.framework on macOS) — containers never run "on
           Windows/macOS" directly, only inside that hidden Linux kernel.
        🔑 On Linux, membership in the `docker` group is root-equivalent —
           it owns the daemon socket, not a sandboxed permission.
        🔑 `docker run hello-world` = (pull if absent) → create → start;
           the exited container still exists until removed or `--rm`'d.
        🔑 `-i` keeps stdin open, `-t` allocates a TTY; together they make
           a shell PID 1 inside the container, and `exit` stops the whole
           container.
        🔑 `docker ps` shows only RUNNING containers; `docker ps -a` shows
           every container, including exited ones holding a name or port.
        🔑 The 12 daily-driver run flags split into four jobs: identity/
           lifecycle, networking, configuration, and resource/filesystem
           control.
        🔑 The CLI's real grammar is `docker <group> <verb> [flags]
           [target]` — legacy shortcuts (`docker ps`, `docker images`) are
           aliases for the same code path.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚠️ "Docker is eating my RAM" on Windows is almost always the WSL2
           VM's appetite — tune `.wslconfig`, not Docker Desktop settings.
        ⚠️ Skipping the `docker group` re-login (`newgrp docker` or a fresh
           shell) is the #1 cause of "permission denied on
           /var/run/docker.sock."
        ⚠️ `--rm` and `--restart` are mutually exclusive at the CLI level —
           Docker refuses the command instantly, it does not silently
           pick one.
        ⚠️ "port is already allocated" almost always means a FORGOTTEN
           container already holds it — `docker ps` before `lsof`.
        ⚠️ Everything typed AFTER the image name is the container's
           COMMAND, not a docker flag — position is grammar, not style.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚡ `docker ps -a --filter status=exited` finds every leftover
           container before it silently squats on a name or a port.
        ⚡ `--help` works at every level (`docker --help`, `docker image
           --help`, `docker image ls --help`) — the fastest docs you own.
        ⚡ When a command errors, decide CLIENT vs DAEMON first (bad
           grammar vs API failure) — it halves the search space before you
           even read the string.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 COMMANDS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        docker version                       # client AND server — daemon reachability
        docker run --rm hello-world          # full pull→create→run→exit path
        docker ps                            # running containers only
        docker ps -a                         # every container, incl. exited
        docker run -it <image> bash          # interactive shell, PID 1 inside
        docker run -d --name <n> -p H:C --env-file .env --restart unless-stopped <img>
        docker logs <container>              # what a detached (-d) container printed

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 DRILL
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🧪 Run nginx four different ways — plain, --rm, -d --name, and -it
        bash inside it — predicting `docker ps -a`'s output BEFORE you run
        each one. Score yourself: 4/4 correct means Ch3 is muscle memory.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 3)
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Q1. On a Windows laptop, where do Linux containers actually run,
            and why doesn't that contradict "containers share the host
            kernel"?
            → Inside Docker Desktop's managed Linux VM (WSL2 backend) — the
              container still shares THAT Linux kernel with every other
              container in the VM; the "host" from the container's point
              of view is the VM, not Windows itself.
                 Windows ─▶ WSL2 Linux VM ─▶ dockerd ─▶ containers (shared kernel)

        Q2. Why does `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER` require a new login/
            shell before it takes effect, and what error appears if you
            skip it?
            → Group membership is read when a shell session STARTS; an
              already-open shell keeps its old group list. Skipping the
              relogin (or `newgrp docker`) produces "permission denied on
              /var/run/docker.sock."

        Q3. Narrate, in order, what happens the FIRST time you run `docker
            run hello-world` on a clean machine, and how the second run
            differs.
            → (1) client sends the request to dockerd, (2) dockerd checks
              the local image cache — not found, (3) pulls hello-world from
              Docker Hub, (4) creates a container from the image, (5) the
              container runs, prints its message, and exits. The second run
              skips steps 2-3's pull entirely — the image is now cached.

        Q4. What do -i and -t each do individually, and what would you
            observe running `docker run -i python:3.11-slim bash` WITHOUT
            -t?
            → -i keeps STDIN open; -t allocates a pseudo-TTY so a shell
              prompt renders correctly. Without -t you'd get a working
              shell but no visible prompt/formatting — commands still run,
              but it "looks broken."

        Q5. After `docker run --rm -it python:3.11-slim bash` then typing
            `exit`, what does `docker ps -a` show, and why?
            → Nothing — `--rm` auto-removes the container the instant its
              main process (the bash shell, PID 1) exits, before `ps -a`
              could ever list it.

        Q6. Write, from memory, a production docker run for easypj: named,
            detached, port 8000, env file, capped at 512m/1.5 cpus,
            restart unless-stopped.
            → docker run -d --name easypj-web -p 8000:8000 \
                 --env-file .env --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 \
                 --restart unless-stopped easypj:v1

        Q7. Compare the four restart policies and say which one a
            production stack should use over `always`.
            → | Policy          | Restarts after crash | Restarts after `docker stop` |
              | no              | never                 | never                        |
              | on-failure[:N]  | only non-zero exit     | never                        |
              | unless-stopped  | yes                    | no (until explicitly started)|
              | always          | yes                    | yes, even after manual stop  |
              Production prefers `unless-stopped`: it survives crashes and
              reboots but still respects a deliberate `docker stop` during
              maintenance — `always` would fight you.

        Q8. Translate `docker volume rm pgdata` and `docker image prune -a`
            into plain English using group/verb/flag/target grammar,
            without running them.
            → `volume rm pgdata`: management group "volume," verb "rm"
              (remove), target "pgdata" — delete the named volume.
              `image prune -a`: management group "image," verb "prune,"
              flag `-a` (all) — remove ALL unused images, not just dangling
              ones.

        Q9. A teammate reports "port is already allocated" starting
            easypj-web on 8000. What are your first two commands, and in
            what order?
            → `docker ps` first (find a forgotten container already
              publishing 8000), then `lsof -i :8000` (or `netstat`) only if
              `docker ps` comes back clean — checking Docker's own state
              before the OS avoids chasing the wrong process.

        Q10. Sort these into CLIENT-side vs DAEMON-side, and state the rule
             that sorts them: "unknown flag: --nam," "Cannot connect to the
             Docker daemon," "No such container: easypj-old," "exec format
             error."
             → CLIENT: "unknown flag: --nam" (bad grammar, never reaches
               the API). DAEMON: "Cannot connect to the Docker daemon,"
               "No such container: easypj-old," "exec format error" (all
               require the daemon to process the request and refuse it).
               Rule: if it fails before the API call, it's the CLIENT; if
               the daemon itself reports the problem, it's the DAEMON.

    [F] PART 1 — KEY TAKEAWAYS
     ✅ Docker kills environment drift by shipping the full userspace as
        one immutable image; containers share the host kernel instead of
        booting their own (Ch1).
     🔑 Five nouns run the rest of this guide: image, container, registry,
        layer, tag — plus the digest that makes an image reference truly
        immutable (Ch2).
     🎯 DCA MAP: Ch1 underlies Image Creation/Mgmt/Registry (20%); Ch2 IS
        that domain directly; Ch3 IS Installation and Configuration (15%).
     🔑 One `docker run` always travels client → dockerd → containerd →
        shim → runc — the shim is why containers outlive a daemon restart
        with live-restore on (Ch1, Ch2.7).
     ✅ A container's writable layer is ephemeral by design — delete the
        container, lose anything not on a volume or pushed to a registry
        (Ch2).
     ✅ Desktop (dev, VM-wrapped) and Engine (prod, bare) are the same
        engine in two packagings — you now have one installed and
        verified (Ch3).
     🔑 Every docker command is `group verb [flags] [target]` — grammar,
        not memorization (Ch3).

    ⚠️ PART 1 — GOTCHAS
     ⚠️ "Docker packages the kernel" is false throughout this part — the
        kernel is always the host's; that's WHY containers are light AND
        why a Windows container needs a Windows kernel underneath.
     ⚠️ `:latest` is a name, not a promise — pulling a newer `:latest`
        never updates a container already running from the old one.
     ⚠️ Deleting a container is destructive by default — its writable
        layer goes with it; volumes (later in this guide) are where this
        gets fixed permanently.
     ⚠️ Docker Desktop is a development tool; it is never the thing
        running easypj in production — that's bare Engine (CE), always.

    ⚡ PART 1 — SPEED TIPS
     ⚡ `docker version` then `docker info` is the two-command health
        check to run on ANY machine before touching anything else.
     ⚡ Read any image reference or command right-to-left when confused —
        defaults fill every gap Docker lets you omit.
     ⚡ `--help` at every level beats memorizing flags — build that reflex
        starting now, not as a fallback later.
