Chapter 7: Image Management — docker image Commands
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Builds multiply: within a week you own fifty
    images, twelve <none> ghosts and a full disk. This chapter is image
    custody — listing, tagging, moving (push/pull/save/load), pruning and
    auditing what you hold. Problem solved here: "which of these easypj
    images is production, why is /var/lib/docker 40 GB, and how do I ship
    an image to a server with no internet?"

    [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~50-70 min · 🎯 DCA: Image Creation,
      Management & Registry (20% — core domain; Ch7 is its command layer)

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
      • List and filter local images by name, dangling state, or
        reference pattern, and format output for scripts (7.1).
      • Explain why one IMAGE ID can carry many tags, and re-tag easypj
        for release, latest, and registry-prefixed names (7.2).
      • Log in, push, and pull easypj to/from a registry, and pin a
        deploy to a digest instead of a movable tag (7.3).
      • Choose save/load over export/import for moving a full image
        offline, and state exactly what export loses (7.4).
      • Run the cleanup ladder (prune → prune -a → system prune
        --volumes) and read `docker system df` before doing it (7.5).
      • Read `docker history` to rank an image's fattest layers and
        `docker inspect` to audit its Env/User/digest (7.6).

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: Chapter 7 IS the "Registry" half of the
      20%-weighted Image Creation, Management & Registry domain —
      expect exam items on tagging, push/pull, and removal semantics.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 7.1 list/filter → 7.2 tag → 7.3 push/pull → 7.4
      save/load (offline) → 7.5 prune/cleanup → 7.6 history/inspect —
      each section hands the next one a cleaner, better-understood
      image store.

    7.1  Listing & Filtering Images
         - docker images (list all)
         - docker image ls (same, newer syntax)
         - Filtering: docker images --filter "dangling=true"
         - Filtering: docker images --filter "reference=python*"
         - Formatting: docker images --format "table {{.Repository}}\t{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}"
         [OUTPUT EXAMPLES: Annotated image listings]

         [TERMINAL: listing with intent — drawn]
            $ docker images --filter "reference=easypj*"
            REPOSITORY   TAG     IMAGE ID       CREATED       SIZE
            easypj       v1.1    3f9a12bc77de   2 hours ago   181MB
            easypj       v1.0    9c31e0a4f552   3 days ago    184MB
            $ docker images --filter "dangling=true" -q    # just the IDs
            77af4d6b9913
            $ docker images --format "{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}} {{.Size}}"
         🎯 GOAL: Find any image by name, hunt every <none> ghost, and
            feed image lists into scripts — no eyeballing walls of text.
         [TECH] dangling=true matches layers whose tag was STOLEN by a
            newer build of the same name — untagged but still on disk.
            --format uses Go templates over fields (.Repository, .Tag,
            .ID, .Size); -q prints IDs only, which is what makes
            `docker rmi $(docker images -f dangling=true -q)` possible.
         [ANALOGY] A warehouse manifest: filters are clipboard queries
            ("aisle easypj*", "unlabeled boxes"), --format picks the
            printout's columns, -q prints barcode stickers only.
         🔬 easypj: every rebuild of easypj:v1 demotes the previous build
            to <none>:<none> — after a day of iterating you hold a dozen
            dangling ghosts. 7.5 deletes them; here you LIST them first.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: rebuild easypj:v1 after touching a file, then
            run the dangling filter above. Verify: yesterday's IMAGE ID
            now shows as <none>:<none> — the tag moved, the bytes stayed.
         📊 SUMMARY: images lists the local store; filters + Go-template
            formats turn it from wallpaper into a queryable database.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: SIZE double-counts shared layers — ten easypj tags
            do not cost 10 × 180 MB; docker system df tells disk truth.

    7.2  Tagging Images Properly
         - docker tag source target
         - docker tag easypj:v1 easypj:latest
         - docker tag easypj:v1 myregistry.com/easypj:v1
         - Multiple tags for same image (same IMAGE ID)
         - Untagging: docker rmi easypj:v1 (removes tag, not image if others exist)
         [DIAGRAM: One IMAGE ID → multiple tags]

         [DIAGRAM:architecture — one IMAGE ID, many name tags]
                              ┌─ easypj:v1.0
            3f9a12bc77de ─────┼─ easypj:latest
            (the bytes)       └─ ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0
            one image on disk — three sticky notes, zero extra megabytes
         🎯 GOAL: Re-name images freely — versions, latest, registry
            prefixes — knowing tags are free and the ID is the identity.
         [TECH] docker tag SRC DST creates another name → same IMAGE ID;
            nothing is copied. The name's PREFIX is routing: tagging as
            ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0 is what makes push go to ghcr (2.3).
            docker rmi easypj:v1.0 removes ONE name; the bytes die only
            when the LAST name (and last container) lets go.
         [ANALOGY] The diagram above: one person (ID), three name badges —
            work alias, nickname, passport name for border crossings
            (registry prefix). Shredding a badge never harms the person.
         🔬 easypj: release ritual — docker tag easypj:v1.1 easypj:latest
            && docker tag easypj:v1.1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1 — one
            build, three names, each with a different job.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: apply both tags above, run docker images,
            then rmi the latest tag. Verify: all three rows shared one
            IMAGE ID; after rmi, v1.1 still exists — only the badge died.
         📊 SUMMARY: tag = alias, ID = identity; the registry prefix in
            the name IS the push destination.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker rmi 3f9a12bc77de` by ID with several tags
            present refuses (or with -f, kills EVERY name) — untag by
            NAME; delete by ID only when one name remains.

    7.3  Pushing & Pulling Images
         - docker push registry/repo:tag
         - docker pull registry/repo:tag
         - Authentication: docker login
         - Docker Hub namespace: username/repo:tag
         - Private registry push workflow
         [TERMINAL: Complete push/pull workflow for easypj]

         [TERMINAL: the full round trip — drawn]
            $ docker login ghcr.io -u you           # token → config.json
            $ docker tag easypj:v1.1 ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1
            $ docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1
            9d3a: Pushed   f2c1: Layer already exists  # dedup, see 2.3
            v1.1: digest: sha256:4be2... size: 1786
            $ ssh server 'docker pull ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1'
         🎯 GOAL: Move easypj laptop → registry → server and pin what the
            server got to a digest, not a hope.
         [TECH] push uploads missing layers + the manifest, then prints
            the manifest DIGEST — record it: deploying by digest
            (ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:4be2...) is immune to tag moves
            (2.5). pull on the server reverses the trip; Docker Hub names
            omit the registry (you/easypj:v1.1 = docker.io implied).
         [ANALOGY] Registered mail: layers are parcels the post office
            already partly holds (dedup), the manifest is the delivery
            slip, and the digest is the tracking number — quote THAT in
            disputes, not "the brown box" (:latest).
         🔬 easypj: CI pushes ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1, records the
            digest, and the deploy step pulls BY DIGEST — what was tested
            is byte-for-byte what runs.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: push v1.1, note the printed digest, then
            `docker pull ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:<it>`. Verify: the
            pull succeeds with no tag at all — content-addressing live.
         📊 SUMMARY: login → tag with registry prefix → push → pull;
            digests, not tags, are the deployable truth.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "denied: requested access to the resource" is
            almost always a missing/wrong NAMESPACE in the name, not a
            password problem — check the prefix before the credentials.

    7.4  Saving & Loading Images (Offline Transfer)
         - docker save -o easypj.tar easypj:v1 (export as tar)
         - docker load -i easypj.tar (import from tar)
         - docker export (container filesystem, NOT image)
         - docker import (create image from filesystem)
         - save vs export: critical difference
         [TABLE: save/load vs export/import comparison]

         [TABLE: save/load vs export/import — drawn]
            | pair           | moves          | layers+tags kept? | CMD? |
            | save → load    | IMAGE          | ✅ history intact | ✅   |
            | export→ import | container's FS | ❌ flattened      | ❌   |
         🎯 GOAL: Carry easypj onto an air-gapped server on a USB stick —
            and never grab export when you meant save.
         [TECH] save serializes the IMAGE: all layers, tags, config —
            load restores it identically, cache-compatible. export tars a
            CONTAINER's merged filesystem: one flat layer, no CMD/ENV/
            EXPOSE — importing it yields an image that does not even know
            how to start. gzip the save (~40% smaller) for transport.
         [ANALOGY] save ships the printing plates (reprint anytime,
            edition data intact); export photocopies one printed book —
            readable, but the plates, metadata and cover are gone.
         🔬 easypj: docker save easypj:v1.1 | gzip > easypj-v1.1.tar.gz →
            USB → `gunzip -c easypj-v1.1.tar.gz | docker load` on the
            offline server: tag, layers and CMD arrive untouched.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: save + load easypj:v1.1, then export a
            container and import it; docker inspect both results.
            Verify: the loaded image kept CMD ["gunicorn", ...]; the
            imported one has Cmd: null — run it and watch it exit
            instantly, which is the whole lesson.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — save → USB → load, across the air-gap]
         ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
         │ easypj:v1.1 │  │ docker save │  │ USB stick  │  │ gunzip |     │
         │ image       │─▶│ | gzip      │─▶│ air-gap    │─▶│ docker load  │
         │ ONLINE host │  │ .tar.gz     │  │ hand-carry │  │ OFFLINE host │
         └─────────────┘  └─────────────┘  └────────────┘  └──────────────┘
         layers + tags + CMD all survive — export/import would not
         💡 docker load never asks first: loading a tarball whose tag
            already exists on the offline host OVERWRITES it immediately,
            no confirmation prompt — run `docker images` before and after
            on any host you don't fully control.

         📊 SUMMARY: save/load = image, layered, metadata kept;
            export/import = flattened container FS, metadata lost.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker save easypj` without a tag saves EVERY
            easypj tag into one (huge) tarball — pipes hide the mistake.

    7.5  Removing Images & Cleanup
         - docker rmi <image> (remove image)
         - docker image prune (remove dangling)
         - docker image prune -a (remove all unused)
         - docker system df (disk usage)
         - docker system prune -a (nuclear: remove ALL unused)
         [BEFORE/AFTER: Disk space freed after cleanup]

         [TERMINAL: cleanup ladder, least → most destructive — drawn]
            $ docker system df               # who eats the disk?
            TYPE          TOTAL  ACTIVE  SIZE    RECLAIMABLE
            Images        23     4       9.8GB   7.1GB (72%)
            Build Cache   118    0       4.2GB   4.2GB
            $ docker image prune             # dangling <none> only: safe
            $ docker image prune -a          # ALL images no container uses
            $ docker builder prune           # build cache
            $ docker system prune -a --volumes   # ☢️ everything unused
         🎯 GOAL: Reclaim gigabytes on a build machine deliberately —
            climbing the ladder above one rung at a time, never jumping.
         [TECH] rmi refuses while ANY container (even Exited) references
            the image — rm the container first. prune deletes dangling
            images (the 7.1 ghosts); prune -a widens to every image with
            zero containers, meaning the next run re-PULLS them. df's
            RECLAIMABLE column is the honest number — shared layers
            counted once.
         [ANALOGY] Cleaning a garage: df is the inventory walk, prune
            tosses unlabeled boxes, prune -a tosses everything not bolted
            to a car, system prune -a --volumes sells the garage — each
            rung is cheaper to regret than the next.
         🔬 easypj: a week of iteration leaves ~15 dangling builds;
            `docker image prune` frees GBs and cannot touch easypj:v1.1
            while easypj-web runs — that reference protects it.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: df → image prune → df again. Verify: the
            Images RECLAIMABLE number fell by roughly the pruned total,
            and every named easypj tag survived.
         📊 SUMMARY: df to diagnose, prune to trim, -a to purge, system
            prune -a --volumes only when you can re-pull and rebuild ALL.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: on CI runners, prune -a also evicts your
            --cache-from sources — the next build goes cold; prune
            surgically there.

    7.6  Image History & Inspection
         - docker image history easypj:v1 (show layers)
         - docker image inspect easypj:v1 (JSON metadata)
         - Understanding image IDs and digests
         - Image signing and verification (Docker Content Trust)
         [OUTPUT EXAMPLES: history and inspect with annotations]


         [TERMINAL: reading an image's autopsy — drawn]
            $ docker history easypj:v1.1
            IMAGE     CREATED BY                                SIZE
            3f9a12bc  CMD ["gunicorn" "easypj.wsgi:applicat…    0B
            <missing> COPY . . # buildkit                      612kB
            <missing> RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r req…   50MB
            <missing> FROM python:3.11-slim                    130MB
            $ docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Env}}' easypj:v1.1
            $ docker inspect -f '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' easypj:v1.1
         🎯 GOAL: Audit any image you did NOT build: where its size comes
            from, what env it injects, and which digest it really is.
         [TECH] history walks layers newest-first: CREATED BY shows each
            instruction, SIZE its cost — the 50 MB pip layer is where
            Chapter 8 aims. <missing> is cosmetic (parent layer IDs not
            stored locally). inspect exposes Config (Env, Cmd, User,
            ExposedPorts) and RepoDigests — the sha256 identity from 2.1.
            Docker Content Trust (DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1) adds signature
            verification on pull for publishers that sign.
         [ANALOGY] history is a geological core sample — every layer's
            thickness on display; inspect is the lab report on the same
            rock: composition, provenance, fingerprint.
         🔬 easypj: before basing on any community image, history it — a
            surprise `curl … | sh` layer or a bloated 400 MB RUN is
            visible in seconds, BEFORE it ever runs on your machine.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: history easypj:v1.1 and rank its three
            fattest layers. Verify: your ranking names pip install and
            the base image first — exactly the targets Chapter 8 attacks.
         📊 SUMMARY: history = per-layer cost and origin; inspect = full
            metadata + digest; audit before you trust.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: history's CREATED BY proves 5.7's warning — any
            ARG/ENV secret consumed by a RUN is readable here forever.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how the local image store actually stores things
      Every image is really three things glued together by digests,
      never by name: a MANIFEST (lists layer digests + the config
      digest), a CONFIG (the JSON `docker inspect` prints — Env, Cmd,
      User...), and the LAYERS themselves (each a tarball, content-
      addressed by its own sha256). Tags are just human labels in a
      small local index pointing at a manifest digest — that index is
      ALL `docker tag` ever edits. `docker rmi` deletes an index entry;
      the layer BYTES only leave disk when the last manifest
      referencing them, across every tag AND every image, is gone —
      which is why ten easypj tags sharing one `FROM python:3.11-slim`
      layer cost that layer's bytes exactly ONCE (7.1's SIZE gotcha,
      explained).
       ┌────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐     ┌───────────────────┐
       │ TAG (name)      │────▶│ MANIFEST         │────▶│ LAYERS (sha256)   │
       │ easypj:v1.1     │     │ digest sha256:.. │     │ shared across ALL │
       │ just a pointer  │     │ + CONFIG digest  │     │ tags that need    │
       │ in local index  │     │ (env/cmd/user)   │     │ that exact layer  │
       └────────────────┘     └─────────────────┘     └───────────────────┘
      retagging rewrites the left box only; deleting an image walks
      right-to-left and only frees a layer when NOTHING points at it.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      ✅ `docker images`/`image ls` read the local index; filters and
        --format turn it into a queryable, scriptable list (7.1).
      ✅ A tag is a free-to-create, free-to-delete pointer; the IMAGE
        ID (and the bytes behind it) is the only real identity (7.2).
      ✅ push/pull move manifests + missing layers; the printed DIGEST
        is the deploy-safe identifier — tags can move, digests can't (7.3).
      ✅ save/load preserve the whole image (layers+tags+config);
        export/import flatten a container's filesystem and lose CMD/
        ENV entirely (7.4).
      ✅ The cleanup ladder is ordered by blast radius: prune (dangling
        only) → prune -a (all unused) → system prune -a --volumes
        (everything) — `docker system df` shows which rung you need (7.5).
      ✅ `docker history` ranks a layer's SIZE and origin instruction;
        `docker inspect` exposes Config + RepoDigests — audit any image
        you did not build with both before trusting it (7.6).
      🎯 DCA relevance: tagging semantics, push/pull/digest behavior,
        and prune/rmi reference rules are classic graded items here.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS (consolidated)
      • SIZE in `docker images` double-counts shared layers — trust
        `docker system df`'s RECLAIMABLE column, not mental arithmetic.
      • `docker rmi <ID>` with multiple tags present either refuses or
        (-f) nukes every tag at once — untag by NAME, delete by ID only
        once one name remains.
      • "denied: requested access" on push is almost always a missing
        registry NAMESPACE in the tag, not a bad password.
      • `docker load` overwrites an existing tag on the target host with
        zero confirmation — diff `docker images` before/after on any
        host you don't fully control.
      • `docker save easypj` with no tag silently bundles EVERY easypj
        tag into one tarball.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      ⚡ `docker rmi $(docker images -f dangling=true -q)` — kill every
        ghost in one line (7.1's filter feeds 7.5's cleanup directly).
      ⚡ `docker inspect -f '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' easypj:v1.1` —
        grab a pinnable digest without parsing JSON by hand.
      ⚡ Pipe `docker save … | gzip` in one command instead of saving
        then compressing separately — one less multi-GB temp file.

    🔑 COMMANDS TO REMEMBER
      docker images --filter "dangling=true"      # find ghost images
      docker tag SRC DST                          # free re-name, same ID
      docker push/pull registry/repo:tag          # move; note the DIGEST
      docker save -o f.tar IMAGE / docker load -i f.tar  # full image, offline
      docker image prune / prune -a               # dangling / all unused
      docker system df                            # honest disk accounting
      docker history IMAGE                        # layer-by-layer cost
      docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Env}}' IMAGE   # audit injected env

    🧪 DRILL (5 min): rebuild easypj:v1 once (touch any file first), then
      in order run `docker images -f dangling=true`, tag the new build
      both `latest` and with a registry prefix, then `docker system df`.
      Done when you can point at the dangling ghost, name all three tags
      sharing its predecessor's ID, and quote the RECLAIMABLE number.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 7)

      Q1: `docker images` shows easypj:v1.0 and easypj:v1.1 both at
          ~181 MB. Does deleting easypj:v1.0 free ~181 MB?
      A1: Almost never — no, not if the two images share layers.
      Explanation: SIZE is per-tag, but layers are shared (7.1's
      gotcha). `docker rmi easypj:v1.0` only frees layers v1.1 does NOT
      also reference — typically just the small COPY . . layer that
      changed; the shared python:3.11-slim base survives untouched.
      Check `docker system df`'s RECLAIMABLE column for the real
      number, not the listed SIZE.

      Q2: After `docker tag easypj:v1.1 easypj:latest`, how many images
          exist on disk, and how many names?
      A2: One image, two names.
      Explanation: `docker tag` never copies bytes — it adds a second
      pointer to the same IMAGE ID (7.2). `docker images` prints two
      ROWS with the same IMAGE ID column; that repeated ID is the proof.
             ┌─ easypj:v1.1
      ID ────┤
             └─ easypj:latest        (same bytes, zero extra MB)

      Q3: `docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.1` fails with "denied:
          requested access to the resource is denied." You are logged
          in correctly. What's the first thing to check?
      A3: The NAMESPACE in the image name, not your credentials.
      Explanation: this error almost always means the repo path
      (`you/easypj`) doesn't match your logged-in account/org, or the
      repo doesn't exist yet on that registry (7.3) — a bad password
      produces a different (401 unauthorized) error.

      Q4: Why should a deploy script pull by DIGEST
          (`ghcr.io/you/easypj@sha256:...`) instead of by tag?
      A4: Because tags are mutable pointers and digests are not.
      Explanation: another `tag`/push can silently repoint
      `easypj:v1.1` at different bytes tomorrow; the digest printed at
      push time (7.3) always resolves to the exact manifest that was
      tested — it is content-addressed, not name-addressed.

      Q5: What's the difference between `docker save` and `docker
          export` for moving easypj to an air-gapped server?
      A5: save moves the IMAGE (layers+tags+config); export moves only
          a flattened CONTAINER filesystem with no CMD/ENV.
      Explanation (7.4):
          | pair            | keeps layers+tags? | keeps CMD? |
          | save → load     | yes                 | yes        |
          | export → import | flattened           | no         |
      An exported-then-imported easypj would need CMD supplied manually
      on every `docker run` — it forgot how to start itself.

      Q6: You run `docker load -i easypj-v1.1.tar.gz` on a server that
          already has an image tagged `easypj:v1.1`. What happens?
      A6: The existing `easypj:v1.1` tag is silently overwritten — no
          confirmation prompt.
      Explanation: this is 7.4's most dangerous gotcha. Always run
      `docker images` before AND after `load` on any shared or
      production host, especially in scripted deploy pipelines.

      Q7: `docker system df` reports Images: TOTAL 23, RECLAIMABLE
          7.1GB (72%). You run `docker image prune` (no -a). Roughly
          how much of that 7.1GB comes back?
      A7: Only the DANGLING portion — likely much less than 7.1GB.
      Explanation: plain `prune` removes only <none> images (7.1's
      ghosts); `prune -a` is required to reclaim images that are merely
      unused-by-a-container but still tagged. Re-run `docker system df`
      after each rung of the ladder (7.5) to see the real delta.

      Q8: On a CI runner you rely on `--cache-from` to speed up builds.
          A teammate runs `docker system prune -a` to "clean up disk."
          What breaks?
      A8: The next build goes fully cold — the cache-from source images
          were exactly what "unused" prune -a just deleted.
      Explanation (7.5's gotcha): CI hosts should prune surgically
      (dangling only, or age-based) rather than blanket `prune -a`,
      because "unused by a running container" and "needed as a cache
      source" are different things prune cannot distinguish.

      Q9: `docker history easypj:v1.1` shows a layer `<missing>` next
          to `RUN pip install ...`. Is the image broken?
      A9: No — `<missing>` is cosmetic.
      Explanation (7.6): it means the PARENT layer's full ID isn't
      stored locally (common after a pull, or once BuildKit collapses
      intermediate IDs) — the layer's SIZE and CREATED BY stay accurate
      and usable for the size audit Chapter 8 depends on.

      Q10: You need to know whether a downloaded community image
           injects a suspicious environment variable before running it.
           Which single command answers that, with zero risk?
      A10: `docker inspect -f '{{.Config.Env}}' <image>`.
      Explanation: `inspect` reads the CONFIG digest (7.6's diagram)
      without ever starting a container — a completely static, safe
      read of exactly what that image would set at runtime, which is
      the whole point of auditing BEFORE you trust it.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
       ┌────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────────┐
       │ LIST/  │─▶│ TAG     │─▶│ PUSH/PULL  │─▶│ SAVE/  │─▶│ PRUNE +    │
       │ FILTER │  │ (free,  │  │ (digest =  │  │ LOAD   │  │ HISTORY/   │
       │ (7.1)  │  │ same ID)│  │ truth,7.3) │  │ (7.4)  │  │ INSPECT    │
       └────────┘  └─────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────┘  └────────────┘
      .vs-prose — Chapter 7 is the full custody lifecycle of an image:
      find it (7.1), name it correctly (7.2), move it to and from a
      registry by a digest you can trust (7.3), carry it offline intact
      when there is no registry at all (7.4), then keep the local store
      honest with a graduated cleanup ladder and an auditable history
      (7.5-7.6). Nothing here changes what is INSIDE an image — that is
      Chapter 8's job; Chapter 7 only ever manages what already exists.


Chapter 8: Optimizing Docker Images — Smaller, Faster, Safer
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: easypj works — as an 850 MB image with 120
    CVEs. Every megabyte is pulled by every deploy, cached on every node
    and scanned by every audit; every package is attack surface. This
    chapter turns a working image into a professional one: right base,
    tight layers, scanned, and — where it fits — distroless. Problem
    solved here: "it runs, but it is fat, slow to ship, and indefensible."

    [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate → 🔴 Advanced (8.6) · ⏱️ ~70-90 min · 🎯 DCA:
      Image Creation, Management & Registry (20%) + Security (15%, 8.5-8.6)

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
      • Put a number on why size matters: pull time, CI bandwidth, and
        CVE count all scale with image weight (8.1).
      • Defend python:3.11-slim over alpine or full Debian for a Django
        app, citing the glibc-vs-musl wheel problem (8.2).
      • Chain and clean RUN instructions in the SAME layer, and explain
        why cleanup in a later layer never shrinks anything (8.3).
      • Apply Django-specific shrink techniques: --no-cache-dir, a
        multi-stage collectstatic, and a prod-only requirements split (8.4).
      • Read a `docker scout quickview` report and separate base-image
        findings from your own layer's findings (8.5).
      • State what distroless removes, why that kills most post-
        exploitation tooling, and what it costs at debug time (8.6).

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: base image choice, layer/cache mechanics, and
      image scanning are all named competencies inside Image Creation,
      Management & Registry (20%) and Security (15%) — Chapter 8 is
      where those two domains overlap hardest.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 8.1 why size matters → 8.2 pick the base → 8.3
      general layer discipline → 8.4 Django-specific application → 8.5
      scan what you built → 8.6 go all the way to distroless — each
      section removes more weight than the last.

    8.1  Why Image Size Matters
         - Smaller = faster push/pull (critical in CI/CD)
         - Smaller = less attack surface (fewer packages to exploit)
         - Smaller = less disk usage on nodes
         - Target: keep images under 200MB for production
         [SIZE COMPARISON GRAPH: easypj before vs after optimization]

         🎯 GOAL: Put numbers on "smaller is better" — pull time, disk,
            CVE count — so optimization is a budget, not an aesthetic.
         [TECH] Size taxes every stage: registry storage, network on each
            pull (CI pulls per job!), node disk, scanner runtime. Attack
            surface scales with PACKAGE COUNT more than bytes — every
            binary is a potential CVE. The 200 MB target is the point
            where a Django+gunicorn+psycopg2 image stops carrying
            anything it never executes.
         [ANALOGY] Airline baggage: every kilo flies on EVERY flight, and
            every extra item is one more thing security must screen. You
            pay per deploy, forever, for weight you packed once.
         [TABLE: what 850 MB vs 180 MB actually costs — drawn]
            | cost            | 850 MB single-stage | 180 MB optimized |
            | pull @ 10 Mbps  | ~11 min             | ~2.4 min         |
            | 20 CI runs/day  | ~17 GB pulled       | ~3.6 GB          |
            | CVE findings    | 120+                | 30-40            |
         🔬 easypj: a 3-line hotfix to jobpost/views.py should deploy in
            seconds; with an 850 MB image the fix waits on an 11-minute
            pull at the worst possible moment.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: docker images easypj + docker history (7.6)
            to find the two heaviest layers. Verify: you can name the
            exact instruction behind each — those are 8.2-8.4's targets.
         [DIAGRAM:layers — 850 MB vs 180 MB, stacked and to scale]
         ┌────────────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────────┐
         │ SINGLE-STAGE   850 MB      │   │ MULTI-STAGE    180 MB      │
         ├────────────────────────────┤   ├────────────────────────────┤
         │ python:3.11 (dev)  268 MB  │   │ python:3.11-slim   130 MB  │
         │ build tools         240 MB │   │ deps (wheels only)  38 MB  │
         │ deps (unpinned)     150 MB │   │ app code             12 MB │
         │ pip cache           180 MB │   │ — build tools: gone —      │
         │ app code             12 MB │   │ — pip cache: gone —        │
         └────────────────────────────┘   └────────────────────────────┘

         850 MB ██████████████████████████████████████████
         180 MB █████████
         easypj: single-stage prototype (850MB) shrinks to 9.7 (180MB).
         💡 The MB→CVE relationship above isn't coincidence: every extra
            package dragged in by a bigger base is one more binary 8.7's
            scanner can flag and one more thing to patch on every rebuild
            — size and audit burden grow together, not separately.

         📊 SUMMARY: size = a recurring tax on ship speed, disk and
            security; under 200 MB is the professional bar for easypj.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: optimizing the APP layer is pointless if the BASE
            is 700 MB — always attack the biggest layer first (8.2).

    8.2  Choosing the Right Base Image
         - Alpine (5MB): smallest but musl libc compatibility issues
         - Slim (40-80MB): Debian-based, good balance for Python
         - Full Debian/Ubuntu (100MB+): most compatible, largest
         - Distroless (20MB): Google's minimal, no shell, ultra-secure
         - Scratch (0MB): completely empty, for static binaries
         [TABLE: Base image comparison — size, compatibility, security, use case]

         [TABLE: base images for a Django app — drawn]
            | base         | size   | verdict for easypj                |
            | python:3.11  | ~268MB | dev toolbox — never ship          |
            | 3.11-slim    | ~130MB | ✅ THE choice: glibc + apt        |
            | 3.11-alpine  | ~50MB  | ⚠️ musl: psycopg2/wheel pain      |
            | distroless   | ~20MB  | 🔴 no shell — 8.6's endgame       |
            | scratch      | 0MB    | static binaries (Go) only — not   |
            |              |        | an option for CPython             |
         🎯 GOAL: Defend "python:3.11-slim" for easypj in one paragraph
            against both the alpine fans and the full-image comfort camp.
         [TECH] The axis is the C library: slim = Debian glibc, so PyPI's
            prebuilt manylinux wheels (psycopg2-binary, Pillow) install
            in seconds. Alpine = musl: many wheels don't apply, pip
            compiles from source — slower builds, subtle libc bugs, and
            the 100 MB you "saved" comes back as gcc in the build stage.
         [ANALOGY] Choosing a venue: full Debian is a furnished mansion
            (pay for rooms you never enter), slim a fitted studio, alpine
            a tiny cabin with NON-STANDARD sockets — half your appliances
            (wheels) need adapters (compilers).
         🔬 easypj: FROM python:3.11-slim + psycopg2-binary → a clean
            40 s install; the same on alpine wants gcc, musl-dev and
            postgresql-dev plus minutes of compiling — for a BIGGER
            effective image.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: time `pip install psycopg2-binary` inside
            python:3.11-slim vs python:3.11-alpine containers. Verify:
            slim installs a wheel in seconds; alpine attempts a source
            build (or fails wanting pg_config) — the table, proven.
         📊 SUMMARY: slim is the Django default: glibc wheels, small
            enough; alpine optimizes bytes at the cost of correctness.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the tag matters twice — 3.11-slim pins the PYTHON
            too; plain python:latest can silently jump interpreter
            versions between builds (2.5's lesson, again).

    8.3  Layer Optimization Techniques
         - Chain RUN commands: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
         - Clean up in same layer: pip cache, apt cache, temp files
         - COPY specific files, not entire directory
         - Use .dockerignore aggressively
         [BEFORE/AFTER DOCKERFILE: Optimized layer structure]

         [CODE: one RUN — install and clean in the same layer]
            RUN apt-get update \
             && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends libpq5 \
             && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
         🎯 GOAL: Make every layer pay rent: nothing installed in layer N
            and deleted in layer N+1, nothing copied that isn't needed.
         [TECH] Layers are additive: a file deleted in a LATER layer
            still ships inside the earlier one (a whiteout entry merely
            hides it), so cleanup only works in the SAME RUN.
            --no-install-recommends halves apt payloads; COPY of specific
            paths beats COPY . . where practical; .dockerignore (5.2) is
            layer optimization too — it shrinks what COPY can even see.
         [ANALOGY] Sedimentary rock: each layer fossilizes forever.
            Burying garbage under a new layer of soil does not remove
            it — the truck must leave DURING the same geological event.
         🔬 easypj: `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` followed by a
            separate `RUN rm -rf /root/.cache` shrinks NOTHING — the
            cache is fossilized in the pip layer; --no-cache-dir (or
            5.7's cache mount) is the correct move.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build one image installing a package and
            rm-ing it in a second RUN, and one doing both in a single
            RUN; compare docker images sizes. Verify: only the single-RUN
            variant got smaller — deletion across layers is a lie.
         📊 SUMMARY: clean in the layer that dirtied; chain related RUNs;
            copy precisely. Layers only ever grow.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: docker history shows a "0 B" layer for the late
            rm — the bytes did not leave, they just went invisible.

    8.4  Python/Django Specific Optimizations
         - Use --no-cache-dir with pip
         - Use slim image instead of full Debian
         - Multi-stage: collect static separately
         - Remove dev dependencies for production
         - Use .dockerignore for __pycache__, .git, env/
         [CODE: Optimized easypj Dockerfile with all techniques applied]

         [CHECKLIST: the Django shrink list — applied to easypj]
            [ ] FROM python:3.11-slim (8.2 — glibc wheels)
            [ ] pip install --no-cache-dir (or 5.7 cache mount)
            [ ] PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 — no .pyc in the image
            [ ] multi-stage: gcc & friends stay in the builder (4.5)
            [ ] collectstatic in builder; final stage gets /app/static
            [ ] prod requirements.txt: no pytest, no debug-toolbar
         🎯 GOAL: Apply every generic technique from 8.2-8.3 in its
            Django-specific form and land easypj under the 200 MB bar.
         [TECH] Split requirements into base/prod/dev files and install
            ONLY prod in the image — pytest, coverage and debug toolbars
            are dev-machine software. collectstatic belongs in the
            builder stage: the final image serves /app/static as plain
            files and never needs the toolchain that produced them.
            PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 is for logs (6.3), not size — but it
            rides the same ENV line.
         [ANALOGY] Touring vs rehearsal gear: the band rehearses with
            spare amps, cables and a sound engineer (dev deps, gcc); the
            tour bus (image) carries only what is played ON STAGE.
         🔬 easypj: dropping dev-only packages plus the multi-stage split
            is the 850 MB → ~180 MB story the 4.5 table promised —
            measured, not vibes.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build easypj with dev requirements, then with
            prod-only; compare docker images, then try
            `docker run --rm easypj:prod python -c "import pytest"`.
            Verify: tens of MB gone AND the import fails — proof the
            ballast (and its CVEs) left the ship.
         📊 SUMMARY: slim base, no pip cache, no bytecode, no dev deps,
            static collected in the builder — Django's 20% that cuts 80%.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: deleting psycopg2's system library goes too far —
            keep libpq5 in the FINAL stage or Django dies at first query.

    8.5  Image Scanning — Docker Scout
         - What is Docker Scout? (vulnerability scanning)
         - docker scout quickview easypj:v1
         - Understanding CVE reports
         - Fixing vulnerabilities: update base, update packages
         - docker scout recommendations
         [TERMINAL: Annotated scout output walkthrough]

         [TERMINAL: scout on easypj — drawn]
            $ docker scout quickview easypj:v1.1
              Target    easypj:v1.1       1C 2H  7M 25L
              Base      python:3.11-slim  0C 1H  5M 22L
            $ docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high easypj:v1.1
            $ docker scout recommendations easypj:v1.1
              ↳ update base image to 3.11-slim (newer point release)
         🎯 GOAL: Read a CVE report like an engineer: what is CRITICAL,
            what lives in YOUR layers vs the base, and what to fix first.
         [TECH] Scout matches the image's SBOM (every package + version)
            against CVE databases; severities run C/H/M/L. The quickview
            split above is the key diagnostic: findings on the BASE row
            are fixed by REBUILDING on a newer base (slim receives
            patches continuously); only the delta above it belongs to
            your requirements.txt. Zero CVEs is not the goal — zero
            UNREVIEWED criticals is.
         [ANALOGY] A building inspection: the report separates faults in
            the foundation you bought (base image) from the walls you
            built (pip layer). You don't re-pour the foundation yourself
            — you take the builder's newer revision.
         🔬 easypj: a Critical in Django lands in YOUR layer — bump the
            pin in requirements.txt and rebuild; a Critical in zlib is
            the base's — pull the fresh 3.11-slim and rebuild. Same
            command, different line changed.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the three commands above on easypj.
            Verify: you can state (a) the critical/high count, (b) the
            base vs your-layer split, (c) the single next action — in
            one minute flat.
         📊 SUMMARY: scan every release; read base vs own-layer findings
            differently; rebuild-on-newer-base is the cheapest patch.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: images do not rot visibly — an UNCHANGED easypj
            image gains CVEs as databases learn; rescan on a schedule,
            not only on rebuild.

    8.6  Distroless Images — The Ultimate Security
         - What is "distroless"? (no shell, no package manager, no utilities)
         - Why distroless? (no shell = attacker can't exec)
         - How to debug distroless containers (kubectl debug, ephemeral containers)
         - Distroless for Python/Go/Java
         [CODE: Distroless Dockerfile for easypj (multi-stage with distroless final)]


         🎯 GOAL: Say precisely what distroless removes, what that buys,
            and what it costs you at 3 AM — then decide for easypj.
         [TECH] Distroless bases (gcr.io/distroless/python3 family) ship
            ONLY a runtime: no shell, no package manager, no coreutils.
            docker exec -it … bash cannot work — there is no bash; most
            of an attacker's post-exploitation toolkit (sh, curl, apt)
            simply does not exist. Debugging shifts to docker cp, logs,
            or ephemeral debug containers ([KUBERNETES GUIDE] covers
            kubectl debug).
         [ANALOGY] A bank vault with no doorway: builders assembled it
            around the contents (multi-stage COPY in), so there is no
            door for burglars — or for the locksmith. You interact only
            through slots designed in advance (port 8000, stdout logs).
         🔬 easypj: multi-stage — the builder on python:3.11-slim does
            pip install + collectstatic; the final distroless stage
            copies site-packages and /app. The 4.7 entrypoint SCRIPT
            needs /bin/sh — distroless forces migrations OUT of startup
            (run them as a separate exec step or one-off container).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build the distroless variant, then try
            docker exec -it easypj-dl sh. Verify: "no such file or
            directory" — the missing shell IS the security feature, and
            docker logs still shows everything gunicorn says (6.3).
         📊 SUMMARY: distroless = runtime-only final stage: minimal CVE
            surface, no shell for attackers or for you; pay with harder
            debugging and no shell-based entrypoint scripts.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: HEALTHCHECK CMD curl … (6.7) breaks too — probe
            with `python -c "import urllib.request; …"` or move health
            probing to the orchestrator [KUBERNETES GUIDE].

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — why deleting in a later layer never shrinks the image
      The storage driver (overlay2, the Linux default) stacks each
      layer as a read-only directory; a container's writable top layer
      merges over all of them. When a LATER layer "deletes" a file that
      existed in an EARLIER layer, overlay2 doesn't erase anything — it
      writes a tiny WHITEOUT marker (a character device, `.wh.<name>`)
      that tells the merged view to HIDE that path. The original bytes
      stay exactly where they were, in the earlier read-only layer,
      forever part of the image you ship. This is precisely why 8.3's
      `RUN pip install ...` followed by a separate `RUN rm -rf
      /root/.cache` saves nothing: the cache is real bytes in layer N,
      and layer N+1 just adds a piece of paper saying "ignore that
      drawer."
       ┌─ layer N   (RUN pip install)   [pip cache: real bytes]        ─┐
       ┌─ layer N+1 (RUN rm -rf cache)  [.wh.cache marker, ~0B]        ─┤
       │  merged view: cache directory invisible — but still on disk   │
       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      the fix is always the SAME RUN: install-and-clean in one
      instruction, so the cache never gets fossilized in its own layer.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      ✅ Size is a recurring tax, not a one-time cost: it multiplies by
        every pull, every CI job, every node — 850MB vs 180MB is an
        11-min vs 2.4-min pull at 10 Mbps (8.1).
      ✅ python:3.11-slim is the Django default: glibc means prebuilt
        manylinux wheels install in seconds; alpine's musl libc forces
        slow, fragile source builds for the same packages (8.2).
      ✅ Layers only ever grow — cleanup MUST happen in the same RUN
        that created the mess, or the bytes are fossilized (8.3).
      ✅ Django's specific 20%: slim base + --no-cache-dir + no .pyc +
        multi-stage collectstatic + prod-only requirements = the
        850MB → ~180MB result, measured not assumed (8.4).
      ✅ `docker scout quickview` splits findings into BASE (fixed by
        rebuilding on a newer base) vs YOUR LAYER (fixed by bumping
        your own pins) — read the split, don't just count CVEs (8.5).
      ✅ Distroless removes the shell and package manager entirely — a
        huge attack-surface win, but it also removes shell-based
        entrypoints and shell-based HEALTHCHECKs (8.6).
      🎯 DCA relevance: expect items on WHY a smaller image is
        preferred and on distinguishing build-time vs runtime
        dependencies — both are graded, not just "best practice."

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS (consolidated)
      • Optimizing the app layer is wasted effort if the BASE image is
        700MB — always attack the biggest layer first (docker history).
      • Alpine's "savings" often come back as gcc/musl-dev needed just
        to compile a wheel that slim gets prebuilt — measure the WHOLE
        build, not just the final base size.
      • Deleting libpq5 to save space in the final stage breaks Django
        at the first database query — psycopg2 needs it at runtime.
      • distroless has no shell: a HEALTHCHECK CMD using curl, or a
        shell ENTRYPOINT script, silently cannot run.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      ⚡ `docker history <image> | head -5` right after any build — the
        two heaviest rows tell you exactly where 8.2-8.4 apply next.
      ⚡ Keep separate requirements/base.txt, requirements/prod.txt,
        requirements/dev.txt from day one — a prod-only build is then
        one `-r requirements/prod.txt` away, no editing required.

    🔑 COMMANDS TO REMEMBER
      docker history <image>                       # find the fat layers
      docker scout quickview <image>                # CVE count, base split
      docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high <image>
      docker scout recommendations <image>          # suggested next fix
      docker images <repo>                          # confirm size after a fix
      docker run --rm <image> python -c "import pytest"  # prove dev deps gone

    🧪 DRILL (10 min): pick any image you built in Part 2, run `docker
      history` on it, name its two heaviest layers, then apply ONE
      technique from 8.2-8.4 and rebuild. Done when `docker images`
      shows a measurably smaller SIZE for the same functionality.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 8)

      Q1: An easypj image is 850MB. A teammate says "that's fine, disk
          is cheap." What's wrong with that argument?
      A1: Disk is only one of four costs — pull time, CI bandwidth, and
          CVE count also scale with size, and none of those are "cheap."
      Explanation (8.1):
          | cost           | 850MB single-stage | 180MB optimized |
          | pull @ 10Mbps  | ~11 min             | ~2.4 min         |
          | 20 CI runs/day | ~17 GB pulled       | ~3.6 GB          |
          | CVE findings   | 120+                | 30-40            |
      The size tax is paid on EVERY deploy, forever — not once at build.

      Q2: Why is python:3.11-slim preferred over python:3.11-alpine for
          easypj, even though alpine is smaller?
      A2: slim uses glibc (Debian), so psycopg2-binary and other
          manylinux wheels install as prebuilt binaries in seconds;
          alpine's musl libc often forces a slow source compile (or
          fails outright without extra build tools).
      Explanation (8.2): the "savings" from alpine's smaller base are
      frequently erased by needing gcc/musl-dev/postgresql-dev in the
      build stage — smaller base, bigger real cost.

      Q3: `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt` in layer 3, followed by
          `RUN rm -rf /root/.cache/pip` in layer 4 — does layer 4
          shrink the final image?
      A3: No — zero bytes recovered.
      Explanation (8.3): overlay filesystems are additive; a later
      layer can only HIDE a file with a whiteout marker, not remove its
      bytes from an already-committed earlier layer. `docker history`
      even shows layer 4 as "0B" — the cache never left, it just became
      invisible in the merged view.

      Q4: Name three Django-specific edits (8.4) that helped shrink
          easypj from 850MB to ~180MB, beyond just changing the base
          image.
      A4: Any three of: --no-cache-dir on pip install; splitting
          requirements into base/prod/dev and installing prod-only;
          running collectstatic in a builder stage (not the final
          image); setting PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1.
      Explanation: each is small alone, but 8.4's checklist stacks all
      of them onto the base-image win from 8.2 for the full result.

      Q5: `docker scout quickview easypj:v1.1` shows `Target 1C 2H 7M
          25L` and `Base 0C 1H 5M 22L`. Where should you look first to
          fix the 1 Critical?
      A5: In YOUR layers, not the base — the base row shows 0 Criticals.
      Explanation (8.5): quickview's two-row split is the diagnostic —
      findings that appear on Target but NOT on Base came from your own
      requirements.txt or code; bump the offending package pin and
      rebuild, rather than chasing the base image.
             Target: 1C 2H  7M 25L   ← includes your own layer
             Base:   0C 1H  5M 22L   ← subtract this to isolate yours

      Q6: An easypj image hasn't been rebuilt in two months, yet a scan
          today shows 15 new CVEs it didn't have at build time. Did the
          image change?
      A6: No — the image is byte-identical; the CVE DATABASE learned
          about new vulnerabilities in the same old packages.
      Explanation (8.5's gotcha): images don't rot by changing, but
      they do rot in the sense of being scanned against an ever-growing
      database — rescanning on a SCHEDULE (not only on rebuild) is the
      only way to catch this.

      Q7: What exactly does "distroless" remove compared to
          python:3.11-slim, and why does that matter for security?
      A7: No shell, no package manager, no coreutils — only the Python
          runtime and your app.
      Explanation (8.6): `docker exec -it <container> bash` cannot work
      because there is no bash; most post-exploitation tooling (sh,
      curl, apt, wget) an attacker would reach for simply does not
      exist in the image at all.

      Q8: Why can't easypj's normal `docker-entrypoint.sh` (which waits
          for the DB, runs migrate, then execs gunicorn) be used
          unmodified in the distroless final stage?
      A8: Because it's a shell script, and distroless has no /bin/sh to
          interpret it.
      Explanation (8.6): the migration/wait logic has to move out of a
      shell entrypoint and into a separate step (a one-off container on
      the builder-stage base, or an exec-form startup distroless CAN
      run) before the final distroless stage can be used.

      Q9: A HEALTHCHECK using `curl -f http://localhost:8000/` worked
          fine on python:3.11-slim. It silently fails after switching to
          distroless. Why?
      A9: distroless has no curl (no shell, no coreutils, no utilities).
      Explanation (8.6's gotcha): the fix is a probe distroless CAN run
      natively — `python -c "import urllib.request; ..."` — or moving
      health probing to the orchestrator entirely ([KUBERNETES GUIDE]).

      Q10: Rank these four techniques by expected size impact for
           easypj, biggest first: (a) --no-cache-dir, (b) slim vs full
           Debian base, (c) multi-stage collectstatic, (d) removing
           dev-only requirements.
      A10: Roughly (b) > (d) ≈ (c) > (a) — the base image swap is the
           single biggest lever (8.1's diagram: 268MB → 130MB before
           anything else changes); dropping dev requirements and moving
           collectstatic out of the final stage are next biggest;
           --no-cache-dir alone saves real but comparatively smaller MBs.
      Explanation: this ordering is exactly why 8.1's gotcha insists on
      attacking the BIGGEST layer first — order of operations matters.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
       ┌──────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  ┌─────────┐  ┌────────────┐
       │ WHY SIZE │─▶│ PICK BASE │─▶│ LAYER +      │─▶│ SCAN    │─▶│ DISTROLESS │

      .vs-prose — Chapter 8 turns a working easypj image into a
      professional one: 8.1 justifies the effort in real pull-time and
      CVE numbers, 8.2 fixes the single biggest lever (the base image),
      8.3-8.4 apply general and Django-specific layer discipline to
      shrink what's left, 8.5 proves the result with a scan you can
      read (base vs your-layer), and 8.6 offers the ceiling —
      distroless — for teams willing to trade shell-based debugging for
      the smallest possible attack surface. Chapter 9 now takes this
      exact toolkit and spends it on easypj, start to finish.

    9.1  Project Structure Review
         - easypj/ (Django project root)
         - jobpost/ (Django app — models, views, urls, admin)
         - Models: Skills, Author, Location, JobPost (with User FK)
         - Dependencies: Django 5.2, gunicorn, psycopg2-binary
         [DIRECTORY TREE DIAGRAM: Full easypj project structure]

         [DIAGRAM:architecture — the easypj tree, container's-eye view]
            easypj/
            ├── manage.py           ← exec target for migrations (6.4)
            ├── requirements.txt    ← COPYed FIRST (cache layer, 4.4)
            ├── Dockerfile          ← this chapter's artifact
            ├── .dockerignore       ← gatekeeper of the context (5.2)
            ├── easypj/             ← settings.py, wsgi.py (gunicorn's
            │                         entry: easypj.wsgi:application)
            └── jobpost/            ← models.py: Skills, Author,
                                      Location, JobPost (FK → User)
         🎯 GOAL: Map every file the container story touches to the
            chapter that consumes it — before writing a single line.
         [TECH] What matters to Docker: requirements.txt pins Django 5.2,
            gunicorn and psycopg2-binary (PostgreSQL is the only database
            in this guide — settings.py reads DB_HOST/DB_NAME/DB_USER/
            DB_PASSWORD from the environment, 12-factor style). wsgi.py
            exposes `application` — the exact dotted path gunicorn's CMD
            names. The database itself is NOT in this tree: it runs as a
            separate container (Part 4 formalizes that).
         [ANALOGY] An architect's site survey: before pouring concrete
            (building images) you mark what exists — load-bearing walls
            (wsgi.py, requirements.txt) vs furniture (everything
            .dockerignore will keep out of the truck).
         🔬 easypj: jobpost/models.py holds Skills, Author, Location and
            JobPost — migrate (via 4.7's entrypoint or 6.4's exec) is
            what turns those classes into PostgreSQL tables at startup.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: in your checkout run `python -c "import
            easypj.wsgi"` and open requirements.txt. Verify: the import
            succeeds and the file pins Django, gunicorn, psycopg2-binary
            — the three names the Dockerfile is about to depend on.
         📊 SUMMARY: know the tree, the wsgi path and the env-driven DB
            settings before Docker enters; the database lives in its own
            container, always.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: hardcoded DB credentials in settings.py sink the
            whole chapter — the container gets its database address from
            the ENVIRONMENT or it is not portable.

    9.2  Writing the Dockerfile
         - Complete Dockerfile for easypj (production-ready)
         - Line-by-line explanation of each instruction
         - Why each choice was made (python:3.11-slim, gunicorn, etc.)
         [DOCKERFILE CODE with extensive annotations]

         🎯 GOAL: Assemble the production Dockerfile from decisions
            already won — and cite the chapter behind every single line.
         [TECH] The file is 4.4's skeleton hardened by 4.6: slim base
            pinned (8.2), requirements-first COPY (5.3), --no-cache-dir
            (8.4), a created appuser + USER before CMD, exec-form
            gunicorn CMD (4.3), EXPOSE 8000 as documentation (4.2).
            Nothing here is new — that is the point: production files
            are arguments you can replay, not folklore you copy.
         [ANALOGY] A chess game's annotated score sheet: every move
            written WITH the reason it was played; a reviewer replays
            the reasoning, not just the moves.
         [CODE: the two lines beginners miss — drawn]
            RUN adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" appuser \
             && chown -R appuser:appuser /app
            USER appuser       # everything after this runs unprivileged
         🔬 easypj: with USER appuser, a hijacked Django process cannot
            apt-get, cannot write outside /app, cannot bind port 80 —
            three attack chapters closed by one line.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build, then `docker run --rm easypj:v1.0
            whoami` and `docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 id -u`.
            Verify: appuser and a non-zero UID — root is gone from
            runtime.
         📊 SUMMARY: every line is a chapter's conclusion: base (8.2),
            order (5.3), cleanup (8.3), USER (4.6), exec CMD (4.3).
            ⚠️ Gotcha: set USER BEFORE CMD but AFTER installs — flip the
            order and pip fails on permissions, or worse, you ship root.

    9.3  Writing .dockerignore
         - Complete .dockerignore for Django projects
         - Why each entry is excluded
         [.dockerignore CODE with annotations]

         🎯 GOAL: Ship the 5.2 ignore file with easypj and prove it does
            its three jobs: speed, cache stability, secret hygiene.
         [TECH] Same entries as 5.2 (.git, __pycache__, env/, .env,
            media/, the Dockerfile itself); the Django-specific stakes:
            env/ would ship a wrong-platform interpreter, .env would
            fossilize SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD into a pullable layer,
            media/ belongs in a volume (Part 6), and host __pycache__ is
            stale bytecode that can shadow fresh code.
         [ANALOGY] The bouncer's list at the build's door — written once,
            enforced identically on every build, no judgment calls at
            2 AM.
         🔬 easypj: the .env next to manage.py holds DB_PASSWORD for
            local runs — precisely why it must NEVER enter the image;
            the container receives it at RUN time (--env-file, 3.5).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker build . 2>&1 | grep "transferring
            context"` before and after adding the file, then
            `docker run --rm easypj:v1.0 ls -a /app`.
            Verify: context shrinks to ~1 MB; no .env, env/ or .git
            inside the image's /app.
         📊 SUMMARY: one dotfile, three protections; copy it into every
            Django repo you ever containerize.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: .dockerignore lives in the CONTEXT ROOT (next to
            the dot in docker build .) — one directory off and it is
            silently ignored, with zero warnings.
