    11.6 Development Workflow with Docker Compose
         - Hot reload with volume mounts (.:/app)
         - docker compose watch (auto-sync + rebuild on changes)
         - Debugging inside compose: docker compose exec
         - Running tests: docker compose run django python manage.py test
         [WORKFLOW DIAGRAM: Edit code → Compose watches → Auto-reload → Test]


         🎯 GOAL: Edit models.py on the host and see the change live in
            the container without rebuilding anything.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — the dev loop, drawn]
            edit jobpost/views.py ─▶ bind mount .:/app ─▶ dev server sees
            the change ─▶ auto-restart ─▶ refresh browser ─▶ repeat
         [TECH] Two hot-reload routes: (a) volumes: [".:/app"] plus a
            reloading server — file changes cross the mount instantly;
            (b) docker compose watch, whose develop.watch actions are
            sync (copy files in), rebuild (Dockerfile/deps changed) and
            sync+restart (config changed). Details in 12.5.
         [ANALOGY] A bind mount is a serving hatch between your editor and
            the container's kitchen: dishes pass through instantly; watch
            is a waiter who also rebuilds the kitchen when the OVEN
            (Dockerfile) itself changes.
         🔬 easypj: the dev override runs command: python manage.py
            runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 with .:/app mounted; tests run one-shot
            in a clean container:
            docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: change a string in a jobpost view, save,
            refresh the page. Verify: visible with NO rebuild; then check
            the test command above exits 0 and leaves nothing behind
            (--rm) in docker ps -a.
         📊 SUMMARY: bind mount + reloading server for code; compose watch
            when you also want rebuild-on-change; run --rm for tests.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: gunicorn does NOT reload by default — dev uses
            runserver or gunicorn --reload; forgetting this makes people
            "fix" it by rebuilding images all day.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — why POSTGRES_PASSWORD only matters on the FIRST boot
      The official postgres image's entrypoint script checks whether
      PGDATA (the volume mount, /var/lib/postgresql/data) already
      contains a data directory. Only on an EMPTY volume does it run
      initdb and consume POSTGRES_DB/POSTGRES_USER/POSTGRES_PASSWORD to
      create the role and database; on every later boot it just starts
      postgres against the existing files and ignores those variables.

         postgres_data volume EMPTY?
              │
              ├─ yes ─▶ entrypoint runs initdb ─▶ creates role/db from
              │          POSTGRES_* env vars ─▶ writes data files
              │
              └─ no ──▶ entrypoint SKIPS initdb ─▶ starts postgres
                         directly against existing files ─▶ POSTGRES_*
                         vars ignored entirely

      This is exactly why 11.2's gotcha holds: the credential now lives
      INSIDE the volume's data files, not in the environment — changing
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env after the first boot changes nothing
      until you either drop the volume (losing all data) or connect
      with psql and run ALTER ROLE yourself.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      - Plan first: build for django, pull for postgres/redis/nginx;
        only postgres gets a persistent volume (postgres_data).
      - postgres/redis stay backend-only; only nginx exposes a host
        port (80) — the frontend/backend network split from 11.1.
      - condition: service_healthy + pg_isready is what makes django
        wait for a database that can actually answer, not just exist.
      - POSTGRES_* env vars are read once, only when the data volume
        is empty — never assume changing .env changes a live database.
      - .env feeds two distinct mechanisms: ${} interpolation into
        compose.yaml, and env_file injection into the container.
      - The daily verb set is up -d / ps / exec ... migrate / logs -f —
        four commands cover cold start through verification.
      - down -v deletes named volumes too; that's the whole difference
        between "restart the stack" and "drop the database."

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
      - Exposing postgres or redis with ports: "for convenience" —
        backend-internal is the default posture from 11.1's plan.
      - Expecting a changed POSTGRES_PASSWORD to take effect on an
        existing volume — it won't, without a volume reset or ALTER ROLE.
      - Editing nginx.conf on the host and expecting nginx to reload it
        automatically — needs `nginx -s reload` or a service restart.
      - Relying on gunicorn's default behavior for hot reload in dev —
        it does not reload; use runserver or gunicorn --reload instead.
      - Running `down -v` when you meant plain `down` — the extra flag
        silently takes the database with it.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      - `docker compose exec postgres psql -U easypj easypj_db` then
        `\dt` for a 10-second schema sanity check.
      - `docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost`
        for a clean, disposable test run that leaves nothing in
        `docker ps -a`.
      - Compare `docker compose logs nginx` against `logs django` side
        by side to separate static-file hits from real app requests.

    🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 11 cheat-card
      docker compose up -d                                   # boot the full stack
      docker compose ps                                       # postgres healthy? 4 running?
      docker compose exec django python manage.py migrate     # apply jobpost's schema
      docker compose exec django python manage.py createsuperuser  # admin access
      docker compose logs -f django                            # confirm gunicorn is listening
      docker compose exec postgres psql -U easypj easypj_db    # \dt to see jobpost tables
      docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost  # one-shot, self-cleaning tests
      docker compose down -v                                    # DANGER: also deletes volumes

    🧪 DRILL — 10 minutes, cold start
      From a clean clone: `docker compose up -d`, then migrate,
      createsuperuser, and curl both `/jobs/` and
      `/static/admin/css/base.css`. Verify: `docker compose ps` shows
      postgres as healthy and all 4 services running BEFORE you open a
      browser — reading the health column first is the habit this
      chapter is training.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 11)

      Q1: For each of easypj's 4 services, is it built or pulled, does
          it get a persistent volume, and which network(s) is it on?
      A: | Service  | Image source        | Volume?              | Networks           |
         | django   | build: .            | no (stateless)       | backend, frontend  |
         | postgres | image: postgres:15  | yes (postgres_data)  | backend only       |
         | redis    | image: redis:7-alpine | no                 | backend only       |
         | nginx    | image: nginx:alpine | no (mounts static:ro)| frontend only      |
      Explanation: this table IS 11.1's planning diagram in tabular
         form — decide these three columns before writing any YAML.

      Q2: Why does postgres get a pg_isready healthcheck, and what does
          condition: service_healthy change about django's startup?
      A: pg_isready confirms postgres can actually accept connections,
         not just that the process exists; service_healthy makes
         django's depends_on wait for that healthy state instead of
         merely "container started" — closing 10.4's gotcha for real.
      Explanation: straight from 11.2's TECH/ANALOGY pairing.

      Q3: What is the gunicorn command 11.2 uses to serve easypj, and
          why does it bind 0.0.0.0 instead of 127.0.0.1?
      A: `gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000
         --workers 3`; binding 0.0.0.0 is required so the process
         accepts connections arriving from OTHER containers (nginx),
         not only from inside its own process.
      Explanation: 11.3's nginx upstream depends on this bind address.

      Q4: In nginx.conf, what does `server django:8000;` resolve to,
          and why does it work without an IP address?
      A: it resolves via Compose's embedded DNS to whichever container
         is currently named "django" on the frontend network — the
         service name is the hostname, so nginx never hardcodes an IP.
      Explanation: this reuses Chapter 10's (10.4) DNS-hostname
         takeaway on a real config file.

      Q5: Draw the request path for a browser hitting
          http://localhost/jobs/ versus /static/admin/css/base.css.
      A:
            /jobs/  ──▶ nginx :80 ──▶ proxy_pass ──▶ django:8000
                                                   (appears in django's logs)
            /static/... ──▶ nginx :80 ──▶ alias /static/ (served from the
                                        `static` volume — ONLY in nginx's logs)
      Explanation: 11.3's PRACTICE step verifies exactly this split by
         comparing `docker compose logs nginx` vs `logs django`.

      Q6: Name Redis's two jobs in easypj and the two logical databases
          they use.
      A: Django cache backend at redis://redis:6379/1 and the Celery
         message broker at redis://redis:6379/0 — one container, two
         DB indexes, no persistence needed for either.
      Explanation: from 11.3's easypj example.

      Q7: What are the two distinct mechanisms .env feeds in Compose,
          and which one carries SECRET_KEY to Django?
      A: (1) ${VAR} interpolation substituted into compose.yaml at
         parse time, and (2) env_file: injecting variables into the
         container at runtime; SECRET_KEY travels via env_file into the
         container environment, read by os.environ["SECRET_KEY"] — it
         never appears in compose.yaml itself.
      Explanation: 11.4's TECH block names both mechanisms explicitly.

      Q8: List the six commands of a cold-start verification, in
          order, and what each one proves.
      A: up -d (build+create+start) -> ps (postgres healthy, 4 running)
         -> exec migrate (schema applied) -> exec createsuperuser
         (admin access exists) -> logs -f django (gunicorn listening)
         -> curl -I /jobs/ (200 OK end to end).
      Explanation: this is 11.5's full TERMINAL sequence.

      Q9: You run `docker compose down` then `up -d` again — does your
          superuser survive? What if you'd run `down -v` instead?
      A: Plain down keeps volumes, so postgres_data (and your
         superuser row) survives intact; down -v deletes named volumes
         too, wiping postgres_data and the database with it.
      Explanation: 11.5's closing gotcha, verified by its own PRACTICE
         step.

      Q10: What's the difference between the two hot-reload routes in
           11.6, and which one also handles a changed requirements.txt?
      A: a bind mount (.:/app) plus a reloading dev server (runserver)
         syncs code instantly but does nothing for dependency changes;
         `docker compose watch`'s develop.watch can also `rebuild` when
         requirements.txt or the Dockerfile changes — the bind-mount
         route cannot.
      Explanation: 11.6's TECH block names both routes and defers the
         full watch mechanics to 12.5.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
         ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Chapter 11, in one picture                                  │

         │   🐍 django (build)  ──▶ 🐘 postgres (healthy, volume)         │

      .vs-prose — Chapter 11 turned Chapter 10's grammar into easypj's
      actual stack: a healthcheck-gated django+postgres core (11.2),

Chapter 12: Docker Compose Advanced Features
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: One compose.yaml now has three masters — your
    laptop, CI, and something production-like — and they disagree about
    ports, mounts and debug flags. This chapter adds the machinery that
    keeps ONE source of truth serving all three: profiles, override files,
    health-gated ordering, watch, and scaling. Problem solved here: "I keep
    editing compose.yaml back and forth between dev and prod."

    [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~90 min · 🎯 DCA: Orchestration (25%)
    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
      - Use profiles to keep optional services (e.g. pgadmin) declared
        in compose.yaml but OUT of the default `up`
      - Split base/override/prod compose files and predict a merge
        result before running `docker compose config`
      - Explain the project's default network, DNS resolution, and
        internal: true isolation for backend-only services
      - Gate startup on real readiness with service_healthy healthchecks
        across all three tiers — postgres, redis, and django itself
      - Choose the right `compose watch` action (sync / rebuild /
        sync+restart) for a given kind of file change
      - Scale a stateless service with --scale and state precisely what
        Compose can and cannot do versus Swarm or Kubernetes
      - Debug any compose.yaml with `docker compose config`, reason
        about env-value precedence, and avoid the common YAML traps
    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: profiles, overrides, health-gated dependencies,
        watch and scaling are all graded under Orchestration (25%,
        Section 6.2) — this chapter is the "beyond the happy path"
        material the domain expects once fundamentals (Ch10) and a real
        stack (Ch11) are in place.
    [E] SECTION MAP: 12.1 profiles (conditional services) -> 12.2
        override files (dev/prod from one base) -> 12.3 networking
        deep dive (DNS + internal:) -> 12.4 depends_on + health checks
        (real readiness) -> 12.5 watch (hot reload) -> 12.6 scaling
        (--scale + its ceiling) -> 12.7 validating/debugging (config,
        precedence, YAML traps) — the file that survives dev, CI, prod.
    12.1 Compose Profiles — Environment-Specific Services
         - What are profiles? (conditional service inclusion)
         - dev profile, prod profile, debug profile
         - docker compose --profile dev up
         [CODE: compose.yaml with profiles]

         🎯 GOAL: Keep optional services (pgadmin, mailhog, celery-beat)
            declared in the file but OUT of the default `up`.
         [TECH] profiles: ["debug"] tags a service; untagged services
            always run, tagged ones only with --profile debug (or the
            COMPOSE_PROFILES env var). One file, N shapes — no copy-paste
            forks of the yaml.
         [CODE: a profile-tagged service — drawn]
              pgadmin:
                image: dpage/pgadmin4
                ports: ["127.0.0.1:5050:80"]
                profiles: ["debug"]
                networks: [backend]
         [ANALOGY] Theatre lighting presets: every lamp is wired
            (declared), but the "rehearsal" preset powers only some.
            --profile picks the preset; the wiring never changes.
         🔬 easypj: pgadmin under profile debug — daily `up` boots 4
            services; `docker compose --profile debug up -d` adds the DB
            GUI on :5050 when you need to eyeball jobpost rows.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: tag pgadmin as above, run plain `up -d`, then
            again with --profile debug. Verify: compose ps shows 4 then 5
            services — and plain `down` needs the profile to remove it.
         📊 SUMMARY: profiles = conditional membership in the stack; one
            file serves dev/debug/prod shapes.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: depends_on a profiled service from an unprofiled
            one and default `up` fails — dependencies must share profiles.

    12.2 Compose Overrides — Multiple Compose Files
         - docker-compose.yml (base)
         - docker-compose.override.yml (dev overrides)
         - docker-compose.prod.yml (production settings)
         - Merging: docker compose -f base.yml -f prod.yml up
         [CODE: 3 compose files with merge explanation]

         🎯 GOAL: Run dev and prod from the SAME base file with two small
            deltas — and predict the merged result before running it.
         [TECH] `docker compose up` auto-loads compose.yaml PLUS
            compose.override.yaml. Explicit -f lists load left→right,
            later files winning per key: scalars replace, maps merge,
            lists (ports, volumes) merge/replace per spec — always confirm
            with `docker compose config`.
         [CODE: the three-file layout — drawn]
            compose.yaml           # base: services, networks, volumes
            compose.override.yaml  # dev: mount .:/app, runserver,
                                   #      DEBUG=True, ports 8000:8000
            compose.prod.yaml      # prod: gunicorn, restart: always,
                                   #      no source mount, no 8000 exposed
            $ docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d
         [ANALOGY] The base file is the house blueprint; overrides are
            transparent sheets laid on top — dev's sheet draws a workbench
            in the living room, prod's sheet bolts the doors. The bottom
            blueprint never changes.
         🔬 easypj: dev override swaps command to runserver and mounts the
            source; the prod file swaps in the gunicorn command and drops
            the mount so the image's COPY'd code is what actually runs.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `docker compose config` twice — once bare,
            once with -f base -f prod. Verify: command, volumes and ports
            differ exactly where the sheets said they would.
         📊 SUMMARY: base + override(s), later file wins; the merged truth
            is whatever compose config prints.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the dev override loads AUTOMATICALLY — on a server,
            forgetting -f can deploy runserver with DEBUG=True.

    12.3 Compose Networking Deep Dive
         - Default network: auto-created, services reachable by name
         - Custom networks: isolation between service groups
         - Network drivers: bridge, host, overlay, none
         - DNS resolution: service name → container IP

         [COMPOSE NETWORKING DIAGRAM — 4 Services Connected]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                 🌐 DOCKER COMPOSE NETWORKING                              │
         │                                                                          │
         │  Network: easypj_default (auto-created by compose)                       │
         │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
         │  │                                                                     │  │
         │  │  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐       │  │
         │  │  │   nginx      │────▶│   django     │────▶│  postgres    │       │  │
         │  │  │  (port 80)   │     │  (port 8000) │     │  (port 5432) │       │  │
         │  │  │              │     │              │     │              │       │  │
         │  │  │  DNS: nginx  │     │  DNS: django │     │ DNS: postgres│       │  │
         │  │  │  PortMap:    │     │  PortMap:    │     │  PortMap:    │       │  │
         │  │  │  80:80       │     │  (internal)  │     │  (internal)  │       │  │
         │  │  └──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘     └──────┬───────┘       │  │
         │  │         │                   │                     │                │  │
         │  │         │    ┌──────────────┘                     │                │  │
         │  │         │    │                                    │                │  │
         │  │         │    │  django can: docker exec django    │                │  │
         │  │         │    │  ping postgres  → resolves! ✅     │                │  │
         │  │         │    │  (compose DNS = service name)      │                │  │
         │  │         │    │                                    │                │  │
         │  │         ▼    ▼                                    │                │  │
         │  │  ┌──────────────┐                                 │                │  │
         │  │  │    redis     │◀────────────────────────────────┘                │  │
         │  │  │  (port 6379) │   django can: docker exec django                  │  │
         │  │  │              │   redis-cli -h redis ping  → PONG ✅              │  │
         │  │  │  DNS: redis  │                                                  │  │
         │  │  └──────────────┘                                                  │  │
         │  │                                                                     │  │
         │  │  EXTERNAL: curl http://localhost:80 → nginx → django                │  │
         │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
         │                                                                          │
         │  💡 Each service can reach any other service by its SERVICE NAME!        │
         │     Compose creates a DNS network automatically. No IPs to remember.     │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Explain every arrow in the compose networking diagram
            above in terms of DNS names, never IPs.
         [TECH] Compose creates <project>_default and attaches every
            service unless you declare networks:. The embedded DNS server
            (127.0.0.11) maps service names → container IPs; a service on
            TWO networks answers on both. internal: true networks get no
            route out of the host — the DB-isolation pattern.
         [ANALOGY] The diagram above is what compose gives you by DEFAULT
            when no networks: key is declared at all: one open-plan room
            where everyone answers to their NAME and can walk to anyone
            else's desk. easypj never actually ships this flat layout —
            Chapter 11's frontend/backend split (11.1-11.3) already built
            the walls: postgres sits in a windowless back office only
            django has a door to; `internal: true` (TECH, above) is what
            removes that office's street exit too. Chapter 14 goes one
            layer deeper into the network model that makes those walls
            work.
         🔬 easypj: django reaches postgres:5432 and redis:6379 by name in
            the diagram; only nginx carries a PortMap (80:80) — everything
            else stays internal exactly as drawn.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker compose exec django ping -c1 postgres`
            then `docker network inspect easypj_default`. Verify: ping's
            reported IP matches postgres in the inspect output.
         📊 SUMMARY: service name = DNS record on the project network;
            custom networks are the isolation tool, port maps the only
            doors to the host.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: container-to-container traffic uses CONTAINER ports
            (django:8000), never host-mapped ones — and localhost inside a
            container is that container, not your laptop.

    12.4 depends_on with Health Checks
         - Problem: depends_on only waits for container START, not READINESS
         - Solution: depends_on with condition: service_healthy
         - Writing health checks for PostgreSQL, Redis, Django
         [CODE: Health check configurations + depends_on with condition]

         🎯 GOAL: Make "started" and "ready" two different words in your
            stack — and gate startup on the second one.
         [TECH] depends_on alone = wait until the container process
            EXISTS. condition: service_healthy = wait until the service's
            own healthcheck passes. Health states: starting → healthy /
            unhealthy — visible in compose ps and docker inspect.
         [CODE: health checks for all three tiers — drawn]
            postgres: test: ["CMD-SHELL","pg_isready -U easypj -d easypj_db"]
            redis:    test: ["CMD","redis-cli","ping"]           # → PONG
            django:   test: ["CMD-SHELL","curl -fs localhost:8000 || exit 1"]
            # each with: interval: 5s, timeout: 3s, retries: 5
         [ANALOGY] A container that started but isn't ready is a shop with
            the lights on and the till not counted. The healthcheck is the
            OPEN sign the shopkeeper flips — service_healthy means "queue
            outside until the sign flips".
         🔬 easypj: without the gate, gunicorn boots first and Django's
            first query hits a postgres still running initdb → connection
            refused → crash loop. With pg_isready gating, cold starts are
            boring — which is the goal.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: remove the condition, `docker compose down &&
            docker compose up -d`, read django's logs; restore it, repeat.
            Verify: crash + restart in run one, clean single boot in two.
         💡 Two more healthcheck fields matter for slow-booting
            services: start_period gives a grace window where failures
            don't count toward retries — useful while django runs
            `migrate` before its own healthcheck can pass. start_interval
            sets a FASTER probe cadence during that same window, so the
            grace period doesn't cost a full `interval` per attempt.
            disable: true turns off a HEALTHCHECK baked into a base
            image without forking the Dockerfile.

         📊 SUMMARY: healthchecks define ready; service_healthy makes
            dependents wait for it.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the healthcheck command runs INSIDE the container —
            curl/pg_isready must exist in that image, or the check fails
            forever and the stack never starts.

    12.5 docker compose watch — Hot Reload
         - Sync: Copy changed files into container
         - Rebuild: Rebuild image when Dockerfile changes
         - Restart: Restart container when config changes
         [CODE: compose.yaml with watch configuration]

         🎯 GOAL: Choose the right watch action — sync, rebuild, or
            sync+restart — for each kind of file easypj changes.
         [CODE: develop.watch for the django service — drawn]
              django:
                develop:
                  watch:
                    - action: sync            # .py, templates → copy in
                      path: .
                      target: /app
                      ignore: [".git/", "*.pyc"]
                    - action: rebuild         # deps changed → new image
                      path: requirements.txt
                    - action: sync+restart    # config → restart process
                      path: easypj/settings.py
                      target: /app/easypj/settings.py
         [TECH] `docker compose watch` runs alongside up: sync copies
            changed files into the RUNNING container (no bind mount
            required); rebuild triggers build + container replacement;
            sync+restart bounces the service after copying.
         [ANALOGY] Three severities of edits to a play mid-run: sync =
            slip the actor a corrected line; sync+restart = redo the
            scene; rebuild = new script, restage the whole play.
         🔬 easypj: views.py edits sync in a blink; touching
            requirements.txt correctly forces the pip-layer rebuild from
            2.4 — watch knows the difference so you don't have to.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `docker compose watch`, edit a jobpost
            template, then add a package to requirements.txt. Verify: the
            first logs "Syncing", the second logs "Rebuilding".
         📊 SUMMARY: watch = a file-event router: sync for code, rebuild
            for deps, sync+restart for config.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: synced files land in the container's writable layer
            — a rebuild discards them; your disk copy (the source of the
            sync) is the only durable one, by design.

    12.6 Scaling Services with Compose
         - docker compose up --scale django=3
         - Load balancing with Nginx
         - Limitations: all on one host (for multi-host, use K8s/Swarm)
         [DIAGRAM: 3 Django containers behind Nginx on single host]

         🎯 GOAL: Run three gunicorn containers behind one nginx and know
            exactly what Compose scaling can and cannot do.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — --scale django=3, drawn]
                          ┌────────────────────┐
               :80 ──────▶│  nginx (1)         │
                          │  upstream easypj   │
                          └──┬──────┬──────┬───┘
                 DNS "django"│      │      │  round-robin
                        ┌────▼─┐ ┌──▼───┐ ┌▼─────┐
                        │ dj-1 │ │ dj-2 │ │ dj-3 │  easypj-django-{1,2,3}
                        │:8000 │ │:8000 │ │:8000 │  no ports: published!
                        └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘
         [TECH] `docker compose up -d --scale django=3` creates N replicas
            of one service. Compose DNS returns all three IPs for
            "django"; nginx resolves and spreads requests. REQUIREMENT:
            a scaled service cannot publish a fixed host port — three
            containers cannot share 8000:8000.
         [ANALOGY] One reception desk (nginx), three clerks (replicas):
            callers dial one NAME and the switchboard (compose DNS) picks
            a clerk. Hiring clerk #4 is one flag, not new YAML.
         🔬 easypj: stateless Django (sessions in redis, uploads in
            volumes, rows in postgres) is WHY scaling works — replica 2
            can answer a request that replica 1 started.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: remove django's ports:, scale to 3, curl
            localhost/jobs/ six times, then read
            `docker compose logs django | grep GET`. Verify: the hits
            spread across django-1/2/3.
         [TABLE: scaling ceiling — Compose vs Swarm vs Kubernetes]
         | Dimension      | Compose       | Swarm           | K8s         |
         | Max hosts      | 1 (this host) | N (swarm nodes) | N (cluster) |
         | Scale command  | --scale svc=3 | service scale   | kubectl/HPA |
         | Auto-scaling   | none, manual  | none, manual    | HPA (auto)  |
         | Failed replica | stays dead    | rescheduled     | rescheduled |
         | Cross-host LB  | n/a (1 host)  | routing mesh    | Service/LB  |
         easypj's `--scale django=3` above IS the entire Compose row — the
         other two columns are what Part 10 (Swarm) and the Kubernetes
         guide add once one host stops being enough.

         💡 Compose has no scheduler at all — `--scale` launches N
            containers once and stops; if host capacity runs out mid-scale
            the command just errors, unlike Swarm/K8s, which hold a
            desired-replica-count and keep retrying in the background.

         [TABLE: capping resources — two syntaxes for the same goal]
         | Need         | Plain attribute      | deploy: (Swarm, C.7)  |
         | Hard mem cap | mem_limit: 512m      | limits.memory: 512M   |
         | Soft mem tgt | mem_reservation:256m | reservations.memory   |
         | CPU share    | cpus: "0.50"         | limits.cpus: "0.50"   |
         easypj's django service can set `cpus: "1.00"` directly for a
         plain `docker compose up`; the deploy: block only takes effect
         under `docker stack deploy` (Swarm mode, C.7).

         📊 SUMMARY: --scale = N replicas on ONE host behind DNS
            round-robin; real multi-host scaling is Swarm (Part 10) or
            [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
            ⚠️ Gotcha: scaling with ports: "8000:8000" still set kills
            replica 2 with "port is already allocated" — 3.7's old friend.

    12.7 Validating & Debugging Compose Files
         - docker compose config: render the MERGED, interpolated truth
         - ${VAR:-default} and ${VAR:?error} interpolation syntax
         - Env precedence: shell > --env-file > .env > env_file > image ENV
         - Top YAML traps: tabs, unquoted ports, boolean strings
         - compose config --services / --volumes for quick sanity lists

         🎯 GOAL: Debug any "compose does something weird" in one move:
            render the merged truth and read what the engine actually saw.
         [TECH] `docker compose config` parses ALL -f files, applies
            override merging, resolves profiles and substitutes every
            ${VAR} — its output is the ONLY file the engine acts on.
            Interpolation grammar: ${VAR} (empty if unset), ${VAR:-8000}
            (default if unset/empty), ${VAR:?msg} (abort loudly if unset).
         [TABLE: env value precedence — highest wins]
            1 | shell env of the compose command  | export DEBUG=True
            2 | --env-file FILE flag              | --env-file .env.prod
            3 | .env beside compose.yaml          | POSTGRES_PASSWORD=…
            4 | env_file: inside the service      | runtime-only vars
            5 | ENV in the image's Dockerfile     | last-resort defaults
         [TABLE: top YAML traps — trap | what YAML does | fix]
            TAB indentation   | hard parse error       | spaces, always
            ports: [22:22]    | sexagesimal int 1342   | quote "22:22"
            DEBUG: false      | boolean, not string    | quote "false"
            COUNTRY: NO       | YAML 1.1 → false       | quote "NO"
         [ANALOGY] compose config is asking the pharmacist to print the
            FINAL prescription after every doctor's note was merged — you
            argue with that paper, not with the sticky notes (-f files).
         🔬 easypj: SECRET_KEY=${SECRET_KEY:?set it in .env} makes prod
            fail fast instead of running with an empty key, while
            PORT=${PORT:-8000} lets a fresh clone boot with zero setup.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: break the file on purpose — indent one line
            with a TAB, then unquote a port as 22:22. Run compose config
            after each. Verify: config names the tab's line number, and
            shows the port parsed into a number you never wrote.
         📊 SUMMARY: compose config = merged, interpolated, validated
            truth; ${VAR:-} for dev ergonomics, ${VAR:?} for prod safety.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: compose config prints RESOLVED secrets in plain
            text — pipe it to your eyes, never into a ticket or a commit.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how Compose actually MERGES multiple -f files
      `docker compose -f a.yml -f b.yml config` does not just
      concatenate the files — each YAML type merges by a different rule:
      scalars (strings/numbers/booleans) in a LATER file REPLACE the
      earlier value; maps (environment as key: value, labels) are
      merged key-by-key; sequences written as a plain YAML list
      (a service's `ports:` or `volumes:`) are REPLACED wholesale by a
      later file's list, not appended to it.

         compose.yaml:       command: gunicorn ...            (scalar)
         compose.prod.yaml:  command: gunicorn --workers 4    ← REPLACES
         ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         compose.yaml:       environment: {DEBUG: "True"}        (map)
         compose.override:   environment: {LOG_LEVEL: info}   ← MERGES
         result:              {DEBUG: "True", LOG_LEVEL: info}
         ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
         compose.yaml:       ports: ["8000:8000"]               (list)
         compose.prod.yaml:  ports: []                        ← REPLACES
         result:              ports: []   (nothing published at all)

      This is exactly why 12.7's rule — "always confirm with docker
      compose config" — is not optional caution. It is the only way to
      know which merge rule applied to a given key without memorizing
      the entire compose-spec merge algorithm.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      - profiles = conditional stack membership; untagged services
        always run, tagged ones need --profile (or COMPOSE_PROFILES).
      - compose.override.yaml auto-loads; explicit -f lists load
        left-to-right, later files winning per the merge rules above.
      - the project's default network gives every service DNS-by-name;
        internal: true removes any route out of the host entirely.
      - started != healthy; service_healthy gates real readiness across
        all three tiers — postgres, redis, and django's own healthcheck.
      - watch routes: sync (code), rebuild (deps/Dockerfile changed),
        sync+restart (config changed) — three severities, one tool.
      - --scale needs a stateless service with NO fixed host port;
        Compose scaling is single-host, manual, with no self-healing.
      - `docker compose config` is the one command that prints what the
        engine will actually run — the final word in any dispute.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
      - depends_on crossing a profile boundary — an unprofiled service
        depending on a profiled one breaks the default `up`.
      - compose.override.yaml loading automatically on a server —
        forgetting -f can deploy dev settings (runserver, DEBUG=True).
      - a healthcheck command that doesn't exist INSIDE the image
        (curl, pg_isready) — the check fails forever, stack never starts.
      - scaling a service that still has a fixed `ports:` mapping set —
        replica 2 dies with "port is already allocated."
      - unquoted YAML values (ports: 22:22, DEBUG: false, COUNTRY: NO)
        silently reinterpreted as numbers or booleans.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
      - `docker compose config --services` / `--volumes` for a quick
        sanity list without reading the whole merged file.
      - `${VAR:?msg}` on any secret that must never silently boot empty
        in production.
      - `docker compose ps` (health column) to read a service's actual
        health state instead of guessing from raw logs.

    🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 12 cheat-card
      docker compose --profile debug up -d                          # include profiled services
      docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d     # explicit merge, prod
      docker compose config                                          # merged, interpolated truth
      docker compose config --services                              # quick service sanity list
      docker compose up -d --scale django=3                          # N replicas, one host
      docker compose watch                                           # sync/rebuild/sync+restart loop
      docker compose ps                                              # health column, per-service

    🧪 DRILL — 10 minutes
      Tag one service `profiles: ["debug"]`, run plain `up -d` then
      `--profile debug up -d`, and note the service count change in
      `compose ps`. Then run `docker compose config` once bare and once
      with `-f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml`. Verify: you can name
      every line that changed and WHY (scalar replace, map merge, or
      list replace) before reading the diff.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 12)

      Q1: pgadmin is tagged `profiles: ["debug"]`. What does plain
          `docker compose up -d` do, and what changes with --profile
          debug?
      A: plain up boots the 4 untagged services only; adding
         --profile debug brings pgadmin in as a 5th — `compose ps`
         shows 4 services, then 5.
      Explanation: 12.1's easypj example, verified by its own PRACTICE
         step.

      Q2: Fill in the env-value precedence table, highest wins first.
      A: | 1 | shell env of the compose command | export DEBUG=True |
         | 2 | --env-file FILE flag              | --env-file .env.prod |
         | 3 | .env beside compose.yaml          | POSTGRES_PASSWORD=… |
         | 4 | env_file: inside the service      | runtime-only vars |
         | 5 | ENV in the image's Dockerfile     | last-resort defaults |
      Explanation: straight from 12.7's precedence table.

      Q3: The base file's override sets `command: runserver`; the prod
          file swaps to gunicorn and drops the source mount. Which
          command runs under `-f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up`?
      A: gunicorn — later -f files win on scalar keys like `command:`,
         and compose.prod.yaml is listed last.
      Explanation: 12.2's three-file layout example.

      Q4: What's the difference between a network with no `internal:`
          flag and one with `internal: true`?
      A: a default network still lets its services reach the internet
         (and, via published ports, the host); `internal: true` removes
         ALL outside routing — services on it can only reach each
         other, matching postgres/redis's backend-isolation pattern.
      Explanation: 12.3's TECH/ANALOGY pairing on custom networks.

      Q5: Write the three healthcheck commands used for postgres,
          redis, and django respectively.
      A: postgres: `pg_isready -U easypj -d easypj_db`; redis:
         `redis-cli ping` (expects PONG); django:
         `curl -fs localhost:8000 || exit 1`.
      Explanation: 12.4's per-tier healthcheck block.

      Q6: Draw the watch decision path for (a) editing a template,
          (b) adding a pip package, (c) editing settings.py.
      A:
            template edit          ──▶ action: sync         ──▶ copied in instantly
            requirements.txt edit  ──▶ action: rebuild       ──▶ new image built
            settings.py edit       ──▶ action: sync+restart  ──▶ copied + process restarted
      Explanation: 12.5's develop.watch example for the django service.

      Q7: Why does scaling django to 3 replicas REQUIRE removing its
          `ports: "8000:8000"` line first?
      A: three containers cannot all bind the same host port; a scaled
         service must rely on the internal network plus nginx's
         DNS-based upstream instead of a fixed host port mapping.
      Explanation: 12.6's scaling diagram and closing gotcha.

      Q8: Per 12.6's scaling-ceiling table, what happens to a failed
          replica under Compose versus Swarm/Kubernetes?
      A: Compose: the replica "stays dead," no rescheduling; Swarm/K8s:
         the replica is automatically rescheduled to restore the
         desired count.
      Explanation: this is the exact row-by-row contrast in 12.6's
         [TABLE: scaling ceiling].

      Q9: What's the difference between `${VAR:-8000}` and
          `${VAR:?msg}`, and which one should guard SECRET_KEY in prod?
      A: `:-default` substitutes a default when VAR is unset/empty
         (dev ergonomics); `:?msg` aborts `up` loudly with msg when VAR
         is unset — SECRET_KEY should use `:?msg` so prod never boots
         with a blank key.
      Explanation: 12.7's interpolation grammar and easypj example.

      Q10: Name the three YAML traps from 12.7's table and the fix for
           each.
      A: TAB indentation (hard parse error) → use spaces, always;
         `ports: [22:22]` (parsed as a sexagesimal number) → quote
         "22:22"; `DEBUG: false` / `COUNTRY: NO` (YAML booleans) →
         quote them as strings, "false"/"NO".
      Explanation: 12.7's [TABLE: top YAML traps], reproduced exactly.

    [F] PART 4 KEY TAKEAWAYS
      - Compose turns N `docker run` commands into one declarative file
        plus one command, namespaced per project so stacks never collide.
      - easypj's real stack: django (build, stateless) + postgres
        (volume) + redis (no volume) + nginx (only published port),
        split across backend/frontend networks.
      - Healthchecks + service_healthy are what make depends_on mean
        "ready," not just "started" — the gap opened in Ch10 and closed
        by Ch12.
      - .env is the one place secrets live: ${} interpolation feeds
        compose.yaml, env_file feeds the running container.
      - Profiles + override files let ONE base file serve dev/debug/
        prod shapes without copy-paste forks of the YAML.
      - `docker compose config` is the final word on what any set of
        -f files, profiles, and env values actually resolve to.
      - Compose scaling (--scale) is single-host and manual; real
        multi-host scaling is Swarm (Part 10) or the Kubernetes bridge (Part 9).

    ⚠️ PART 4 GOTCHAS
      - Treating depends_on as a readiness gate without
        condition: service_healthy attached.
      - Running `down -v` when the intent was just to restart the
        stack — it deletes named volumes (and the database) too.
      - Publishing db/cache ports "for convenience" — backend-internal
        is Part 4's default posture, not an oversight to fix.
      - Letting compose.override.yaml auto-load on a server meant to
        run the explicit prod file (-f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml).

    ⚡ PART 4 SPEED TIPS
      - Run `docker compose config` before touching any "weird" stack —
        look at the resolved truth before touching anything else.
      - Alias `dc` to `docker compose` and read the health column in
        `compose ps` before ever opening a browser.
      - `docker compose logs -f <service>` beats grepping four separate
        `docker logs` streams by hand.

PART 5: DOCKER NETWORKING — HOW CONTAINERS COMMUNICATE                   🟡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    THINK BEFORE PART 5:
      What runs where?    → virtual cables & switches inside the Linux kernel.
      What talks to what? → container → veth → bridge → NAT → outside world.
      What breaks first?  → DNS — names don't resolve on the DEFAULT bridge.

    [PART 5 INTRO]
    Part 4 closed with a Compose stack that "just worked" — nginx found
    django, django found postgres, and nobody asked why. Part 5 opens that
    box. Every container easypj runs sits inside its own network
    namespace, deaf and mute to everything else, until Docker wires it
    onto a virtual network that has a name server sitting at 127.0.0.11.
    Chapter 13 teaches that wiring in the abstract (the CNM model, the
    five drivers, the docker0 bridge, embedded DNS); Chapter 14 spends
    that vocabulary on easypj specifically, building a real two-network
    topology on purpose instead of trusting Compose's defaults; Chapter 15
    covers everything that departs from the default path — host mode,
    real-LAN drivers, multi-host overlays — plus the debugging toolbox for
    when the wiring itself is the incident.

    What Part 5 unlocks: containers that FIND each other by name,
    containers that CANNOT reach each other when they shouldn't (postgres
    reachable only from django, never from nginx), and the confidence to
    read a `docker network inspect` or an `iptables -t nat -L` dump
    instead of restarting things and hoping.

    🧠 ANALOGY — Part 5 in one picture
    Docker networking is an office building wired one floor at a time.
    Chapter 13 installs the building's phone system in the abstract —
    extensions, a directory, an operator (CNM nouns, the five drivers,
    docker0, embedded DNS). Chapter 14 moves easypj's actual staff in: the
    receptionist (nginx) sits in the lobby, the account manager (django)
    carries a badge for both the lobby AND the vault floor, and the vault
    (postgres, redis) has no line to the street at all. Chapter 15 is the
    building's advanced systems — a private line straight to another
    office (host networking), a real street address for one office
    instead of a shared switchboard (macvlan/ipvlan), a pneumatic tube to
    sister buildings (overlay), and the phone company's own trace-the-wire
    kit for when a call won't connect (netshoot, iptables).

    Read the map as a sentence: Ch13 teaches what a Docker network IS,
    Ch14 spends that vocabulary designing easypj's OWN networks on
    purpose, and Ch15 covers everything that ISN'T the default bridge
    path — plus how to prove, with tools instead of guesses, which rung
    of the stack actually broke.

                     │
