Chapter 13: Docker Networking Fundamentals
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Compose "just worked" — nginx found django,
    django found postgres — and you deserve to know why. This chapter opens
    the hood: the CNM model, the five drivers, the docker0 bridge and the
    embedded DNS server. Problem solved here: "containers talk to each
    other and I'm treating it as magic I can't debug."

    [A] META: 🟡 INTERMEDIATE  ·  ⏱️ ~75-90 min  ·  🎯 DCA DOMAIN: Networking
        (15% of the exam) — this chapter is CORE to that domain.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
         • Name the three CNM nouns (sandbox, endpoint, network) and point
           at each one inside a running container (13.1)
         • Pick the right network driver — bridge/host/none/overlay/
           macvlan-ipvlan — for a given use case (13.2)
         • Explain why the DEFAULT docker0 bridge has no name resolution
           while a user-defined bridge does (13.3)
         • Drive the full network lifecycle: create, connect, inspect,
           disconnect, rm, prune (13.4)
         • Trace a DNS lookup through the embedded 127.0.0.11 resolver and
           use --network-alias for extra names (13.5)
         • State in one sentence why --link is legacy and should never
           appear in new easypj configuration (13.5)

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: This chapter maps directly onto the DCA
        "Networking" domain (15% of the exam) — CNM vocabulary, driver
        selection and DNS behavior are graded competencies, not
        background theory.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 13.1 the model (CNM) → 13.2 the 5 drivers → 13.3 the
        default driver in depth (bridge) → 13.4 the command lifecycle →
        13.5 how names resolve (DNS) — each section hands the next one
        vocabulary it immediately reuses.

    13.1 How Docker Networking Works
         - Container Network Model (CNM)
         - Sandbox, Endpoint, Network
         - Network namespaces and virtual Ethernet pairs
         - docker0 bridge (default)
         [ARCHITECTURE DIAGRAM: CNM components]

         🎯 GOAL: Name the three CNM nouns — sandbox, endpoint, network —
            and point at each one inside a running container.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — CNM on one host, drawn]
            ┌──────────────────── HOST ────────────────────┐
            │                                              │
            │  SANDBOX C1 (netns)      ┌────────────────┐  │
            │  [eth0]══ENDPOINT═══════▶│                │  │
            │                          │    NETWORK     │  │
            │  SANDBOX C2 (netns)      │    (docker0)   │  │
            │  [eth0]══ENDPOINT═══════▶│                │  │
            │                          └───────┬────────┘  │
            │                                  ▼ NAT       │
            └──────────────────────────────────┼───────────┘
                                               ▼ outside world
         [TECH] Sandbox = the container's private network namespace (own
            interfaces, routes, port table). Endpoint = one veth pair: one
            end becomes eth0 INSIDE the sandbox, its twin plugs into a
            network. Network = a virtual switch that a libnetwork driver
            implements — docker0 by default.
         [ANALOGY] Hotel wiring: sandbox = the room's own wall sockets,
            endpoint = the cable from room to patch panel, network = the
            patch panel itself. The diagram is that wiring closet.
         🔬 easypj: `docker exec easypj-web ip addr` shows eth0@ifXX — the
            veth's inside end; `ip link` on the host shows its twin
            attached to the bridge.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run both commands above and match the ifXX
            index across host and container. Verify: the numbers pair up —
            you just traced one endpoint end to end.
         📊 SUMMARY: sandbox (namespace) + endpoint (veth pair) + network
            (bridge/driver) — every Docker network is these three nouns.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a container can hold MANY endpoints (one per
            network) but exactly ONE sandbox — multi-homed, never
            multi-brained.

    13.2 Network Drivers Overview
         - bridge: Default, containers on same host (docker0)
         - host: Container uses host's network directly (no isolation)
         - none: No networking (loopback only)
         - overlay: Multi-host Swarm networking
         - ipvlan/macvlan: Assign physical IP to container

         [DOCKER NETWORK DRIVERS — ARCHITECTURE COMPARISON]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                     🌐 5 NETWORK DRIVERS VISUALIZED                        │
         │                                                                          │
         │  1. BRIDGE (default)          2. HOST                  3. NONE            │
         │  ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐  │
         │  │ Host OS          │        │ Host OS          │     │ Host OS      │  │
         │  │ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  │        │ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  │     │ ┌──┐         │  │
         │  │ │C1│ │C2│ │C3│  │        │ │C1│ │C2│ │C3│  │     │ │C1│         │  │
         │  │ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘  │        │ │  shares host   │     │ │lo only│    │  │
         │  │  docker0 bridge │        │ │  network!      │     │ │       │    │  │
         │  │  (NAT to host)  │        │ └──────────────────┘     │ │127.0.0│    │  │
         │  │  -p 8080:80     │        │  ⚠️ No isolation         │ └──────────────┘  │
         │  └──────────────────┘        │  ✅ Max performance      │  🔒 Max security  │
         │                              └──────────────────┘                      │
         │  4. OVERLAY (Swarm)                             5. MACVLAN/IPVLAN       │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐   │
         │  │         overlay network (VXLAN)       │       │ Physical Network │   │
         │  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐        │       │ 192.168.1.0/24   │   │
         │  │  │ 🐝 Node 1 │    │ 🐝 Node 2 │        │       │ ┌──┐  ┌──┐      │   │
         │  │  │ ┌──┐┌──┐ │    │ ┌──┐┌──┐ │        │       │ │C1│  │C2│      │   │
         │  │  │ │C1││C2│ │◀═══▶│ │C3││C4│ │        │       │ │.5│  │.6│      │   │
         │  │  │ └──┘└──┘ │    │ └──┘└──┘ │        │       │ └──┘  └──┘      │   │
         │  │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘        │       │  Gets REAL IPs!  │   │
         │  │  Multi-host communication! ✅         │       └──────────────────┘   │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────┘                               │
         │                                                                          │
         │  [DRIVER SELECTION GUIDE]                                                │
         │  | Driver    | Isolation | Multi-Host | Performance | Use Case          │
         │  | bridge    | ✅ Good  | ❌ No      | 🟡 Medium   | Default, most apps │
         │  | host      | ❌ None  | ❌ No      | 🟢 Max      | High-perf, no isol.│
         │  | none      | ✅ Max   | ❌ No      | 🟢 N/A      | Security-sensitive │
         │  | overlay   | ✅ Good  | ✅ Yes     | 🟡 Medium   | Swarm clusters     │
         │  | macvlan   | ✅ Good  | ❌ No      | 🟢 High     │ Legacy apps, own IP│
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Pick the right driver from the 5-driver diagram above in
            one sentence per use case.
         [TECH] Drivers are libnetwork plugins answering one question:
            what does the endpoint plug INTO? bridge → virtual switch +
            NAT; host → nothing, share the host's stack; none → loopback
            only; overlay → a VXLAN tunnel spanning hosts; macvlan/ipvlan
            → the physical NIC itself, with real LAN addresses.
         [ANALOGY] Housing options for the same tenant: bridge = apartment
            with a shared front desk (NAT), host = living in the lobby,
            none = a bunker, overlay = sister buildings with a private
            skybridge, macvlan = your own street address. All five are
            drawn above — same containers, different walls.
         🔬 easypj: everything in Parts 4-5 runs on user-defined BRIDGE
            networks; overlay arrives when easypj meets Swarm (Part 10);
            host mode fits only a latency-obsessed metrics agent.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker network ls` on a fresh engine. Verify:
            exactly bridge, host and none exist — the other drivers appear
            only when YOU create networks with them.
         📊 SUMMARY: bridge (default, NAT), host (no isolation), none
            (absolute isolation), overlay (multi-host), macvlan/ipvlan
            (real LAN presence) — the selection table above is the recap.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: --network host silently IGNORES -p — there is
            nothing to map when there is no NAT layer.

    13.3 Bridge Networks — The Default
         - How bridge networking works
         - docker network create my-bridge
         - DNS resolution: container name → IP
         - Port mapping: -p 8080:80

         [BRIDGE NETWORK — DEEP DIVE]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                     🌉 BRIDGE NETWORK ARCHITECTURE                         │
         │                                                                          │
         │  EXTERNAL WORLD (Internet / LAN)                                         │
         │       │                                                                  │
         │       │  curl http://host:8080                                           │
         │       ▼                                                                  │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
         │  │                         HOST (192.168.1.100)                       │   │
         │  │                                                                   │   │
         │  │  ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────────────┐   │   │
         │  │  │  eth0 (physical) │         │       docker0 bridge          │   │   │
         │  │  │  192.168.1.100   │  NAT    │       172.17.0.1              │   │   │
         │  │  └────────┬─────────┘◀────────│                               │   │   │
         │  │           │                   │  -p 8080:80 → routes to C2:80│   │   │
         │  │           │                   │                               │   │   │
         │  │           │     ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐                │   │   │
         │  │           │     │             │             │                │   │   │
         │  │           │     ▼             ▼             ▼                │   │   │
         │  │           │  ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐               │   │   │
         │  │           │  │  C1  │    │  C2  │    │  C3  │               │   │   │
         │  │           │  │.0.2  │    │.0.3  │    │.0.4  │               │   │   │
         │  │           │  │ easypj│   │nginx │    │redis │               │   │   │
         │  │           │  │:8000 │    │:80   │    │:6379 │               │   │   │
         │  │           │  └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘               │   │   │
         │  │           │                                                  │   │   │
         │  │           │  ❌ C1 pings "nginx" by NAME → fails (no DNS here) │  │   │
         │  │           │  ✅ C1 pings 172.17.0.3 by IP → works (docker0 has │  │   │
         │  │           │     NO embedded DNS — that's only on user-defined  │  │   │
         │  │           │     bridges, see 13.4/13.5)                        │  │   │
         │  │           └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │   │
         │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Trace curl http://host:8080 through the bridge diagram
            above hop by hop — and explain both DNS lines at its bottom.
         [TECH] A user-defined bridge = a Linux bridge + a subnet + the
            embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11. The DEFAULT docker0 bridge LACKS
            that DNS: containers on it resolve nothing by name. Inbound:
            eth0:8080 → DNAT (the -p rule) → 172.17.0.3:80. Outbound:
            container → bridge → MASQUERADE → eth0 → world.
         [ANALOGY] The diagram is an office building: eth0 is the street
            entrance, docker0 the internal corridor, -p 8080:80 the sign
            "deliveries for suite 8080 go to room .0.3". DNS is the
            receptionist — and the DEFAULT corridor has no receptionist.
         🔬 easypj: `docker network create easypj-net`, then run postgres
            and easypj-web on it — settings.py can say HOST="postgres"
            precisely because a USER-DEFINED bridge has DNS.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run two alpines on the default bridge and ping
            by name (fails); repeat on a created network (works). Verify:
            both results — this is the single most-asked Docker
            networking interview question.
         📊 SUMMARY: bridge = switch + NAT; user-defined bridges add DNS
            and isolation — ALWAYS prefer them over docker0.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: containers on DIFFERENT bridges cannot talk at all
            — isolation is per-bridge, not per-host.

    13.4 docker network Commands
         - docker network ls (list networks)
         - docker network create (create network)
         - docker network inspect (view network details)
         - docker network connect (connect container)
         - docker network disconnect (disconnect)
         - docker network rm (remove network)
         - docker network prune (remove unused)
         [TERMINAL: All network commands with output examples]

         🎯 GOAL: Drive the whole network lifecycle — create, wire,
            inspect, unwire, destroy — with the commands below.
         [TERMINAL: full lifecycle, drawn]
            $ docker network create --driver bridge easypj-net
            $ docker network ls                  # bridge/host/none + yours
            $ docker run -d --name web --network easypj-net nginx
            $ docker network connect easypj-net some-running-container
            $ docker network inspect easypj-net  # subnet, gateway,
                                                 # "Containers": {…}
            $ docker network disconnect easypj-net web
            $ docker network rm easypj-net       # refuses if still in use
            $ docker network prune               # sweep unused networks
         [TECH] connect/disconnect operate on RUNNING containers — a new
            veth (eth1) appears inside, live. inspect is the map: subnet,
            gateway, and every attached container's IP and MAC.
         [ANALOGY] Patch-panel operations: create = mount a new panel,
            connect = plug a cable in, inspect = read the port labels,
            prune = rip out panels with no cables left in them.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: create easypj-net, connect a running alpine,
            run `ip addr` inside before and after. Verify: eth1 appears on
            connect and vanishes on disconnect — live rewiring, no
            restart.
         [DIAGRAM:state — network lifecycle, drawn]
            CREATED  (docker network create, 0 endpoints, no traffic)
               │  docker run --network=... / docker network connect
               ▼
            CONNECTED  (≥1 container attached, veth live, DNS active)
               │  docker network disconnect (or the last container exits)
               ▼
            DISCONNECTED  (0 endpoints again — same state as CREATED)
               │  docker network rm (refuses if any endpoint remains)
               ▼
            REMOVED  (object gone; docker network ls no longer lists it)
         ↺ CONNECTED can also loop straight back to CONNECTED — connect
           another container without passing through DISCONNECTED.
         easypj: `easypj-net` (13.3) cycles through all four states on
         every plain `docker compose down` followed by `up -d`.

         💡 Disconnecting a container from a network never stops it — it
            only removes that one interface (eth1, etc). A container only
            goes fully network-less if you disconnect its LAST network,
            and even DNS lookups inside it start failing at that point.

         📊 SUMMARY: ls/create/inspect/connect/disconnect/rm/prune — the
            complete verb set; inspect is your debugging home base.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: network rm refuses while ANY container is still
            attached ("active endpoints") — disconnect or remove the
            tenants first.

    13.5 Container DNS & Service Discovery
         - Built-in DNS server (127.0.0.11)
         - Container name resolution
         - --network-alias for multiple names
         - --link (legacy, avoid)
         [DIAGRAM: DNS resolution flow between containers]


         🎯 GOAL: Explain who answers when a container asks "who is
            postgres?" — and what --network-alias adds on top.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — one DNS lookup between containers, drawn]
            django asks "postgres" ─▶ /etc/resolv.conf → 127.0.0.11
              ─▶ embedded DNS (dockerd) ─▶ known name on THIS network?
                 ├─ yes ─▶ answer 172.20.0.3 (container IP)
                 └─ no  ─▶ forward to the host's upstream DNS
         [TECH] Every container on a user-defined network gets resolv.conf
            pointing at 127.0.0.11; dockerd answers for container names,
            compose service names and every --network-alias; unknown names
            are forwarded upstream. Aliases allow many names → one
            container, or one name → many containers (poor man's LB).
         [ANALOGY] The embedded DNS is the office receptionist: colleagues
            by first name (container names), departments by role
            (aliases), and unknown visitors get pointed to the city
            directory (upstream DNS).
         🔬 easypj: `--network-alias db` on postgres lets legacy config
            using HOST="db" and new config using HOST="postgres" both
            resolve to the same container.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker exec easypj-web cat /etc/resolv.conf`,
            then run nslookup postgres from inside. Verify: nameserver
            127.0.0.11, and an answer inside the network's subnet.
         📊 SUMMARY: 127.0.0.11 = dockerd's per-network phonebook; aliases
            add extra names; unknown names go upstream.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: --link is legacy and effectively dead — it predates
            user-defined networks; a tutorial using it is an OLD tutorial.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — why docker0 never got DNS
         docker0 is a Linux bridge device created once at dockerd startup;
         every container's veth peer attaches to it as a bridge port. A
         user-defined bridge is just ANOTHER Linux bridge created on
         demand by `docker network create`, but wired to a daemon
         subsystem docker0 was never retrofitted with: an embedded DNS
         process reachable at 127.0.0.11:53 inside every container's
         namespace (via an iptables DNAT rule dockerd installs
         per-container). docker0 predates that feature — Docker's
         earliest releases had exactly one flat bridge and no DNS to
         embed — and was left alone for backward compatibility while
         new bridges got name resolution on top. The DOCKER-ISOLATION
         iptables chains that block traffic between DIFFERENT bridges,
         by contrast, apply to EVERY bridge dockerd manages, docker0
         included — isolation was never a user-defined-only feature.

         dockerd starts
            │
            ├─▶ creates docker0 (Linux bridge) ── no DNS (legacy default)
            │                                      still isolated from
            │                                      every OTHER bridge
            └─▶ `docker network create X` ──▶ new bridge "br-xxxx"
                                               ├─ iptables DNAT:
                                               │  127.0.0.11:53 → embedded DNS
                                               └─ DOCKER-ISOLATION rule vs
                                                  every OTHER bridge
         Recap: it isn't that docker0 is "broken" — it only missed the
         DNS upgrade; per-bridge isolation has always applied to it too.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
         ✅ CNM = sandbox (netns) + endpoint (veth) + network (bridge or
            driver) — every Docker network is built from these three nouns.
         ✅ 5 drivers cover every case: bridge (default), host (no
            isolation), none (loopback only), overlay (multi-host),
            macvlan/ipvlan (real LAN IP).
         ✅ docker0 has NO embedded DNS — only user-defined bridges get
            127.0.0.11 name resolution.
         ✅ The full network lifecycle is create → connect → inspect →
            disconnect → rm, with `prune` sweeping anything at zero
            endpoints.
         ✅ `network connect`/`disconnect` operate on RUNNING containers
            live — no restart required.
         ✅ Container names, compose service names, and every
            --network-alias are ALL answered by the embedded DNS; unknown
            names are forwarded upstream.
         🎯 DCA relevance: driver selection and DNS behavior are directly
            graded exam competencies, not just background reading.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
         - --network host silently ignores -p — there is no NAT layer
           left for it to configure.
         - Containers on the default docker0 bridge cannot resolve each
           other by NAME — the single most common beginner "networking is
           broken" report.
         - `docker network rm` refuses while any container is still
           attached ("has active endpoints").
         - Containers on two DIFFERENT bridges cannot talk at all, even
           knowing each other's name — isolation is per-bridge, not
           per-host.
         - --link is legacy; any tutorial still using it predates
           user-defined networks entirely.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
         - `docker network inspect NET --format '{{json .Containers}}'`
           for a fast attached-container list without wading through the
           full JSON dump.
         - Default every `docker network create` to an explicit --subnet
           from day one — re-subnetting later means recreating the
           network from scratch.

    🔑 COMMANDS
         $ docker network ls                        # bridge/host/none + yours
         $ docker network create --driver bridge X   # new bridge network
         $ docker network inspect X                  # subnet, gateway, members
         $ docker network connect X container        # live-attach, running
         $ docker network disconnect X container     # live-detach, keeps running
         $ docker network rm X                       # fails if endpoints remain
         $ docker network prune                      # remove every unused net
         $ docker exec CONTAINER cat /etc/resolv.conf  # confirm 127.0.0.11

    🧪 DRILL (10 min): Create a user-defined bridge, run two alpine
         containers on it, ping one from the other BY NAME (works). Then
         run a THIRD alpine on the default bridge and try to ping either
         of the first two, by name and by IP (both fail). Verify: you can
         state in one sentence why the third container failed differently
         from a plain DNS miss.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 13)

         Q1: What are the three nouns of the Container Network Model
             (CNM), and what real object does each map to?
             A: Sandbox = the container's network namespace; Endpoint =
                one veth pair (one end becomes eth0 inside the sandbox);
                Network = the virtual switch a driver implements.
                SANDBOX (netns) ══ENDPOINT(veth)══▶ NETWORK (bridge/driver)
                one per container    one per network JOINED    one per docker network
             Explanation: this is 13.1's wiring-closet model — a
             container can hold many endpoints but exactly one sandbox.

         Q2: How would you prove, from the host AND from inside a
             container, that one specific veth pair connects them?
             A: Inside: `docker exec CONTAINER ip addr` shows
                `eth0@ifXX`. On the host: `ip link` lists a matching
                `vethXXXXX@ifYY` attached to the bridge — the ifXX/ifYY
                indices identify the two ends of the SAME pair.
             Explanation: this is exactly 13.1's PRACTICE lab — tracing
             one endpoint end to end.

         Q3: Which driver fits (a) a latency-critical metrics agent,
             (b) a 3-node Swarm cluster, (c) a legacy scanner needing a
             real LAN IP, (d) a security-sensitive container with no
             network at all?
             A: (a) host  (b) overlay  (c) macvlan  (d) none.
                | Driver  | Isolation | Multi-Host | Performance |
                | host    | None      | No         | Max         |
                | overlay | Good      | Yes        | Medium      |
                | macvlan | Good      | No         | High        |
                | none    | Max       | No         | N/A         |
             Explanation: the 13.2 selection table maps one dominant need
             to one driver each — memorize the mapping, not just the names.

         Q4: Two running containers both know each other's name, yet
             `ping other-container` fails with "bad address." Most likely
             cause and fix?
             A: Both are on the DEFAULT docker0 bridge, which has no
                embedded DNS. Fix: create a user-defined bridge and run
                both containers on it.
             Explanation: 13.3's single most-asked interview scenario.

         Q5: In one sentence each — what happens to (a) an inbound
             packet hitting a published port, and (b) an outbound packet
             leaving a container for the internet?
             A: (a) DNAT rewrites the destination from host:port to
                container-IP:port before routing. (b) MASQUERADE (SNAT)
                rewrites the container's source IP to the host's outbound
                IP so replies can find their way back.
             Explanation: 13.3's TECH block — the two halves of every
             bridge-network conversation with the outside world.

         Q6: List, in order, the four states a Docker network passes
             through from creation to deletion, and what drives each
             transition.
             A: CREATED ─(run --network / network connect)─▶ CONNECTED
                ─(disconnect, or last container exits)─▶ DISCONNECTED
                ─(network rm)─▶ REMOVED. CONNECTED can also loop straight
                back to CONNECTED by attaching another container.
             Explanation: 13.4's lifecycle diagram — `docker compose down`
             then `up -d` cycles easypj-net through all four states.

         Q7: If you disconnect a container from its ONLY remaining
             network, does the container stop? What actually breaks?
             A: No — it keeps running, fully network-isolated (loopback
                only); DNS lookups and outbound connections stop working
                until it's reconnected.
             Explanation: 13.4's 💡 callout — disconnecting never stops a
             container, it only removes an interface.

         Q8: Walk through what happens, step by step, when a container
             asks "who is postgres?"
             A: /etc/resolv.conf points at 127.0.0.11 → the embedded DNS
                (dockerd) checks its per-network table → if "postgres" is
                a known name on THIS network it answers with the
                container's IP; otherwise the query is forwarded upstream.
             Explanation: 13.5's DNS-lookup diagram, restated as prose.

         Q9: Give a concrete easypj example of --network-alias solving a
             real naming problem.
             A: `--network-alias db` on the postgres container lets old
                config expecting HOST="db" and new config using
                HOST="postgres" both resolve to the SAME container.
             Explanation: 13.5 — one container, two names, zero code
             changes.

         Q10: Why should a Docker tutorial that still uses --link be
              treated as outdated?
              A: --link predates user-defined networks and their embedded
                 DNS entirely; everything it did is now handled better,
                 and by default, by a user-defined bridge — its presence
                 is itself evidence the material is old.
              Explanation: 13.5's closing gotcha.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
         ┌──────────────────── CHAPTER 13 — THE WHOLE PICTURE ───────────────────┐
         │  CNM: SANDBOX(netns) ══ENDPOINT(veth)══▶ NETWORK (one of 5 drivers)   │
         │                                                │                     │
         │                       ┌────────────────────────┼───────────────┐     │
         │                       ▼                        ▼               ▼     │
         │              docker0 (default)        user-defined bridge   host/none/│
         │              NAT, NO DNS               NAT + DNS @127.0.0.11 overlay/ │
         │                                                │              macvlan │
         │                                  create→connect→inspect→disconnect→rm │
         │                                  (13.4 lifecycle — all of it, live)   │
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         .vs-prose — Every Docker network, regardless of which of the five
         drivers backs it, is built from the same three CNM nouns: a
         sandbox (the container's private namespace), an endpoint (the
         veth pair connecting it), and a network (the virtual switch a
         driver implements). The fork that causes the most beginner pain
         is docker0 vs a user-defined bridge — identical NAT behavior, but
         only the user-defined one wires up the embedded 127.0.0.11 DNS
         server that lets containers find each other by name. Every
         action on a network — create, connect, inspect, disconnect,
         remove — happens live, on running containers, which is exactly
         why Chapter 14 can wire and rewire easypj's topology without ever
         restarting the stack.


Chapter 14: Networking easypj Containers
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Theory becomes architecture here — Chapter
    13's bridges and DNS get applied to easypj on purpose: a backend
    network the internet can never reach, a frontend network nginx guards,
    and a database with NO published port. Problem solved here: "my stack
    works, but every service is one -p flag away from the public internet."

    [A] META: 🟡 INTERMEDIATE  ·  ⏱️ ~90-105 min  ·  🎯 DCA DOMAIN: Networking
        (15% of the exam) — applied/design chapter.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
         • Design a two-network topology that isolates postgres from
           nginx entirely, with django as the only dual-homed tier (14.1)
         • Create custom networks with explicit --subnet/--gateway
           instead of trusting auto-allocation (14.2)
         • Attach containers to one or two networks, at run time and
           live, and prove reachability with ping in both directions
           (14.3)
         • Explain precisely what EXPOSE does (metadata only) versus what
           -p does (a real DNAT rule) (14.4)
         • Choose the right publish syntax for a given exposure need —
           loopback-only, all-EXPOSEd, UDP, container-to-container (14.4)
         • Encode the entire two-network design as a compose.yaml
           networks: section, including internal: true (14.5)
         • Verify isolation from inside running containers with exec +
           ping, not just by reading the compose file (14.1-14.5)

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: A direct, hands-on application of the DCA
        "Networking" domain to a real multi-service stack — subnet
        planning, publish semantics and compose network placement all
        appear on the exam in this exact shape.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 14.1 design the two networks → 14.2 create them
        explicitly → 14.3 wire containers by hand (CLI) → 14.4 EXPOSE vs
        -p → 14.5 the same design as compose.yaml — each section repeats
        the SAME topology at an increasing level of automation.

    14.1 Network Design for easypj Stack
         - Backend network: Django + PostgreSQL + Redis
         - Frontend network: Nginx + Django
         - Database isolation: PostgreSQL NOT exposed to host
         [ARCHITECTURE DIAGRAM: Two networks with services placed]

         🎯 GOAL: Place easypj's four services on two networks so the
            blast radius of a compromised nginx is one hop — not the DB.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — the two-network design, drawn]
            internet ──▶ host:80
                          │
            ┌─ frontend ──▼────────────────────────┐
            │  [nginx] ───────▶ [django]           │
            └───────────────────────┬──────────────┘
            ┌─ backend ─────────────┼──────────────┐
            │  [postgres] ◀── [django] ──▶ [redis] │
            │  (no ports:)             (no ports:) │
            └──────────────────────────────────────┘
         [TECH] django is dual-homed (frontend + backend); nginx sees ONLY
            django; postgres/redis sit backend-only with zero published
            ports. Add internal: true to backend and its members also lose
            the NAT route out — no ingress, no egress.
         [ANALOGY] A bank branch: frontend is the customer hall, django
            the teller window, backend the vault corridor. The teller
            works both zones; customers never enter the corridor; the
            vault has no street door AT ALL (no ports:).
         🔬 easypj: JobPost rows and User password hashes — everything
            valuable lives in postgres, and postgres is reachable ONLY as
            postgres:5432 from backend members. No -p, no exposure.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: from nginx, try `wget -qO- postgres:5432`;
            repeat from django. Verify: nginx cannot even RESOLVE the name
            (different network); django connects.
         📊 SUMMARY: two networks, one dual-homed app tier, zero published
            DB ports — this diagram is the reference posture for Part 7.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "it's just dev" is how 5432 ends up on 0.0.0.0 —
            design the isolation BEFORE the first up, not after the first
            breach.

    14.2 Creating Custom Networks for easypj
         - docker network create easypj-backend
         - docker network create easypj-frontend
         - docker network inspect easypj-backend
         [TERMINAL: Network creation and inspection]

         🎯 GOAL: Create both easypj networks with explicit subnets and
            read an inspect output like a map.
         [TERMINAL: create + inspect, drawn]
            $ docker network create easypj-frontend
            $ docker network create --subnet 172.28.0.0/24 \
                --gateway 172.28.0.1 easypj-backend
            $ docker network inspect easypj-backend
                "Driver": "bridge",
                "Subnet": "172.28.0.0/24",
                "Containers": {}        # empty — nothing attached yet
         [TECH] Without --subnet, dockerd allocates the next free pool
            from default-address-pools (2.7). Explicit subnets buy stable
            firewall rules and no collisions with the office VPN's ranges.
         [ANALOGY] Naming the corridors before moving furniture: create
            networks first, then attach containers — better than letting
            every docker run improvise its own hallway.
         🔬 easypj: two creates, ten seconds — the entire architecture of
            14.1 now EXISTS, waiting for tenants.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: create both networks, then `docker network ls`
            and inspect each. Verify: driver bridge, distinct subnets,
            empty Containers — and you can say which subnet is backend.
         📊 SUMMARY: create (optionally --subnet), inspect to confirm;
            networks are cheap — name them like you mean it.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a subnet overlapping your VPN or LAN silently
            blackholes traffic — the #1 "Docker broke my VPN" cause; pick
            ranges like 172.28.x.x deliberately.

    14.3 Connecting Containers to Networks
         - docker run --network easypj-backend ...
         - docker network connect easypj-frontend django-container
         - Verify: docker exec django ping postgres
         [TERMINAL: Connection + verification workflow]

         🎯 GOAL: Attach each easypj container to its planned network(s) —
            at run time and live — and prove the wiring in both directions.
         [TERMINAL: wire the stack by hand, drawn]
            $ docker run -d --name postgres --network easypj-backend \
                -e POSTGRES_DB=easypj_db -e POSTGRES_USER=easypj \
                -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pg-pass postgres:15
            $ docker run -d --name django --network easypj-backend \
                --env-file .env easypj:v1
            $ docker network connect easypj-frontend django  # 2nd network!
            $ docker run -d --name nginx --network easypj-frontend \
                -p 80:80 nginx:alpine
            $ docker exec django ping -c1 postgres    # backend    ✅
            $ docker exec nginx  ping -c1 django      # frontend   ✅
            $ docker exec nginx  ping -c1 postgres    # FAILS — by design
         [TECH] --network at run time attaches the FIRST network; further
            ones need docker network connect (live — adds eth1). The
            failing third ping is the design working: nginx and postgres
            share no network, so not even DNS crosses.
         [ANALOGY] Issuing keycards: django gets two (both corridors),
            nginx one, postgres one — and the ping test is walking each
            corridor rattling every door.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the block above. Verify: two pings answer;
            the third says "bad address" — name resolution itself refused.
         📊 SUMMARY: --network at birth, network connect for the second
            home; verify with exec + ping in the directions you expect AND
            the one you don't.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: docker run accepts only ONE --network flag — the
            "django on both" step MUST be a separate connect (Compose does
            this for you; the raw CLI makes you feel it).

    14.4 Port Publishing & Exposure
         - EXPOSE in Dockerfile (documentation only!)
         - -p (publish) in docker run (actual mapping)
         - Short syntax: -p 8000:8000
         - Long syntax in compose: protocol, mode
         [TABLE: Port mapping scenarios with examples]

         🎯 GOAL: Stop confusing EXPOSE with -p forever, and pick the
            right publish syntax per scenario.
         [TECH] EXPOSE in a Dockerfile is pure METADATA — documentation
            for humans and input for -P. Only -p/--publish (or compose
            ports:) creates the DNAT rule that makes a container reachable
            from outside (full mechanics: 15.6).
         [TABLE: publish scenarios — need | flag | result]
            laptop dev           | -p 8000:8000           | host:8000 → app
            loopback only        | -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 | not LAN-visible
            random host port     | -p 8000                | ephemeral high
            all EXPOSEd ports    | -P                     | quick demos
            container→container  | (no flag at all)       | DNS + port
            UDP service          | -p 514:514/udp         | proto explicit
         [ANALOGY] EXPOSE is the "doorbell here" sticker printed on the
            blueprint; -p actually wires the doorbell to the street. A
            sticker never rang anything.
         🔬 easypj: nginx gets -p 80:80 — the ONLY publish in the stack;
            django, postgres and redis rely on container-to-container DNS:
            row five of the table.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run easypj:v1 (EXPOSE 8000) without -p; curl
            localhost:8000 (fails), then docker exec nginx curl
            django:8000 (works). Verify: EXPOSE published exactly nothing.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — EXPOSE vs -p, what each ACTUALLY touches]
            EXPOSE 8000 in Dockerfile          (easypj's Django port)
               └─▶ stored in image JSON (Config.ExposedPorts) ─▶ done.
                   no daemon action, no kernel rule, ever fires.

            -p 8000:8000 in `docker run` / compose `ports:`
               └─▶ dockerd creates the container ─▶ writes an iptables
                   nat-table DNAT rule in the DOCKER chain ─▶ reachable
                   from outside (full packet path: 15.6)

         💡 EXPOSE's only runtime effect is enabling `-P` (capital):
            with zero EXPOSE lines, `docker run -P` publishes nothing —
            it just reads the image's ExposedPorts list and maps each one
            to a random host port. It invents nothing on its own.

         📊 SUMMARY: EXPOSE documents, -p publishes; container-to-
            container needs neither — DNS name + container port.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: -p 8000:8000 binds 0.0.0.0 — your "local dev" is
            LAN-visible at the coffee shop; the 127.0.0.1: prefix is one
            keystroke of paranoia that pays for itself.

    14.5 Service Discovery in Compose
         - Compose creates a default network automatically
         - Services reachable by service name (DNS)
         - Example: Django connects to postgres://postgres:5432/db
         - Custom networks in Compose
         [CODE: compose.yaml with network configuration]


         🎯 GOAL: Encode the ENTIRE 14.1 design — both networks, all
            placements — as ten lines of compose.yaml.
         [CODE: networks section of easypj's compose.yaml — drawn]
            services:
              nginx:    { networks: [frontend], ports: ["80:80"] }
              django:   { networks: [frontend, backend] }
              postgres: { networks: [backend] }
              redis:    { networks: [backend] }
            networks:
              frontend: {}
              backend:
                internal: true    # no NAT out — the vault corridor
         [TECH] Compose creates real networks named <project>_frontend /
            <project>_backend and registers every service in the embedded
            DNS of each network it joins. DATABASE_URL uses the service
            name: postgres://easypj:pg-pass@postgres:5432/easypj_db.
         [ANALOGY] 14.3 wired the stack by hand, cable by cable; this file
            is the same wiring as a printed patch-panel chart — applied
            with one `up`, reproducible forever.
         🔬 easypj: the manual demo (14.3) and this yaml produce the SAME
            three ping results — nginx→django yes, django→postgres yes,
            nginx→postgres refused.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker compose up -d`, then re-run 14.3's
            three pings via compose exec. Verify: identical outcomes with
            zero manual connects — the file did the wiring.
         📊 SUMMARY: service name = one DNS record per joined network;
            networks: is the placement column of your architecture diagram.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: internal: true also blocks OUTBOUND traffic — a
            backend-internal django could not pip install or call a
            payments API; that is why django, not postgres, is dual-homed.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — what internal: true actually removes
         A normal user-defined bridge gets a MASQUERADE (SNAT) rule in
         the nat POSTROUTING chain, letting its containers reach the
         internet through the host's default route. When a compose
         network is declared `internal: true`, dockerd creates the
         bridge WITHOUT that MASQUERADE rule and without a route out of
         the bridge's subnet at all — it isn't just firewalled, there is
         structurally no path out. That is why postgres and redis on
         easypj-backend can't reach PyPI or any external host even if a
         misconfigured process tried.

         normal user-defined bridge:              internal: true bridge:
         container─▶bridge─▶MASQUERADE─▶eth0        container─▶bridge─▶(no route out)
         ─▶ internet                                 ✗ no MASQUERADE rule installed
         Recap: internal: true is a routing decision, not a rule you
         could accidentally bypass from inside the container.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
         ✅ Two networks, one dual-homed service (django) = the smallest
            blast radius for a compromised edge container (nginx).
         ✅ Explicit --subnet/--gateway beats auto-allocation — stable
            firewall rules, no VPN/LAN collisions.
         ✅ `docker run` accepts only ONE --network flag; a second
            attachment is always a live `docker network connect`.
         ✅ EXPOSE is metadata (Config.ExposedPorts) — it opens nothing;
            only -p/-P/compose ports: create real DNAT rules.
         ✅ internal: true removes BOTH inbound reachability AND outbound
            routing — decide which service needs real internet access
            before flagging a network internal.
         ✅ Compose creates real, inspectable networks named
            <project>_<name> and registers every joined service in each
            network's DNS.
         🎯 DCA relevance: subnet planning, publish-syntax variants, and
            compose networks: topology are all directly examinable.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
         - "It's just dev" is how 5432 ends up bound to 0.0.0.0 — design
           isolation before the first `up`, not after an incident.
         - A subnet overlapping your VPN or office LAN silently
           blackholes traffic — pick deliberate ranges like 172.28.x.x.
         - internal: true blocks egress too — a backend-internal django
           couldn't call an external payments API, which is exactly why
           django (not postgres) is the dual-homed service.
         - `docker run --network` only accepts one value — there is no
           comma-separated shortcut for two networks at creation time.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
         - `docker compose config` renders the fully-resolved networks:
           section — read it once before `up` to catch topology mistakes
           on paper.
         - Bind dev-only debug ports as `-p 127.0.0.1:PORT:PORT` by
           muscle memory; typing the loopback prefix costs less than a
           LAN leak.

    🔑 COMMANDS
         $ docker network create --subnet 172.28.0.0/24 \
             --gateway 172.28.0.1 easypj-backend
         $ docker network create easypj-frontend
         $ docker run -d --name postgres --network easypj-backend \
             postgres:15
         $ docker network connect easypj-frontend django   # 2nd network, live
         $ docker exec nginx ping -c1 postgres              # expect: fails
         $ docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.ExposedPorts}}' easypj:v1
         $ docker compose config --format json | jq .networks

    🧪 DRILL (15 min): Stand up easypj's two networks by hand (14.2-14.3),
         then bring up the SAME stack via `docker compose up -d` using the
         compose.yaml from 14.5, and diff the two `docker network
         inspect` outputs. Verify: same subnets, same isolation, same
         three ping outcomes — only the amount of typing changed.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 14)

         Q1: Why is django the ONLY dual-homed service in easypj's design,
             and what would break if nginx were dual-homed instead?
             A: django must reach both nginx (frontend, to serve
                responses) and postgres/redis (backend, to serve data);
                if nginx were also on backend it could reach postgres
                directly, defeating the entire isolation design.
                internet──▶[nginx]──▶[django]──▶[postgres]/[redis]
                            frontend         backend (no ports:)
             Explanation: 14.1's two-network diagram — the blast radius
             of a compromised nginx must stop at django.

         Q2: What TWO things does `internal: true` remove from a compose
             network, not just one?
             A: Both inbound reachability from other networks AND
                outbound routing to the internet — there is no MASQUERADE
                rule and no default route out, so there's structurally no
                path, not just a firewalled one.
             Explanation: ties 14.1's design to this chapter's Under the
             Hood deep-dive.

         Q3: Why does easypj-backend use an explicit --subnet
             (172.28.0.0/24) instead of Docker's auto-allocated pool?
             A: Auto-allocated pools can collide with a VPN or office LAN
                range, silently blackholing traffic — the #1 "Docker
                broke my VPN" cause; explicit subnets are deliberate and
                auditable.
             Explanation: 14.2's gotcha, restated as a why-question.

         Q4: django needs to join TWO networks. Why can't one `docker run
             --network` do that, and what's the real two-step sequence?
             A: `docker run --network` accepts only one value. Sequence:
                `docker run --network easypj-backend --name django ...`
                followed by a live `docker network connect
                easypj-frontend django`.
             Explanation: 14.3 — the raw CLI makes you feel a step
             Compose normally hides.

         Q5: From nginx, `wget -qO- postgres:5432` fails even though
             nginx knows the string "postgres." Why, precisely?
             A: nginx and postgres share no network, so nginx can't even
                RESOLVE the name — it's a resolution failure ("bad
                address"), not a connection refusal.
             Explanation: 14.3's third ping — the design working exactly
             as intended.

         Q6: A Dockerfile has `EXPOSE 8000` and the container runs with
             no -p flag at all. Can a LAN machine reach port 8000? Can
             another container on the same Docker network?
             A: LAN: no — EXPOSE is metadata only, it opens nothing.
                Same network: yes — container-to-container traffic needs
                neither EXPOSE nor -p, only the DNS name and the actual
                listening port.
                | need                | flag/config            |
                | laptop dev          | -p 8000:8000            |
                | loopback only       | -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000  |
                | container→container | (no flag at all)        |
             Explanation: 14.4's publish-scenario table, condensed.

         Q7: What is the concrete difference between `-p 8000:8000` and
             `-p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000`?
             A: The first binds 0.0.0.0 — reachable from the LAN (or the
                internet, if the host is public); the second binds only
                loopback — reachable only from the host itself.
             Explanation: 14.4's closing gotcha.

         Q8: An image has zero EXPOSE lines. What does `docker run -P` do?
             A: Nothing — -P only maps ports already listed in the
                image's ExposedPorts; with zero EXPOSE lines there is
                nothing for it to publish.
             Explanation: 14.4's 💡 callout.

         Q9: Translate easypj's 14.1 design into the compose.yaml
             networks: keys each service needs.
             A: nginx: [frontend]; django: [frontend, backend]; postgres:
                [backend]; redis: [backend]; top-level: frontend: {},
                backend: {internal: true}.
             Explanation: 14.5's networks: section, restated as a
             mapping.

         Q10: After `docker compose up -d`, which three exec-based ping
              tests prove the design works, and what result does each
              expect?
              A: nginx→django (works), django→postgres (works), nginx→
                 postgres (fails/refused) — the third one failing IS the
                 success condition.
              Explanation: 14.5 reproducing 14.3's manual results with
              zero manual connects.

         ┌──────────────────── CHAPTER 14 — EASYPJ'S REAL TOPOLOGY ──────────────┐
         │  internet ──▶ [nginx :80] ──▶ [django] ──▶ [postgres] (no ports:)     │
         │               frontend net    dual-homed  └──▶ [redis]  (no ports:)  │
         │                                            backend net (internal:true)│
         │  EXPOSE = metadata only  │  -p/-P/ports: = real iptables DNAT rules  │
