         .vs-prose — Chapter 14 turns Chapter 13's vocabulary into a real,
         defensible topology: two networks, one dual-homed app tier, and
         databases with zero published ports. EXPOSE never opens anything
         by itself — only -p, -P, or compose's ports: key create the
         iptables rules that make a container reachable from outside —
         and internal: true removes both the inbound AND the outbound
         path for the tier that holds the data. This exact posture is
         what every later Part of the guide assumes is already standing.


Chapter 15: Advanced Docker Networking
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: The last 10% of Docker networking causes 90%
    of the 2 a.m. pages: host-mode surprises, containers that need real
    LAN IPs, multi-host overlays, and "the app is fine but the network
    isn't" mysteries. This chapter arms you with the exotic drivers, a
    proper toolbox (netshoot), and the iptables truth behind -p. Problem
    solved here: "I can wire containers, but I can't DEBUG the wiring."

    [A] META: 🔴 ADVANCED  ·  ⏱️ ~110-130 min  ·  🎯 DCA DOMAIN: Networking
        (15% of the exam) — advanced/edge-case chapter.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
         • Decide when --network host is a legitimate performance choice
           versus a foot-gun (15.1)
         • Choose macvlan vs ipvlan by the one criterion that matters —
           MAC-per-container or not (15.2)
         • Explain how VXLAN lets containers on different hosts share one
           subnet, and which ports an overlay needs open (15.3)
         • Walk a fixed 4-rung debugging ladder — inspect → nslookup →
           nc -zv → netshoot-in-netns — instead of guessing (15.4)
         • Apply a 10-rule default-deny network security checklist to
           easypj (15.5)
         • Trace one inbound packet through PREROUTING/DOCKER/DNAT/
           FORWARD to explain why ufw never sees published-port traffic
           (15.6)

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: Covers the advanced edge of the DCA "Networking"
        domain: driver selection beyond bridge, Swarm overlay basics, and
        the security/troubleshooting competencies graded at the "why did
        this actually break" level.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 15.1 host mode → 15.2 macvlan/ipvlan → 15.3 overlay
        (multi-host) → 15.4 the debugging ladder → 15.5 security
        checklist → 15.6 the iptables truth behind -p — three exotic
        drivers, then the tools and posture to run (and defend) any of
        them in production.

    15.1 Host Networking
         - When to use --network host (maximum performance)
         - When NOT to use (port conflicts, reduced isolation)
         - Comparison: bridge vs host performance
         [TABLE: Bridge vs Host networking trade-offs]

         🎯 GOAL: Decide in one breath when --network host is the right
            tool and when it is a foot-gun.
         [TABLE: bridge vs host — dimension | bridge | host]
            isolation      | own netns, own IP     | NONE — host's stack
            port mapping   | -p required (NAT)     | -p IGNORED silently
            performance    | NAT + veth overhead   | native wire speed
            port conflicts | impossible (mapped)   | app fights the host
            multi-instance | many per host port    | one owner per port
            DNS names      | embedded 127.0.0.11   | host's resolv.conf
         [TECH] --network host deletes the sandbox boundary: the container
            shares the host's interfaces, routes and port table. gunicorn
            binding :8000 binds the HOST's :8000 — no veth, no bridge, no
            DNAT hop (which is exactly where the performance win is).
         [ANALOGY] Bridge = your own hotel room with mail forwarding; host
            = sleeping in the lobby. Fastest path to the front door, zero
            privacy, and only ONE guest can claim the sofa.
         🔬 easypj: never for django or postgres; plausible for a
            node-exporter-style metrics agent that must see the host's
            real interfaces to be useful at all.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker run --rm --network host alpine ip
            addr`, then compare with the host's own ip addr. Verify:
            IDENTICAL interface lists — the isolation is simply gone.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — bridge path vs host path, drawn]
            BRIDGE (default, needs -p 8080:80)
            client ─▶ host eth0:8080 ─▶ NAT/DNAT ─▶ docker0 bridge ─▶
              veth pair ─▶ container eth0 (172.17.0.x) ─▶ app :80
            3 translation hops; container gets its OWN IP + port table

            HOST (--network host, -p has no effect)
            client ─▶ host eth0:80 ─▶ app :80 (same netns as the host)
            0 translation hops; container has the HOST's IP and the
            HOST's port table — binding :80 in the container binds :80
            on the host, port conflicts and all
         easypj: :80 above is nginx's own port (14.4) — bridge is what
         easypj actually runs; host mode is the road not taken.

         💡 Compose spells this `network_mode: host` (not `networks:`) —
            the moment it's set, `ports:` on that service does nothing,
            and Compose logs a warning saying so, which is the fastest
            way to confirm host mode is actually active.

         📊 SUMMARY: host mode trades ALL network isolation for native
            speed and real-interface visibility; rare, deliberate,
            Linux-only.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: on Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) host mode attaches
            to the hidden VM's network, not your laptop's — "works only on
            the Linux server" is the tell.

    15.2 Macvlan / IPvlan Networking
         - Macvlan: Container gets its own MAC address
         - IPvlan: Container shares MAC but has own IP
         - Use case: Legacy apps that need physical network presence
         [DIAGRAM: Macvlan vs IPvlan architecture]

         🎯 GOAL: Give a container a REAL address on the office LAN — and
            choose macvlan vs ipvlan by one criterion: MAC count.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — macvlan vs ipvlan, drawn]
            physical LAN 192.168.1.0/24 ── switch ── router
                               │
                           host eth0
                  ┌────────────┴────────────┐
              MACVLAN sub-ifs          IPVLAN L2 sub-ifs
              C1 .50  MAC aa:aa        C1 .50 ┐ share the
              C2 .51  MAC bb:bb        C2 .51 ┘ host's MAC
              (a MAC per container:    (one MAC on the wire:
               switch sees them all)    port-security friendly)
         [TECH] Both drivers bond container sub-interfaces to the parent
            NIC (-o parent=eth0), skipping bridge and NAT entirely — DHCP
            servers, printers and legacy scanners see a first-class LAN
            citizen. macvlan mints one MAC per container; ipvlan reuses
            the host's MAC and differs only at L3.
         [ANALOGY] macvlan = each container gets its own house on the
            street (own mailbox, own nameplate); ipvlan = apartments in
            the host's building — one street door (MAC), many unit
            numbers (IPs).
         🔬 easypj: not for the web stack — but a legacy license server or
            an IoT integration that must ARP on the real LAN is the
            genuine use case.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: create a macvlan network with your LAN's
            subnet and -o parent=eth0, run alpine with --ip, then ping it
            from ANOTHER machine. Verify: an outside device reaches a
            container with no -p anywhere in sight.
         📊 SUMMARY: real-LAN presence without NAT; macvlan = MAC per
            container, ipvlan = shared MAC — pick ipvlan when switches or
            wifi filter MACs.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the HOST cannot reach its own macvlan containers
            (kernel hairpin restriction) — plan a macvlan shim interface
            or accept host-blindness.

    15.3 Overlay Networking (Swarm)
         - Multi-host container communication
         - VXLAN tunneling
         - Encryption (--opt encrypted)
         [DIAGRAM: Overlay network across 3 Swarm nodes]

         🎯 GOAL: Explain how two containers on DIFFERENT machines share
            one subnet — and what --opt encrypted changes.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — one overlay, three nodes, drawn]
            overlay easypj-net 10.0.9.0/24 (VXLAN)
            ┌── node1 ───┐   ┌── node2 ───┐   ┌── node3 ───┐
            │ [django]   │   │ [django]   │   │ [postgres] │
            │  10.0.9.3  │   │  10.0.9.4  │   │  10.0.9.5  │
            └────╥───────┘   └────╥───────┘   └────╥───────┘
                 ╚═══ UDP 4789 ═══╩═ VXLAN tunnels ╝
                 (containers' L2 frames ride inside UDP packets)
         [TECH] VXLAN wraps container Ethernet frames in UDP/4789 packets
            between nodes; each node's kernel unwraps and delivers as if
            one switch spanned the cluster. Needs Swarm mode (Part 10) for
            the control plane; --opt encrypted adds IPsec between nodes.
         [ANALOGY] Sister office buildings with a pneumatic tube system:
            interoffice envelopes (frames) ride inside courier capsules
            (UDP packets); staff just write room numbers (10.0.9.x) and
            never see the tubes.
         🔬 easypj: on a 3-node Swarm, django on node1 dials postgres:5432
            exactly as it did in Compose — the connection string never
            learns the database moved machines.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: docker swarm init, join a second node, create
            an attachable overlay, run alpine on each, ping across.
            Verify: tcpdump on eth0 shows UDP 4789 while the ping runs.
         📊 SUMMARY: overlay = one virtual switch across hosts via VXLAN;
            encrypt with --opt encrypted; deep dive in Part 9, CNI
            equivalents in [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
            ⚠️ Gotcha: overlays need 2377/tcp, 7946/tcp+udp and 4789/udp
            OPEN between nodes — a cloud security group eats one and
            "overlay is broken" tickets follow.

    15.4 Network Troubleshooting Tools
         - docker run --rm alpine ping <target>
         - docker run --rm nicolaka/netshoot (swiss army knife)
         - docker run --rm alpine nslookup <hostname>
         - docker run --rm curlimages/curl <url>
         - docker network inspect (see connected containers)
         [PRACTICAL: Debugging connectivity between easypj containers]

         🎯 GOAL: Debug "django can't reach postgres" with a fixed 4-rung
            ladder instead of random restarts.
         [TERMINAL: the debugging ladder, drawn]
            # 1. Is the target on the network I think it is?
            $ docker network inspect easypj-backend | grep -A3 Name
            # 2. Does DNS resolve from the source's viewpoint?
            $ docker run --rm --network easypj-backend alpine \
                nslookup postgres
            # 3. Is the PORT open (not just the host alive)?
            $ docker run --rm --network easypj-backend \
                nicolaka/netshoot nc -zv postgres 5432
            # 4. Full toolbox INSIDE the source's own netns:
            $ docker run --rm -it --network container:django \
                nicolaka/netshoot        # tcpdump, dig, ss, curl, iperf
         [TECH] Rung 4's --network container:django joins django's OWN
            network namespace — you see its eth0, its resolv.conf, its
            routes, without installing one tool into the app image.
         [ANALOGY] A plumber's ladder: check the house is on the street
            (inspect), the address resolves (nslookup), the tap opens
            (nc -zv), then put your ear on THIS house's pipes (netshoot
            inside the same netns).
         🔬 easypj: classic finding — rung 2 fails because django ran with
            --network easypj-frontend only; one `docker network connect
            easypj-backend django` later, rungs 2-4 go green.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: break the stack on purpose (disconnect django
            from backend), walk the ladder, fix, re-walk. Verify: you can
            name WHICH rung failed and why — that sentence is the skill.
         📊 SUMMARY: inspect → nslookup → nc -zv → netshoot-in-netns; four
            rungs diagnose 95% of container connectivity tickets.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a NEW container on the same network is NOT the same
            as the source's netns — wrong resolv.conf or per-container
            rules only show up via --network container:<name>.

    15.5 Network Security Basics
         - Principle of least privilege: only expose what's needed
         - Internal-only networks (no host port mapping)
         - Docker network encryption (Swarm)
         - Network policies (with K8s, not native Docker)
         [BEST PRACTICE CHECKLIST: 10 network security rules]

         🎯 GOAL: Ship a default-deny network posture for easypj — every
            open path a decision, never an accident.
         [CHECKLIST: 10 network security rules — drawn]
            □ 1  Publish NOTHING but the edge (nginx :80/:443)
            □ 2  DB/cache on internal: true networks — no NAT either way
            □ 3  Bind dev-only ports to 127.0.0.1, never 0.0.0.0
            □ 4  One network per trust zone; dual-home only the app tier
            □ 5  Never --network host for internet-facing services
            □ 6  Encrypt overlays that cross datacenters (--opt encrypted)
            □ 7  icc=false on the default bridge (2.7) — or don't use it
            □ 8  Explicit subnets — auditable firewall rules, no VPN wars
            □ 9  Re-scan `docker ps` for 0.0.0.0 leaks after every change
            □ 10 Know -p bypasses ufw (15.6) — audit the DOCKER chain too
         [TECH] Docker networking is default-ALLOW inside a network and
            default-DENY across networks — segmentation IS the firewall.
            Rules 1-4 are pure topology; 5-10 are the host-level escape
            hatches people forget they opened.
         [ANALOGY] Castle design: one gate (nginx), an inner keep with no
            outside door (internal: true), separate courtyards per trust
            zone — and rule 10 is checking the tunnel the drawbridge
            keeper (iptables) dug without telling the guards (ufw).
         🔬 easypj: the 14.1 design already scores rules 1, 2 and 4;
            adding 127.0.0.1 binds for dev tools and explicit subnets
            completes the posture in one afternoon.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run
            docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Ports}}' on your stack.
            Verify: exactly ONE 0.0.0.0 entry (nginx) — any other line is
            a checklist violation with your name on it.
         📊 SUMMARY: segment first, publish least, bind narrow, audit the
            iptables reality; NetworkPolicies extend this — see
            [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Docker recreates its iptables rules on daemon
            restart — hand-edited firewall "fixes" silently vanish; encode
            policy in networks and daemon.json, not ad-hoc iptables.

    15.6 How -p Really Works — NAT, iptables & the Published-Port Path
         - Packet path: eth0 → PREROUTING → DOCKER chain → DNAT → container
         - docker-proxy: the userland fallback (localhost + hairpin cases)
         - Binding scopes: -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 vs -p 5432:5432 (0.0.0.0)
         - Why ufw/firewalld rules never see published-port traffic
         - Reading the truth: iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n

         🎯 GOAL: Trace one inbound packet from the wire to gunicorn and
            explain why your ufw "deny 8000" rule never fired.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — the published-port path, drawn]
            client:54321 ─▶ host eth0 :8000
              ─▶ nat PREROUTING ─▶ DOCKER chain
                   match tcp dpt:8000 → DNAT to 172.18.0.4:8000
              ─▶ FORWARD (DOCKER-USER first, then DOCKER)
              ─▶ bridge ─▶ veth ─▶ container eth0 ─▶ gunicorn :8000
            reply: conntrack rewrites the source back — the client
            never sees 172.18.0.4
         [TECH] -p writes iptables rules, not proxies: a nat-table DNAT in
            the DOCKER chain rewrites the destination BEFORE routing.
            docker-proxy (one process per published port) survives only as
            a userland fallback for localhost and hairpin traffic. ufw's
            INPUT rules never match because DNATed traffic traverses
            FORWARD, not INPUT — the one hook Docker guarantees you is the
            DOCKER-USER chain.
         [ANALOGY] The mailroom rewrites the envelope's address (DNAT) at
            the loading dock BEFORE the receptionist (INPUT/ufw) ever sees
            it — complaining to the receptionist about deliveries she
            never handles is the whole "ufw doesn't block Docker" bug.
         🔬 easypj: -p 5432:5432 "just to debug" DNATs the whole internet
            to PostgreSQL even with ufw deny 5432 active. The fix is
            binding scope: -p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 makes the DNAT rule
            itself match only loopback destinations.
         [TERMINAL: see it with your own eyes, drawn]
            $ sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n | grep 5432
              DNAT tcp -- 0.0.0.0/0 ... dpt:5432 to:172.18.0.3:5432
            $ ps aux | grep docker-proxy    # one per published port
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: publish nginx as -p 8080:80, add ufw deny
            8080, curl from another machine (still answers!); re-run with
            -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80. Verify: LAN curl now refused, localhost
            fine — and the iptables line shows the 127.0.0.1 match.
         📊 SUMMARY: -p = kernel DNAT in the DOCKER chain + conntrack
            replies; docker-proxy is a niche fallback; firewall Docker in
            DOCKER-USER (or bind narrow), never in INPUT.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: -p with no address means 0.0.0.0 AND [::] — the
            port answers on every interface the host owns, cloud-public
            IP included.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — the firewall chain order Docker actually uses
         Inbound traffic to a published port does not hit iptables'
         INPUT chain at all — it is DNATed in the nat table's DOCKER
         chain and then evaluated in the filter table's FORWARD chain, in
         a fixed order: DOCKER-USER first (a chain Docker guarantees it
         will never flush or manage — the one stable hook for your own
         rules), then DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-1/2 (blocking cross-bridge
         traffic by default, rewritten on every daemon restart), then
         DOCKER (the per-container ACCEPT rules Docker manages itself).
         This ordering is WHY 15.5's checklist rule about auditing
         DOCKER-USER matters, and why 15.6's ufw story happens at all.

         nat:PREROUTING ─▶ DOCKER (DNAT rewrite) ─▶ filter:FORWARD
            │
            ▼
         filter:DOCKER-USER    (empty by default — YOUR rules survive here)
            │
            ▼
         filter:DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-1/2   (blocks cross-bridge traffic)
            │
            ▼
         filter:DOCKER   (per-container ACCEPT rules Docker manages)
            │
            ▼
         destination container
         Recap: if you want a firewall rule Docker will never silently
         delete out from under you, DOCKER-USER is the only chain built
         for that purpose.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
         ✅ --network host deletes the sandbox boundary entirely — native
            speed, zero isolation, one owner per host port.
         ✅ macvlan mints one MAC per container; ipvlan shares the host's
            MAC and differs only at L3 — pick ipvlan when switches or
            wifi filter by MAC count.
         ✅ Overlay tunnels container frames inside VXLAN (UDP/4789)
            between Swarm nodes; --opt encrypted adds IPsec on top.
         ✅ The 4-rung ladder (inspect → nslookup → nc -zv →
            netshoot-in-netns) diagnoses the large majority of
            connectivity tickets without guesswork.
         ✅ -p writes a real iptables DNAT rule in the DOCKER chain —
            docker-proxy is only a niche fallback for loopback/hairpin
            cases, not the common path.
         ✅ ufw/firewalld INPUT rules never see published-port traffic
            because DNATed packets traverse FORWARD, not INPUT.
         🎯 DCA relevance: driver trade-offs, Swarm overlay basics, and
            the DNAT mental model are all directly examinable.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
         - On Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows), host mode attaches to the
           hidden VM's network, not your physical laptop's — "only works
           on the Linux server" is the tell.
         - The host cannot reach its OWN macvlan containers (a kernel
           hairpin restriction) — plan a macvlan shim interface or accept
           host-blindness.
         - Overlay needs 2377/tcp, 7946/tcp+udp and 4789/udp open between
           EVERY node — one blocked port in a cloud security group and
           "overlay is broken" tickets follow.
         - -p with no address means 0.0.0.0 AND [::] — the port answers
           on every interface the host owns, including a cloud-public IP.
         - Docker rewrites its iptables rules on every daemon restart —
           hand-edited firewall "fixes" outside DOCKER-USER silently
           vanish.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
         - Keep `nicolaka/netshoot` pulled locally — it's the one image
           worth caching before you need it at 2 a.m.
         - `iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n | grep <port>` answers "is this
           actually published, and to where" faster than re-reading
           compose files.

    🔑 COMMANDS
         $ docker run --rm --network host alpine ip addr        # host mode has zero isolation
         $ docker network create -d macvlan --subnet 192.168.1.0/24 \
             -o parent=eth0 lanX
         $ docker swarm init && docker network create -d overlay \
             --attachable easypj-net
         $ docker run --rm --network easypj-backend alpine nslookup postgres  # rung 2
         $ docker run --rm --network easypj-backend nicolaka/netshoot \
             nc -zv postgres 5432                                # rung 3
         $ docker run --rm -it --network container:django nicolaka/netshoot  # rung 4
         $ sudo iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n                     # the real DNAT rules
         $ docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Ports}}'            # scan for 0.0.0.0 leaks

    🧪 DRILL (15 min): Publish nginx with `-p 8080:80`, add `ufw deny
         8080`, curl it from another machine (still answers!), then
         re-publish as `-p 127.0.0.1:8080:80` and repeat. Verify: LAN curl
         is now refused, localhost still works, and you can point at the
         exact iptables line that changed.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 15)

         Q1: List three concrete differences between bridge and host
             networking, and explain why testing "host mode" on Docker
             Desktop for Mac doesn't prove what you think it proves.
             A: isolation (own netns vs none), port mapping (-p required
                vs ignored), performance (NAT overhead vs native). On
                Desktop, host mode attaches to the HIDDEN Linux VM's
                network, not your Mac/Windows interfaces.
                | dimension | bridge              | host              |
                | isolation | own netns, own IP   | NONE              |
                | port map  | -p required (NAT)   | -p IGNORED        |
             Explanation: 15.1's bridge-vs-host table plus its Desktop
             gotcha.

         Q2: You run a container with `--network host -p 9000:80`. What
             actually happens to the -p flag?
             A: It's silently ignored — there is no NAT/sandbox layer for
                -p to configure; the app binds directly to the host's own
                port 80, not 9000.
             Explanation: 15.1's core trap.

         Q3: What ONE criterion decides macvlan vs ipvlan, and why can't
             the Docker HOST reach a container on a macvlan network?
             A: MAC count — macvlan gives each container its own MAC
                (real LAN citizen); ipvlan shares the host's MAC. The
                host can't reach its own macvlan containers due to a
                kernel hairpin restriction.
             Explanation: 15.2's criterion plus its closing gotcha.

         Q4: How do two containers on DIFFERENT hosts share one subnet
             under an overlay network, which ports must be open between
             nodes, and what does --opt encrypted add?
             A: Container frames are wrapped in UDP/4789 (VXLAN) packets
                between nodes; Swarm's control plane also needs 2377/tcp
                and 7946/tcp+udp. --opt encrypted adds IPsec between the
                nodes.
                node1[django]═╗           ╔═[django]node2   ╔═[postgres]node3
                       UDP 4789 tunnels (VXLAN) ═════════════╝
             Explanation: 15.3's diagram and required-ports list.

         Q5: Put these in the correct debugging order and say what each
             rung answers: nc -zv, network inspect, netshoot-in-netns,
             nslookup.
             A: 1) network inspect — is the target on the network I
                think it is; 2) nslookup — does DNS resolve from the
                source's viewpoint; 3) nc -zv — is the port actually
                open; 4) netshoot in the source's netns — full toolbox
                from the exact failing vantage point.
             Explanation: 15.4's 4-rung ladder.

         Q6: What does `--network container:django` actually do, and why
             is it more revealing than running netshoot on the SAME
             Docker network as django?
             A: It joins netshoot to django's OWN network namespace (same
                eth0, same resolv.conf, same routes) instead of giving it
                a fresh namespace on the same network — so it sees
                exactly what django sees, quirks included.
             Explanation: 15.4's rung 4.

         Q7: Pick three rules from the security checklist and say what
             concrete easypj mistake each prevents.
             A: Rule 1 (publish only the edge) prevents postgres/redis
                ports leaking to 0.0.0.0; Rule 2 (internal: true on DB/
                cache) prevents any outbound path from the vault tier;
                Rule 3 (bind dev ports to 127.0.0.1) prevents a "just for
                debugging" -p from being LAN-visible at a coffee shop.
             Explanation: 15.5's 10-rule checklist, applied.

         Q8: Trace one inbound packet to a published port from the wire
             to the application, and explain why `ufw deny <port>` does
             not stop it.
             A: client → host eth0 → nat:PREROUTING → DOCKER chain (DNAT
                rewrite) → filter:FORWARD → bridge → veth → container
                eth0 → app. ufw's rules live in INPUT; DNATed traffic to
                a container traverses FORWARD instead, so ufw never sees
                it.
                client:54321─▶eth0:8000─▶PREROUTING─▶DOCKER(DNAT)─▶FORWARD─▶container
             Explanation: 15.6's packet-path diagram, restated.

         Q9: How does adding `127.0.0.1:` to a -p flag change the actual
             iptables rule created?
             A: The DNAT rule's destination-address match narrows from
                0.0.0.0/0 (any interface) to loopback only — packets
                arriving on any OTHER interface never match, so they're
                never DNATed to the container.
             Explanation: 15.6's binding-scope mechanics.

         Q10: If you want a custom firewall rule Docker will never
              silently delete, which iptables chain should you use, and
              why?
              A: DOCKER-USER — Docker guarantees it never flushes or
                 manages that chain itself, unlike DOCKER and
                 DOCKER-ISOLATION-STAGE-1/2, which it rewrites on every
                 daemon restart.
              Explanation: this chapter's Under the Hood deep-dive.

         .vs-prose — Chapter 15 is everything that departs from Chapter
         14's default bridge path: host mode trades all isolation for
         native speed, macvlan/ipvlan hand a container a first-class spot
         on the physical LAN, and overlay stretches one virtual switch
         across Swarm nodes over VXLAN. The chapter's real payoff is
         operational — a fixed four-rung debugging ladder that turns
         "the network is broken" into a rung number, and the iptables
         truth that -p is a kernel DNAT rule living in the DOCKER chain,
         which is exactly why a host-level firewall like ufw can look
         perfectly configured and still never see the traffic it thinks
         it's blocking.

    [F] PART 5 KEY TAKEAWAYS
         ✅ Every Docker network, regardless of driver, is built from the
            same three CNM nouns: sandbox, endpoint, network (Ch13).
         ✅ User-defined bridges are the ONLY ones with embedded DNS
            (127.0.0.11); the default docker0 has none (Ch13).
         ✅ easypj's production posture is two networks, one dual-homed
            service (django), and ZERO published ports on postgres/redis
            (Ch14).
         ✅ EXPOSE documents; only -p/-P/compose ports: create real DNAT
            rules — the difference is metadata versus iptables (Ch14).
         ✅ Exotic drivers (host/macvlan/ipvlan/overlay) trade isolation
            for performance or reach; none of them fit django/postgres in
            Part 5's default posture (Ch15).
         ✅ Every connectivity failure localizes to one of four rungs: is
            it on the network, does DNS resolve, is the port open, what
            does the source's OWN netns actually see (Ch15).
         🎯 DCA relevance: this Part alone covers the entire DCA
            "Networking" domain (15% of the exam) — CNM, drivers, DNS,
            publish semantics, and the security/debugging competencies.

    ⚠️ PART 5 GOTCHAS
         - The single most-asked Docker interview question is Ch13.3's
           demo: names don't resolve on docker0, but do on a user-defined
           bridge — know it cold.
         - "It's just dev" is how -p 5432:5432 ends up reachable from the
           whole internet, ufw rule or not (Ch14, Ch15.6) — ufw's INPUT
           chain never sees DNATed traffic.
         - internal: true blocks egress as well as ingress — decide which
           service needs real internet access before flipping the flag
           (Ch14).
         - host/macvlan modes both trade away something structural
           (isolation, or host-to-container reachability) — never adopt
           them "for a little more speed" without reading the full
           trade-off table first (Ch15).

    ⚡ PART 5 SPEED TIPS
         - Default every `docker network create` to an explicit --subnet
           — renaming or re-subnetting later means recreating the
           network from scratch.
         - Keep the 4-rung ladder (inspect → nslookup → nc -zv →
           netshoot-in-netns) as your FIRST move on any "container can't
           reach container" ticket, before touching a single Dockerfile.

         (sandbox, endpoint, network) and the one fact that resolves the
         most common Docker confusion: only user-defined bridges carry
         the embedded DNS server, never the default docker0. Chapter 14
         spends that vocabulary on easypj specifically, landing on two
         networks, one dual-homed django, and databases with no published
         ports at all — the reference posture every later Part assumes.
         Chapter 15 covers everything that departs from that default

         macvlan/ipvlan when a container needs to be a first-class

PART 6: DOCKER STORAGE — VOLUMES & PERSISTENT DATA                        🟡
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    THINK BEFORE PART 6:
      What runs where?    → the container; the DATA lives in a named volume.
      What talks to what? → container mount point → volume/bind/tmpfs → disk.
      What breaks first?  → `docker rm -v` — one flag deletes volumes too.

    [PART 6 INTRO]
    Every part so far has treated the container as the whole story: build
    it (Part 3), run it (Part 2), compose it (Part 4), network it (Part
    5). Part 6 asks the question all of those parts quietly deferred —
    when a container dies, and every container eventually dies, on
    purpose or by crash, what happens to the DATA it was holding? For
    easypj that is not academic. The `db` container holds every Skills,
    Author, Location, JobPost, and User row jobpost has ever had; the
    `django` container's filesystem holds every uploaded resume and every
    asset `collectstatic` produced. Part 6 is the difference between a
    container restart being a non-event and a container restart being an
    outage.

    By the end of Part 6, easypj's postgres_data, django_media, and
    django_static are named Docker volumes — objects that outlive any
    container mounting them — and you can explain, back up, restore, and
    choose the right persistence mechanism (volume, bind mount, or
    tmpfs) for any new data easypj ever needs to hold.

    🧠 ANALOGY — Part 6 in one picture:
    A container is a hotel room; a volume is a safety-deposit box in the
    hotel's vault. Housekeeping (`docker rm`) clears the room completely
    between guests — fine, because nothing irreplaceable ever lived
    there. The vault box is a separate object with its own key: whatever
    room you're in tonight, the box is reachable, and it survives every
    checkout. Chapters 16-18 are: what a vault box even is (16), which of
    your belongings actually need one (17), and how the hotel's vault is
    built underneath the floor (18).

    [WITHOUT vs WITH PERSISTENT STORAGE — easypj]
         ┌───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┐
         │ WITHOUT persistent storage         │ WITH persistent storage   │
         ├───────────────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┤
         │ `docker compose down` empties the  │ `docker compose down`     │
         │ jobpost database                   │ leaves postgres_data alone│
         │ Every uploaded resume is gone      │ django_media keeps every  │
         │ after a container restart          │ upload across restarts    │
         │ collectstatic output vanishes      │ django_static persists    │
         │ with the django container          │ (or rebuilds instantly)   │
         │ No backup strategy exists — one    │ pg_dump + tar backups     │
         │ bad `rm` is permanent data loss    │ exist AND are test-restored│
         │ Scaling to a 2nd host loses the DB │ NFS/cloud volume drivers  │
         │ unless it also moves by hand       │ let any host reach it     │
         └───────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘
    In short: every row on the right is a `docker compose down` (or
    worse) that easypj now survives without incident.

    [PART 6 SUMMARY + IMPLEMENTATION — read before the chapters]
    Part 6's implementation, end to end: Chapter 16 hands you three real
    mount types (volume, bind mount, tmpfs — npipe is Windows-only
    plumbing, never application data); Chapter 17 assigns each easypj
    data path exactly one of them and proves the assignment survives
    `docker compose down`, a UID mismatch, and a database restore;
    Chapter 18 explains the storage-driver and volume-driver layers a
    volume secretly depends on, so a Swarm rollout in Part 10 doesn't
    surprise you with an empty "local" volume on a new node.
         easypj data path             Chapter 17 decision          Backed by
         ────────────────────         ──────────────────────        ────────
         postgres data dir     ──▶    named volume (17.2)     ──▶   host disk
         django media uploads  ──▶    named volume (17.3)     ──▶   host disk
         django static files   ──▶    named volume, :ro nginx ──▶   (Ch 18)
         decrypted secret       ──▶    tmpfs (17.5)            ──▶   RAM only
         your working copy      ──▶    bind mount (17.4, dev)  ──▶   host disk
    In short: five data categories, three real mount types, one already
    -tested backup — that is the entirety of what Part 6 implements.
Chapter 16: Docker Storage Fundamentals
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Every container you have run so far dies with
    its data intact only by accident — kill it and whatever it wrote is
    gone. Chapter 16 replaces that accident with a deliberate choice:
    volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs, each solving a different persistence
    problem. Skip this chapter and easypj's PostgreSQL data, and every
    user upload, evaporates on the next `docker compose down`.

    [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~60-75 min · 🎯 DCA: Storage
        & Volumes domain (10% of the exam) — a core chapter, not
        supplementary background.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after Chapter 16 you can:
    • State exactly what survives and what dies when a container is
      removed (16.1).
    • Name Docker's four mount types — volume, bind mount, tmpfs,
      npipe — and pick the correct one from a need, not a guess (16.2).
    • Explain why a volume's lifecycle is independent of any container
      that mounts it, and create one with `docker volume create` (16.3).
    • Run all five `docker volume` subcommands (create, ls, inspect,
      rm, prune) and read their output correctly (16.4).
    • Tell an anonymous volume from a named one, and explain why only
      named volumes are safe to rely on long-term (16.3-16.4).
    • Read a `docker volume inspect` Mountpoint and locate a volume's
      real files on the host filesystem (16.4).

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: Chapter 16 is graded directly under the Storage &
        Volumes domain (10%) — volumes vs bind mounts vs tmpfs is exam
        content, not just production hygiene.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 16.1 the ephemeral-container problem -> 16.2 the
        four mount types -> 16.3 volumes in depth -> 16.4 the `docker
