    16.1 The Ephemeral Container Problem
         - Containers are ephemeral: data dies with the container
         - Problem: PostgreSQL data must survive container restarts
         - Problem: User uploads in easypj must persist

         [EPHEMERAL CONTAINER vs PERSISTENT VOLUME]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │              💾 THE EPHEMERAL CONTAINER PROBLEM                            │
         │                                                                          │
         │  WITHOUT VOLUMES (Data dies with container):                             │
         │  ┌─────────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────┐                     │
         │  │ Container: postgres │     │ Container: DELETED  │                     │
         │  │ ┌─────────────────┐ │     │                     │                     │
         │  │ │ /var/lib/       │ │     │  💀 DB GONE!        │                     │
         │  │ │   postgresql/   │ │ ──▶ │  💀 Users GONE!     │                     │
         │  │ │   data/         │ │ rm  │  💀 Orders GONE!    │                     │
         │  │ │   (20 GB DB)    │ │     │  💀 Everything!     │                     │
         │  │ └─────────────────┘ │     └─────────────────────┘                     │
         │  └─────────────────────┘                                                │
         │                                                                          │
         │  WITH VOLUMES (Data survives container):                                 │
         │  ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐                │
         │  │ Container: postgres │         │ Container: DELETED  │                │
         │  │ ┌─────────────────┐ │         │                     │                │
         │  │ │ /var/lib/       │ │         │  Container gone,    │                │
         │  │ │   postgresql/   │ │    ──▶  │  but...             │                │
         │  │ │   data/         │ │   rm    │                     │                │
         │  │ └───────┬─────────┘ │         └─────────────────────┘                │
         │  └─────────┼───────────┘                                               │
         │            │ mount                                                      │
         │            ▼                                                            │
         │  ┌─────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────┐                │
         │  │ 📦 VOLUME: pg_data  │────────▶│ 📦 VOLUME: pg_data  │                │
         │  │ /var/lib/docker/    │  new    │ STILL HERE! ✅      │                │
         │  │ volumes/pg_data/    │  cont.  │ Mount to new        │                │
         │  │ (20 GB, persistent) │         │ container!          │                │
         │  └─────────────────────┘         └─────────────────────┘                │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: State exactly what dies with a container and what a
            volume protects — before you ever lose real easypj data.
         [TECH] A container's writable layer lives inside the container's
            storage-driver directory; `docker rm` deletes that layer along
            with everything the process wrote. The WITHOUT VOLUMES half of
            the diagram above IS this deletion. A volume is a separate,
            named object Docker manages outside that layer — mounting one
            over /var/lib/postgresql/data routes writes there instead, as
            the WITH VOLUMES half of the diagram shows.
         [ANALOGY] A hotel room vs a safety-deposit box: whatever you leave
            in the room (writable layer) gets cleared at checkout (rm); the
            box (volume) sits in the vault regardless of which room you
            book next — same building, independent lifecycle.
         🔬 easypj: `docker run postgres` with no -v, then `docker rm -f`,
            then `docker volume ls` — nothing there; the 20 GB dataset the
            diagram warns about was never anything but container-local.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run postgres WITHOUT a volume, INSERT one row,
            `docker rm -f` it, start a fresh postgres container. Verify:
            the row is gone — you just reproduced the top half of the
            diagram with your own data.
         📊 SUMMARY: containers are disposable compute; volumes are where
            anything that must outlive a container has to live.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker compose down` (no -v) keeps named volumes,
            but `docker compose down -v` deletes them — one flag away from
            the WITHOUT VOLUMES scenario in production.

    16.2 Storage Types Overview
         - Volumes: Managed by Docker (/var/lib/docker/volumes/)
         - Bind mounts: Any host directory mounted into container
         - tmpfs mounts: In-memory only (Linux), never on disk
         - Named pipes (npipe): Windows only

         [4 STORAGE TYPES — VISUAL COMPARISON]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                    💾 DOCKER STORAGE MOUNT TYPES                           │
         │                                                                          │
         │  1. VOLUME (Recommended)           2. BIND MOUNT                         │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐              │
         │  │ Docker manages:      │          │ You manage:          │              │
         │  │ ┌──────────────────┐ │          │ ┌──────────────────┐ │              │
         │  │ │ Container        │ │          │ │ Container        │ │              │
         │  │ │ /app/data ─────┐ │ │          │ │ /app/data ─────┐ │ │              │
         │  │ └────────────────┼─┘ │          │ └────────────────┼─┘ │              │
         │  │                  │   │          │                  │   │              │
         │  │  ┌───────────────▼─┐ │          │  ┌───────────────▼─┐ │              │
         │  │  │ 📦 my-volume    │ │          │  │ 📁 /home/me/    │ │              │
         │  │  │ /var/lib/docker │ │          │  │    data/        │ │              │
         │  │  │ /volumes/...    │ │          │  │ (any host path) │ │              │
         │  │  └────────────────┘ │          │  └────────────────┘ │              │
         │  │  ✅ Managed backup  │          │  ⚠️ Permissions issues│              │
         │  │  ✅ Driver plugins  │          │  ✅ Dev hot-reload   │              │
         │  └──────────────────────┘          └──────────────────────┘              │
         │                                                                          │
         │  3. tmpfs (RAM disk)               4. npipe (Windows only)               │
         │  ┌──────────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────┐              │
         │  │ ┌──────────────────┐ │          │ Windows named pipes  │              │
         │  │ │ Container        │ │          │ for Docker API comm. │              │
         │  │ │ /tmp ───┐       │ │          │ (rarely used)        │              │
         │  │ └─────────┼───────┘ │          └──────────────────────┘              │
         │  │           │         │                                                 │
         │  │  ┌────────▼───────┐ │          [STORAGE TYPE DECISION MATRIX]         │
         │  │  │ 🧠 RAM (tmpfs) │ │          | Type   |Persists|Speed  |Use Case   │
         │  │  │ NEVER on disk! │ │          | Volume |✅ Yes |Fast   |DB data,    │
         │  │  │ Fast, volatile │ │          |        |       |       |uploads     │
         │  │  └────────────────┘ │          | Bind   |✅ Yes |Fast   |Dev reload, │
         │  │  ✅ Secrets/temp    │          |        |       |       |config files│
         │  └──────────────────────┘          | tmpfs  |❌ No  |🚀Fastest|Secrets,  │
         │                                   |        |       |       |temp files │
         │                                   | npipe  |N/A   |N/A    |Windows IPC│
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Pick the correct one of Docker's four mount types for a
            given easypj need, on sight.
         [TECH] The 4 STORAGE TYPES diagram above draws the real split:
            volumes (Docker-managed, under /var/lib/docker/volumes/), bind
            mounts (you pick the host path), tmpfs (RAM only, Linux),
            npipe (Windows IPC, not a data store). Only the first three
            ever hold application data; npipe never does.
         [ANALOGY] Renting a Docker-managed storage unit (volume) vs
            using your own garage (bind mount) vs a whiteboard wiped
            nightly (tmpfs) — each box in the diagram above is one of
            those three real-world containers for your stuff.
         [TABLE: pick the mount — need | type]
            Survive restart, don't care where on disk | volume
            Edit code live from your host editor        | bind mount
            Secret that must never touch disk           | tmpfs
         🔬 easypj: postgres data → volume; `./app:/app` while coding →
            bind mount; a decrypted API key for one request → tmpfs.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: for each easypj directory (media/, static/,
            your working copy, a decrypted secret), name its mount type
            using ONLY the decision table above. Verify against 17.1-17.5.
         📊 SUMMARY: four mount types, three real choices — volume, bind,
            tmpfs — decided by durability and disk-visibility needs.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: bind mounts inherit host file permissions/UID
            exactly — the #1 cause of "permission denied" in a container.

    16.3 Docker Volumes — The Recommended Way
         - What are volumes? (Docker-managed storage)
         - docker volume create my-volume
         - docker run -v my-volume:/data ...
         - Volumes survive container deletion
         - Volume drivers (local, nfs, cloud-specific)

         [VOLUME LIFECYCLE — INDEPENDENT OF CONTAINERS]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                     🔄 VOLUME LIFECYCLE                                   │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ┌─────────┐   create    ┌─────────┐   mount    ┌─────────┐            │
         │  │ Nothing │────────────▶│ 📦Volume│──────────▶│Container│            │
         │  │         │             │ (empty) │            │ uses it │            │
         │  └─────────┘             └────┬────┘            └────┬────┘            │
         │                               │                      │                  │
         │                               │   Container writes   │                  │
         │                               │◄─────────────────────┘                  │
         │                               │                                         │
         │                               │   Container deleted                     │
         │                               │   ┌─────────┐                          │
         │                               │   │Container│ 💀                       │
         │                               │   │ DELETED │                          │
         │                               │   └─────────┘                          │
         │                               │                                         │
         │                               ▼                                         │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐                          │
         │  │ 📦 Volume STILL EXISTS with all data!   │                          │
         │  │ docker volume ls → my-volume            │                          │
         │  │ docker run -v my-volume:/data new-img   │◀── Remount!             │
         │  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘                          │
         │                                                                          │
         │  💡 KEY INSIGHT: Volume lifecycle is COMPLETELY separate from container! │
         │     docker volume rm my-volume ← ONLY way to delete the volume.         │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Explain why a volume's lifecycle is independent of every
            container that ever mounts it.
         [TECH] The VOLUME LIFECYCLE diagram above shows the real sequence:
            `docker volume create` makes an empty object with no owning
            container; `-v name:/path` mounts it; deleting the container
            leaves the volume untouched; only `docker volume rm` removes
            it. Volumes can also be created implicitly by the first `-v`.
         [ANALOGY] A shared storage locker with its own key, not tied to
            any one tenant: tenants (containers) move in and out, the
            locker (volume) and its contents outlast every one of them —
            exactly the "STILL EXISTS" box the diagram ends on.
         🔬 easypj: `docker volume create pgdata`, mount it into postgres,
            `docker rm -f` the container, `docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/
            postgresql/data postgres` again — same rows, new container.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker volume create test`, run alpine with
            `-v test:/data`, write a file, remove the container, run a
            SECOND alpine with the same volume. Verify: `cat /data/file`
            in container #2 prints what container #1 wrote.
         📊 SUMMARY: volumes are first-class Docker objects that outlive
            containers by design — remount, don't recreate, to keep data.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: an anonymous volume (`-v /data`, no name) is just as
            persistent but nearly impossible to find later — always name
            volumes you intend to keep.

    16.4 docker volume Commands
         - docker volume ls (list volumes)
         - docker volume create (create)
         - docker volume inspect (details + mountpoint)
         - docker volume rm (remove)
         - docker volume prune (remove unused)
         [TERMINAL: All volume commands with output examples]


         🎯 GOAL: Run the five `docker volume` subcommands from memory and
            read their output correctly.
         [TERMINAL: the volume command set, drawn]
            $ docker volume create pgdata
            pgdata
            $ docker volume ls
            DRIVER    VOLUME NAME
            local     pgdata
            $ docker volume inspect pgdata
            [{"Mountpoint": "/var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data", ...}]
            $ docker volume rm pgdata
            pgdata
            $ docker volume prune
            WARNING! This will remove all unused local volumes.
            Total reclaimed space: 0B
         [TECH] `inspect` is the command that matters most: it prints the
            real Mountpoint on the host — the ONE place you can `ls` a
            volume's contents without going through a container at all.
         🔬 easypj: `docker volume inspect pgdata` on the host, then
            `sudo ls` that Mountpoint to confirm PostgreSQL's real files
            exist even while every easypj container is stopped.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: create, inspect, and remove a throwaway volume;
            note the Mountpoint path each time. Verify: `docker volume ls`
            returns empty after `rm` — no orphaned entry left behind.
         [DIAGRAM:state — volume lifecycle, drawn]
            CREATED  (docker volume create, or auto via first -v, empty)
               │  docker run -v name:/path ... (mount into a container)
               ▼
            MOUNTED  (≥1 container has it attached, data can change)
               │  docker rm the container(s) that had it mounted
               ▼
            UNMOUNTED  (0 containers attached — data is UNTOUCHED)
               │  docker volume rm name (refuses if still mounted)
               ▼
            REMOVED  (data deleted from /var/lib/docker/volumes/, gone)
         ↺ UNMOUNTED loops straight back to MOUNTED any time — that loop
           IS 16.3's whole point: data outlives any one container.
         easypj: `postgres_data` (17.2) lives almost entirely in that
         MOUNTED ⇄ UNMOUNTED loop — it should never see REMOVED.

         💡 A volume can be MOUNTED into a STOPPED container — "mounted"
            tracks attachment, not whether the container is running. That
            is why `docker volume rm` refuses even for a volume attached
            only to a container you have not started in weeks.

         📊 SUMMARY: create/ls/inspect/rm/prune cover the full volume
            lifecycle from the CLI; inspect is your window into the host.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker volume prune` deletes EVERY unused volume,
            not just Docker's guesses — a stopped-but-not-removed backup
            container's volume is safe, but nothing else is.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how the daemon actually tracks a volume
    Every named volume is really two things on disk: a metadata record
    the daemon keeps (which driver owns it, when it was created, which
    containers currently reference it) and the data directory itself,
    always at `/var/lib/docker/volumes/<name>/_data` for the `local`
    driver. `docker volume inspect` (16.4) prints exactly that
    Mountpoint because there is no path translation left to hide.
         Container mount request: -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
              │
              ▼
         dockerd's volume subsystem
              │  1. look up "pgdata" in its local metadata store
              │  2. if missing, driver="local" creates it right here:
              ▼
         /var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data   (the real files live here)
              │
              ▼
         bind-mounted into the container's mount namespace at
         /var/lib/postgresql/data — the container's kernel-level view
         IS this host directory, not a copy of it.
    Bind mounts skip the metadata step entirely — the kernel just maps a
    host path directly into the container's mount namespace, which is
    why `docker volume ls` never lists bind mounts: they were never
    Docker-managed objects to begin with.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ✅ Containers are disposable compute; anything that must outlive one
       belongs in a volume, never in the writable layer.
    ✅ Docker has four mount types — volume, bind mount, tmpfs, npipe —
       and only the first three ever hold real application data.
    ✅ A volume's lifecycle is independent of any container: create,
       mount, unmount, remount, and only `docker volume rm` deletes it.
    ✅ Anonymous volumes persist exactly like named ones but are nearly
       impossible to find again — name everything you intend to keep.
    ✅ `docker volume inspect` is your window into the host filesystem —
       the Mountpoint is a real, `ls`-able path.
    ✅ `docker volume prune` deletes EVERY unused local volume, not a
       curated subset — read its warning before confirming.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    • `docker compose down -v` deletes named volumes; plain `down` does
      not — one flag is the entire difference between safe and gone.
    • Bind mounts inherit host file permissions/UID exactly — the #1
      source of "permission denied" errors inside a container.
    • An anonymous volume (`-v /data`, no name) still needs `docker
      volume rm <hash>` to clean up — it just never gets an easy name.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    • `docker volume inspect <name> -f '{{.Mountpoint}}'` prints just the
      path — skip reading the full JSON blob by eye.
    • `docker volume ls -f dangling=true` lists only unused volumes
      BEFORE you prune, so you know exactly what is about to be deleted.

    🔑 COMMANDS
        docker volume create pgdata          # make a named volume
        docker volume ls                     # list all volumes
        docker volume inspect pgdata         # show driver + Mountpoint
        docker volume rm pgdata              # delete (fails if in use)
        docker volume prune                  # delete ALL unused volumes
        docker run -v pgdata:/data alpine    # mount a named volume
        docker run -v /data alpine           # mount an ANONYMOUS volume
        docker run -v "$(pwd)":/app alpine   # bind mount (host path=source)

    🧪 DRILL (5 min): create a volume named `drillvol`, run alpine with
        it mounted at /data, write one file, remove the container, run a
        SECOND alpine with the same volume mounted. `cat` the file. Stop
        the clock the moment you see its contents print.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 16)

    Q1: You run a postgres container with no `-v` flag, insert rows,
        then `docker rm -f` it. Are the rows recoverable?
        A: No. With no volume, PostgreSQL's data directory lives only in
        the container's writable layer, which `docker rm` deletes along
        with the container.
        Explanation: this is the WITHOUT VOLUMES half of 16.1's diagram —
        nothing outside the container's storage-driver layer ever held
        the data, so there is nothing left to recover.

    Q2: What are Docker's four mount types, and which of them never
        holds application data?
        A: volume, bind mount, tmpfs, and npipe. npipe never holds
        application data — it is Windows-only IPC plumbing, not storage.
        Explanation:
            | Type   | Persists | Speed   | Typical use            |
            | volume | Yes      | Fast    | DB data, uploads       |
            | bind   | Yes      | Fast    | Dev hot-reload, config |
            | tmpfs  | No       | Fastest | Secrets, temp files    |
            | npipe  | N/A      | N/A     | Windows daemon IPC     |

    Q3: Why is a bind mount the wrong default for a database's data
        directory even though it also "persists"?
        A: It works, but it ties the container to the host's exact
        filesystem layout and inherits host file permissions/UID
        exactly — the #1 cause of container permission errors.
        Explanation: 16.2's decision table routes "survive restart,
        don't care where on disk" to a volume specifically because
        Docker manages the path and permissions for you.

    Q4: You mount the same named volume into two different containers,
        one after the other. What does the second container see?
        A: Whatever the first container wrote — the volume's data is
        independent of both containers.
        Explanation: this is 16.3's VOLUME LIFECYCLE diagram in miniature:
             create → mount → write → rm container → STILL EXISTS → remount
        The volume never re-enters existence; it simply never left.

    Q5: What is the difference between a named volume and an anonymous
        volume, in terms of what happens to your data?
        A: Nothing — both persist identically. The only difference is
        that a named volume has a human-readable name; an anonymous one
        only has a long hash.
        Explanation: 16.3's gotcha exists precisely because anonymous
        volumes are just as durable as named ones, only harder to manage.

    Q6: What does `docker volume inspect pgdata` show that `docker
        volume ls` does not?
        A: The Mountpoint — the real host path
        (`/var/lib/docker/volumes/pgdata/_data`) where the volume's files
        actually live, plus driver and label metadata.
        Explanation: `ls` only lists names and drivers; `inspect` lets
        you `ls` the real files from the host directly, no container
        needed.

    Q7: Does plain `docker compose down` delete named volumes defined
        under a compose file's top-level `volumes:` key?
        A: No. Named volumes survive; only containers and the default
        network are removed.
        Explanation: 16.1's closing gotcha is exactly this — `docker
        compose down -v` is the one-flag difference that deletes them.

    Q8: A volume is currently mounted only into a container you stopped
        (not removed) three weeks ago. Can you `docker volume rm` it?
        A: No — Docker refuses because the volume is still "mounted"
        (attached), even though the container is not running.
        Explanation: 16.4's state diagram tracks MOUNTED vs UNMOUNTED by
        attachment, not by running state — remove the container first.

    Q9: What does `docker volume prune` actually delete?
        A: EVERY volume with zero containers currently referencing it —
        not a curated guess, all of them.
        Explanation: 16.4's gotcha warns exactly about this — a volume
        you meant to keep but forgot to attach anywhere is fair game.

    Q10: You need a directory that changes as fast as possible and must
         NEVER touch disk, even briefly. Which mount type do you reach
         for, and why not a volume?
         A: tmpfs — it is backed by RAM only. A volume still round-trips
         through the storage driver to real disk (or the VM disk on
         Desktop), which tmpfs skips entirely.
         Explanation: 16.2's four-way comparison marks tmpfs as the only
         type explicitly "never on disk."

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
         ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │            💾 CHAPTER 16 — THE FOUR MOUNT TYPES              │
         │                                                              │
         │   docker rm  ──▶  writable layer: GONE   (16.1)              │
         │                                                              │
         │   ┌────────┐  ┌───────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌───────┐          │
         │   │ VOLUME │  │BIND MOUNT │  │ tmpfs  │  │ npipe │          │
         │   │Docker- │  │you-       │  │RAM     │  │Windows│          │
         │   │managed │  │managed    │  │only    │  │IPC only│         │
         │   │persist │  │persist    │  │no persist│ │  N/A  │          │
         │   └────────┘  └───────────┘  └────────┘  └───────┘          │
         │        │                                                     │
         │        ▼                                                     │
         │   create → mount → write → container dies → STILL THERE     │
         │   (16.3/16.4 volume lifecycle — independent of any container)│
         └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         .vs-prose — Chapter 16 draws one hard line: a container's
         writable layer dies with `docker rm`, full stop, but a volume is
         a separate Docker-managed object whose lifecycle you control
         explicitly with `docker volume create`/`rm`. Bind mounts and
         tmpfs round out the other two real choices — host-path-managed
         persistence and RAM-only non-persistence — while npipe is
         Windows plumbing, not a data store. Chapter 17 spends its entire
         length deciding which of these four every easypj directory gets.

Chapter 17: Persistent Data for easypj
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Chapter 16 gave you three storage tools;
    this chapter decides which easypj directory gets which one, and
    proves each choice under real failure. Skip it and the result stays
    vague instead of exact: postgres_data on the DB, scoped media and
    static volumes, dev-only bind mounts that never reach production,
    and a backup you have actually restored at least once.

    [A] META: 🟡 Intermediate · ⏱️ ~90-120 min (hands-on
        heavy) · 🎯 DCA: Storage & Volumes domain (10%) — this chapter is
        where the domain's "backup/restore patterns for volumes"
        objective actually lives.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after Chapter 17 you can:
    • Sort any easypj data path into "irreplaceable" or "rebuildable"
      and justify the call (17.1).
    • Mount a named volume onto PostgreSQL's data directory so `docker
      compose down` never touches jobpost's rows (17.2).
    • Give Django media uploads and collected static files their own
      volumes, with nginx reading django_static read-only (17.3).
    • Use a bind mount for live code reload in dev without letting that
      habit reach production (17.4).
    • Reach for tmpfs, correctly, for one specific class of secret or
      scratch data (17.5).
    • Run a real `pg_dump`-based backup AND restore cycle for jobpost,
      not just a tar of the raw data directory (17.6).
    • Automate that backup on a schedule, retain N days, and prove it
      restorable with a periodic test (17.7).

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: Chapter 17 is the applied half of the Storage &
        Volumes domain (10%) — the exam expects real volume configuration
        on real services and sound backup/restore reasoning, not just
        the vocabulary Chapter 16 introduced.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 17.1 decide what must persist -> 17.2 volume the
        database -> 17.3 volume Django's media/static -> 17.4 bind-mount
        for dev only -> 17.5 tmpfs for secrets -> 17.6 pg_dump backup/
        restore -> 17.7 automate and prove the backup actually works.
    17.1 What Needs to Persist in easypj?
         - PostgreSQL data directory (/var/lib/postgresql/data)
         - Django media files (user uploads)
         - Django static files (collected by collectstatic)
         - Application logs
         [DATA MAP: Which directories need persistence]

         🎯 GOAL: Name the four easypj data categories and the ONE
            question that decides each one's mount type.
         [TABLE: easypj data map — data | must persist? | where]
            PostgreSQL data dir  | yes, always | named volume (17.2)
            Django media uploads | yes, always | named volume (17.3)
            Django static files  | rebuildable | named volume (17.3)
            Application logs     | usually     | volume or log driver
         [TECH] "Must persist" means: would losing it on the next
            `docker rm` be a data-loss incident (DB rows, user uploads)
            or just a rebuild step (collectstatic output, cached logs)?
            Only the first category is non-negotiable.
         [ANALOGY] Sorting moving boxes into "irreplaceable" (family
            photos → DB rows, uploads) vs "can be bought again"
            (furniture from a catalog → generated static files).
         🔬 easypj: delete django_static and one `collectstatic` rebuilds
            it; delete postgres_data and every JobPost, Skills, Author,
            Location, and User row is gone with no rebuild possible.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: list every path easypj writes to at runtime
            and mark each irreplaceable or rebuildable. Verify: your list
            matches the four rows in the table above.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — easypj containers ─▶ persistent path]
            postgres ─▶ postgres_data ─▶ /var/lib/postgresql/data
              (rows: Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, User — 17.2)
            django   ─▶ django_media  ─▶ /app/media  (uploads, 17.3)
            django   ─▶ django_static ─▶ /app/static (generated, 17.3)
            nginx    ─▶ django_static ─▶ /app/static (:ro, reads only)
            redis    ─▶ (none — cache only, nothing here worth keeping)

         💡 redis has NO volume on purpose — 17.1's table already marks
            cache data as disposable; giving redis a volume would just be
            extra disk I/O for data you already decided to lose.

         📊 SUMMARY: irreplaceable data gets a volume without debate;
            rebuildable output gets one anyway, but for convenience.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: application logs feel disposable until an incident
            review needs last week's — decide log retention on purpose,
            not by accident, in Chapter 17.6.

    17.2 Volume Setup for PostgreSQL
         - Named volume: postgres_data
         - Mount: /var/lib/postgresql/data
         - Backup strategy: docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data alpine tar czf - /data > backup.tar.gz
         [CODE: compose.yaml with PostgreSQL volume]
         [BACKUP/RESTORE COMMANDS]

         🎯 GOAL: Mount a named volume onto PostgreSQL's data directory so
            `docker compose down` never touches jobpost's rows.
         [CODE: compose.yaml — postgres_data volume, drawn]
            services:
              db:
                image: postgres:16
                environment:
                  POSTGRES_DB: jobpost
                  POSTGRES_USER: jobpost_user
                volumes:
                  - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
            volumes:
              postgres_data:
         [TECH] `postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data` is the ONE mount
            that matters — that path is where postgres's own data files
            live; everything else in the container is disposable image
            content, rebuildable from `postgres:16` at any time.
         [ANALOGY] The volume is the filing cabinet; the postgres
            container is just this month's clerk operating it — replace
            the clerk (docker rm db), hire a new one, cabinet untouched.
         [TERMINAL: backup / restore commands, drawn]
            $ docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
                alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tar.gz -C /data .
            $ docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
                alpine tar xzf /backup/pgdata.tar.gz -C /data
         🔬 easypj: after this change, `docker compose down && docker
            compose up -d` restarts the whole stack — Skills, Author,
            Location, JobPost, and User rows survive untouched.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker compose down`, `docker compose up -d`,
            then `docker compose exec db psql -U jobpost_user -d jobpost
            -c "SELECT count(*) FROM jobpost_jobpost;"`. Verify: the count
            matches what it was before you brought the stack down.
         📊 SUMMARY: one named volume on one path turns PostgreSQL from
            disposable to durable — the container above it stays stateless.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: compose prefixes volume names with the PROJECT
            name (`<dir>_postgres_data`) unless you set `name:
            postgres_data` explicitly under the top-level volumes:.

    17.3 Volume Setup for Django Media & Static
         - Named volume: django_media, django_static
         - Mount: /app/media, /app/static
         - Nginx serving static files from volume
         [CODE: compose.yaml with all volumes]

         🎯 GOAL: Give Django media uploads and collected static files the
            same durability postgres just got — without conflating them.
         [CODE: compose.yaml — django_media & django_static, drawn]
            services:
              django:
                volumes:
                  - django_media:/app/media
                  - django_static:/app/static
              nginx:
                volumes:
                  - django_static:/app/static:ro
            volumes:
              postgres_data:
              django_media:
              django_static:
         [TECH] django_static is mounted :ro into nginx — nginx only ever
            READS what `collectstatic` wrote into the SAME volume from
            the django container; two services, one volume, one direction.
         [ANALOGY] A shared print tray: Django prints (writes) pages into
            it, nginx only ever picks pages up (reads) — the :ro flag is
            the label on nginx's side saying "no writing here".
         🔬 easypj: a user's uploaded resume PDF lands in django_media via
            a FileField; nginx never touches media — Django (or a signed
            URL) serves that path directly.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: upload a file through easypj's admin, `docker
            volume inspect django_media` for its Mountpoint, `sudo ls` it
            on the host. Verify: the uploaded filename appears there.
         📊 SUMMARY: three named volumes now cover DB rows, user uploads,
            and generated static assets — none of it lives in a container.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: skipping `:ro` on nginx's static mount doesn't break
            anything today, but it lets a compromised nginx write into a
            path Django trusts — least privilege, even on volumes.

    17.4 Bind Mounts for Development
         - Live code reload: -v .:/app (mount project root)
         - Why not in production
         - Permissions issues (especially on Linux)
         - :ro flag (read-only mount)
         [CODE: dev compose override with bind mounts]

         🎯 GOAL: Get live code reload in dev without ever baking that
            habit into the production image.
         [CODE: compose.override.yaml — dev bind mount, drawn]
            services:
              django:
                volumes:
                  - .:/app                  # live host code, read-write
                  - django_media:/app/media
                command: python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000
         [TECH] compose.override.yaml auto-merges over compose.yaml on
            plain `docker compose up` (12.2's file-merge rules) — the
            bind mount and dev command apply locally, never in a prod
            build where this file is intentionally absent.
         [ANALOGY] A whiteboard clipped over the framed production poster:
            erase and redraw all day (bind mount), then unclip it (deploy
            without the override) and the original poster is untouched.
         🔬 easypj: edit views.py in your editor, runserver inside the
            container sees the change immediately — no rebuild, no
            `docker cp`, because .:/app IS your working directory.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: with the override active, change a Django
            template's text, refresh the browser. Verify: the new text
            appears with no `docker compose build` in between.
         📊 SUMMARY: bind mounts trade isolation for iteration speed — the
            right trade in dev, the wrong one in prod (5.2's .dockerignore
            already blocks dev-only mounts from leaking into an image).
            ⚠️ Gotcha: on Linux, files the container writes appear owned
            by the CONTAINER's UID on your host — mismatched UIDs between
            image and host user are the #1 "why can't I edit this" bug.

    17.5 tmpfs Mounts — In-Memory Storage
         - What is tmpfs? (RAM-based, never written to disk)
         - Use case: temporary cache, secrets that must not hit disk
         - --tmpfs /tmp:exec (allow execution)
         - Performance comparison: tmpfs vs volume vs bind mount
         [TABLE: tmpfs use cases and limitations]

         🎯 GOAL: Decide, without hesitating, when tmpfs beats a volume
            for one specific easypj value.
         [TABLE: tmpfs — use case | limitation]
            Decrypted DB creds for one process | gone on container stop
            Session cache faster than a volume | capped by --tmpfs-size
            Scratch space for image processing  | counts against host RAM
         [TECH] tmpfs is a RAM-backed filesystem the KERNEL exposes — it
            never touches the storage driver or the host disk at all;
            `--tmpfs /tmp:size=64m` caps it so one runaway write can't
            exhaust host memory.
         [ANALOGY] A whiteboard, not a notebook: fast to write on, but
            wiped the instant the room (container) is vacated — nothing
            written there was ever meant to be found later.
         🔬 easypj: mounting `--tmpfs /run/secrets:size=1m` for a
            decrypted DATABASE_URL keeps it out of both the image layer
            and any volume backup that might leak it.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run
            `docker run --tmpfs /tmp:size=16m alpine df -h /tmp`.
            Verify: /tmp shows filesystem type tmpfs sized 16m, not the
            container's overlay root.
         [TABLE: read/write speed — tmpfs vs volume vs bind, approx.]
         | Mount type | Backing store          | Linux host  | Desktop VM  |
         | tmpfs      | RAM (kernel), no disk  | fastest     | fastest     |
         | volume     | host/VM disk, overlay2 | near-native | near-native |
         | bind mount | host disk, direct      | near-native | 5-20x slower|
         easypj: `/run/secrets` (tmpfs) and `postgres_data` (volume) never
         feel this gap; a `.:/app` bind mount (17.4) is exactly where
         Desktop's per-file overhead shows up during pip installs.

         💡 On Docker Desktop, some teams dodge the bind-mount penalty by
            mounting the repo once, then copying it into a named volume
            before running tests or builds — trading one slow copy for a
            fast volume for the rest of the run.

         📊 SUMMARY: tmpfs trades persistence for speed and secrecy —
            perfect for secrets and scratch space, wrong for anything
            easypj needs tomorrow.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: tmpfs on Docker Desktop for Windows isn't native
            Linux tmpfs — it's backed by the Desktop VM's RAM, not the
            host you think you have.

    17.6 Backup & Restore Strategies
         - Volume backup: docker run --rm -v vol:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/vol.tar.gz -C /data .
         - Volume restore: reverse the process
         - Database-specific: pg_dump inside container
         - Automated backup with CronJobs
         [TERMINAL: Complete backup/restore workflow]


         🎯 GOAL: Run one real pg_dump-based backup and restore cycle for
            jobpost end to end, not just tar the raw data files.
         [TERMINAL: pg_dump backup/restore workflow, drawn]
            $ docker compose exec db pg_dump -U jobpost_user jobpost \
                > jobpost_backup.sql
            $ ls -lh jobpost_backup.sql
            -rw-r--r-- 1 you you 42K jobpost_backup.sql
            $ docker compose exec -T db psql -U jobpost_user jobpost \
                < jobpost_backup.sql
         [TECH] `pg_dump` produces a logical, version-portable SQL dump —
            unlike 17.2's `tar` of the raw data directory, this restores
            cleanly onto a DIFFERENT postgres minor version and can target
            a brand-new, empty database.
         [ANALOGY] A recipe card vs a frozen dish: the tar backup (17.2)
            is the frozen meal — only reheats in an identical oven; the
            pg_dump SQL is the recipe — any working kitchen can cook it.
         🔬 easypj: `pg_dump -U jobpost_user jobpost` captures every row
            across Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User in one
            portable .sql file you can commit to encrypted backup storage.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: dump jobpost, drop and recreate the database,
            restore the dump. Verify: `SELECT count(*) FROM
            jobpost_jobpost;` returns the same number as before the drop.
         📊 SUMMARY: tar the volume for fast whole-disk snapshots; pg_dump
            for portable, restorable, version-safe database backups.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `psql < dump.sql` needs `-T` on `docker compose
            exec` (disable pseudo-TTY) or the piped stdin silently fails.

    17.7 Automated Backups — cron + pg_dump Pattern
         - Host cron vs a dedicated backup sidecar container that wakes
           on a schedule (a sidecar travels with the compose stack; host
           cron does not)
         - `pg_dump | gzip` streamed straight to a timestamped file on a
           mounted backup volume — never written inside the ephemeral
           database container itself
         - Retention policy: keep the last N days, prune older archives
           automatically so the backup volume never grows unbounded
         - The RESTORE drill: a backup nobody has restored is not a
           backup — schedule a periodic test restore into a throwaway
           postgres container and diff the row counts

         🎯 GOAL: Stand up an automated, retained, and PROVEN-restorable
            backup for easypj's PostgreSQL data.
         [TECH] Two valid schedulers: host cron calling `docker exec db
            pg_dump ...` from outside, or a sidecar service in
            compose.yaml running its own loop over the compose network —
            the sidecar deploys with the stack, host cron does not.
            Either way, `pg_dump` streams SQL to stdout; piping through
            gzip before it touches disk keeps a growing jobpost
            database's backups small.
         [ANALOGY] A fire drill, not a fire extinguisher on the wall: an
            extinguisher (backup file) never test-fired might be empty.
            The RESTORE drill is pulling the pin once a month on purpose,
            on a THROWAWAY building, to prove it still sprays.
         [CODE: sidecar backup service in compose.yaml, drawn]
            services:
              db-backup:
                image: postgres:16
                depends_on: [db]
                environment:
                  PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
                volumes:
                  - ./backups:/backups
                entrypoint: >
                  sh -c "while true; do
                  pg_dump -h db -U jobpost_user jobpost |
                  gzip > /backups/jobpost_$(date +%F_%H%M).sql.gz;
                  find /backups -name '*.sql.gz' -mtime +7 -delete;
                  sleep 86400; done"
         🔬 easypj: the service above dumps the jobpost database (Skills,
            Author, Location, JobPost, and User tables) daily, gzips it
            into ./backups on the host, and prunes anything past 7 days
            with `find -mtime +7` — a three-line retention policy.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run db-backup once by hand (`docker compose
            run --rm db-backup`), then RESTORE it into a fresh container:
            `gunzip -c backups/latest.sql.gz | docker exec -i newpg psql
            -U jobpost_user jobpost`. Verify: `SELECT count(*) FROM
            jobpost_jobpost;` matches the original database.
         📊 SUMMARY: schedule the dump, compress it, prune old copies,
            and — the step everyone skips — actually restore one on a
            recurring basis.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a backup volume on the SAME Docker host as the
            database is not disaster recovery — one disk failure takes
            both; ship backups off-host (S3, another server) for real DR.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how Compose actually names the volume on disk
    When compose.yaml declares a service volume as `postgres_data:/var/
    lib/postgresql/data`, "postgres_data" is not the final volume name on
    disk — Compose prefixes it with the PROJECT name (the directory name,
    or `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME`/`-p` override) unless the top-level
    `volumes:` entry sets `name:` explicitly. This is exactly 17.2's
    gotcha: two unrelated projects both naming a volume `postgres_data`
    never collide, because they resolve to different real names.
         compose.yaml (project dir: "easypj")
              service volume ref: postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
                          │
                          ▼
              Compose resolves the top-level `volumes:` entry
                          │
              ┌───────────┴────────────────┐
              │ no `name:` override        │  `name: postgres_data` set
              ▼                             ▼
        real volume = "easypj_postgres_data"  real volume = "postgres_data"
        (docker volume ls shows THIS)         (docker volume ls shows THIS)
    Either way, `docker compose down` (no -v) never touches the volume
    object regardless of its resolved name — the prefixing only affects
    how you would reference it with plain `docker volume` commands
    OUTSIDE of Compose.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ✅ Sort data first, mount second: irreplaceable data (DB rows, user
       uploads) always gets a volume; rebuildable output (static files)
       gets one too, but for convenience, not survival.
    ✅ postgres_data mounts onto exactly one path that matters:
       /var/lib/postgresql/data — everything else in that container is
       disposable image content.
    ✅ django_static is shared between django (writes) and nginx (reads
       :ro) — one volume, one direction, least privilege enforced by the
       mount flag itself.
    ✅ Bind mounts are a dev-only convenience (compose.override.yaml);
       they never belong in the production image or a prod compose file.
    ✅ tmpfs is for the one class of data that must never survive even
       briefly on disk — decrypted secrets, not application state.
    ✅ pg_dump produces a portable, version-safe SQL backup; a raw tar of
       the volume only reheats on an identical postgres version.
    ✅ An untested backup is not a backup — schedule the restore drill,
       not just the dump.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    • Compose prefixes volume names with the project name unless `name:`
      is set explicitly under the top-level `volumes:` key.
    • On Linux, files a bind-mounted container writes appear owned by
      the CONTAINER's UID on the host — a UID mismatch is the #1 "why
      can't I edit this" bug in dev.
    • `psql < dump.sql` through `docker compose exec` needs `-T` to
      disable the pseudo-TTY, or piped stdin silently fails.
    • A backup volume on the SAME host as the database is not disaster
      recovery — ship it off-host before calling it "backed up."

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    • `docker compose exec -T db pg_dump ...` — add `-T` up front for any
      piped exec, not just restores, to avoid TTY surprises.
    • Alias a one-line backup: `alias pjbackup='docker compose exec -T db
      pg_dump -U jobpost_user jobpost | gzip > backup_$(date +%F).sql.gz'`

    🔑 COMMANDS
        docker compose exec db pg_dump -U jobpost_user jobpost > b.sql   # backup
        docker compose exec -T db psql -U jobpost_user jobpost < b.sql   # restore
        docker run --rm -v postgres_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup \
          alpine tar czf /backup/pgdata.tar.gz -C /data .                # raw tar backup
        docker volume inspect django_media -f '{{.Mountpoint}}'          # find uploads on host
        docker compose run --rm db-backup                                # run backup sidecar once
        docker compose up -d                                             # applies override automatically

    🧪 DRILL (10 min): `docker compose exec db pg_dump -U jobpost_user
        jobpost > drill.sql`, drop and recreate the jobpost database,
        restore drill.sql, then re-run 17.6's row-count query. Stop the
        clock once the count matches.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 17)

    Q1: Which easypj data path is non-negotiable to persist, and which
        is merely convenient?
        A: PostgreSQL's data directory is non-negotiable — losing it
        loses every Skills, Author, Location, JobPost, and User row.
        Django's collected static files are convenient — losing them
        costs one `collectstatic` re-run.
        Explanation: 17.1's data map draws exactly this line:
            | Path                       | Must persist? |
            | postgres data dir          | Yes, always   |
            | django_static (generated)  | Rebuildable   |

    Q2: What single path does the `postgres_data` volume mount onto, and
        why does nothing else in that container need a volume?
        A: /var/lib/postgresql/data. Everything else in the postgres
        container is image content, rebuildable from `postgres:16` at
        any time.
        Explanation: 17.2's compose.yaml mounts exactly this one path —
        mounting more would just be unnecessary extra durability.

    Q3: Why is django_static mounted `:ro` into nginx but read-write
        into django?
        A: Django is the only service that WRITES static files (via
        collectstatic); nginx only ever needs to READ them to serve.
        Explanation:
            django (write) ──▶ django_static (volume) ──▶ nginx (:ro, read-only)
        17.3's gotcha calls this out directly — skipping `:ro` doesn't
        break anything today but violates least privilege if nginx is
        ever compromised.

    Q4: You edit a Django template on your host while the dev container
        runs with a bind mount active. Do you need to rebuild the image
        to see the change?
        A: No — the bind mount means the container's /app IS your
        working directory; runserver picks it up immediately.
        Explanation: 17.4's compose.override.yaml example is precisely
        this — `.:/app` plus `runserver`, no `docker cp`, no rebuild.

    Q5: A file the container wrote through a bind mount now appears
        owned by a strange numeric UID on your host. What caused it?
        A: The container process's UID (not necessarily matching your
        host user's UID) wrote the file directly onto the host path.
        Explanation: 17.4's gotcha names this the #1 "why can't I edit
        this" bug — bind mounts inherit host permissions exactly, in
        both directions.

    Q6: Why keep a decrypted DATABASE_URL in a tmpfs mount instead of a
        named volume?
        A: tmpfs never touches disk or the storage driver, so the
        decrypted value cannot leak into a volume backup or an image
        layer; it disappears the moment the container stops.
        Explanation: 17.5 makes this exact case for `/run/secrets`.

    Q7: What can a `pg_dump` backup do that a raw `tar` of postgres_data
        cannot?
        A: Restore cleanly onto a DIFFERENT postgres minor version, or
        into a brand-new empty database — the tar only reheats on an
        identical setup.
        Explanation: 17.6's recipe-card-vs-frozen-meal analogy is built
        on exactly this distinction.

    Q8: Your `psql < dump.sql` restore through `docker compose exec`
        hangs or silently does nothing. What flag did you forget?
        A: `-T`, to disable the pseudo-TTY that `exec` allocates by
        default — piped stdin needs it disabled.
        Explanation: 17.6's gotcha names this exact failure mode.

    Q9: What is the difference between scheduling backups with host cron
        versus a db-backup sidecar service in compose.yaml?
        A: A sidecar deploys and travels WITH the compose stack; host
        cron lives outside it and must be set up separately per host.
        Explanation: 17.7 lists both as valid, but only the sidecar is
        guaranteed present wherever the stack is deployed.

    Q10: Why is a daily jobpost backup sitting only in ./backups on the
         SAME Docker host not real disaster recovery?
         A: One disk failure destroys the live database AND every local
         backup at once — they share the same failure domain.
         Explanation: 17.7's closing gotcha requires shipping backups
         off-host (S3, another server) for that reason.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │        📦 CHAPTER 17 — easypj's STORAGE ASSIGNMENTS            │
         │                                                                │
         │  postgres ──▶ postgres_data (volume) ──▶ DB rows     (17.2)   │
         │  django   ──▶ django_media  (volume) ──▶ uploads     (17.3)   │
         │  django   ──▶ django_static (volume) ──▶ generated   (17.3)   │
         │  nginx    ──▶ django_static (:ro)     ──▶ reads only (17.3)   │
         │  dev only ──▶ .:/app (bind mount)     ──▶ live reload(17.4)   │
         │  secrets  ──▶ /run/secrets (tmpfs)    ──▶ RAM only   (17.5)   │
         │                                                                │
         │  pg_dump → gzip → retained N days → TEST-RESTORED (17.6/17.7)│
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         .vs-prose — Chapter 17 turns Chapter 16's four abstract mount
         types into six concrete decisions for easypj: the database and
         user uploads get durable named volumes, static files get a
         volume shared read-only with nginx, dev convenience gets a bind
         mount that never reaches production, and one decrypted secret
         gets tmpfs. The chapter doesn't stop at "it's backed up" — 17.7
         insists the backup has actually been restored at least once
         before it counts.

Chapter 18: Advanced Storage Topics
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Volumes (Chapters 16-17) solved DATA
    persistence; this chapter opens the box underneath — how Docker
    itself stores image layers and a container's writable layer on
    disk. Skip it and two real incidents have no explanation: a host
    filesystem change wiping every image, and one file edit taking
    seconds instead of milliseconds — both trace to the mechanics here.

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~60-75 min · 🎯 DCA: Storage &
        Volumes domain (10%), overlapping Installation & Configuration
        (15%) — storage drivers appear explicitly under both domain maps.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after Chapter 18 you can:
    • Name Docker's default storage driver, explain why it replaced
      aufs/devicemapper, and read the active driver off a running daemon
      (18.1).
    • Distinguish a STORAGE driver (image/container layers) from a
      VOLUME driver (where volume data physically lives) (18.1-18.2).
    • Choose `local` vs `nfs` vs a cloud volume driver based on whether
      storage must be reachable from more than one host (18.2).
    • Create and mount an NFS-backed volume, and state its main
      performance trade-off (18.3).
    • Explain overlay2's LowerDir/UpperDir/WorkDir/MergedDir model and
      predict which layer a given file edit lands in (18.4).
    • Read `docker diff` output and connect what it reports back to
      copy-on-write (18.4).

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: storage drivers are listed explicitly under BOTH
        the Storage & Volumes domain (10%, "storage drivers") and the
        Installation & Configuration domain (15%, "daemon configuration,
        storage drivers") — Chapter 18 is graded twice over.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 18.1 storage drivers (image/container layers) ->
        18.2 volume drivers (local/nfs/cloud) -> 18.3 NFS volumes in
        practice -> 18.4 overlay2 internals and copy-on-write.
    18.1 Storage Drivers (Overlay2, aufs, etc.)
         - What is a storage driver? (manages image layers and container filesystem)
         - overlay2: Default, best performance, recommended
         - aufs, devicemapper, btrfs, zfs: legacy/niche
         - docker info | grep "Storage Driver"
         [TABLE: Storage driver comparison]

         🎯 GOAL: Name the default storage driver, say why it won, and
            read it back out of a running daemon.
         [TABLE: storage driver comparison — driver | status]
            overlay2      | default since Docker 18.09, best all-round
            aufs          | legacy, older kernels only, overlay2 replaced it
            devicemapper  | legacy CentOS/RHEL path, slower, more fragile
            btrfs / zfs   | niche, needs that host filesystem specifically
         [TECH] A storage driver manages how IMAGE LAYERS and a
            container's writable layer are stored and merged on disk —
            it is orthogonal to volumes (16.3), which bypass it entirely.
            overlay2 uses the kernel's native OverlayFS — no extra kernel
            module, which is why it displaced aufs/devicemapper.
         [ANALOGY] The storage driver is the warehouse's shelving system;
            volumes are a separate locker room down the hall — reshelving
            the warehouse (changing storage drivers) never touches what's
            in the lockers.
         🔬 easypj: whichever driver is active, `postgres_data` (a named
            volume) is completely unaffected — only easypj's own IMAGE
            layers and its container's writable layer go through it.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `docker info | grep "Storage Driver"`.
            Verify: it prints `overlay2` on any current Docker install —
            anything else is worth investigating, not assuming.
         📊 SUMMARY: overlay2 is the correct default almost everywhere;
            legacy drivers exist for legacy kernels, not new decisions.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: changing storage drivers wipes ALL local images and
            containers (each keeps its own on-disk layout) — named
            volumes under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ are untouched by this.

    18.2 Volume Drivers & Plugins
         - Local driver (default)
         - NFS driver (network file system)
         - Cloud drivers: AWS EBS, Azure Disk, GCE Persistent Disk
         - Third-party: REX-Ray, Portworx, NetApp
         [TABLE: Volume driver comparison — persistence, performance, cloud]

         🎯 GOAL: Explain what a volume DRIVER changes vs a storage driver,
            and when easypj would ever need one besides `local`.
         [TABLE: volume driver comparison — driver | persists beyond host]
            local (default)      | no — lives on this one Docker host
            nfs                  | yes — shared network filesystem
            cloud (EBS/Azure/GCE)| yes — cloud block storage, one AZ
            REX-Ray / Portworx   | yes — multi-host, replicated, HA
         [TECH] `docker volume create --driver <name>` swaps WHERE and HOW
            volume data is stored; the container-side mount point and
            your application code never change — only the backing plugin.
         [ANALOGY] Choosing a moving company for the SAME storage unit:
            local is a truck to your own garage; nfs/cloud drivers are a
            truck to a shared warehouse other buildings can also reach.
         🔬 easypj: single-host deploys use `local` for postgres_data with
            zero config; a multi-host Swarm deploy of easypj (Part 10)
            needs `nfs` or a cloud driver so ANY node can mount the DB.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `docker info | grep -A3 "Plugins"` and
            find the Volume line. Verify: `local` is listed even if
            nothing else is installed — it ships with every Docker Engine.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — local vs nfs vs cloud volume topology]
            LOCAL: Host A [ vol ] — only Host A's containers ever see it
                   Host B [ vol ] — a DIFFERENT volume, same name, no link

            NFS:   Host A ─┐
                   Host B ─┼─▶ NFS server ─▶ ONE shared export
                   Host C ─┘    (every host mounts the SAME data)

            CLOUD: Host A ─▶ EBS / Azure Disk / GCE PD (block volume)
                   Host B    ✗ cannot also attach it — single-AZ, usually
                               single-node, cloud block storage

         easypj: `postgres_data` today is the LOCAL case — a Swarm
         rollout (Part 10) needs NFS or a cloud driver so postgres can
         start on ANY node.

         💡 This is why naive `docker service create --mount
            source=postgres_data` on Swarm is a trap: Swarm may reschedule
            the postgres task onto a DIFFERENT node, where "postgres_data"
            is a brand-new, EMPTY local volume — not the one with your data.

         📊 SUMMARY: `local` covers single-host easypj entirely; only
            multi-host orchestration forces a networked volume driver.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a `local` volume is invisible to every OTHER host —
            moving a container to a new Swarm node does NOT move its
            local-driver data with it; that's exactly what 18.3 solves.

    18.3 NFS Volumes in Docker
         - docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=192.168.1.100,rw --opt device=:/path
         - Use case: shared storage across multiple Docker hosts
         [CODE: NFS volume creation and usage]

         🎯 GOAL: Create and mount an NFS-backed volume so postgres_data
            is reachable from more than one Docker host.
         [TERMINAL: NFS volume creation and usage, drawn]
            $ docker volume create --driver local \
                --opt type=nfs \
                --opt o=addr=192.168.1.100,rw \
                --opt device=:/exports/pgdata \
                nfs_pgdata
            $ docker run -d --name db \
                -v nfs_pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16
         [TECH] Despite `--driver local`, `--opt type=nfs` tells the LOCAL
            driver to mount a remote NFS export as its backing store —
            no separate plugin install needed for basic NFSv3/v4 shares.
         [ANALOGY] A shelving unit (local driver) bolted to a wall that
            happens to be a shared warehouse's wall (the NFS server) — any
            other room (Docker host) with a door to that warehouse reaches
            the identical shelf.
         🔬 easypj: two easypj web nodes on separate hosts both mount
            nfs_pgdata; whichever node currently runs the db container,
            the SAME PostgreSQL files back it — the basis for HA failover.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: create the NFS volume above (or a loopback NFS
            export for practice), mount it into alpine on TWO hosts, write
            a file from host A. Verify: host B's mount shows that file.
         📊 SUMMARY: NFS volumes turn Docker's single-host `local` driver
            into a shared, multi-host-reachable one — only the volume's
            creation flags differ, not your application code.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: NFS adds real network latency to every filesystem
            call — a chatty database on NFS is often SLOWER than expected;
            benchmark before trusting it under production write load.

    18.4 Container Filesystem Internals
         - Union filesystem (Overlay2)
         - Copy-on-Write explained
         - Image layers = LowerDir, Container layer = UpperDir
         - Merged view: what the container sees
         [DIAGRAM: Overlay2 layers — LowerDir, UpperDir, WorkDir, Merged]

         🎯 GOAL: Explain copy-on-write well enough to predict which
            layer a given file edit actually lands in.
         [DIAGRAM:layers — Overlay2 merged view, drawn]
            ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
            │ MergedDir = what the CONTAINER actually sees │
            ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
            │ UpperDir  = container's writable layer (CoW) │
            ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
            │ LowerDir N   = image layer, read-only        │
            │   ...        = older image layers, read-only │
            │ LowerDir 1   = base image layer, read-only   │
            ├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
            │ WorkDir   = overlay's internal scratch space │
            └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         [TECH] Overlay2 unions every LowerDir (one per read-only image
            layer, bottom = base image) with one writable UpperDir into
            a single MergedDir. Editing an existing file triggers
            copy-up: the WHOLE file copies from its LowerDir into
            UpperDir first, THEN the write applies — never in place.
         [ANALOGY] Tracing paper over a printed map: the map (LowerDirs)
            never changes; every correction you draw lands on the sheet
            on top (UpperDir); lift the tracing paper (rm the container)
            and the original map is exactly as printed.
         🔬 easypj: editing one line of manage.py inside a RUNNING
            container copy-ups the entire file into UpperDir — that
            change is lost on `docker rm`, which is exactly why 17.4's
            bind mount, not live-editing the image, is the dev pattern.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker exec` into a running container, `echo
            x >> /app/manage.py`, then `docker diff <container>`.
            Verify: manage.py is listed with a `C` (changed) — that line
            lives only in UpperDir until the container is removed.
         📊 SUMMARY: LowerDirs are read-only and shared across every
            container from an image; UpperDir is one container's private,
            disposable delta — volumes (16.3) are the only escape from it.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: copy-up cost scales with FILE size, not edit size —
            appending one byte to a 2 GB log file copies all 2 GB into
            UpperDir first; that's a real, measurable latency spike.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how overlay2 represents a DELETED file
    Copy-on-write (18.4) explains how EDITS land in UpperDir, but
    deletion is trickier: overlay2 cannot remove a file from a read-only
    LowerDir. Instead, deleting a file that exists in any LowerDir makes
    overlay2 create a WHITEOUT — a character device file (major/minor
    number 0/0) with the same name, in UpperDir. The kernel's overlay
    driver treats any whiteout as "this file does not exist in the
    merged view," even though the original bytes still sit untouched in
    the image layer below.
         rm /app/old_config.py  (file exists in a LowerDir, image layer)
              │
              ▼
         overlay2 CANNOT touch the read-only LowerDir
              │
              ▼
         creates a WHITEOUT marker in UpperDir: c000 old_config.py
              │
              ▼
         MergedDir view: old_config.py appears GONE
         (the real bytes are still in the LowerDir, completely untouched)
    This is why `docker diff` (18.4's drill) reports a deleted file as
    `D` — it is reading the whiteout marker in UpperDir, not scanning for
    absence. It also explains why deleting a huge file INSIDE a container
    does not shrink the underlying image at all: the bytes never leave
    the LowerDir; only a tiny whiteout marker was added.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ✅ A storage driver manages image layers + the container's writable
       layer; a volume driver manages where VOLUME data physically lives
       — the two are completely orthogonal.
    ✅ overlay2 is the default since Docker 18.09 because it uses the
       kernel's native OverlayFS, no extra kernel module required.
    ✅ Changing storage drivers wipes ALL local images/containers; named
       volumes under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ are untouched by the change.
    ✅ `local` covers single-host easypj completely; multi-host
       orchestration (Swarm/K8s) is the only reason to reach for nfs or a
       cloud volume driver.
    ✅ A `local` volume is invisible to every other Docker host — moving
       a container to a new node does NOT bring its data with it.
    ✅ overlay2's MergedDir = LowerDir(s) [read-only] + UpperDir
       [writable] + WorkDir [internal scratch] — deletions become
       whiteout markers, not real removal from the image.
    ✅ Copy-up cost scales with FILE size, not edit size — appending one
       byte to a multi-GB file still copies the whole file first.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    • Switching storage drivers is not a config tweak — it deletes every
      local image and container; plan a re-pull, do not discover this in
      production.
    • `docker service create --mount source=postgres_data` on Swarm can
      silently create a brand-new EMPTY local volume if the task lands on
      a node that has never seen that name before.
    • NFS adds real network latency to every filesystem call — benchmark
      a chatty database on NFS before trusting it under write load.
    • Deleting a large file inside a container does not reclaim host disk
      space — the bytes remain in the image's LowerDir; only a whiteout
      marker was added.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    • `docker info | grep "Storage Driver"` — the fastest way to confirm
      overlay2 (or catch a legacy driver) without digging through JSON.
    • `docker diff <container>` before assuming a file is gone for good —
      `D` means whiteout, not "unrecoverable from the image."

    🔑 COMMANDS
        docker info | grep "Storage Driver"            # confirm overlay2 is active
        docker info | grep -A3 "Plugins"                # list available volume drivers
        docker volume create --driver local \
          --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=HOST,rw \
          --opt device=:/export/path nfsvol             # NFS-backed volume
        docker diff <container>                         # A/C/D changes vs image
        docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}' <ctr>  # raw LowerDir/UpperDir paths

    🧪 DRILL (10 min): `docker exec` into any running container, delete a
        file that shipped in the image, then run `docker diff` and
        `docker inspect -f '{{.GraphDriver.Data}}'` on it. Find the
        whiteout's effect in the diff output. Stop the clock once you can
        explain, out loud, why the image itself did not shrink.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 18)

    Q1: What does a storage driver manage that a volume driver does not?
        A: A storage driver manages IMAGE layers and the container's own
        writable layer; a volume driver manages where a VOLUME's data
        physically lives. They never overlap.
        Explanation: 18.1's warehouse-shelving-vs-locker-room analogy
        makes this split explicit.

    Q2: Why did overlay2 replace aufs and devicemapper as the default?
        A: It uses the kernel's native OverlayFS directly — no extra
        kernel module to install or maintain.
        Explanation: 18.1's table marks aufs/devicemapper as legacy paths
        tied to older kernels or specific distros.

    Q3: You switch your daemon's storage driver from overlay2 to
        something else. What happens to your images, and what happens to
        your named volumes?
        A: All local images and containers are wiped (each driver keeps
        its own layout); named volumes under /var/lib/docker/volumes/ are
        completely untouched.
        Explanation: 18.1's closing gotcha states this split exactly —
        volumes bypass the storage driver entirely (16.3).

    Q4: A Swarm service uses `--mount source=postgres_data` with the
        default `local` volume driver, and the scheduler reschedules the
        task onto a brand-new node. What data does the task see?
        A: An empty volume — `local` volumes are per-host; the new node
        has never created a "postgres_data" volume before.
        Explanation: 18.2's gotcha calls this out as a real trap for
        naive Swarm deployments.

    Q5: What does `--opt type=nfs` change about a volume created with
        `--driver local`?
        A: It tells the local driver to back the volume with a remote NFS
        export instead of local disk — no separate plugin install needed
        for basic NFS shares.
        Explanation: 18.3's terminal example shows exactly this flag
        combination creating `nfs_pgdata`.

    Q6: Why might a chatty database perform WORSE on an NFS volume than
        expected, even though NFS "works"?
        A: NFS adds real network latency to every filesystem call —
        something a local disk-backed volume never incurs.
        Explanation: 18.3's closing gotcha explicitly warns to benchmark
        before trusting NFS under production write load.

    Q7: In the overlay2 model, which directory is writable, and which
        directories are shared read-only across every container from the
        same image?
        A: UpperDir is the one writable layer, private to that container.
        Every LowerDir is read-only and shared by ALL containers started
        from that image.
        Explanation:
            UpperDir (writable, private to one container)
                 │
            LowerDir N...1 (read-only, shared by every container from this image)
        18.4's layers diagram stacks the LowerDirs under one UpperDir.

    Q8: You append one byte to a 2 GB log file inside a running
        container. Roughly how much data does copy-on-write actually
        copy?
        A: The entire 2 GB — copy-up cost scales with FILE size, not edit
        size; the whole file moves into UpperDir before the byte is
        appended.
        Explanation: 18.4's closing gotcha names this exact scenario as a
        real, measurable latency spike.

    Q9: You `rm` a file inside a container that originally shipped in the
        base image. Does this shrink the image on disk?
        A: No. overlay2 cannot modify the read-only LowerDir; it adds a
        whiteout marker in UpperDir instead. The original bytes remain in
        the image layer.
        Explanation:
            rm file (exists in LowerDir) → whiteout added to UpperDir →
            MergedDir shows it gone, LowerDir bytes completely untouched
        This chapter's Under the Hood section walks through this exact
        whiteout mechanism.

    Q10: What does `docker diff <container>` report for a file that was
         deleted inside the container versus one that was only edited?
         A: A deleted file shows `D`; an edited file shows `C` (changed).
         Both are reads of UpperDir — `D` reflects a whiteout marker, `C`
         reflects a copied-up, modified file.
         Explanation: 18.4's practice drill uses `docker diff` to observe
         the `C` case directly; the Under the Hood section extends it to
         the `D` case.

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │         🔧 CHAPTER 18 — WHAT'S UNDERNEATH A VOLUME              │
         │                                                                │
         │  STORAGE DRIVER (overlay2)          VOLUME DRIVER (local/nfs/ │
         │  manages image + writable layer      cloud) — manages volume  │
         │  ┌─────────────────────────┐         data location            │
         │  │ MergedDir (what you see)│         ┌──────────────────────┐ │
         │  │ UpperDir (writable, CoW)│         │ local: this host only│ │
         │  │ LowerDir N..1 (RO image)│         │ nfs/cloud: shared    │ │
         │  │ WorkDir (scratch)       │         │ across hosts         │ │
         │  └─────────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘ │
         │       edits → copy-up             volumes (16.3) live OUTSIDE │
         │       deletes → whiteout          this entire diagram         │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         .vs-prose — Chapter 18 opens the box that Chapters 16-17 left
         closed: overlay2 is the storage driver managing every image
         layer and each container's private, copy-on-write UpperDir,
         while a completely separate volume driver (local by default, nfs
         or cloud for multi-host) decides where a named volume's actual
         bytes live. The two never overlap — changing one never touches
         the other — which is exactly why postgres_data survived every
         experiment in Chapter 17 regardless of what the storage driver
         was doing underneath it.
