    [F] PART 6 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ✅ A container's writable layer is disposable; anything that must
       outlive `docker rm` belongs in one of Docker's three real
       persistence mechanisms — volume, bind mount, or tmpfs (Ch 16).
    ✅ Volumes are first-class objects with their own lifecycle: create,
       mount, unmount, remount, and only `docker volume rm` deletes them
       (Ch 16).
    ✅ easypj now assigns storage on purpose: postgres_data (DB rows),
       django_media (uploads), and django_static (:ro into nginx) are
       named volumes; dev-only code reload uses a bind mount; one
       decrypted secret uses tmpfs (Ch 17).
    ✅ A backup is not proven until it has been restored — pg_dump plus a
       scheduled, retained, and TEST-RESTORED cycle is the real bar, not
       just a cron job that runs (Ch 17).
    ✅ Storage drivers (overlay2) manage image/container layers; volume
       drivers (local/nfs/cloud) manage where volume data lives — the two
       never overlap, and volumes bypass the storage driver entirely
       (Ch 18).
    ✅ `local` volumes are single-host only — any multi-host
       orchestration (Swarm in Part 10) needs NFS or a cloud volume
       driver instead (Ch 18).
    ✅ overlay2's copy-on-write means edits copy the WHOLE file into
       UpperDir first and deletes become whiteout markers, not real
       removal from the image (Ch 18).

    ⚠️ PART 6 GOTCHAS
    • `docker compose down -v` deletes named volumes; plain `down` does
      not — the single most consequential flag in this entire part.
    • Bind mounts inherit host UID/permissions exactly, and Compose
      silently prefixes volume names with the project name unless you set
      `name:` explicitly — both are top "why doesn't this match what I
      expected" traps.
    • A `local` volume never travels with a rescheduled Swarm task — the
      new node gets a brand-new EMPTY volume of the same name.
    • A backup living only on the same host as the database it protects
      is not disaster recovery, and an untested backup is not a backup
      at all.

    ⚡ PART 6 SPEED TIPS
    • `docker volume inspect <name> -f '{{.Mountpoint}}'` — jump straight
      to the host path, skip the full JSON dump.
    • `docker info | grep "Storage Driver"` — one line to confirm
      overlay2 (or catch something unexpected) on any host.
    • Always add `-T` to any `docker compose exec` you pipe stdin into
      (restores especially) to avoid the silent pseudo-TTY failure.

         .vs-prose — Part 6 turns "containers are disposable" from a
         warning into a design habit: Chapter 16 supplies the four real
         mount types, Chapter 17 assigns each one to a specific easypj
         path and proves the assignment survives real failure (a restart,
         a UID mismatch, a full database restore), and Chapter 18
         explains the overlay2 storage driver and the local/nfs/cloud
         volume drivers working underneath every one of those decisions.
         Walk into Part 7 knowing that postgres_data, django_media, and
         django_static all outlive any container — and any host, once
         Part 9-10 puts easypj on Swarm or Kubernetes.
PART 7: DOCKER SECURITY — PROTECTING YOUR CONTAINERS                     🔴

    [PART 7 INTRO]
    Every easypj container built in Parts 2-6 runs — but "runs" and "runs
    safely" are different claims. By default a container starts as root,
    keeps every standard Linux capability, has a writable filesystem, and
    trusts whatever base image `FROM` pointed at last Tuesday. Part 7 closes
    that gap: Chapter 19 gives you the primitives (namespaces, capabilities,
    seccomp, AppArmor, non-root, read-only rootfs), Chapter 20 assembles them
    into an ordered hardening checklist you actually run against easypj, and
    Chapter 21 proves the result with scanners, a host benchmark, and an SBOM.

    This is the part where a single RCE stops meaning "the whole host is
    owned." By the last page of Chapter 21 you will have a non-root, capped,
    read-only easypj container whose secrets never touch `docker inspect`,
    whose daemon is locked down, and whose image ships with a Docker Scout
    scan and a CIS Benchmark score you can hand to an auditor.

    🧠 ANALOGY. Parts 1-6 built easypj a house — walls, plumbing, a working
    front door. Part 7 is the security retrofit on that SAME house: Chapter
    19 installs the locks, alarm, and reinforced windows (the primitives);
    Chapter 20 is the locksmith actually fitting them to THIS house's real
    doors and windows (easypj's Dockerfile, compose file, and daemon);
    Chapter 21 is the independent inspector who tests every lock, files a
    report, and signs off that the house meets code — not "we think it's
    safe" but "here is the score that proves it."

Chapter 19: Container Security Fundamentals
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    THINK BEFORE PART 7:
      What runs where?    → same shared kernel — the boundary is SOFTWARE now.
      What talks to what? → namespaces/caps/seccomp gate what a process can
                            touch; the daemon socket gates who is "root".
      What breaks first?  → one over-privileged flag (--privileged, a mounted
                            docker.sock) collapses every other control at once.

    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: A container is not a security boundary by default —
    it is a shared-kernel process wearing isolation. This chapter builds the
    defense-in-depth model: namespaces, capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor, non-
    root users, and a read-only root filesystem, each an independent layer.
    Problem solved: "my container runs as root with full capabilities, and one
    RCE in Django would own the whole host."

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~2.5h · Security domain (15%) — this chapter
        is the core of that domain, section-for-section.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
         ✅ Name the three container-specific attack classes (breakout,
            supply chain, runtime abuse) and give an easypj example of each
            (19.1).
         ✅ Draw the 10-layer security onion from memory and name the kernel
            feature or tool behind each layer (19.2).
         ✅ Run easypj as a non-root user via `USER` in the Dockerfile or
            `--user`, and verify it with `docker exec ... id` (19.3).
         ✅ Apply `--cap-drop ALL` / `--cap-add` correctly, and explain why
            CAP_SYS_ADMIN is treated as near-root (19.4).
         ✅ Run easypj with `--read-only` plus the right `--tmpfs` mounts
            without breaking app writes (19.5).
         ✅ Explain what the default seccomp profile blocks and read an
            AppArmor denial out of the audit log (19.6).
         ✅ Identify `--privileged` and `seccomp=unconfined` on sight as the
            anti-patterns that erase every other control in this chapter.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: this chapter underlies the Security domain (15%) —
        non-root users and capabilities are examined directly; Chapter 20
        applies these primitives to easypj, Chapter 21 measures the result.

    [E] SECTION MAP (you are here):
         19.1 why it matters → 19.2 the 10-layer onion (this chapter's
         spine) → 19.3 non-root → 19.4 capabilities → 19.5 read-only rootfs
         → 19.6 seccomp/AppArmor — each later section is one onion layer
         from 19.2, made concrete.

    19.1 Why Container Security Matters
         - Shared kernel = shared risk
         - Container breakout: escaping to host
         - Supply chain attacks: malicious base images
         - Real incidents: cryptojacking, data exfiltration
         [STATS: Container security breach statistics]

         🎯 GOAL: State the three container-specific attack classes and why a
            shared kernel raises the stakes.
         [TECH] Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel exploit or a
            misconfigured capability can escape to the host (breakout).
            Three classes: (1) breakout via over-privileged containers,
            (2) supply-chain via malicious/vulnerable base images, (3)
            runtime abuse — cryptojacking, data exfiltration from a popped app.
         [ANALOGY] Apartments sharing one foundation: a fire in one unit
            (kernel-level compromise) threatens the whole building, unlike
            detached houses (VMs) with separate foundations.
         [TABLE: attack class → easypj exposure]
            Breakout     | root container + host mount → host takeover
            Supply chain | unpinned base image ships a backdoored lib
            Runtime      | popped Django worker mines crypto / exfiltrates DB
         🔬 easypj: a single RCE in a JobPost upload handler, in a root
            container with the docker socket mounted, is not "one app hacked" —
            it is the whole host and every other container compromised.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `docker scout quickview` (or trivy) on your base
            image. Verify: it lists CVEs you inherited for free — the supply-
            chain surface you did not write but still ship.
         📊 SUMMARY: shared kernel means container security is HOST security;
            breakout, supply chain, and runtime abuse are the three fronts.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "it's just a container" is the mindset that gets hosts
            owned — treat every container as internet-facing and hostile.

    19.2 Docker Security Architecture
         - Namespaces (isolation): PID, NET, IPC, MNT, UTS, USER, CGROUP
         - Control Groups (cgroups): resource limiting
         - Capabilities: fine-grained permissions (CAP_NET_BIND, etc.)
         - Seccomp: system call filtering
         - AppArmor/SELinux: mandatory access control

         [DOCKER SECURITY — LAYERS OF DEFENSE AROUND CONTAINER]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                  🔐 DOCKER SECURITY — ONION OF DEFENSE                      │
         │                                                                          │
         │                           ┌───────────┐                                  │
         │                           │  🐳 Your   │                                 │
         │                           │ Container │                                 │
         │                           └─────┬─────┘                                 │
         │                                 │                                        │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┐    │
         │  │  LAYER 1: User Namespace     │  🔑 USER instruction in Dockerfile│    │
         │  │  (uid=1000, not root!)       │  docker run --user 1000:1000      │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 2: Capabilities       │  🎯 Drop all, add back only needed│    │
         │  │  (not full root!)            │  --cap-drop ALL                   │    │
         │  │                              │  --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE       │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 3: Seccomp Profile    │  🚫 Block dangerous syscalls      │    │
         │  │  (system call filter)        │  ~300 of ~350+ allowed; 44 out    │    │
         │  │                              │  Blocked: mount, reboot, etc.     │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 4: AppArmor/SELinux   │  📋 Mandatory Access Control      │    │
         │  │  (per-process profiles)      │  Limit file access per container  │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 5: Cgroups            │  💪 Limit CPU, RAM, disk I/O     │    │
         │  │  (resource limits)           │  --memory=512m --cpus=1.5         │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 6: Read-Only Root FS  │  📖 --read-only (immutable!)      │    │
         │  │  (no writes to root)         │  + tmpfs for /tmp, /run           │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 7: Network Isolation  │  🌐 No port exposure unless -p    │    │
         │  │  (bridge/host/none)          │  Internal networks only            │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 8: Image Scanning     │  🔍 docker scout quickview         │    │
         │  │  (CVE detection)             │  Trivy, Snyk, Grype                │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 9: Content Trust      │  ✍️ Docker Content Trust (DCT)     │    │
         │  │  (image signing)             │  DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1            │    │
         │  ├──────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤    │
         │  │  LAYER 10: Host Security     │  🖥️ Docker Bench Security          │    │
         │  │  (daemon config, CIS)        │  Secure daemon.json config         │    │
         │  └──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘    │
         │                                                                          │
         │  🏆 RESULT: Even if attacker escapes one layer, 9 more to go!           │
         │     Defense in depth = multiple independent security controls.           │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Name each layer of the security onion and the kernel feature
            behind it.
         [TECH] The onion diagram above is defense in depth: user namespace
            (drop root), capabilities (split root's powers), seccomp (filter
            syscalls), AppArmor/SELinux (mandatory access control), cgroups
            (resource caps), read-only rootfs, network isolation, image
            scanning, content trust, host/CIS hardening — 10 independent rings.
         [ANALOGY] The onion IS the analogy: an attacker peeling one layer
            still faces nine more, each a different lock needing a different
            key — no single failure is game over.
         [DIAGRAM:layers — the load-bearing four, from the onion]
            namespaces   → what a container can SEE (PID/NET/MNT/USER...)
            capabilities → which root powers it KEEPS (drop the rest)
            seccomp      → which SYSCALLS it may call (~44 blocked default)
            AppArmor     → which FILES/ops the profile permits
         🔬 easypj: web tier needs almost none of root's power — drop all caps,
            keep the default seccomp profile, run as uid 1000, mount rootfs
            read-only; that alone removes most of the breakout surface.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker inspect` a default container and find its
            CapAdd/CapDrop, SecurityOpt, and Privileged fields. Verify: by
            default caps are the standard set and Privileged is false.
         📊 SUMMARY: security is layered, not a single switch — namespaces +
            caps + seccomp + AppArmor + non-root + read-only compound.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `--privileged` collapses the ENTIRE onion at once
            (all caps, all devices, no seccomp) — it is the anti-pattern the
            whole diagram exists to prevent.

    19.3 Running as Non-Root User
         - Default: container runs as root (dangerous!)
         - USER instruction in Dockerfile
         - Creating a non-root user: RUN addgroup && adduser
         - --user flag: docker run --user 1000:1000
         [CODE: Dockerfile with non-root user for easypj]

         🎯 GOAL: Make easypj run as a non-root user and prove it.
         [TECH] Containers default to UID 0 (root). If the process is root and
            an attacker breaks out, they are root on the host. Fix: create a
            user in the Dockerfile and switch with USER, or override at runtime
            with `--user 1000:1000`. The app must own the paths it writes.
         [ANALOGY] Handing the new hire a visitor badge, not the master key:
            they can do their job, but they cannot open the server room even
            if they wander off.
         [CODE: Dockerfile — non-root easypj]
            FROM python:3.12-slim
            RUN addgroup --system app && adduser --system --ingroup app app
            WORKDIR /app
            COPY --chown=app:app . .
            RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
            USER app
            CMD ["gunicorn", "easypj.wsgi:application", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000"]
         🔬 easypj: gunicorn now runs as uid "app"; a breakout lands as an
            unprivileged user with no host root, no ability to load kernel
            modules, no write to system paths.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker exec <ctr> id`. Verify: uid is NOT 0 (e.g.
            uid=100(app)); try to write /etc/passwd and get permission denied.
         📊 SUMMARY: USER app turns a root container into an unprivileged one —
            the single highest-value hardening step, one line long.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: switching to non-root can break writes to /app/static,
            /app/media, or a bind mount — chown those paths (or use a volume
            the user owns) or the app crashes on first write.

    19.4 Linux Capabilities
         - What are capabilities? (splitting root's power)
         - Default capabilities given to containers
         - --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE
         - CAP_SYS_ADMIN danger (≈ root)
         [TABLE: Common capabilities — risk, when needed]

         🎯 GOAL: Drop all Linux capabilities and add back only what easypj
            actually needs.
         [TECH] Root's power is split into ~40 capabilities. Docker grants a
            default subset; best practice is `--cap-drop ALL` then
            `--cap-add` the few required. CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE lets a process
            bind ports <1024; CAP_SYS_ADMIN is a near-root grab-bag and should
            never be added to an app container.
         [ANALOGY] Instead of one master key (root), a ring of labeled keys;
            hand out only "bind low port" and take back the rest — especially
            the "does everything" master (SYS_ADMIN).
         [TABLE: capabilities for easypj]
            NET_BIND_SERVICE | bind :80/:443       | add only if needed
            CHOWN / SETUID   | entrypoint privs    | usually droppable
            SYS_ADMIN        | ~= root             | NEVER add to the app
            NET_RAW          | ping / raw sockets  | drop (blocks spoofing)
         🔬 easypj: gunicorn binds 8000 (>1024) behind nginx, so easypj needs
            ZERO added capabilities: `--cap-drop ALL` and it still runs fine.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run easypj with `--cap-drop ALL`. Verify: the app
            still serves; then `--cap-drop ALL` a container that pings and
            watch ping fail (NET_RAW gone) — proof caps are actually enforced.
         📊 SUMMARY: drop ALL, add back the minimum — most web apps need none,
            and SYS_ADMIN is the capability to fear.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `--privileged` is NOT "all capabilities" — it is caps
            PLUS device access PLUS no seccomp; even --cap-add ALL is safer.

    19.5 Read-Only Root Filesystem
         - --read-only flag
         - tmpfs for writable locations: --tmpfs /tmp, --tmpfs /run
         - Django: /tmp needs to be writable for WSGI sockets
         [CODE: Read-only container configuration for easypj]


         🎯 GOAL: Run easypj with a read-only root filesystem plus tmpfs for
            the few writable paths.
         [TECH] `--read-only` mounts the container's root filesystem immutable,
            so a compromised process cannot drop a binary, edit configs, or
            persist. Genuinely writable spots (/tmp, /run, WSGI sockets) get
            explicit `--tmpfs` mounts; real data goes on named volumes.
         [ANALOGY] A hotel room bolted shut except for one labeled scratchpad
            (tmpfs): guests can jot a note, but they cannot repaint the walls
            or hide anything for the next occupant.
         [CODE: read-only easypj container]
            docker run --read-only \
              --tmpfs /tmp \
              --tmpfs /run \
              -v media:/app/media \
              easypj:v1
         🔬 easypj: Django + gunicorn need /tmp for sockets and uploads-in-
            progress; those go on tmpfs, media persists on a volume, and the
            rest of the filesystem is frozen against tampering.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run easypj `--read-only` with no tmpfs and watch it
            fail writing /tmp; add `--tmpfs /tmp` and it starts. Verify: `touch
            /etc/x` inside is denied while `touch /tmp/x` works.
         📊 SUMMARY: read-only rootfs + narrow tmpfs + volumes = an immutable
            container where writes are a deliberate, listed exception.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: forgetting a required writable path (/tmp, /run, cache)
            makes the app crash on boot — enumerate them and add tmpfs, do not
            abandon --read-only.

    19.6 Seccomp & AppArmor in Practice
         - Default seccomp profile blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls of ~350+
         - Custom profile = a JSON allow/deny list passed with --security-opt
         - --security-opt seccomp=unconfined DISABLES the filter (danger!)
         - AppArmor docker-default confines file/capability/network per process
         - Denials surface as EPERM in the app and in the host audit log

         🎯 GOAL: Explain what the default seccomp and AppArmor profiles block,
            and where a denial shows up.
         [TECH] Seccomp filters syscalls: Docker's default profile allows the
            common ~300 and blocks ~44 dangerous ones (mount, reboot,
            kexec_load, ptrace of others, etc.). A custom profile is JSON
            (defaultAction + a syscalls allow-list) passed via
            `--security-opt seccomp=profile.json`. AppArmor's docker-default
            profile independently confines file access and capabilities per
            container process.
         [ANALOGY] Seccomp is the bouncer checking each SYSCALL against a
            guest list at the kernel door; AppArmor is building security
            deciding which ROOMS (files) that guest may enter once inside.
         [TERMINAL: inspect and apply]
            $ docker run --rm alpine grep Seccomp /proc/1/status  # 2 = filtered
            $ docker run --security-opt seccomp=custom.json easypj:v1
            $ docker run --security-opt apparmor=docker-default easypj:v1
            # denials appear as EPERM; on the host:
            $ dmesg | grep -i apparmor    # DENIED audit lines
         🔬 easypj: the default profiles are enough for Django + gunicorn —
            easypj never calls mount() or reboot(); keep them on and only write
            a custom profile if a library needs a specifically blocked syscall.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run a container with `--security-opt
            seccomp=unconfined` and one without; compare
            `grep Seccomp /proc/1/status`. Verify: 0 (unconfined) vs 2
            (filtered) — proof the profile is really attached.
         📊 SUMMARY: keep the default seccomp + AppArmor profiles on; they cost
            nothing and block whole syscall/file-access attack classes for free.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `seccomp=unconfined` and `--privileged` both strip the
            seccomp filter entirely — a container that "only works" unconfined
            is telling you it is doing something the default rightly blocks.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how the onion is actually enforced by the kernel
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Every layer in 19.2's onion is a real Linux kernel mechanism, not a
        Docker invention. `docker run` translates your flags into an OCI
        runtime spec that runc hands to the kernel in one sequence, before
        your process ever executes:
          • NAMESPACES are created with `clone()`/`unshare()` using flags
            like CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWNS, CLONE_NEWUSER —
            this is what 19.2's "what a container can SEE" actually is.
          • CAPABILITIES are a set of bitmasks (permitted, effective,
            inheritable, bounding, ambient) that runc sets on the
            container's init process via `capset()` before exec —
            `--cap-drop ALL` simply clears bits instead of leaving
            Docker's default subset in place.
          • SECCOMP is a BPF program attached with the `seccomp()` syscall;
            the KERNEL evaluates it on every syscall the process makes for
            the rest of its life — a denial is a kernel-level EPERM, not
            something Docker or your app decided at runtime.
        AppArmor/SELinux (19.6) is a separate Linux Security Module hooked
        into the same syscall path, checking file/network/capability access
        against a loaded profile — it runs alongside seccomp, not instead
        of it.

        [ENFORCEMENT CHAIN — one `docker run` to a filtered, capped process]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  docker run --cap-drop ALL --read-only \                         │
        │             --security-opt seccomp=default.json easypj:v1        │
        │                     │                                            │
        │                     ▼                                            │
        │  containerd + runc build an OCI spec: namespace list,            │
        │  capability bitmask, seccomp BPF program, mount list             │
        │                     │                                            │
        │                     ▼                                            │
        │  KERNEL: clone() w/ ns flags + capset() bitmask + seccomp() BPF  │
        │                     │                                            │
        │                     ▼                                            │
        │  gunicorn (PID 1 inside): every syscall it makes is now checked  │
        │  against BOTH the capability set AND the seccomp filter          │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ⚠️ This is exactly why `--privileged` is so total: it sets the
        capability bitmask to all-1s, attaches NO seccomp filter, and grants
        raw device access — three independent kernel controls erased by one
        flag, which is why 19.2/19.4 call it the onion's single point of
        failure.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🔑 Containers share the host kernel — a breakout is a HOST
           compromise, not just an app compromise (19.1).
        🔑 Three attack classes: breakout (over-privileged container),
           supply chain (malicious/vulnerable base image), runtime abuse
           (a popped app mining crypto or exfiltrating data) (19.1).
        🔑 The security onion is 10 independent layers — namespaces, caps,
           seccomp, AppArmor/SELinux, cgroups, read-only rootfs, network
           isolation, image scanning, content trust, host/CIS hardening;
           one failed layer still leaves nine more (19.2).
        🔑 `USER app` (non-root) is the single highest-value, one-line fix —
           a breakout as uid 1000 is not host root (19.3).
        🔑 `--cap-drop ALL` then add back only what's proven necessary —
           easypj's web tier needs zero added capabilities (19.4).
        🔑 `--read-only` + narrow `--tmpfs` mounts make the filesystem an
           explicit allow-list of writable paths, not a free-for-all (19.5).
        🔑 Default seccomp blocks ~44 dangerous syscalls; AppArmor's
           docker-default independently confines file/capability access;
           denials surface as EPERM and in the host audit log (19.6).

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚠️ `--privileged` is NOT "all capabilities" — it is caps + device
           access + no seccomp, all at once; it erases the whole onion.
        ⚠️ Switching to non-root breaks writes to paths the new user doesn't
           own (`/app/static`, `/app/media`, bind mounts) — chown them
           first, don't abandon USER.
        ⚠️ Forgetting a required tmpfs path (`/tmp`, `/run`) under
           `--read-only` crashes the app on boot instead of degrading
           gracefully — enumerate real writable paths before enabling it.
        ⚠️ `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` silently strips the syscall
           filter — a container that "only works" unconfined is telling
           you it needs a syscall the default profile rightly blocks.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚡ `docker inspect <ctr> --format '{{.HostConfig.Privileged}}'` — a
           one-line sanity check that a container is NOT privileged.
        ⚡ `docker run --rm alpine grep Seccomp /proc/1/status` — 2 means
           filtered, 0 means unconfined; a 5-second proof the flag applied.
        ⚡ `dmesg | grep -i apparmor` right after a mysterious permission
           error — a silent AppArmor DENY often looks like an app bug.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 COMMANDS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        docker inspect <c> --format '{{.HostConfig.CapAdd}} {{.HostConfig.CapDrop}}'
                                             # what caps were added/dropped
        docker run --user 1000:1000 easypj:v1        # force non-root
        docker run --cap-drop ALL easypj:v1          # drop every capability
        docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run easypj:v1
        docker run --security-opt seccomp=unconfined ...  # DANGER, testing only
        docker exec <ctr> id                          # verify uid != 0
        dmesg | grep -i apparmor                      # AppArmor DENY lines
        docker run --rm alpine grep Seccomp /proc/1/status  # 2 = filtered

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 DRILL
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🧪 Take any easypj container started with plain defaults. In 10
        minutes: (1) `docker inspect` it and record Privileged/CapAdd/
        CapDrop. (2) re-run it with `--user 1000:1000 --cap-drop ALL
        --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run`. (3) confirm it still serves
        a request. (4) `docker exec ... id` and confirm uid != 0. All four
        steps passing with the app still healthy IS this chapter.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 19)
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Q1. Why does a shared kernel make container security fundamentally
            different from VM security?
            → A container is a process on the HOST kernel; a breakout
              escapes directly to the host, unlike a VM's separate kernel
              behind a hypervisor boundary (19.1). This is why 19.2's
              namespaces/caps/seccomp exist as SOFTWARE boundaries — there
              is no hardware isolation backing them up.

        Q2. List the three container-specific attack classes from 19.1 and
            give one easypj example of each.
            → Breakout (root container + host mount → host takeover),
              supply chain (unpinned base image ships a backdoored lib),
              runtime abuse (a popped Django worker mines crypto). Each
              needs a different defense: breakout is 19.3-19.6, supply
              chain is Chapter 21's scanning.

        Q3. List, inner to outer, the 10 layers of 19.2's security onion.
            → (1) user namespace/non-root, (2) capabilities, (3) seccomp,
              (4) AppArmor/SELinux, (5) cgroups, (6) read-only rootfs,
              (7) network isolation, (8) image scanning, (9) content trust,
              (10) host/CIS hardening.
                 🐳 container → 1 userns → 2 caps → 3 seccomp → 4 AppArmor
                 → 5 cgroups → 6 read-only → 7 network → 8 scan → 9 trust
                 → 10 host/CIS — each ring independent of the others.

        Q4. What single Dockerfile line converts a root container into an
            unprivileged one, and why does it matter?
            → `USER app` (after creating the user). A breakout as root is
              host root; a breakout as uid 1000 is not (19.3) — the
              highest payoff-per-line change in the whole chapter.

        Q5. You add `USER app` to easypj's Dockerfile and the container now
            crashes writing to `/app/media`. What happened, and the fix?
            → The `app` user doesn't own `/app/media`. Fix: `COPY --chown=
              app:app` in the build, or chown the mounted volume (19.3's
              gotcha — non-root breaks unowned writable paths).

        Q6. What does `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE` do, and
            why does easypj's gunicorn setup not even need the add-back?
            → Drops all ~40 Linux capabilities, then re-adds only the power
              to bind ports <1024. easypj's gunicorn binds :8000 (>1024)
              behind nginx, so it runs fine with ZERO added capabilities.
                 NET_BIND_SERVICE | bind <1024   | rarely needed by app tier
                 SYS_ADMIN        | ~= root      | never add to the app
                 NET_RAW          | ping/raw     | drop (blocks spoofing)

        Q7. Why does `--privileged` collapse the ENTIRE onion at once
            rather than just one layer?
            → It sets capabilities to all-1s, disables seccomp filtering,
              AND grants device access simultaneously — three layers gone
              in one flag (19.2/19.4), which is exactly why the chapter
              calls it the anti-pattern the onion exists to prevent.

        Q8. A container runs with `--read-only` and no tmpfs mounts. What
            happens when gunicorn tries to write a WSGI socket to `/tmp`,
            and how do you fix it?
            → The write fails (read-only filesystem) and the app crashes on
              boot. Fix: add `--tmpfs /tmp` (and `/run` if used) —
              enumerate real writable paths instead of abandoning
              `--read-only` (19.5).

        Q9. Roughly how many syscalls does Docker's default seccomp profile
            block, and what shows up when a blocked one is attempted?
            → ~44 dangerous syscalls (mount, reboot, kexec_load, etc.) out
              of ~350+; a blocked call surfaces as EPERM in the app and can
              appear in the host's audit log (19.6).

        Q10. How do you PROVE, from inside a running container, that
             seccomp filtering is actually attached rather than assumed?
             → `grep Seccomp /proc/1/status` — 2 means filtered
               (SECCOMP_MODE_FILTER), 0 means unconfined/disabled (19.6) —
               never trust a security flag without a kernel-reported check.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — "Chapter 19, the onion in motion"
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  🐳 DEFAULT CONTAINER   root, all caps, no seccomp filter, writable │
    │         │  apply the onion, layer by layer...                      │
    │         ▼                                                          │
    │  👤 19.3 non-root USER → 🎯 19.4 cap-drop ALL → 🚫 19.6 seccomp/   │
    │  AppArmor → 📖 19.5 read-only + tmpfs                              │
    │         │                                                          │
    │         ▼                                                          │
    │  🔒 HARDENED CONTAINER   a breakout now lands as an unprivileged,  │
    │     capped, syscall-filtered process on a frozen filesystem        │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    .vs-prose — Chapter 19 in one line: a default container is root, fully
    capped, unfiltered, and writable everywhere (19.1), the security onion
    names ten independent layers standing between an attacker and the host
    (19.2), and 19.3-19.6 make four of the highest-value layers concrete on
    easypj — non-root, dropped capabilities, seccomp/AppArmor, and a
    read-only filesystem — so that a single RCE stops meaning "game over"
    and starts meaning "an unprivileged process that can't write, can't
    call dangerous syscalls, and can't escalate." Chapter 20 now turns
    these primitives into an ordered checklist for the whole easypj stack.


Chapter 20: Securing the easypj Stack
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Chapter 19 gave you the security primitives; this
    chapter assembles them into a hardened easypj stack — a concrete checklist,
    real secrets handling, a locked-down daemon, image signing, and the rootless
    option. Problem solved: "I know about capabilities and seccomp, but what is
    the actual, ordered list of things I must do to ship easypj safely?"

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~2h · Security domain (15%) — secrets
        management and daemon hardening are graded directly.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
         ✅ Apply the 10-item hardening checklist to easypj in priority
            order and explain why each item earns its place (20.1).
         ✅ Move SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD out of ENV vars into mounted
            secret files, and explain why ENV leaks via `docker inspect`
            (20.2).
         ✅ Explain why `docker.sock` is root-equivalent, and configure
            hardened daemon.json settings (userns-remap, icc, no-new-
            privileges) (20.3).
         ✅ Sign and verify easypj images with Docker Content Trust and
            explain what DCT does and does not protect (20.4).
         ✅ Explain rootless containers (Podman or Docker rootless) and
            when they beat a root daemon for security (20.5).
         ✅ State, from memory, why mounting docker.sock is more dangerous
            in common CI use than `--privileged` on a single container.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: this chapter IS the Security domain (15%) applied
        end-to-end — secrets management, daemon configuration, and least-
