        Installation and Configuration domain (15%) via daemon.json.

    [E] SECTION MAP (you are here):
         20.1 the ordered checklist (this chapter's spine) → 20.2 secrets
         (not ENV) → 20.3 the daemon socket & daemon.json → 20.4 signing &
         Content Trust → 20.5 rootless/Podman — each section hardens one
         more surface Chapter 19 named.

    20.1 Security Hardening Checklist
         - Use specific base image tags (not :latest)
         - Run as non-root user
         - Drop all capabilities, add back only needed
         - Use read-only root filesystem
         - Scan images for vulnerabilities (Docker Scout)
         - Use secrets, not environment variables for sensitive data
         - Limit resources (--memory, --cpus)
         - Use health checks
         - Enable Docker Content Trust (DCT)
         - Keep Docker Engine updated
         [CHECKLIST: 10 security items for easypj]

         🎯 GOAL: Apply an ordered hardening checklist to easypj and know why
            each item earns its place.
         [TECH] The high-value controls, in priority order: pin base image
            tags (not :latest), run non-root, `--cap-drop ALL`, read-only
            rootfs + tmpfs, scan images (Scout/Trivy), secrets NOT in ENV,
            resource limits (--memory/--cpus), health checks, Content Trust,
            keep the Engine patched. Each maps to a layer of the onion.
         [ANALOGY] A pre-flight checklist: pilots do not "remember" to lower
            the gear, they READ the list every time — hardening is a list you
            run on every deploy, not a thing you recall.
         [CHECKLIST: easypj hardening — top items]
            [ ] base image pinned (python:3.12-slim, not :latest)
            [ ] USER app (non-root)          [ ] --cap-drop ALL
            [ ] --read-only + tmpfs /tmp     [ ] --memory / --cpus set
            [ ] secrets via file, not ENV    [ ] HEALTHCHECK defined
            [ ] image scanned, 0 criticals   [ ] Engine + base patched
            [ ] Content Trust (DCT) enabled
         🔬 easypj: a single `docker run` line for easypj web carries USER,
            cap-drop, read-only, tmpfs, memory limit and a health check — the
            checklist rendered as flags on one command.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: take a plain easypj run command and add every
            checklist flag one at a time, confirming the app still boots after
            each. Verify: the final container passes `docker scout quickview`
            and runs as non-root with limits set.
         📊 SUMMARY: hardening is a repeatable checklist, ordered by payoff —
            pin, de-root, de-cap, freeze, scan, limit, sign, patch.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: :latest silently changes under you between builds —
            an unpinned base is an unreviewed dependency upgrade every deploy.

    20.2 Secrets Management
         - Problem: ENV vars visible in docker inspect
         - Docker secrets (Swarm only): encrypted at rest, in transit
         - docker secret create, docker service --secret
         - For non-Swarm: .env file mounted as volume (limited)
         - Third-party: HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager
         [CODE: Swarm secrets for Django SECRET_KEY, DB_PASSWORD]

         🎯 GOAL: Keep easypj's SECRET_KEY and DB password out of environment
            variables and image layers.
         [TECH] ENV vars leak: they show in `docker inspect`, `/proc/1/environ`,
            and child processes. Swarm secrets are encrypted at rest + in
            transit and appear only as files under /run/secrets. Non-Swarm:
            mount a file and read it, or use Vault/AWS Secrets Manager. NEVER
            bake secrets into a Dockerfile — they persist in image layers.
         [ANALOGY] ENV secrets are a password on a sticky note on the monitor
            (anyone glancing sees it); a mounted secret file is the password in
            a sealed envelope handed only to the one process that needs it.
         [CODE: file-based secret for easypj]
            services:
              web:
                environment:
                  DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
                secrets:
                  - db_password
            secrets:
              db_password:
                file: ./secrets/db_password.txt   # gitignored
         🔬 easypj: Django reads SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD from files at
            /run/secrets/*; `docker inspect web` shows only the FILE PATH, never
            the secret value.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: set a secret via ENV, run `docker inspect | grep -i
            secret`, and see it in plain text; switch to a file secret and
            inspect again. Verify: the value is no longer visible in inspect.
         📊 SUMMARY: secrets belong in mounted files (or a vault), never in ENV
            or image layers — inspect and layer history are both readable.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a secret ARG/ENV in an early Dockerfile stage is baked
            into that layer forever — even if a later stage unsets it; use
            build secrets (`--mount=type=secret`) instead.

    20.3 Securing the Docker Daemon
         - Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) — root equivalent
         - Never expose Docker daemon to internet without TLS
         - Docker daemon configuration (daemon.json)
         - User namespace remapping (userns-remap)
         [CODE: daemon.json security settings]

         🎯 GOAL: Lock down the Docker daemon and understand why the socket is
            the crown jewel.
         [TECH] /var/run/docker.sock is the daemon's API endpoint, and the
            daemon runs as ROOT. Anyone who can talk to that socket can run
            `docker run -v /:/host --privileged` and own the entire host —
            mounting the socket into a container is handing that container
            root on the host. Harden the daemon in daemon.json: userns-remap,
            no-new-privileges, disable inter-container comms, never expose the
            API over TCP without mutual TLS.
         [ANALOGY] docker.sock is the master key to the whole building. A
            container with the socket mounted is a tenant holding that master
            key — polite until it is not, then every door is already open.
         [CODE: daemon.json hardening]
            {
              "userns-remap": "default",
              "no-new-privileges": true,
              "icc": false,
              "live-restore": true,
              "log-driver": "json-file",
              "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}
            }
         🔬 easypj: NO easypj container ever mounts docker.sock. A CI job that
            "needs Docker" is the classic trap — that mount makes the CI
            container root on the runner host (see 22.6 for safe options).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `docker run -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/
            docker.sock alpine` and from inside, list host containers via the
            API. Verify: you can see and control the host's Docker — proof the
            socket = root. Then DON'T do this in production.
         📊 SUMMARY: the socket is root-equivalent; guard it like root, never
            mount it casually, and never expose the API without TLS.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` grants
            full host root to whatever runs in that container — the single
            most dangerous flag in common use. Treat it as host --privileged.

    20.4 Image Signing & Content Trust
         - Docker Content Trust (DCT): sign and verify images
         - DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker pull
         - Notary: the signing server
         - docker trust commands
         [TERMINAL: DCT setup and verification workflow]

         🎯 GOAL: Sign easypj images and make pulls verify signatures.
         [TECH] Docker Content Trust (DCT) signs image tags with Notary so a
            consumer can verify an image was published by you and not tampered
            with. `export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` makes push sign and pull
            REFUSE unsigned/altered tags. `docker trust` manages signer keys.
         [ANALOGY] A wax seal on a letter: the recipient (pull) checks the seal
            is intact and yours before trusting the contents; a broken or
            missing seal means reject, do not open.
         [TERMINAL: sign + enforce for easypj]
            $ export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
            $ docker push easypj/web:v1.2.3     # prompts for signing key
            $ docker trust inspect easypj/web:v1.2.3 --pretty
            $ docker pull easypj/web:v1.2.3     # verifies before pulling
            $ docker pull easypj/web:tampered   # ERROR: no valid trust data
         🔬 easypj: production hosts run with DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1, so a
            compromised registry serving a swapped easypj image is rejected at
            pull time instead of silently deployed.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: enable DCT, push a signed tag, then try to pull a
            tag you never signed. Verify: the signed pull works and the
            unsigned one is refused with a trust-data error.
         📊 SUMMARY: DCT = signed, verifiable image tags; turn it on in prod so
            "pull" also means "prove it is authentic and unmodified".
            ⚠️ Gotcha: DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 only protects tags you actually
            SIGNED — an unsigned :latest simply fails to pull, and losing your
            root signing key means you can never sign that repo again.

    20.5 Podman vs Docker — Rootless Containers
         - What is Podman? (daemonless, rootless by default)
         - podman vs docker CLI compatibility (alias docker=podman)
         - Rootless Docker mode
         - Why rootless matters
         [COMPARISON TABLE: Docker vs Podman — 10 dimensions]


         🎯 GOAL: Explain rootless containers and when Podman beats Docker for
            security.
         [TECH] Podman is daemonless and rootless by default: containers run
            as your user via user namespaces, so "root" inside maps to your
            unprivileged UID outside — no root daemon, no socket to steal.
            Docker offers rootless mode too (dockerd as a non-root user). The
            CLIs are near-identical (`alias docker=podman` often just works).
         [ANALOGY] Docker's default is a valet (the root daemon) who parks
            everyone's car with the master key; rootless/Podman gives each
            driver their own limited key — no central master to hijack.
         [TABLE: Docker vs Podman — security dimensions]
            Daemon        | Docker: root daemon | Podman: none (fork/exec)
            Default user  | root                | rootless
            Socket risk   | docker.sock = root  | no daemon socket
            Systemd units | via daemon          | native `podman generate`
            Compose       | docker compose      | podman-compose / quadlet
         🔬 easypj: on a shared CI runner, running the easypj build under
            rootless Podman means a build-time compromise cannot escalate to
            host root — there is no root daemon to reach.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run easypj under `podman run` (or rootless docker)
            and check `id` on the host for the container process. Verify: it
            maps to your UID, not 0 — root inside ≠ root outside.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — who actually launches the container?]
            DOCKER (root daemon mediates every container):
            ┌────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌────────────┐
            │ docker │──▶│ dockerd │──▶│ easypj web │
            │  CLI   │   │  (root) │   │   (root)   │
            └────────┘   └─────────┘   └────────────┘
                  │ docker.sock = root-equiv access

            PODMAN (client forks the container itself, no daemon):
            ┌────────┐                        ┌─────────────────┐
            │ podman │──no-daemon,no-socket──▶│    easypj web   │
            │  CLI   │                        │ (you, not root) │
            └────────┘                        └─────────────────┘

         💡 Under the hood: rootless (Podman or Docker) leans on Linux user
            namespaces plus `newuidmap`/`newgidmap` to remap container UID 0 to
            your real UID, and slirp4netns/pasta for networking — a rootful
            daemon gets real bridges and raw sockets that rootless simply cannot.

         📊 SUMMARY: rootless (Podman, or Docker rootless mode) removes the
            root daemon and the root-equivalent socket — a strictly smaller
            attack surface for multi-tenant and CI hosts.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: rootless cannot bind ports <1024 without extra config
            and some volume/network features differ — test easypj under it
            before assuming drop-in parity.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — userns-remap and why docker.sock is really root
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        20.3's `userns-remap` setting doesn't touch the container process at
        all — it changes what UID 0 INSIDE a container maps to OUTSIDE it.
        The daemon reads ranges from `/etc/subuid` and `/etc/subgid` (e.g.
        `dockremap:231072:65536`) and asks the kernel to remap the
        container's entire UID/GID space into that unprivileged host range.
        Root inside becomes uid 231072 on the host — a kernel exploit that
        would normally hand over host root instead hands over an ordinary,
        powerless host account.

        docker.sock is dangerous for an unrelated reason: it is a Unix
        domain socket owned by root, and the DAEMON listening on it runs as
        root by default. Anyone who can write to that socket is not calling
        a sandboxed API — they are handing arbitrary container specs
        (including `--privileged`, `-v /:/host`) to a root process that will
        execute them without question.

        [WHY MOUNTING docker.sock = HANDING OVER HOST ROOT]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  container WITH docker.sock mounted                              │
        │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
        │  │ curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock \                   │ │
        │  │   -d '{"Image":"alpine","HostConfig":{"Privileged":true,    │ │
        │  │        "Binds":["/:/host"]}}' http://localhost/containers/  │ │
        │  │   create                                                    │ │
        │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
        │                     │  daemon (ROOT) obeys — it cannot tell a    │
        │                     │  "friendly" caller from a hostile one      │
        │                     ▼                                            │
        │           a NEW privileged container with the WHOLE host         │
        │           filesystem bind-mounted at /host — game over           │
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        ⚠️ userns-remap and "mount docker.sock into a container" are
        opposite instincts: one shrinks what root can do, the other hands
        root out to whoever asks nicely.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🔑 The hardening checklist is ordered by payoff: pin the base
           image, de-root, de-cap, freeze the filesystem, scan, limit
           resources, add health checks, sign, keep the Engine patched
           (20.1).
        🔑 ENV vars leak — they show in `docker inspect`,
           `/proc/1/environ`, and child processes; secrets belong in
           mounted files (or Vault/Secrets Manager), never ENV or a
           Dockerfile layer (20.2).
        🔑 A secret ARG/ENV baked into an early build stage persists in
           that layer forever, even if a later stage unsets it — use
           `--mount=type=secret` build secrets instead (20.2).
        🔑 `docker.sock` is root-equivalent — mounting it into any
           container hands that container the power to create a
           `--privileged` container with the host filesystem bind-mounted
           (20.3).
        🔑 `userns-remap`, `no-new-privileges`, and `icc: false` are three
           daemon.json settings that shrink what a compromised container
           (or its root) can actually do (20.3).
        🔑 Docker Content Trust (DCT) makes `pull` also mean "verify this
           tag was signed by us and untampered" — but it only protects
           tags you actually signed (20.4).
        🔑 Rootless containers (Podman, or Docker's rootless mode) remove
           the root daemon and the root-equivalent socket entirely — a
           strictly smaller attack surface for CI and multi-tenant hosts
           (20.5).

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚠️ An unpinned `:latest` base silently changes between builds — an
           unreviewed dependency upgrade shipping on every deploy.
        ⚠️ A secret baked into ANY build stage's ENV/ARG stays in that
           image layer forever, regardless of what later stages do.
        ⚠️ `-v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` is functionally
           `--privileged` for the WHOLE HOST, not just that one container —
           the single most dangerous flag in common CI use.
        ⚠️ DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 does not make an unsigned `:latest`
           magically safe — it just fails the pull; losing your root
           signing key means you can never sign that repo again.
        ⚠️ Rootless containers cannot bind ports <1024 without extra
           configuration and some volume/network features differ — test
           easypj under it before assuming drop-in parity.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚡ `docker inspect <c> | grep -i -A2 env` right after any incident —
           the fastest way to see exactly what secrets an image/container
           exposed.
        ⚡ Grep your Dockerfiles for `ENV.*(SECRET|PASSWORD|KEY|TOKEN)` in
           CI — the fastest way to catch a baked-in secret before it ships.
        ⚡ `docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}'` shows userns-remap
           and seccomp status on a host in one line.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 COMMANDS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        docker inspect web --format '{{.Config.Env}}'   # what ENV actually ships
        docker secret create db_password ./secret.txt   # Swarm: encrypted secret
        docker service create --secret db_password ...  # mount it at runtime
        export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1                    # sign on push, verify on pull
        docker trust inspect easypj/web:v1 --pretty      # who signed this tag
        podman run --rm easypj:v1                        # rootless, no daemon
        docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}'      # userns-remap/seccomp status

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 DRILL
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🧪 Take easypj's current DB_PASSWORD, passed today as an ENV var.
        In 15 minutes: (1) `docker inspect | grep -i password` and confirm
        it's visible in plain text. (2) switch to a mounted secret file per
        20.2's compose snippet. (3) re-run inspect and confirm the value no
        longer appears — only the file path does.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 20)
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Q1. List the hardening checklist's first four items in priority
            order and say why pinning comes before scanning.
            → Pin the base tag (not :latest), run non-root, `--cap-drop
              ALL`, read-only rootfs + tmpfs. Pinning comes first because
              you cannot meaningfully scan or reason about an image whose
              base silently changes underneath you (20.1).

        Q2. Why does `docker inspect web` leak SECRET_KEY if it's passed as
            an ENV var, and what replaces it?
            → ENV vars are stored in the container's config and shown
              verbatim by `docker inspect` and readable from
              `/proc/1/environ`. Replace with a mounted secret file (Swarm
              secret, or a plain file volume) that Django reads at startup
              (20.2).
                 ENV SECRET_KEY=abc123     → visible in `docker inspect`
                 /run/secrets/secret_key   → file path only in inspect

        Q3. A Dockerfile does `ARG DB_PASSWORD` then `RUN echo $DB_PASSWORD
            > /tmp/x && rm /tmp/x` in one layer, believing the secret is
            gone. Is it actually gone? Why or why not?
            → No — the ARG value and everything the RUN step touched are
              baked into that layer's diff; deleting the file in the SAME
              layer removes it from the final filesystem view, but the
              value can still be extracted from layer history/build cache
              (20.2's gotcha). Use `--mount=type=secret` instead, which
              never writes the secret into a layer at all.

        Q4. Why is mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` into a container
            functionally equivalent to giving it `--privileged` on the
            whole HOST, not just itself?
            → The socket is the daemon's API, and the daemon runs as root.
              A container with the socket can ask the daemon to create a
              NEW container with `--privileged` and `-v /:/host`, and the
              root daemon will comply — it cannot distinguish a friendly
              caller from a hostile one (20.3).

        Q5. Name three daemon.json keys that hardening changes and what
            each one does.
            → `userns-remap` (remaps container UID 0 to an unprivileged
              host UID), `no-new-privileges` (blocks privilege escalation
              via setuid binaries), `icc: false` (disables default inter-
              container communication on the bridge network) (20.3).

        Q6. What does Docker Content Trust actually verify on `docker
            pull`, and what happens if you pull a tag you never signed?
            → It verifies the image manifest was signed by a trusted key
              (via Notary) and matches what was pushed — untampered and
              authentic. Pulling an unsigned/tampered tag with DCT enabled
              FAILS with a trust-data error rather than silently pulling it
              (20.4).

        Q7. Your team loses the Content Trust root signing key. What is
            the practical consequence for that repository?
            → You can never sign new releases of that repository under the
              old key/trust data again — it is not a "reset password"
              situation, which is why 20.4 treats the root key as something
              to protect as carefully as the docker.sock socket itself.

        Q8. Compare Docker's default architecture to Podman's for ONE
            security property: what happens to "root inside the
            container" in each?
            → Docker (root daemon): root inside typically IS root outside
              unless userns-remap is on. Podman (rootless by default): root
              inside maps to YOUR unprivileged UID outside via user
              namespaces — there is no root daemon to escalate to (20.5).
                 DOCKER: CLI ▶ dockerd (root) ▶ easypj web (root)
                 PODMAN: CLI ▶ easypj web (you, not root) — no daemon

        Q9. Why does 20.3 call `docker.sock` "the crown jewel" rather than
            just another dangerous flag?
            → Every other control in Chapters 19-20 (non-root, cap-drop,
              read-only, secrets) can be bypassed in one step if a
              container also holds the socket — it is root-equivalent
              access that overrides everything else on the host.

        Q10. Put the ordered hardening checklist, secrets handling, daemon
             lockdown, signing, and rootless together: what is the ONE
             thing NONE of them prove, and which chapter does?
             → None of Chapter 20 measures whether the hardening actually
               worked or whether new CVEs have appeared since the image
               was built — that verification, scanning, and CIS scoring is
               Chapter 21's job.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — "Chapter 20, the checklist made real"
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  📋 20.1 CHECKLIST      pin → non-root → cap-drop → read-only →     │
    │                          scan → limits → healthcheck → sign → patch │
    │         │                                                          │
    │         ▼                                                          │
    │  🔐 20.2 SECRETS        files/vault, never ENV or a Dockerfile layer│
    │         │                                                          │
    │         ▼                                                          │
    │  🗝️ 20.3 THE DAEMON     docker.sock = root; userns-remap,          │
    │                          icc:false, no-new-privileges shrink root  │
    │         │                                                          │
    │         ▼                                                          │
    │  ✍️ 20.4 SIGNING        DCT: pull also means "verify authentic"     │
    │         │                                                          │
    │         ▼                                                          │
    │  🚫 20.5 ROOTLESS       Podman/rootless Docker: no root daemon      │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    .vs-prose — Chapter 20 takes every primitive Chapter 19 named and turns
    it into things you actually DO to easypj: an ordered checklist you run
    on every deploy (20.1), secrets that live in mounted files instead of a
    leaky ENV var or a baked-in layer (20.2), a daemon whose root socket is
    guarded and whose config actively shrinks what a compromised root
    process can do (20.3), image signing that makes "pull" mean "verify"
    (20.4), and a rootless option that removes the root daemon altogether
    for the highest-risk hosts (20.5). What none of this chapter can tell
    you is whether it actually worked — that measurement is Chapter 21.


Chapter 21: Docker Security Scanning & Compliance
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Hardening you cannot measure is faith, not
    security. This chapter is the instrumentation: scanning images for CVEs
    (Scout, Trivy), auditing the host against the CIS Benchmark (Docker Bench),
    generating an SBOM of everything you ship, and wiring all of it into CI.
    Problem solved: "how do I PROVE, on every build, that easypj has no known
    critical vulnerabilities and follows the benchmark?"

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced · ⏱️ ~2h · Security domain (15%) — image scanning
        (Docker Scout) is examined directly; this chapter is the
        measurement layer for the whole DCA Security domain.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
         ✅ Run `docker scout quickview/cves/recommendations/compare` on
            easypj and act on each command's output (21.1).
         ✅ Run Docker Bench Security against a host and map its PASS/WARN
            output back to a concrete daemon.json or run-flag fix (21.2).
         ✅ Scan easypj with Trivy and wire `--exit-code` into a CI gate
            (21.3).
         ✅ Generate an SBOM for easypj (SPDX or CycloneDX) and use it to
            answer "are we affected by CVE-X?" without a rebuild (21.4).
         ✅ Explain what the CIS Docker Benchmark covers and which of its
            checks are image-level versus host-wide (21.5).
         ✅ Explain why a clean scan is a point-in-time result and must be
            re-run on every build, not trusted forever.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: this chapter IS the measurable half of the Security
        domain (15%) — Docker Scout and vulnerability scanning are graded
        directly; it closes out Chapters 19-20's hardening with proof.

    [E] SECTION MAP (you are here):
         21.1 Docker Scout (the vendor-native scanner) → 21.2 Docker Bench
         Security (host CIS audit) → 21.3 Trivy (open-source alternative)
         → 21.4 SBOM (the durable inventory) → 21.5 CIS Benchmark (the
         standard the bench script measures) — scan the image, audit the
         host, inventory everything, then name the standard behind it all.

    21.1 Docker Scout Deep Dive
         - docker scout quickview <image>
         - docker scout cves <image>
         - docker scout recommendations <image>
         - docker scout compare <image1> <image2>
         - Scout in CI/CD pipelines
         [TERMINAL: Complete docker scout workflow for easypj]

         🎯 GOAL: Use Docker Scout to find, explain, and fix CVEs in the easypj
            image.
         [TECH] Scout analyzes an image's SBOM against CVE databases.
            `quickview` gives a severity summary; `cves` lists each finding;
            `recommendations` suggests base-image bumps; `compare` diffs two
            tags. It runs locally and in CI, failing a build over a policy.
         [ANALOGY] A home inspector for your image: quickview is the one-page
            summary, cves is the full defect list, recommendations is "replace
            this old water heater", compare is "before vs after the repairs".
         [TERMINAL: the Scout workflow on easypj]
            $ docker scout quickview easypj:v1
              Critical 0  High 3  Medium 12  Low 20
            $ docker scout cves easypj:v1 --only-severity critical,high
            $ docker scout recommendations easypj:v1   # e.g. slim → newer slim
            $ docker scout compare easypj:v1 --to easypj:v2
         🔬 easypj: quickview flags 3 highs from an old base; `recommendations`
            says bump python:3.12-slim to the latest patch, which
            `docker scout compare` then confirms cleared them.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: scan easypj:v1, bump the base image one patch
            version, rebuild, and `docker scout compare` old vs new. Verify:
            the high-severity count drops in the comparison.
         📊 SUMMARY: Scout turns "is my image safe?" into a measured, diffable
            number — quickview to triage, recommendations to fix, compare to prove.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a clean scan is a POINT-IN-TIME result; new CVEs land
            daily, so re-scan on every build and on a schedule, not once.

    21.2 Docker Bench Security
         - Automated checks against CIS Docker Benchmark
         - docker run --rm --pid host --net host --cap-add audit_control -v /var/lib:/var/lib -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v /etc:/etc docker/docker-bench-security
         [OUTPUT: Annotated docker-bench-security report]

         🎯 GOAL: Audit the Docker host against the CIS Benchmark with Docker
            Bench Security.
         [TECH] docker-bench-security is a script (shipped as a container) that
            checks host config, daemon.json, image, and runtime settings
            against the CIS Docker Benchmark, emitting [PASS]/[WARN]/[INFO]
            per check. It reads host paths, so it needs several host mounts and
            pid/net host to inspect the real daemon.
         [ANALOGY] A code-compliance inspector walking your building with the
            official checklist, ticking each rule PASS or WARN — the CIS
            Benchmark is the building code.
         [TERMINAL: run the benchmark]
            $ docker run --rm --net host --pid host --cap-add audit_control \
              -v /var/lib:/var/lib -v /etc:/etc \
              -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
              docker/docker-bench-security
              [WARN] 2.1  - Restrict network traffic between containers (icc)
              [PASS] 4.1  - Ensure a user for the container is created
         🔬 easypj: the bench WARNs that icc is enabled — feeding the exact
            daemon.json fix (icc:false) already recommended in 20.3.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run docker-bench-security and pick the top 3 WARNs.
            Verify: each maps to a concrete daemon.json or run-flag change you
            can apply, then re-run to see it flip to PASS.
         📊 SUMMARY: Docker Bench converts the CIS Benchmark into an automated
            PASS/WARN report — the host-hardening counterpart to image scanning.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the bench itself needs docker.sock + host mounts to run;
            treat it as a trusted, one-off audit tool, not a long-lived
            container, and remove it after.

    21.3 Trivy — Open Source Vulnerability Scanner
         - What is Trivy? (Aqua Security's scanner)
         - trivy image easypj:v1
         - trivy fs /path/to/dockerfile
         - Trivy in CI/CD
         [TERMINAL: Trivy output for easypj image]

         🎯 GOAL: Scan easypj with Trivy as an open-source, CI-friendly
            alternative to Scout.
         [TECH] Trivy (Aqua Security) scans images, filesystems, and IaC for
            CVEs and misconfigurations. `trivy image easypj:v1` reports OS and
            language-package vulnerabilities; `--exit-code 1 --severity
            CRITICAL,HIGH` fails a CI job on serious findings; `trivy fs .`
            scans a source tree before it is ever built.
         [ANALOGY] A free, open-source metal detector you can run anywhere —
            on the finished image, on the raw source, or wired to the CI gate —
            no vendor account required.
         [TERMINAL: Trivy on easypj]
            $ trivy image easypj:v1
              Total: 15 (HIGH: 3, CRITICAL: 0)
            $ trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 easypj:v1
            $ trivy fs --scanners vuln,misconfig .
         🔬 easypj: the same 3 highs Scout found appear in Trivy with fix
            versions; CI runs `trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL`
            so a critical CVE hard-fails the easypj pipeline.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `trivy image` on easypj, then again with
            `--exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH` and check `$?`. Verify:
            exit 0 when clean, 1 when a high/critical exists — a usable CI gate.
         📊 SUMMARY: Trivy is a free, scriptable scanner for images, filesystems
            and IaC — the open-source workhorse of a scanning gate.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Trivy caches its vuln DB; in air-gapped/CI runs update or
            mount the DB explicitly, or you scan against a stale database and
            miss fresh CVEs.

    21.4 SBOM (Software Bill of Materials)
         - What is an SBOM? (list of all components in an image)
         - docker sbom easypj:v1
         - Syft + Grype tools
         - SBOM formats: SPDX, CycloneDX
         [CODE: SBOM generation and interpretation]

         🎯 GOAL: Generate an SBOM for easypj and use it to answer "are we
            affected by CVE-X?" instantly.
         [TECH] An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) is a machine-readable list
            of every component + version in an image. `docker sbom` (or Syft)
            emits SPDX/CycloneDX; feed it to Grype to match against CVEs. When
            the next Log4j-style bug drops, you grep the SBOM instead of
            rebuilding and rescanning everything.
         [ANALOGY] The ingredients label on the package: when a recall hits
            "batch of ingredient X", you read labels to find affected products
            — you do not re-cook every meal to check.
         [CODE: SBOM generate + match]
            $ docker sbom easypj:v1 -o spdx-json > easypj.sbom.json
            $ syft easypj:v1 -o cyclonedx-json > easypj.cdx.json
            $ grype sbom:easypj.sbom.json          # CVEs from the SBOM alone
            $ grep -i "django" easypj.sbom.json    # which version do we ship?
         🔬 easypj: the SBOM lists Django 5.x, psycopg, gunicorn and every OS
            lib with exact versions; a new psycopg CVE is answered by grepping
            the file, no rebuild required.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: generate easypj's SBOM, then find the exact Django
            and psycopg versions in it. Verify: the versions match
            `pip freeze` inside the container.
         [TABLE: SPDX vs CycloneDX — which SBOM format?]
            Dimension | SPDX                     | CycloneDX
            Steward   | Linux Fdn (ISO 5962)     | OWASP Foundation
            Born from | license/provenance       | AppSec / CVE tracking
            Tooling   | syft -o spdx-json        | syft -o cyclonedx-json
            easypj    | license audit of deps    | feeds Grype CVE match

         💡 One nuance the CODE above doesn't show: CycloneDX has native VEX
            (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) support, letting you attach
            "CVE-X is present but NOT exploitable here" statements that Grype can
            honor — SPDX only gained comparable VEX linkage in its 3.0 spec.

         📊 SUMMARY: an SBOM is the durable inventory of what you shipped — the
            fastest path from "is CVE-X in our stack?" to a yes/no answer.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: an SBOM is a SNAPSHOT of one build; regenerate it per
            image tag, and store it as a build artifact — a stale SBOM answers
            the wrong version's question.

    21.5 CIS Docker Benchmark Overview
         - What is CIS Benchmark? (security configuration standard)
         - Key checks: Host configuration, Docker daemon, Container runtime
         - Automated compliance with docker-bench-security
         [TABLE: CIS Benchmark categories and key checks]

         🎯 GOAL: Describe what the CIS Docker Benchmark covers and how to
            check compliance automatically.
         [TECH] The CIS Docker Benchmark is a consensus security-configuration
            standard grouped into sections: Host config, Docker daemon config,
            daemon files/permissions, container images, container runtime, and
            operations. docker-bench-security automates most checks; the
            benchmark is the WHAT, the bench script is the HOW-to-measure.
         [ANALOGY] CIS is the published building code; Docker Bench is the
            inspector who walks the site with that code in hand. You can read
            the code yourself, but the inspector makes it a checklist.
         [TABLE: CIS Docker sections → example check]
            Host config   | audit the docker daemon & files
            Daemon config | icc=false, no-new-privileges, live-restore
            Images        | non-root USER, no secrets in layers
            Runtime       | --cap-drop, --read-only, --memory limits
         🔬 easypj: nearly every easypj control so far — non-root, cap-drop,
            read-only, memory limits, hardened daemon.json — is a specific CIS
            line item; the benchmark is a rollup of Chapters 19-21.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: pick one check from each CIS section and confirm
            easypj meets it (e.g. Images → USER set, Runtime → cap-drop ALL).
            Verify: docker-bench PASSes those exact lines for your container.
         📊 SUMMARY: CIS is the standard, Docker Bench is the meter — together
            they turn "is easypj hardened?" into a section-by-section score.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: CIS is guidance, not law — some checks (e.g. auditd
            rules, AppArmor) are host-wide and cannot be satisfied from a
            Dockerfile alone; hardening spans the host, not just the image.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how a scanner turns image layers into a CVE list
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Scout, Trivy, and Grype all do fundamentally the same three-step job
        (21.1, 21.3, 21.4), even though their UIs differ:
          • INVENTORY: unpack every image layer and read each package
            manager's own metadata — `dpkg`'s /var/lib/dpkg/status, `apt`'s
            equivalents, Python's installed-package metadata (the same data
            `pip freeze` reads), any lockfile present. This list of
            {name, version, ecosystem} tuples IS the SBOM (21.4) —
            scanning and SBOM generation are the same first step.
          • IDENTIFY: each package is turned into a standard identifier —
            a CPE (Common Platform Enumeration) or a PURL (Package URL,
            e.g. `pkg:pypi/django@5.2.5`) — because CVE databases (NVD,
            OSV, distro security trackers) are indexed by these, not by
            free-text names.
          • MATCH: the identifiers are looked up against a downloaded CVE
            feed. A hit means "this exact version range is listed against
            this CVE"; the severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) comes from
            the feed's CVSS score, not from the scanner itself.

        [FROM IMAGE LAYERS TO A CVE LIST]
        ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  easypj:v1 layers  ──▶  dpkg/pip package metadata (= the SBOM)   │
        │                              │                                    │
        │                              ▼                                    │
        │                  pkg:pypi/django@5.2.5, pkg:deb/openssl@3.0.2...  │
        │                              │                                    │
        │                              ▼                                    │
        │         match against CVE feed (NVD/OSV/distro trackers)          │
        │                              │                                    │
        │                              ▼                                    │
        │            Critical 0  High 3  Medium 12  Low 20  (21.1's output)│
        └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        💡 This is WHY an SBOM answers "are we affected by CVE-X" without a
        rebuild (21.4): the inventory step already happened, so a new CVE
        just needs a MATCH against data you already have, not a new scan.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🔑 Docker Scout gives quickview (triage), cves (the full list),
           recommendations (the fix), and compare (before vs after) — one
           tool covering the whole find-explain-fix loop (21.1).
        🔑 Docker Bench Security automates the CIS Docker Benchmark into a
           PASS/WARN/INFO report — CIS is the standard, Bench is the meter
           (21.2, 21.5).
        🔑 Trivy is a free, open-source, CI-friendly alternative to Scout —
           `--exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH` makes it a real CI gate
           (21.3).
        🔑 An SBOM (SPDX or CycloneDX) is the durable inventory of exactly
           what shipped — the fastest path from "is CVE-X in our stack?" to
           a yes/no answer, without a rebuild (21.4).
        🔑 Scanning and SBOM generation are the same first step: unpack
           layers, read package-manager metadata, identify packages by
           CPE/PURL, then match against a CVE feed.
        🔑 A clean scan is a POINT-IN-TIME result — new CVEs land daily, so
           re-scan on every build and on a schedule, not once (21.1).
        🔑 CIS is guidance, not law — some checks (auditd rules, AppArmor)
           are host-wide and cannot be satisfied from a Dockerfile alone;
           hardening spans the host, not just the image (21.5).

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚠️ GOTCHAS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚠️ Treating a clean scan as permanent — CVE databases update daily,
           so yesterday's clean image can be today's critical finding.
        ⚠️ Docker Bench itself needs `docker.sock` and host mounts to run —
           treat it as a trusted, one-off audit tool, not a long-lived
           container, and remove it after.
        ⚠️ Trivy's vulnerability DB is cached locally — in air-gapped or CI
           runs, update or mount the DB explicitly, or you scan against a
           stale database and miss fresh CVEs.
        ⚠️ An SBOM is a snapshot of ONE build — regenerate it per image
           tag and store it as a build artifact; a stale SBOM answers the
           wrong version's question.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ⚡ SPEED TIPS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ⚡ `docker scout quickview` before every push — a 5-second severity
           summary beats finding out from an auditor.
        ⚡ `trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1` as your
           first CI security gate — free, fast, and scriptable.
        ⚡ Keep the last build's SBOM alongside the image tag — the next
           Log4j-style CVE is a `grep`, not a rebuild-and-rescan.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🔑 COMMANDS
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        docker scout quickview easypj:v1               # severity summary
        docker scout cves easypj:v1 --only-severity critical,high
        docker scout compare easypj:v1 --to easypj:v2   # before vs after
        trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL,HIGH easypj:v1
        docker sbom easypj:v1 -o spdx-json > easypj.sbom.json
        grype sbom:easypj.sbom.json                     # CVEs from the SBOM
        docker run --rm --net host --pid host --cap-add audit_control \
          -v /var/lib:/var/lib -v /etc:/etc \
          -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
          docker/docker-bench-security                  # CIS host audit

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 DRILL
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        🧪 In 15 minutes: run `docker scout quickview easypj:v1`, note the
        High/Critical count, bump the base image one patch version, rebuild,
        and `docker scout compare` old vs new. Then generate an SBOM and
        `grep -i django` it to confirm the version matches `pip freeze`
        inside the container.

    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 21)
    ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Q1. What do `docker scout quickview`, `cves`, `recommendations`,
            and `compare` each answer?
            → quickview: how bad is it (severity counts). cves: exactly
              which CVEs. recommendations: what to change (e.g. a newer
              base tag). compare: did the fix actually help, tag vs tag
              (21.1).

        Q2. Why is a clean `docker scout quickview` on Monday not a
            guarantee of a clean scan on Friday?
            → CVE databases are updated continuously as new vulnerabilities
              are disclosed; a scan is a snapshot against the feed at that
              moment, so the same unchanged image can score differently a
              few days later (21.1's gotcha).

        Q3. What is Docker Bench Security actually checking, and why does
            it need `--pid host --net host` plus several host mounts?
            → It audits the HOST's Docker configuration (daemon.json,
              filesystem permissions, running containers) against the CIS
              Docker Benchmark, so it needs visibility into the real host
              process tree, network namespace, and files — those flags and
              mounts are what give it that visibility (21.2).

        Q4. A Docker Bench run reports `[WARN] 2.1 - Restrict network
            traffic between containers (icc)`. What is the concrete fix?
            → Set `"icc": false` in daemon.json and restart the daemon —
              the exact fix already covered in 20.3, now surfaced as a
              measured finding instead of a recommendation (21.2).

        Q5. Compare Trivy and Docker Scout on ONE dimension: what do you
            need to use each, and why might a team run both?
            → Scout is bundled with the Docker CLI/Hub and needs no extra
              install; Trivy is standalone open source with no vendor
              account required. Teams often run both because they draw
              from overlapping-but-not-identical CVE sources, catching
              more than either alone (21.1, 21.3).

        Q6. What exit code does `trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity
            CRITICAL,HIGH easypj:v1` return when the image is clean versus
            when it has a High finding, and why does that matter for CI?
            → Exit 0 when clean, exit 1 when a High/Critical exists — a
              non-zero exit is what lets a CI pipeline actually FAIL the
              build instead of just printing a warning nobody reads (21.3).

        Q7. What is an SBOM, and how does it let you answer "are we
            affected by the newest CVE?" without touching the image?
            → A Software Bill of Materials — a machine-readable list of
              every component + exact version shipped. Since the CVE
              matching step (see Under the Hood) just needs identifiers,
              you grep/feed the EXISTING SBOM against the new CVE instead
              of re-unpacking and re-scanning the image (21.4).
                 new CVE announced → grep easypj.sbom.json → yes/no, instant

        Q8. Your team needs to attach a "CVE-X is present but not
            exploitable in our deployment" statement that a scanner can
            honor. Which SBOM format natively supports this, and what is
            the mechanism called?
            → CycloneDX, via native VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability
              eXchange) support — SPDX only gained comparable VEX linkage
              in its 3.0 spec (21.4).

        Q9. List three CIS Docker Benchmark sections and one example check
            from each, and say which are image-level versus host-wide.
            → | Section        | Example check                      | Level      |
              | Host config    | audit the daemon & its files       | host-wide  |
              | Daemon config  | icc=false, no-new-privileges       | host-wide  |
              | Images         | non-root USER, no secrets in layers| image-level|
              (21.5).

        Q10. Why does 21.5 say CIS is "guidance, not law," and give one
             example of a check no Dockerfile change alone can satisfy?
             → Some CIS checks require host-level configuration (auditd
               rules, AppArmor profile loading) that no image build can
               set — hardening spans the host as well as the image, which
               is why Chapter 20's daemon.json work and Chapter 21's
               scanning are BOTH necessary, not either/or (21.5).

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — "Chapter 21, hardening you can measure"
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  🔍 21.1 SCOUT           quickview → cves → recommendations →       │
    │                           compare: find, explain, fix, prove        │

    │         │                                                          │

    .vs-prose — Chapter 21 is Part 7's proof layer: Docker Scout and Trivy
    turn "is easypj's image safe?" into a diffable severity count (21.1,
    21.3), Docker Bench turns "is the host configured safely?" into a
    PASS/WARN report against the CIS Benchmark (21.2, 21.5), and an SBOM
    turns "what exactly did we ship?" into a durable inventory that answers
    the next CVE without a rebuild (21.4). None of it is a one-time check —
    re-scanning on every build is what keeps Chapters 19-20's hardening
    honest as new vulnerabilities are disclosed.



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    [F] PART 7 KEY TAKEAWAYS
     ✅ A default container is root, fully capped, unfiltered, and writable
        everywhere — Part 7 turns each of those defaults into a deliberate,
        hardened choice (Ch19).
     🔑 The security onion is 10 independent layers; Ch19 makes four of the
        highest-value ones concrete on easypj (non-root, cap-drop, seccomp/
        AppArmor, read-only rootfs) before Ch20 assembles the rest.
     🎯 DCA MAP: Ch19 underlies Security (15%) with capabilities and non-
        root users; Ch20 IS secrets management and daemon configuration;
        Ch21 IS image scanning — together they cover the domain end-to-end.
     🔑 `docker.sock` is root-equivalent — mounting it into any container is
        functionally `--privileged` for the WHOLE HOST, not just itself
        (Ch20).
     ✅ Secrets belong in mounted files or a vault, never ENV vars or a
        Dockerfile layer — ENV leaks via `docker inspect` and layer history
        never forgets (Ch20).
     ✅ Hardening is a claim until it is measured: Docker Scout/Trivy scan
        the image, Docker Bench audits the host against the CIS Benchmark,
        and an SBOM makes "are we affected by CVE-X?" a grep, not a
        rebuild (Ch21).
     🔑 A clean scan is a POINT-IN-TIME result — re-scan on every build and
        on a schedule, because Chapters 19-20's hardening only stays true
        until the next disclosed CVE (Ch21).

    ⚠️ PART 7 GOTCHAS
     ⚠️ `--privileged` and `seccomp=unconfined` both erase multiple onion
        layers in one flag — treat either on sight as "this needs review,"
        never as a quick fix.
     ⚠️ Non-root, read-only, and secrets-as-files all commonly break on
        FIRST deploy because a path isn't owned, a tmpfs mount is missing,
        or a secret file isn't wired up — expect one iteration, don't panic.
     ⚠️ Mounting `docker.sock` into any container (including a CI runner
        that "just needs Docker") hands that container host root — there is
        almost always a safer alternative.
     ⚠️ A passing scan or CIS Benchmark today is not a permanent state —
        treat Chapter 21's tools as a recurring gate, not a one-time audit.

    ⚡ PART 7 SPEED TIPS
     ⚡ `docker inspect <c> --format '{{.HostConfig.Privileged}} {{.HostConfig.CapDrop}}'`
        — a one-line health check for the two flags that matter most.
     ⚡ Run `docker scout quickview` before every push — cheaper than
        finding out from an auditor or an incident.
     ⚡ When something breaks after hardening, check ownership (non-root),
        tmpfs paths (read-only), and secret wiring (files) — in that order,
        those three explain almost every Part 7 regression.

    [G] PART 7 VISUAL SUMMARY — "from default container to measured-safe"
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │  Ch19 — THE PRIMITIVES      Ch20 — APPLIED TO easypj   Ch21 — PROVEN│
    │  namespaces, caps,          ordered checklist,         Scout/Trivy  │
    │  seccomp, AppArmor,         secrets as files,          scans, Docker│

    │  the 10-layer onion         signed images, rootless    SBOM answers │
    │         │                          │                        │       │

    │                                     ▼                                │
    │           A non-root, capped, read-only easypj container whose      │

    .vs-prose — Part 7 in one line: Chapter 19 replaced "a container is
    isolated by default" with the real model — a shared kernel wearing ten
    independent software layers of defense; Chapter 20 applied four of the
    highest-value layers to easypj's actual Dockerfile, compose file, and
    daemon, plus secrets, signing, and a rootless option; and Chapter 21
    turned "we hardened it" into a measured claim with Docker Scout, Docker
    Bench, Trivy, an SBOM, and a CIS Benchmark score. Nothing about what
    easypj DOES has changed — only how safely it runs and how provably that
    safety holds, which is exactly what Part 8 now ships.

    THINK BEFORE PART 8:
      What runs where?    → the build runs on a CI RUNNER, not your laptop; the
                            image is the artifact that moves to the registry.
      What talks to what? → runner → Docker build → registry → deploy target;
                            every stage is itself a container for consistency.
      What breaks first?  → the build strategy: dind vs a mounted docker.sock —
                            the socket mount makes the CI job root on the runner.

    [PART 8 INTRO]
    Parts 1-7 got easypj built, run, composed into a multi-container stack,
    networked, given real storage, and hardened — but every one of those
    steps still happened because a human sat down and typed a command.
    Part 8 removes the human from the loop: from here on, a `git push`
    builds, tests, scans, and versions an easypj image by itself, and the
    exact image that passes CI is the exact image that reaches production.
    This is the part where "I can build/run/compose easypj" becomes
    "easypj ships itself, safely, on every commit."

    Honesty check: parts of this part go beyond the DCA exam blueprint —
    Chapter 22 (pipeline automation) and Chapter 24 (testing strategy) are
    production depth, not graded DCA content. Chapter 23 (tagging,
    versioning, promotion) IS graded — it sits squarely inside the Image
    Creation, Management & Registry domain (20% of the exam, Section 6.3).

    Parts 1-7 taught you to be a skilled solo cook: you can build the dish

    End to end, Part 8 wires easypj into one push-to-prod path: a commit
    triggers a pipeline (Ch22) that builds ONE image, tags it traceably and
    promotes that same digest through environments purely by retagging
    (Ch23), while tests at every layer — unit, integration against real
    Postgres, e2e, image structure, and Dockerfile lint — gate whether that
    digest is even allowed to move (Ch24).

        push ──▶ [Ch22: CI builds + tests + scans easypj] ──▶ [Ch23: tag &
        promote ONE digest dev→staging→production] ──▶ prod pull
                          ▲
                          └── [Ch24: tests gate every hop above]

      This is the loop that now runs, unattended, on every commit to
      easypj.

Chapter 22: Docker in CI/CD Pipelines
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: The "works on my machine" problem returns with a
    vengeance in CI — different runners, different tool versions, flaky tests.
    This chapter makes Docker the constant: build, test, scan and push easypj
    inside containers on GitHub Actions, GitLab CI and Jenkins, so every stage
    runs in an identical environment. Problem solved: "my tests pass locally but
    the CI build is a different machine I cannot reproduce."

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced   ⏱️ ~3-3.5 hrs   🎯 DCA: not a graded domain on
        its own — full CI/CD pipeline design is production depth beyond the
        DCA blueprint — but it is the operational context for the graded
        Image Creation, Management & Registry domain (20%, see Ch23).

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
        - Explain why every stage of a CI/CD pipeline should run inside a
          container, and practice "build once, promote by tag."
        - Write a GitHub Actions workflow that logs in, tags, builds and
          pushes easypj using docker/login-action, docker/metadata-action
          and docker/build-push-action.
        - Write a GitLab CI pipeline for easypj and justify a dind vs
          docker.sock choice for the build job.
        - Write a Jenkins declarative pipeline that uses the Docker
          Pipeline plugin with credentials from Jenkins' store, never
          hardcoded in the Jenkinsfile.
        - Decide when to offload easypj builds to Docker Build Cloud for a
          shared cache and multi-arch (amd64+arm64) speed.
        - Choose a CI build strategy — dind, socket mount, or rootless
          kaniko/buildah — by weighing isolation against root-on-host risk.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: not graded directly — the DCA exam does not examine
        specific CI/CD platforms — but this chapter builds the production
        muscle that makes the graded tagging/registry domain (Ch23) matter
        in the first place.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 22.1 why Docker belongs in CI/CD → 22.2 GitHub Actions
        → 22.3 GitLab CI → 22.4 Jenkins → 22.5 Docker Build Cloud → 22.6
        choosing a build strategy (dind vs socket vs rootless) — three
        concrete platforms bracketed by the "why" up front and the "how
        safely" at the end.

    22.1 Why Docker in CI/CD?
         - Consistent build environment
         - No "works on my machine" in CI
         - Parallel testing in isolated containers
         - Easy artifact management (images = artifacts)

         [CI/CD PIPELINE — DOCKER AT EVERY STAGE]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                    🚀 CI/CD PIPELINE WITH DOCKER                           │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────┐ │
         │  │ 👨‍💻 Push  │   │ 🏗️ Build │   │ 🧪 Test  │   │ 🔍 Scan │   │ 📦 Push  │ │
         │  │  Code   │──▶│  Image  │──▶│  Image   │──▶│  Image  │──▶│  Image   │ │
         │  └─────────┘   └─────────┘   └──────────┘   └─────────┘   └──────────┘ │
         │       │             │              │              │             │         │
         │       ▼             ▼              ▼              ▼             ▼         │
         │  ┌─────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌─────────┐   ┌──────────┐ │
         │  │ GitHub  │   │ docker  │   │ docker   │   │ docker  │   │ docker   │ │
         │  │ /GitLab │   │ build   │   │ compose  │   │ scout   │   │ push     │ │
         │  │         │   │ -t      │   │ run test │   │ quick-  │   │ registry │ │
         │  │ Trigger │   │ easypj  │   │ django   │   │ view    │   │ easypj   │ │
         │  │ on push │   │ :ci-123 │   │ test     │   │ easypj  │   │ :v1.2.3  │ │
         │  └─────────┘   └─────────┘   └──────────┘   └─────────┘   └──────────┘ │
         │                                                                  │       │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
         │  │                                                                      │
         │  ▼                                                                      │
         │  ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐    │
         │  │ 🚢 Deploy│   │ 🏃 Smoke │   │ 📊 Monitor│   │ 🔄 Auto-Rollback │    │
         │  │  to K8s  │──▶│  Tests   │──▶│  Health  │──▶│  (if unhealthy)  │    │
         │  │ kubectl  │   │ curl     │   │ Prometheus│   │ kubectl rollout  │    │
         │  │ apply    │   │ /health  │   │ Grafana   │   │ undo             │    │
         │  └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────┘   └──────────────────┘    │
         │                                                                          │
         │  🔑 EVERY step runs in a Docker container → IDENTICAL environment!       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Explain why every CI/CD stage in the pipeline diagram runs
            inside a container.
         [TECH] The pipeline diagram above is push → build → test → scan → push
            → deploy → smoke → monitor → rollback, and EACH stage runs in a
            Docker container. The image built in stage 2 IS the artifact that
            flows through the rest — the exact bytes tested are the exact bytes
            deployed, eliminating environment drift between CI and prod.
         [ANALOGY] A factory conveyor (the diagram): the same part is stamped,
            inspected, and boxed at stations that never touch the part with
            bare hands — every station is a sealed, identical booth (container).
         [DIAGRAM:flow — the artifact is the image]
            build  → easypj:ci-<sha>   (one immutable artifact)
            test   → run tests IN that image
            scan   → Scout/Trivy that same image
            push   → retag ci-<sha> → v1.2.3 (rebuild NOTHING)
            deploy → pull v1.2.3 to prod
         🔬 easypj: `docker build -t easypj:ci-$SHA` once; tests, scan and the
            production tag all reference that one build — what CI green-lit is
            byte-for-byte what ships.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build an image tagged with the git SHA, run the
            test suite inside it, then retag it as a release. Verify: the
            release digest equals the tested digest (`docker inspect` --format
            '{{.Id}}') — no rebuild between test and ship.
         📊 SUMMARY: Docker makes CI/CD deterministic — build the artifact once,
            then test/scan/deploy that identical image through every stage.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: rebuilding at the deploy stage (instead of retagging the
            tested image) reintroduces drift — you would ship an image nobody
            tested. Build once, promote by tag.

    22.2 GitHub Actions + Docker
         - docker/login-action (authenticate)
         - docker/build-push-action (build and push)
         - docker/metadata-action (tags and labels)
         - Complete workflow for easypj
         [CODE: .github/workflows/docker.yml for easypj]

         🎯 GOAL: Build, scan and push easypj from a GitHub Actions workflow.
         [TECH] The official actions do the heavy lifting: docker/login-action
            authenticates to the registry, docker/metadata-action derives tags
            + labels from git refs, and docker/build-push-action builds
            (with buildx cache) and pushes. Secrets come from GitHub Actions
            secrets, never hardcoded.
         [ANALOGY] Prebuilt LEGO modules for the pipeline: you snap login +
            metadata + build-push together instead of hand-writing docker CLI
            in shell — fewer sharp edges, tested by millions.
         [CODE: .github/workflows/docker.yml — core steps]
            - uses: docker/login-action@v3
              with:
                username: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }}
                password: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}
            - uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
              with: { images: easypj/web }
            - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
              with:
                push: true
                tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
                cache-from: type=gha
                cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
         🔬 easypj: a push to main builds easypj/web tagged with both the SHA
            and the branch, scans it, and pushes — with GHA layer caching so
            unchanged pip layers are not rebuilt.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: add the three actions to a workflow and push a
            commit. Verify: the run logs show login → metadata tags → a pushed
            image, and the registry now lists the new tag.
         📊 SUMMARY: login + metadata + build-push actions give easypj a
            cached, tagged, pushed image on every commit with minimal YAML.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: registry creds MUST be GitHub secrets, never inline in
            the YAML — the workflow file is in the repo for everyone to read.

    22.3 GitLab CI + Docker
         - .gitlab-ci.yml with Docker
         - docker-in-docker (dind) vs docker socket binding
         - Complete GitLab CI pipeline for easypj
         [CODE: .gitlab-ci.yml for easypj]

         🎯 GOAL: Build easypj in GitLab CI and pick between dind and socket
            binding.
         [TECH] GitLab CI runs each job in a container. To build images you
            either run docker:dind as a privileged service (a full Docker
            daemon inside the job) or bind the host's docker.sock. dind is
            isolated but needs --privileged; the socket bind is lighter but
            gives the job root on the runner (see 22.6).
         [ANALOGY] dind is bringing your own portable forge to the job site
            (heavy, but yours); the socket bind is borrowing the landlord's
            master forge — convenient until the job burns the building down.
         [CODE: .gitlab-ci.yml — dind build]
            build:
              image: docker:27
              services:
                - docker:27-dind
              variables:
                DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs"
              script:
                - docker build -t easypj:ci-$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA .
                - docker push easypj:ci-$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA
         🔬 easypj: the GitLab pipeline builds easypj:ci-<sha> in a dind
            service, runs `docker compose run tests`, then pushes — all inside
            ephemeral job containers that vanish after the run.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: write a two-job pipeline (build, test) using dind.
            Verify: the build job produces an image the test job can run, and
            the pipeline goes green only when tests pass.
         📊 SUMMARY: GitLab jobs are containers; build images via dind
            (isolated, privileged) or a socket bind (light, risky) — 22.6 picks.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: dind needs --privileged, which disables the seccomp/cap
            protections from Part 7 for that job — isolate dind runners and
            never reuse them for untrusted code.

    22.4 Jenkins + Docker
         - Jenkinsfile with Docker agent
         - docker.build(), docker.push()
         - Complete Jenkins pipeline for easypj
         [CODE: Jenkinsfile for easypj]

         🎯 GOAL: Build and push easypj from a Jenkins declarative pipeline.
         [TECH] Jenkins runs stages on agents; the Docker Pipeline plugin adds
            `docker.build()`, `.push()`, and `docker.image().inside {}` to run
            steps inside a container. Agents need Docker access (a dind sidecar
            or a mounted socket) with the same trade-off as every other CI.
         [ANALOGY] Jenkins is the veteran foreman with a huge plugin toolbox;
            the Docker Pipeline plugin is the attachment that lets the foreman
            hand each task to a sealed container crew.
         [CODE: Jenkinsfile — build + push]
            pipeline {
              agent any
              stages {
                stage('Build') { steps { script {
                  img = docker.build("easypj:ci-${env.GIT_COMMIT}")
                } } }
                stage('Push') { steps { script {
                  docker.withRegistry('', 'registry-creds') { img.push() }
                } } }
              }
            }
         🔬 easypj: Jenkins builds easypj:ci-<commit>, runs the Django test
            suite via `img.inside { sh 'python manage.py test' }`, and pushes
            only if the stage is green.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: create a Build + Push pipeline with the Docker
            plugin and a credentials ID. Verify: the build stage produces an
            image and the push stage authenticates via the stored credential,
            not a plaintext password.
         📊 SUMMARY: Jenkins + Docker Pipeline plugin gives declarative
            build/test/push stages with credentials pulled from Jenkins' store.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker.withRegistry` credential IDs live in Jenkins'
            credential store — hardcoding a registry password in the Jenkinsfile
            leaks it to everyone with repo read access.

    22.5 Docker Build Cloud
         - Remote builds in the cloud
         - Faster builds (no local resource drain)
         - Shared build cache across team
         - docker buildx build --builder cloud-xxx
         [TERMINAL: Docker Build Cloud workflow]


         🎯 GOAL: Offload easypj image builds to Docker Build Cloud for speed
            and a shared cache.
         [TECH] Docker Build Cloud runs buildx builds on remote, beefy builders
            with a persistent, team-shared cache. `docker buildx build
            --builder cloud-<org>-<name>` sends the build context up; results
            (and cache) are shared, so a teammate's cached layers speed YOUR
            build. Multi-arch (amd64+arm64) builds run in parallel remotely.
         [ANALOGY] A shared industrial kitchen instead of everyone cooking on a
            camping stove: bigger burners, and the prep one cook did (cache) is
            ready for the next — nobody re-chops the same onions.
         [TERMINAL: build easypj in the cloud]
            $ docker buildx create --driver cloud easypj/builder
            $ docker buildx build --builder cloud-easypj-builder \
                --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
                -t easypj/web:v1 --push .
         🔬 easypj: the slow pip-install layer, cached in Build Cloud from the
            last run, is reused so a one-line code change rebuilds easypj in
            seconds instead of minutes — on CI runners that stay small.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build easypj once on Build Cloud, change only a
            source file, build again. Verify: the second build reuses the
            cached dependency layers (CACHED in the log) and finishes far faster.
         📊 SUMMARY: Build Cloud = remote builders + shared cache + easy multi-
            arch — faster CI without bigger local/runner machines.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the build CONTEXT is uploaded to the cloud — a fat
            context (node_modules, .git, media) is slow and may leak files;
            tighten .dockerignore before pointing builds at the cloud.

    22.6 dind vs Socket Mount — Choosing a CI Build Strategy
         - Building images in CI needs a Docker engine SOMEWHERE — three ways
         - docker:dind --privileged: isolated daemon, but privileged = risky
         - -v /var/run/docker.sock: light, but = ROOT on the runner host
         - Rootless builders (kaniko, buildah) need no daemon and no privilege
         - Choose by trust level of the code and the runner's blast radius

         🎯 GOAL: Choose a CI build strategy by weighing isolation against the
            root-on-host risk, and know the rootless escape hatch.
         [TECH] Three strategies. (1) docker:dind: a full daemon inside the job,
            requires --privileged — isolated per-job but privileged disables
            Part-7 protections. (2) Socket mount
            (-v /var/run/docker.sock:...): reuses the host daemon, so the job
            is ROOT on the runner (see 20.3) — fast but a breakout owns every
            build. (3) Rootless: kaniko or buildah build images in userspace
            with NO daemon and NO privilege.
         [ANALOGY] dind = your own locked workshop trucked in (heavy, self-
            contained); socket mount = a key to the landlord's workshop
            (convenient, but they can burn the block); kaniko/buildah = a
            portable 3D printer that needs no workshop at all.
         [TABLE: pick a CI build strategy]
            Strategy       | Isolation | Host risk       | Needs
            docker:dind    | high      | privileged job  | --privileged svc
            socket mount   | low       | ROOT on runner  | docker.sock bind
            kaniko/buildah | high      | none (rootless) | no daemon
         🔬 easypj: on a shared runner, easypj images are built with kaniko —
            no daemon, no privilege, no socket — so a poisoned dependency in a
            build cannot escalate to the runner host or other tenants.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build easypj three ways — dind, socket mount,
            kaniko — and for each check `id` / privilege of the build process.
            Verify: only kaniko/buildah run unprivileged with no host daemon
            access; the socket-mount job can control the host's Docker.
         📊 SUMMARY: dind for isolation at the cost of --privileged; socket
            mount only on fully trusted, single-tenant runners; kaniko/buildah
            when you want image builds with neither a daemon nor root.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: mounting docker.sock into a CI job is the most common
            "temporary" CI hack that ships to production runners — it hands
            every pipeline root on the host; prefer rootless builders.

    [G] UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 — why a docker.sock mount is equivalent to root
        The `docker` CLI is a thin client: every command, including
        `docker build`, is just an HTTP request sent over a Unix socket
        (/var/run/docker.sock) to the dockerd API. There is no extra
        authorization layer on top of the socket — the ability to WRITE to
        that socket file IS the authorization. Whoever can talk to it can
        ask dockerd to do anything the engine can do, including starting a
        --privileged container that bind-mounts the host's `/` and chroots
        into it. That is also why membership in the local `docker` group
        has always been documented as root-equivalent, and why 22.6 calls a
        CI socket mount "ROOT on the runner," not just "convenient."

        [DIAGRAM: what a docker.sock mount actually grants]
        CI job container
          │  docker build ...   (an HTTP-over-Unix-socket API call — no more)
          ▼
        /var/run/docker.sock  — no auth beyond "can this process write here?"
          │
          ▼
        dockerd  (runs as root on the HOST, not in any job's container)
          │  can start --privileged containers, mount host paths, etc.
          ▼
        HOST KERNEL — anything dockerd can do, the CI job can now request.

    [H] KEY TAKEAWAYS 🔑
        ✅ Build once, promote by tag: bake the image ONE time, then run
           test/scan/push/deploy against that exact same artifact.
        ✅ GitHub Actions: login-action + metadata-action + build-push-
           action = authenticate, derive tags, build (cached) and push.
        ✅ GitLab CI jobs are themselves containers; get Docker access via
           dind (isolated, privileged) or a docker.sock bind (light, risky).
        ✅ Jenkins' Docker Pipeline plugin (`docker.build()`, `.push()`)
           reads registry creds from Jenkins' credential store, never from
           the Jenkinsfile text.
        ✅ Docker Build Cloud gives a team a shared, persistent build cache
           and painless multi-arch builds without bigger local machines.
        ✅ Three CI build strategies trade isolation for convenience: dind
           (privileged), socket mount (root on host), kaniko/buildah
           (rootless, no daemon).
        🎯 DCA relevance: not a graded topic itself, but Image Creation &
           Registry (20%) assumes you can reliably produce the images it
           tests you on — this chapter is how that production actually runs.

    [I] GOTCHAS ⚠️
        - Rebuilding at the deploy stage (instead of retagging the already-
          tested image) silently reintroduces environment drift.
        - Hardcoding registry passwords in workflow YAML or a Jenkinsfile
          leaks them to anyone with read access to the repo.
