        - dind requires --privileged, which disables the seccomp/capability
          protections Part 7 spent a whole part establishing.
        - A fat build context (stray node_modules, .git, media files)
          uploaded to a remote builder is slow and can leak files — tighten
          .dockerignore before pointing builds at the cloud.
        - A "just this once" docker.sock mount tends to survive into
          production runners — treat it as a permanent decision.

    [J] SPEED TIPS ⚡
        - Cache dependency layers with `cache-from/to: type=gha` (GitHub
          Actions) or Build Cloud's shared cache instead of reinstalling
          pip packages on every run.
        - Prefer `docker buildx build --builder cloud-...` for multi-arch
          images over emulated (QEMU) builds — remote native builders are
          dramatically faster.

    [K] COMMANDS TO REMEMBER 🔑
        docker build -t easypj:ci-$SHA .                  # tag by git SHA
        docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' easypj:ci-$SHA  # confirm Image ID
        docker buildx create --driver cloud ORG/BUILDER   # register cloud builder
        docker buildx build --builder cloud-ORG-BUILDER \
          --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t easypj:v1 --push .
        docker push easypj:ci-$SHA                        # push the tested image
        # GitLab dind service:   services: [ docker:27-dind ]
        # Jenkins build+push:    docker.build("easypj:ci-${env.GIT_COMMIT}")

    [L] PRACTICE DRILL 🧪
        ⏱️ 10 minutes, no notes: write a 3-step GitHub Actions job — login,
        build+tag easypj with `${{ github.sha }}`, push — from memory, then
        compare it against the workflow in 22.2 and list what you missed.

    [M] LAB Q&A 🧪 — Chapter 22 (10 questions)

        Q1: In the 22.1 pipeline diagram, why does EVERY stage (build, test,
            scan, push, deploy, smoke, monitor, rollback) run in a Docker
            container instead of directly on the runner?
        A1: So every stage executes in an IDENTICAL environment, and so the
            image built in stage 2 is the same artifact tested, scanned,
            and deployed later — no "works in build, breaks in deploy" gap.
        Explanation: The diagram's own key line spells this out: "EVERY
            step runs in a Docker container → IDENTICAL environment." A
            bare-metal runner step would reintroduce the "works on my
            machine" problem this chapter exists to kill.

        Q2: What does "build once, promote by tag" mean, and what breaks it?
        A2: Build the image exactly once (e.g. easypj:ci-<sha>), then reuse
            that SAME image for test, scan, and every deploy target by
            adding/moving tags — never running `docker build` again to move
            it forward. Rebuilding at any later stage breaks it.
        Explanation: A second build can pull a different base-image digest
            or dependency version even from an unchanged Dockerfile,
            producing bytes nobody actually tested. 23.2 restates this as
            "promote by retagging the tested digest, never rebuild."

        Q3: Match each GitHub Action to its job in the easypj workflow
            (table).
        A3:
            Action                     | Job
            docker/login-action@v3     | authenticate to the registry
            docker/metadata-action@v5  | derive tags + labels from git refs
            docker/build-push-action@v6| build (with buildx cache) + push
        Explanation: These are official, widely-used actions that replace
            hand-rolled `docker login`/`build`/`push` shell steps with
            tested, declarative YAML — fewer places for a typo to leak a
            credential or mistag an image.

        Q4: Why must the registry username/password in 22.2's workflow come
            from `${{ secrets.REGISTRY_USER }}` / `secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN`
            rather than being typed directly into docker.yml?
        A4: Because the workflow YAML lives in the repository, readable by
            anyone with repo access; GitHub Actions secrets are encrypted
            and injected only at run time, never displayed in logs or diffs.
        Explanation: This is the same discipline 22.4 requires for Jenkins
            credentials — plaintext creds in pipeline-as-code is one of the
            most common real-world leak vectors.

        Q5: Compare dind and docker.sock-mount as GitLab CI build strategies
            (table), and say which one 22.6 recommends for a shared runner.
        A5:
            Strategy     | Isolation | Host risk      | Needs
            dind         | high      | privileged job | --privileged service
            socket mount | low       | ROOT on runner | docker.sock bind
            Recommended for a shared/multi-tenant runner: neither — use a
            rootless builder (kaniko/buildah, per 22.6).
        Explanation: dind isolates but disables Part-7 protections via
            --privileged; the socket mount is faster to set up but hands
            the job root on the host — acceptable only on trusted,
            single-tenant runners.

        Q6: In the Jenkins pipeline from 22.4, where do registry credentials
            come from, and why not a plaintext password in the Jenkinsfile?
        A6: From Jenkins' own credential store, referenced by ID (e.g.
            `docker.withRegistry('', 'registry-creds')`) — never written
            into the pipeline script itself.
        Explanation: The Jenkinsfile is typically versioned in the same
            repo as the app; a hardcoded password there is readable by
            anyone with repo access, exactly like the GitHub Actions case.

        Q7: What two problems does Docker Build Cloud solve for a team
            building easypj, and what's the context-upload gotcha?
        A7: (1) Slow local/CI builds — remote, beefier builders finish
            faster. (2) Duplicated work — a persistent, TEAM-SHARED cache
            means one teammate's cached layers speed up everyone's builds.
            Gotcha: the whole build CONTEXT uploads to the cloud, so a fat
            context (missing .dockerignore entries) is slow and can leak
            files.
        Explanation: 22.5's pip-install-layer example shows this directly —
            a cached dependency layer from a prior run turns a one-line
            code change into a seconds-long rebuild instead of minutes.

        Q8: List 22.6's three CI build strategies from HIGHEST to LOWEST
            isolation, and name the one true "no daemon, no privilege"
            option.
        A8: kaniko/buildah (rootless) and dind (privileged) both give high
            isolation; socket mount gives low isolation. Only kaniko/
            buildah need neither a daemon nor elevated privilege.
        Explanation: dind's isolation costs a privileged service; kaniko/
            buildah get similar/better isolation with NO daemon and NO
            privilege at all, which is why 22.6 calls them the rootless
            escape hatch for shared runners.

        Q9: Using the Under-the-Hood diagram above, explain in one sentence
            why mounting docker.sock into a CI job is described as handing
            it "ROOT on the runner."
        A9: Because writing to docker.sock is the ONLY authorization check
            dockerd applies, and dockerd itself runs as root on the host —
            so any process that can reach the socket can ask the root
            daemon to do anything, including mounting the host filesystem.
        Explanation: This is exactly the mechanism 22.6's table summarizes
            as "socket mount | low isolation | ROOT on runner."

        Q10: A shared runner builds untrusted third-party pull-request code
             for easypj. Which build strategy from 22.6 should it use, and
             why is dind not a safe enough answer here either?
        A10: kaniko or buildah — the only strategies that need neither a
             Docker daemon nor elevated privilege. dind still requires
             --privileged, which is a real host escape surface even though
             it is more isolated than a socket mount.
        Explanation: 22.6's own guidance is to choose "by trust level of
             the code and the runner's blast radius" — untrusted PR code is
             exactly the case that justifies the rootless-but-slower option.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 22
        push ──▶ build (ONE image) ──▶ test ──▶ scan ──▶ push ──▶ deploy
                     │
                     ├─ GitHub Actions  (login + metadata + build-push actions)
                     ├─ GitLab CI       (dind service OR docker.sock bind)
                     ├─ Jenkins         (Docker Pipeline plugin + stored creds)
                     └─ Build Cloud     (remote builder, shared cache, multi-arch)
        underneath ALL of them, one choice: dind (privileged) │ socket
        mount (root-on-host) │ kaniko/buildah (rootless)

        .vs-prose — Chapter 22 automates what Parts 1-7 did by hand: one
        `docker build` produces the ONE image that flows, untouched,
        through test, scan and deploy, on GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or
        Jenkins, optionally offloaded to Docker Build Cloud for speed and a
        shared cache. Every platform still has to answer the same
        underlying question — how does the CI job get Docker access, and at
        what cost — dind (isolated, but privileged), a docker.sock mount
        (fast, but root on the runner host), or a rootless builder like
        kaniko/buildah (neither)? That choice, not the YAML syntax, is the
        real decision this chapter teaches.


Chapter 23: Docker Image Versioning & Promotion
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: A pile of images called :latest is an outage
    waiting to happen — you cannot say what is running or roll back to what
    worked. This chapter imposes discipline: deterministic tags, promotion by
    RETAGGING the tested image across environments, registry topology, and
    signing in the pipeline. Problem solved: "which exact easypj image is in
    production, and how do I promote or roll back without rebuilding?"

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced   ⏱️ ~2.5-3 hrs   🎯 DCA: GRADED — Image Creation,
        Management & Registry (20% of the exam); tagging and promotion are
        explicit exam topics (Section 6.3) — registry design here builds
        on the registries the domain map credits to Ch2/7.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
        - Choose between immutable tags (git SHA, semver, combined) and
          moving tags (:latest, branch names) for the right situation.
        - Promote an easypj image dev → staging → production by RETAGGING
          one tested digest, never rebuilding.
        - Design a registry topology for easypj (single vs split dev/prod,
          pull-through mirrors) with a retention policy that won't delete
          your emergency rollback tag.
        - Sign easypj images in CI with Docker Content Trust and enforce
          signed-only pulls on deploy hosts.
        - Answer "which exact image is running in production?" using tags
          plus digest comparison, not guesswork.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: directly graded. Image tagging, versioning, and
        promotion appear by name under the Image Creation, Management &
        Registry domain (20%) in this guide's DCA domain map (Section 6.3) —
        study this chapter as exam content, not just best practice.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 23.1 tagging strategies → 23.2 promotion by retagging →
        23.3 registry topology & retention → 23.4 signing with Docker
        Content Trust in CI — a straight line from "name the image" to
        "prove which name can be trusted."

    23.1 Image Tagging Strategies for CI/CD
         - Git commit SHA: easypj:abc1234
         - Semantic version: easypj:1.2.3
         - Branch-based: easypj:main, easypj:develop
         - Environment-based: easypj:staging, easypj:production
         - Combined: easypj:1.2.3-abc1234
         [TABLE: Tagging strategy — pros, cons, use case]

         🎯 GOAL: Pick a tagging scheme that makes every easypj image
            identifiable and reproducible.
         [TECH] Tags are pointers, not versions. Use immutable, meaningful
            tags: the git SHA (easypj:abc1234) for exact traceability, semver
            (easypj:1.2.3) for releases, and combined (easypj:1.2.3-abc1234).
            Moving tags (:latest, :main) are convenient but ambiguous — never
            deploy prod from a moving tag.
         [ANALOGY] A SHA tag is a fingerprint (unique, permanent); :latest is a
            nickname that points at whoever answers today — fine for a chat,
            useless for a subpoena.
         [TABLE: tagging strategy trade-offs]
            git SHA  | exact, ugly     | CI builds, traceability
            semver   | human, released | public releases
            branch   | :main, :develop | moving, dev convenience
            combined | 1.2.3-abc1234   | best of both, prod deploys
         🔬 easypj: CI tags every build easypj:ci-<sha>; on release it is
            retagged easypj:1.2.3-<sha>, so prod runs a tag that names both the
            human version AND the exact commit.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build easypj and tag it three ways (SHA, semver,
            combined) pointing at the same image. Verify: `docker images`
            shows three tags, one IMAGE ID — tags are labels on one artifact.
         [DIAGRAM:decision — which tag scheme, when?]
            ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
            │ What is this build FOR?                                      │
            ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
            │ CI job / every commit   ──▶ easypj:ci-<sha>   (traceable)    │
            │ dev / feature branch    ──▶ easypj:main/:dev  (moving, ok)   │
            │ public release          ──▶ easypj:1.2.3      (semver)       │
            │ production deploy       ──▶ easypj:1.2.3-<sha> (both, exact) │
            └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         💡 CI gotcha not shown above: Docker tags cannot contain `/`, so a
            branch named `feature/new-search` cannot become
            `easypj:feature/new-search` — CI sanitizes it to
            `easypj:feature-new-search` before `docker build -t`, or the push fails.

         📊 SUMMARY: prefer immutable SHA/semver tags for anything deployed;
            reserve moving tags for local convenience only.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: :latest is just a default tag, not "newest" — it points
            wherever it was last pushed, which may be an OLD or broken build.

    23.2 Image Promotion Across Environments
         - Dev → Staging → Production promotion pipeline
         - Retagging vs rebuilding (retag!)
         - Promotion gates: tests, scans, approvals
         [FLOWCHART: Image promotion pipeline]

         🎯 GOAL: Promote one tested easypj image dev → staging → prod by
            RETAGGING, never rebuilding.
         [TECH] The image that passed tests is the artifact; promotion just
            adds an environment tag/registry ref to that SAME digest.
            Rebuilding per environment reintroduces drift — a fresh build could
            pull a different base or dependency. Gates (tests, scans, approval)
            guard each hop, but the bytes never change.
         [ANALOGY] A passport getting stamps at each border: same person (same
            digest) admitted to each country (environment) — you do not issue a
            brand-new person at every crossing.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — promote by digest]
            build easypj@sha256:abc  →  test+scan (gate)  →  tag :staging
              →  smoke (gate)  →  tag :production   [same digest throughout]
         🔬 easypj: `docker tag easypj@sha256:abc easypj:production` and push —
            production now points at the exact digest that cleared staging, with
            zero chance of a surprise rebuild.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: build once, promote by retagging staging→production,
            and compare Image IDs with `docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}'`.
            Verify: staging and production tags share one identical Image ID.
         📊 SUMMARY: promote by moving a tested DIGEST through environments;
            gates decide, but the image bytes are immutable end to end.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker build` at the promotion step is the classic
            anti-pattern — it silently produces a DIFFERENT image than the one
            you tested. Retag the digest; never rebuild to promote.

    23.3 Registry Strategies
         - Single registry, multiple repositories
         - Multiple registries (dev on Docker Hub, prod on ECR)
         - Registry mirroring and caching
         - Retention policies: how long to keep images
         [DIAGRAM: Multi-registry architecture]

         🎯 GOAL: Design easypj's registry layout and retention so images are
            findable, secure, and not infinite.
         [TECH] Options: one registry with many repos (simple), or split
            registries (dev on Docker Hub, prod on a private ECR/GHCR) for a
            security boundary. A pull-through mirror caches upstream images to
            cut bandwidth and rate limits. Retention policies expire old tags
            so storage does not grow forever.
         [ANALOGY] Registries are warehouses: one big shared warehouse vs a
            public receiving dock (dev) feeding a secured bonded warehouse
            (prod), with a local depot (mirror) so you do not truck from the
            factory every time.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — easypj registry topology]
            CI ──push──▶ dev registry (Docker Hub)
                              │ promote (retag, copy)
                              ▼
            prod pull ◀── private prod registry (ECR/GHCR)
            base images ◀── pull-through mirror (cache)
         🔬 easypj: CI pushes easypj:ci-<sha> to the dev registry; a promotion
            job copies the approved digest into the private prod registry, which
            production hosts are the only ones allowed to pull from.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: configure a pull-through mirror and pull a base
            image twice. Verify: the second pull is served from the mirror
            cache (faster, no upstream hit) — check the mirror's logs.
         [TABLE: registry options side by side]
            Dimension | Docker Hub      | ECR / GHCR      | Pull mirror
            Cost      | free/paid tier  | pay-per-GB      | bandwidth only
            Access    | org + public    | IAM / SSO       | upstream's ACL
            Retention | no auto-expiry  | lifecycle rule  | TTL / space cap
            easypj    | CI pushes here  | prod pulls only | caches base img

         💡 Why the mirror row matters: Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls
            (100/6hr) and free authenticated accounts (200/6hr) — a CI fleet
            pulling `python:3.12-slim` on every easypj build can hit that
            ceiling fast; a mirror absorbs the repeats as one cached hit.

         📊 SUMMARY: separate dev/prod registries for a trust boundary, mirror
            upstream to save bandwidth, and set retention so storage is bounded.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: no retention policy = a registry that grows without
            limit; but retention that is too aggressive can delete the exact
            old tag you need for an emergency rollback — exempt release tags.

    23.4 Docker Content Trust in CI/CD
         - Signing images in CI/CD
         - DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 in pipeline
         - Key management for signing
         [CODE: CI/CD sign + verify workflow]


         🎯 GOAL: Sign easypj images inside CI so only pipeline-produced images
            can be deployed.
         [TECH] Set DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 in the pipeline so the push step
            signs the tag; deployment hosts pull with DCT on and reject
            anything unsigned. Signing keys are injected as CI secrets (a
            delegation key, NOT the root key), and the root key stays offline.
         [ANALOGY] The pipeline is a notary that stamps every release document;
            production refuses to act on any document without the notary's
            seal — and the notary's master stamp lives in a vault, not the office.
         [CODE: sign in CI, verify on deploy]
            # CI (push step)
            export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
            export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST_REPOSITORY_PASSPHRASE=$CI_SIGN_KEY
            docker push easypj/web:1.2.3        # signs on push
            # deploy host
            export DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1
            docker pull easypj/web:1.2.3        # refuses if unsigned/altered
         🔬 easypj: only the CI pipeline holds the delegation signing key, so a
            developer pushing an unsigned easypj image by hand cannot get it
            deployed — prod's DCT-on pull rejects it.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: sign a tag in a pipeline job, then push an unsigned
            tag manually and try to pull both with DCT=1. Verify: the CI-signed
            tag pulls, the hand-pushed one is refused.
         📊 SUMMARY: signing in CI + DCT-enforced pulls makes the pipeline the
            ONLY path to production — provenance you can enforce, not just hope.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: guard signing keys like production creds — a leaked
            delegation key lets an attacker sign malicious images that pass
            verification; keep the ROOT key offline and rotate delegations.

    [G] UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 — tags are pointers, digests are identity
        A Docker "tag" (easypj:1.2.3) is nothing but a human-readable label
        a registry maps to a content digest — a sha256 hash computed from
        the image's manifest (which itself references the config and every
        layer's digest). `docker tag` never copies bytes; it just writes a
        new pointer in the local image store, which is why 23.1's practice
        step shows THREE tags sharing ONE Image ID. Pushing multiple tags
        pushes the same layers once and updates multiple pointers in the
        registry. Because the digest is a hash OF the content, it cannot be
        forged to match different bytes — which is exactly the property
        23.2's "promote by digest" and 23.4's signing both depend on.

        [DIAGRAM: tag (pointer) vs digest (identity)]
        easypj:ci-abc1234 ─┐
        easypj:1.2.3-abc1234├──▶ sha256:9f8e7d... (ONE manifest, ONE set of layers)
        easypj:production  ─┘
        Retagging = adding/moving a pointer above. Rebuilding = a NEW
        digest, even if the Dockerfile text didn't change.

    [H] KEY TAKEAWAYS 🔑
        ✅ Tags are named pointers; digests (sha256:...) are the actual
           content identity — many tags can share one digest.
        ✅ :latest is not "the newest build," it is just wherever that tag
           was last pushed — possibly an old or broken image.
        ✅ Promotion = retagging the ALREADY-tested digest across
           environments; running `docker build` at the promotion step is
           the anti-pattern this chapter warns against repeatedly.
        ✅ Split dev/prod registries create a real security boundary; a
           pull-through mirror cuts bandwidth and dodges Docker Hub's
           anonymous/free pull-rate limits.
        ✅ Retention policies must exempt release tags, or automated
           cleanup can delete the one image you need for a rollback.
        ✅ Docker Content Trust signs on push and can block unsigned pulls
           on deploy hosts, making the CI pipeline the only path to prod.
        🎯 DCA relevance: this is graded material — the exam expects you to
           know tagging strategy and promotion, not just registry commands.

    [I] GOTCHAS ⚠️
        - Docker tags cannot contain `/` — a branch like `feature/new-
          search` must be sanitized (e.g. to `feature-new-search`) before
          `docker build -t`, or the push fails.
        - Rebuilding to "promote" silently produces a DIFFERENT image than
          the one that passed tests — the classic anti-pattern.
        - No retention policy = unbounded registry growth; an overly
          aggressive one can delete the exact old tag an incident needs.
        - A leaked delegation signing key lets an attacker sign malicious
          images that still pass Content Trust verification.

    [J] SPEED TIPS ⚡
        - `docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}'` to compare two tags' Image
          IDs directly instead of trusting tag names alone.
        - Point CI's base-image pulls at a pull-through mirror to avoid
          Docker Hub's 100/6hr (anonymous) or 200/6hr (free auth) limits.

    [K] COMMANDS TO REMEMBER 🔑
        docker tag easypj:ci-$SHA easypj:1.2.3-$SHA    # add a pointer, no rebuild
        docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}' easypj:1.2.3  # read the local Image ID
        docker tag easypj@sha256:abc easypj:production  # promote by digest
        DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker push easypj/web:1.2.3  # sign on push
        DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1 docker pull easypj/web:1.2.3  # refuse unsigned
        docker images easypj                              # all tags, one ID

    [L] PRACTICE DRILL 🧪
        ⏱️ 8 minutes: build easypj once, tag it three ways (SHA, semver,
        combined), then run `docker images | grep easypj` and confirm all
        three tags list the SAME Image ID.

    [M] LAB Q&A 🧪 — Chapter 23 (10 questions)

        Q1: Why is deploying production from `:latest` risky, per 23.1?
        A1: `:latest` is just a default/moving tag, not a guarantee of
            "newest" — it points wherever it was last pushed, which could
            be an old or even broken build.
        Explanation: 23.1's gotcha states this directly; moving tags are
            fine for local convenience but ambiguous for anything deployed.

        Q2: Compare the four tagging schemes from 23.1 (table).
        A2:
            Scheme   | Example              | Best for
            git SHA  | easypj:abc1234       | CI builds, exact traceability
            semver   | easypj:1.2.3         | public/human releases
            branch   | easypj:main/:develop | moving, dev convenience only
            combined | easypj:1.2.3-abc1234 | production deploys (both)
        Explanation: Matches 23.1's decision diagram exactly — CI commits
            get SHA tags, releases get semver, prod gets combined so it is
            both human-readable and exactly traceable.

        Q3: Walk through promoting an easypj image from staging to
            production WITHOUT rebuilding — what commands, what do you
            verify?
        A3: `docker tag easypj@sha256:<digest> easypj:production` then push;
            verify with `docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}'` that staging and
            production tags report the identical Image ID.
        Explanation: This is 23.2's core practice step — promotion moves a
            pointer, and the verification step proves no rebuild occurred.

        Q4: Why does running `docker build` at the promotion step count as
            an anti-pattern rather than just "extra safety"?
        A4: A fresh build can silently pull a different base-image digest
            or dependency version, producing an image that is NOT what
            passed tests/scans in the earlier stage — you would ship an
            image nobody tested.
        Explanation: 23.2 calls this out explicitly: "docker build at the
            promotion step... silently produces a DIFFERENT image."

        Q5: Compare single-registry and split dev/prod registry topologies
            for easypj (table).
        A5:
            Dimension | Single registry        | Split dev/prod
            Setup     | simpler                | two registries to manage
            Security  | one trust boundary      | dev/prod separated
            easypj use| fine for small teams    | CI pushes dev, prod pulls
                      |                         | only from the private one
        Explanation: 23.3 recommends splitting when a security boundary
            between "anyone can push here" (dev) and "only vetted images
            land here" (prod) matters.

        Q6: What concrete problem does a pull-through mirror solve for a CI
            fleet that builds easypj constantly?
        A6: It caches upstream base images (e.g. python:3.12-slim) locally,
            so repeated pulls hit the mirror instead of the public
            registry — avoiding Docker Hub's 100/6hr (anon) or 200/6hr
            (free auth) rate limits and cutting bandwidth.
        Explanation: 23.3's callout states this exact numeric limit and
            names it as the reason the mirror row matters for a CI fleet.

        Q7: Why must a retention policy exempt release tags?
        A7: Because automated cleanup that is too aggressive can delete the
            exact old tag you need to roll back to during an incident —
            retention should be bounded but release/rollback tags kept.
        Explanation: 23.3's gotcha pairs both failure modes: no retention
            (unbounded growth) and over-aggressive retention (losing a
            needed rollback target) — the fix is exempting release tags.

        Q8: What does setting `DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1` do differently on a
            `push` versus a `pull`?
        A8: On push, it SIGNS the tag using the configured signing key. On
            pull, it REFUSES to pull anything unsigned or altered since it
            was signed.
        Explanation: 23.4's CI/deploy-host code block shows exactly this
            split — sign in the CI push step, enforce on the deploy host's
            pull.

        Q9: Why should the root Content Trust signing key stay offline
            while CI only holds a delegation key?
        A9: Because CI secrets can leak; a leaked DELEGATION key only lets
            an attacker sign images (which you can rotate away), while a
            leaked ROOT key compromises the entire trust chain permanently.
        Explanation: 23.4's gotcha: "guard signing keys like production
            creds... keep the ROOT key offline and rotate delegations."

        Q10: CI tries to build a branch named `feature/new-search` as
             `easypj:feature/new-search`. What happens, and what's the fix?
        A10: The `docker build -t` / push fails because Docker tags cannot
             contain a `/` (it is reserved for the repository path). CI
             sanitizes the branch name first, e.g. to
             `easypj:feature-new-search`.
        Explanation: This is the CI gotcha called out directly under 23.1's
             tagging diagram.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 23
        one digest ── tag:ci-<sha> ── tag:1.2.3-<sha> ── tag:production
                          (all three point at the SAME sha256 manifest)
        dev registry (CI pushes) ──promote(retag)──▶ prod registry (pulls only)
                                                          ▲
                                              signed on push (DCT) │ enforced
                                              on pull (DCT) — unsigned refused

        .vs-prose — Chapter 23 replaces "which image is live?" guesswork
        with discipline: tag deterministically (SHA for traceability,
        semver for releases, combined for prod), promote by retagging one
        tested digest through dev → staging → production instead of
        rebuilding at every hop, keep dev and prod registries separated
        with sane retention, and sign in CI so Docker Content Trust makes
        the pipeline the only route an image can take to production.


Chapter 24: Container Testing Strategies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: A green unit-test suite that never touched a real
    database or the actual image proves little about what you ship. This chapter
    layers container testing — unit, integration against real PostgreSQL,
    full-stack e2e, plus image-level structure tests and Dockerfile linting — so
    the thing you deploy is the thing you tested. Problem solved: "tests pass but
    the container still breaks in prod on a missing file, bad env, or real DB."

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced   ⏱️ ~2.5-3 hrs   🎯 DCA: not a graded domain on
        its own — container testing strategy is not in the DCA blueprint —
        but structure tests and linting reinforce the graded Image
        Creation, Management & Registry domain (20%).

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
        - Place unit, integration, e2e, and image tests on the container
          testing pyramid and explain why the count shrinks as you climb.
        - Run the easypj test suite inside a disposable container wired to
          real PostgreSQL with `docker compose run --rm`, gating CI on the
          exit code.
        - Spin up a throwaway, version-matched PostgreSQL container per
          test run with Testcontainers instead of a shared test database.
        - Write container-structure-test specs that assert facts about the
          BUILT image (files, command output, metadata like non-root USER).
        - Lint the easypj Dockerfile with Hadolint and fix its top
          warnings before they become production incidents.
        - Recognize an "ice-cream cone" test shape (mostly slow e2e) as a
          CI-time smell and correct it.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: not graded directly — the DCA exam does not examine
        testing methodology — but Hadolint and structure tests operationalize
        the Dockerfile/image best practices the graded Image Creation &
        Management domain (20%) does test you on.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 24.1 the testing pyramid → 24.2 `compose run` against
        real Postgres → 24.3 Testcontainers (programmatic disposable DBs) →
        24.4 container structure tests (the image at rest) → 24.5 Hadolint
        (the Dockerfile itself) — narrowing from "does the app behave" to
        "is the artifact itself sound."

    24.1 Testing Pyramid for Containers
         - Unit tests: Inside container, test Django views/models
         - Integration tests: Container + PostgreSQL
         - End-to-end tests: Full Compose stack
         - Image tests: Dockerfile linting, vulnerability scan
         [PYRAMID DIAGRAM: Container testing pyramid]

         🎯 GOAL: Place each kind of easypj test on the container testing
            pyramid and know the cost/coverage trade-off.
         [TECH] Bottom-up: many fast UNIT tests (Django view/model logic against
            a lightweight PostgreSQL test DB), fewer INTEGRATION tests (the app
            container + a full real PostgreSQL), fewer still END-TO-END tests
            (the whole compose stack), and cross-cutting IMAGE tests (structure
            tests, scans, lint). Higher = more realistic, slower, fewer.
         [ANALOGY] A food-safety program: taste each ingredient (unit), taste
            the mixed dish (integration), serve a test table the full meal
            (e2e), and inspect the kitchen itself (image tests) — more effort
            as you climb, so you run fewer at the top.
         [PYRAMID DIAGRAM: easypj container tests]
                     ╱────────────╲       e2e: full compose stack
                    ╱  e2e (few)   ╲      (slow, most realistic)
                   ╱────────────────╲
                  ╱ integration: web ╲    + real PostgreSQL
                 ╱────────────────────╲
                ╱  unit: views/models  ╲  (many, fast)
               └────────────────────────┘
            image tests (structure + scan + lint) wrap every layer
         🔬 easypj: hundreds of unit tests on JobPost/Skills logic, a dozen
            integration tests hitting real PostgreSQL, a couple of e2e flows
            (post a job → search → apply), all green before an image ships.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: count your easypj tests by layer. Verify: the shape
            is a pyramid (unit ≫ integration ≫ e2e), not an ice-cream cone
            (mostly slow e2e) — the cone is a CI-time smell.
         📊 SUMMARY: many fast unit tests, fewer real-DB integration tests, a
            handful of e2e, plus image tests — coverage where it is cheapest.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: easypj uses PostgreSQL, so tests must run against a real
            Postgres test database (never sqlite) — sqlite would pass tests that
            break on Postgres-specific SQL and migrations.

    24.2 Testing with docker compose run
         - docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test
         - docker compose run --rm django python manage.py test jobpost
         - Exit code handling in CI/CD
         [TERMINAL: Test execution and results]

         🎯 GOAL: Run the easypj test suite in a throwaway container wired to a
            real PostgreSQL, and fail CI on a bad exit code.
         [TECH] `docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test` starts a
            one-off container on the compose network (so it reaches the db
            service) and removes it after. The command's exit code is the test
            result — 0 pass, non-zero fail — which CI checks to gate the build.
         [ANALOGY] Renting a car for a single test drive: you get the exact
            same model (image) wired to the real roads (db service), then hand
            it back (--rm) — no residue, repeatable every time.
         [TERMINAL: test easypj against real Postgres]
            $ docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test
              Ran 214 tests in 12.4s — OK
            $ docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test jobpost
            $ echo $?          # 0 = pass, non-zero = CI fails the job
         🔬 easypj: the test container connects to the compose `db` service (a
            real PostgreSQL), so migrations and Postgres-specific queries are
            exercised exactly as they will be in production.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the suite with a deliberately failing test and
            inspect `$?`. Verify: exit code is non-zero and, in CI, that
            non-zero halts the pipeline before build/push.
         📊 SUMMARY: `compose run --rm` gives disposable, network-connected test
            runs whose exit code is the CI gate — real DB, no leftovers.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker compose run` does NOT publish the service's
            ports by default and starts its OWN deps — use --rm and depends_on
            so the db is up, or the first test fails on a refused connection.

    24.3 Testcontainers — Real Database in Tests
         - What is Testcontainers? (throwaway containers for testing)
         - Python: testcontainers-python
         - Django tests with real PostgreSQL container
         - pytest-docker plugin
         [CODE: Django test with Testcontainers for PostgreSQL]

         🎯 GOAL: Spin up a throwaway PostgreSQL per test run with
            Testcontainers so tests own their database.
         [TECH] Testcontainers starts real containers programmatically from the
            test code, hands back the dynamic host/port, and tears them down
            after. testcontainers-python (or pytest-docker) boots a PostgreSQL
            container, points Django at it, runs migrations, and destroys it —
            no shared, stateful test DB to pollute between runs.
         [ANALOGY] Each test crew gets a brand-new rehearsal stage built on
            demand and demolished after — no fighting over one shared stage
            that the last crew left a mess on.
         [CODE: Testcontainers PostgreSQL for easypj]
            from testcontainers.postgres import PostgresContainer
            with PostgresContainer("postgres:16") as pg:
                url = pg.get_connection_url()   # dynamic host:port
                os.environ["DATABASE_URL"] = url
                # run Django migrations + tests against THIS Postgres
         🔬 easypj: CI runs the JobPost/User integration tests against a fresh
            postgres:16 container that exactly matches production's version —
            catching Postgres-specific migration and query bugs early.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: write one test that stands up a PostgresContainer,
            applies migrations, and creates a JobPost. Verify: the row exists
            during the test and the container is gone afterward (`docker ps`).
         📊 SUMMARY: Testcontainers = programmatic, disposable, version-matched
            PostgreSQL per test — real-DB fidelity without a shared test server.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Testcontainers needs a Docker daemon available to the
            test process — in CI that means dind or a socket, with the same
            trust trade-off as 22.6; budget for container startup time too.

    24.4 Container Structure Tests
         - Google's Container Structure Test framework
         - Test: file existence, command output, metadata
         - container-structure-test test --image easypj:v1 --config tests.yaml
         [CODE: container-structure-test config for easypj]

         🎯 GOAL: Assert facts about the built easypj IMAGE — files, commands,
            metadata — independent of the app's own tests.
         [TECH] Google's container-structure-test runs a YAML spec against an
            image: command tests (run X, assert output/exit), file existence
            tests (path present, right mode/owner), file content tests (regex),
            and metadata tests (USER, EXPOSE, ENTRYPOINT). It validates the
            IMAGE, not runtime behavior.
         [ANALOGY] A pre-delivery vehicle inspection: not a test drive, but a
            checklist that the right engine, the correct VIN, and all the parts
            are actually bolted in before the car leaves the lot.
         [CODE: container-structure-test for easypj]
            schemaVersion: 2.0.0
            commandTests:
              - name: python present
                command: python
                args: ["--version"]
                expectedOutput: ["Python 3.12.*"]
            fileExistenceTests:
              - name: app code copied
                path: /app/manage.py
                shouldExist: true
            metadataTest:
              user: "app"                 # asserts non-root USER
         🔬 easypj: the structure test asserts /app/manage.py exists, python is
            3.12, and USER is "app" — catching a broken Dockerfile (missing
            COPY, wrong base, forgotten USER) before the image is ever deployed.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `container-structure-test test --image easypj:v1
            --config tests.yaml` with a rule that USER is app. Verify: it PASSES;
            then remove USER from the Dockerfile, rebuild, and watch it FAIL.
         [TABLE: the three test categories]
            Category  | Example assertion           | What it catches
            File      | /app/manage.py, mode 0644   | missing COPY/context
            Command   | `python --version` ~3.12.*  | drifted base image
            Metadata  | USER app, EXPOSE 8000       | forgotten USER/port

         💡 The framework actually ships a fourth kind — fileContentTests
            (regex match against a file's contents, e.g. confirming
            DEBUG=False survived into the built settings.py) — rarer than the
            three above, but the only one that proves a config VALUE, not
            just a file's existence.

         📊 SUMMARY: structure tests lock the image's shape — files, versions,
            and metadata like non-root USER — as an independent build gate.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: structure tests check the image at REST, not running
            behavior — they confirm USER app is SET, not that the app works as
            that user; pair them with integration tests, do not substitute.

    24.5 Dockerfile Linting
         - Hadolint: Dockerfile linter
         - hadolint Dockerfile
         - Common warnings and how to fix them
         - Integrating hadolint in CI/CD
         [CODE: ShellCheck + Hadolint in CI pipeline]

         🎯 GOAL: Lint the easypj Dockerfile with Hadolint and fix the warnings
            it flags before they cost you in prod.
         [TECH] Hadolint parses a Dockerfile and applies best-practice rules
            (DLxxxx) plus embedded ShellCheck on RUN lines: pin apt versions,
            avoid `latest`, use `--no-install-recommends`, don't run as root,
            combine RUN layers, prefer COPY over ADD. It exits non-zero on
            findings, so it drops straight into CI.
         [ANALOGY] A spell-checker for your Dockerfile: it will not run the
            build, but it underlines the sloppy phrasing (unpinned apt, stray
            ADD, root user) that turns into bugs and bloat later.
         [CODE: hadolint in CI]
            $ hadolint Dockerfile
              DL3007 warning: Using latest is prone to errors
              DL3008 warning: Pin versions in apt-get install
              DL3002 warning: Last USER should not be root
            # CI gate (fail on warnings)
            $ hadolint --failure-threshold warning Dockerfile
         🔬 easypj: Hadolint flags an unpinned `apt-get install libpq-dev` and
            a missing USER in the easypj Dockerfile — the exact issues that
            cause non-reproducible builds and root containers from Part 7.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `hadolint Dockerfile` on easypj, fix the top
            three warnings, and re-run. Verify: the warning count drops and
            `--failure-threshold warning` now exits 0 — a passing CI lint gate.
         📊 SUMMARY: Hadolint + ShellCheck catch Dockerfile smells (unpinned
            deps, ADD, root, :latest) at lint time — cheapest fix in the pipeline.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: linting is static — a clean Hadolint run does NOT mean
            the image builds or runs; it means the Dockerfile follows best
            practices. Keep build + structure + integration tests alongside it.

    [G] UNDER THE HOOD 🔧 — how Testcontainers actually cleans up after itself
        Testcontainers talks to the same Docker API easypj's own tooling
        uses (via docker.sock or DOCKER_HOST) to start a real container —
        e.g. postgres:16 — publishing its port to a RANDOM free host port so
        parallel CI runs never collide. It then applies a wait strategy
        (poll a port, or watch for a log line like "database system is
        ready") before handing the test code a connection URL. To guarantee
        cleanup even if the test process crashes mid-run, Testcontainers
        starts a small companion container (the "Ryuk" resource reaper)
        that watches for the test process's session to end and force-
        removes every container/network it created — so a crashed test run
        does not leave orphaned PostgreSQL containers behind.

        [DIAGRAM: Testcontainers lifecycle]
        test process ──▶ Docker API ──▶ start postgres:16 (random port)
             │                                    │
             │                              wait strategy (port/log-ready)
             ▼                                    ▼
        run Django migrations + tests ──▶ tear down (+ Ryuk reaper cleanup)

    [H] KEY TAKEAWAYS 🔑
        ✅ The pyramid: many fast unit tests, fewer real-Postgres
           integration tests, a handful of e2e, plus cross-cutting image
           tests wrapping every layer.
        ✅ easypj tests must run against real PostgreSQL, never sqlite —
           Postgres-specific SQL and migrations won't be caught otherwise.
        ✅ `docker compose run --rm` gives disposable, network-connected
           test runs whose exit code is the CI gate.
        ✅ `compose run` does NOT publish ports by default and starts its
           OWN deps — pair with depends_on or the first test hits a refused
           connection.
        ✅ Testcontainers gives version-matched, disposable Postgres per
           test run, with automatic cleanup via the Ryuk reaper even on a
           crash.
        ✅ container-structure-test validates the IMAGE at rest (files,
           commands, metadata) — not runtime behavior; pair with
           integration tests, don't substitute.
        ✅ Hadolint is static analysis on the Dockerfile — a clean run does
           not prove the image builds or runs correctly.

    [I] GOTCHAS ⚠️
        - An "ice-cream cone" shape (mostly slow e2e, few unit tests) is a
          CI-time smell — invert it toward the pyramid.
        - Testcontainers needs a Docker daemon reachable from the test
          process — in CI that's dind or a socket, the same trust trade-
          off as 22.6.
        - Forgetting `depends_on` with `compose run` can fail the first
          test on a refused DB connection even though the service exists.
        - A passing structure test proves USER is SET to "app," not that
          the app actually WORKS correctly running as that user.

    [J] SPEED TIPS ⚡
        - Run `hadolint --failure-threshold warning Dockerfile` as a fast
          pre-build CI gate before spending minutes on a full image build.
        - Periodically count tests by layer (unit vs integration vs e2e) to
          catch a pyramid inversion before it slows down every CI run.

    [K] COMMANDS TO REMEMBER 🔑
        docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test          # full suite, real Postgres
        docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test jobpost  # just jobpost app
        echo $?                                                     # 0 pass / non-zero fail
        container-structure-test test --image easypj:v1 --config tests.yaml
        hadolint Dockerfile                                         # lint, non-zero on findings
        hadolint --failure-threshold warning Dockerfile             # CI gate on warnings+

    [L] PRACTICE DRILL 🧪
        ⏱️ 12 minutes: add one deliberately failing Django test, run it via
        `docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test`, confirm `$?`
        is non-zero, then write one container-structure-test metadata rule
        asserting USER is non-root.

    [M] LAB Q&A 🧪 — Chapter 24 (10 questions)

        Q1: Describe the container testing pyramid for easypj from 24.1 —
            what sits at each layer, and why does the count shrink going up?
        A1:
                     e2e (few)         — full compose stack, slowest, most real
                integration (fewer)    — app container + real PostgreSQL
                   unit (many, fast)   — Django views/models logic
            image tests (structure + scan + lint) wrap every layer
            Higher layers cost more time/realism per test, so you deliberately
            run fewer of them.
        Explanation: Matches 24.1's pyramid diagram directly — hundreds of
            unit tests, a dozen integration tests, a couple of e2e flows.

        Q2: Why must easypj's tests run against real PostgreSQL rather than
            sqlite?
        A2: sqlite would pass tests that break on Postgres-specific SQL and
            migrations, since it doesn't share Postgres's SQL dialect or
            migration behavior.
        Explanation: 24.1's gotcha states this exactly — easypj is
            PostgreSQL-only, so any test DB must be Postgres too.

        Q3: What does `docker compose run --rm web python manage.py test`
            actually do, step by step?
        A3: Starts a one-off `web` container on the compose network (so it
            can reach the `db` service), runs the Django test command
            inside it, exits with the test result's exit code, then removes
            the container (`--rm`).
        Explanation: This is 24.2's TECH explanation verbatim in mechanism —
            the exit code becomes the CI gate.

        Q4: Why can the FIRST test fail with a refused connection even
            though `db` is defined in the compose file?
        A4: `docker compose run` does not publish ports by default and
            starts its own dependency containers — if there's no
            `depends_on`/wait step, the test container can start before
            postgres is ready to accept connections.
        Explanation: 24.2's gotcha calls this out directly as the reason to
            use --rm together with depends_on.

        Q5: What problem does Testcontainers solve that a shared, long-
            lived test database does not?
        A5: It gives each test run its OWN fresh, version-matched
            PostgreSQL container, so tests can't pollute each other's data
            or drift from production's Postgres version.
        Explanation: 24.3 frames this as "no shared, stateful test DB to
            pollute between runs," backed by the code example that spins up
            postgres:16 per run.

        Q6: What Docker-level requirement does Testcontainers have, and
            what's the trade-off it inherits from Chapter 22?
        A6: It needs a Docker daemon reachable from the test process — in
            CI that means dind or a socket mount, with the exact same
            isolation-vs-host-risk trade-off discussed in 22.6.
        Explanation: 24.3's gotcha explicitly cross-references this: "the
            same trust trade-off as 22.6."

        Q7: List container-structure-test's assertion categories with an
            easypj example of each (table).
        A7:
            Category  | Example assertion          | Catches
            File      | /app/manage.py exists       | missing COPY/context
            Command   | `python --version` ~3.12.*  | drifted base image
            Metadata  | USER app, EXPOSE 8000       | forgotten USER/port
            (plus fileContentTests — regex on file contents, e.g. confirming
            DEBUG=False landed in settings.py — the only one that proves a
            config VALUE, not just a file's existence.)
        Explanation: Matches 24.4's table plus its callout about the fourth,
            rarer fileContentTests category.

        Q8: Why doesn't a passing container-structure-test guarantee the
            easypj app works correctly at runtime?
        A8: Structure tests check the image AT REST — files present, a
            command's output, metadata values — not actual running
            behavior; USER being "app" doesn't prove the app functions
            correctly running as that user.
        Explanation: 24.4's gotcha: "pair them with integration tests, do
            not substitute."

        Q9: What kind of issues does Hadolint flag on a Dockerfile, and why
            does it matter for easypj specifically?
        A9: Best-practice rules like unpinned apt/pip versions, use of
            `:latest`, missing `--no-install-recommends`, running as root,
            and stray `ADD` instead of `COPY`. For easypj it caught an
            unpinned `apt-get install libpq-dev` and a missing USER — the
            exact non-reproducible-build and root-container risks from
            Part 7.
        Explanation: Straight from 24.5's example output and its 🔬 easypj
            callout.

        Q10: Why is an "ice-cream cone" test distribution (mostly e2e, few
             unit tests) considered a smell, and what does it cost in CI?
        A10: e2e tests are the slowest and least isolated layer; a cone
             inverts the pyramid so MOST of your test time is spent on the
             most expensive, flakiest layer instead of the cheapest one —
             CI runs take longer and fail for less specific reasons.
        Explanation: 24.1's practice step frames the pyramid shape check
             directly as "the cone is a CI-time smell."

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 24
                     ╱────────────╲       e2e (few, slow, most realistic)
                    ╱  integration  ╲     + real PostgreSQL
                   ╱──────────────────╲
                  ╱   unit (many, fast) ╲
                 └────────────────────────┘
            image tests (structure + Hadolint) wrap every layer above
            compose run --rm (exit code) │ Testcontainers (disposable DB)

        .vs-prose — Chapter 24 makes sure the thing you ship is the thing
        you tested: a pyramid of many fast unit tests, fewer integration
        tests against real PostgreSQL (via `compose run --rm` or
        Testcontainers' disposable, version-matched containers), a handful
        of full-stack e2e runs, and image-level checks — container-
        structure-test for the built image's shape, Hadolint for the
        Dockerfile's hygiene — that catch what application tests never see.



━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
    [F] PART 8 KEY TAKEAWAYS 🔑
        ✅ Every CI/CD stage should run in a container so build, test, scan
           and deploy share one identical environment — build the image
           ONCE and promote that same artifact through every later stage.
        ✅ GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and Jenkins each get Docker access one
           of three ways — dind (isolated, privileged), a docker.sock
           mount (fast, but root on the runner), or rootless kaniko/buildah
           — pick by trust level of the code and the runner's blast radius.
        ✅ Tags are pointers, not versions; promote easypj images dev →
           staging → production by RETAGGING one tested digest, never by
           rebuilding.
        ✅ Registry topology (single vs split dev/prod, pull-through
           mirrors) plus a retention policy that exempts release tags keeps
           images findable, secure, and storage-bounded.
        ✅ Docker Content Trust signing in CI, enforced on deploy-host
           pulls, makes the pipeline the ONLY path an image can take to
           production.
        ✅ A container testing pyramid — many unit, fewer real-Postgres
           integration, a handful of e2e, plus image structure tests and
           Hadolint — proves the shipped artifact actually works.
        🎯 DCA relevance across the part: Ch22 and Ch24 are production
           depth beyond the graded blueprint; Ch23 is directly graded under
           Image Creation, Management & Registry (20%).

    ⚠️ PART 8 GOTCHAS
        - Rebuilding instead of retagging at ANY promotion or deploy step
          silently ships an image nobody actually tested (Ch22, Ch23).
        - A docker.sock mount or a leaked registry/signing credential both
          hand out root-equivalent or ship-anything power — treat both as
          production secrets, not CI convenience (Ch22, Ch23).
        - Retention policies and test pyramids fail in mirror-image ways:
          too little (unbounded registries, ice-cream-cone test suites) or
          too aggressive (deleting your rollback tag, skipping real
          integration coverage) — Part 8 asks for balance, not extremes.

    ⚡ PART 8 SPEED TIPS
        - Cache aggressively (GHA cache, Build Cloud, pull-through mirrors)
          — most of Part 8's slowness is repeated work CI doesn't need to
          redo.
        - Compare Image IDs (`docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}'`), not tag
          names, whenever you need to prove two images are really the same.

    [G] PART 8 VISUAL SUMMARY
        Ch22 AUTOMATE ──▶ Ch23 VERSION & PROMOTE ──▶ Ch24 TEST
        (build once,       (tag + retag one digest    (pyramid + image
         GitHub/GitLab/     dev→staging→prod,          structure + lint
         Jenkins/Build      DCT signing in CI)          gate every hop)
         Cloud, dind/
         socket/kaniko)
              └──────────────── one push-to-prod loop ──────────────────┘

        .vs-prose — Part 8 turns easypj from something you ship by hand
        into something that ships itself: Chapter 22 automates the build-
        test-scan-push pipeline across the major CI platforms and settles
        how that pipeline safely gets Docker access; Chapter 23 makes sure
        the image moving through that pipeline is deterministically tagged
        and promoted by retagging one tested digest, never rebuilt;
        Chapter 24 proves, at every layer from unit tests to the Dockerfile
        itself, that the digest being promoted actually works. Together
        they close the loop this guide opened in Part 3 — build the image
        — by making that build trustworthy enough to run unattended, on
        every single commit.

PART 9: DOCKER TO KUBERNETES — THE BRIDGE                                 🔴
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    THINK BEFORE PART 9:
      What runs where?    → Pods land on whichever node the scheduler picks.
      What talks to what? → kubectl → API server → etcd; scheduler → kubelet.
      What breaks first?  → "one container, one host" — Pods move, IPs don't.

    [PART 9 INTRO]
        Part 9 is the bridge: the moment a single Docker host stops being
        enough — one server dies, or one box can't hold the traffic — is
        the moment Kubernetes becomes the answer, not a Docker upgrade.
        Nothing about the easypj image changes here; the exact same OCI
        image built and tagged back in Part 3 runs unmodified as a
        Kubernetes Pod. What changes is who decides WHERE it runs, WHO
        replaces it when it dies, and HOW a new version replaces an old
        one without dropping a single request.

        This is explicitly the DCA→CKA bridge, not new DCA exam material.
        Chapters 25-27 exist so a Docker-certified engineer can look at a
        Kubernetes cluster and recognize every noun already learned in
        Parts 1-8, wearing a new name — not to add graded exam content.

    🧠 ANALOGY (Part 9 — the whole bridge):
        Docker is a single restaurant kitchen: one chef (the daemon), one
        set of stoves (the host), one line of dishes (containers). The
        moment that kitchen can't serve the whole city, you don't teach
        the chef new recipes — you open a restaurant CHAIN. Kubernetes is
        the head office: it doesn't cook, it decides which kitchen makes
        which dish, replaces a kitchen that burns down, and rolls out a
        new menu one kitchen at a time so the chain never closes.

    [HOW THE CHAPTERS FIT — Part 9 map]
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  Ch25                    Ch26                     Ch27           │
        │  Docker→K8s Transition   Deploy easypj to K8s     Deployment     │
        │  (why / when / nouns)    (real YAML, real cluster) Strategies    │
        │  ┌────────────────┐      ┌────────────────┐      ┌─────────────┐│
        │  │ single-host     │ ──▶ │ Deployment +    │ ──▶ │ rolling      ││
        │  │ limits, noun    │     │ Service +       │     │ update,      ││
        │  │ map, Dockerfile │     │ ConfigMap/Secret│     │ rollback,    ││
        │  │ →Deploy journey │     │ scaling         │     │ probes, envs ││
        │  └────────────────┘      └────────────────┘      └─────────────┘│
        └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Read the map as a sentence: "Understand WHY you'd leave Docker
        alone (25), actually GET easypj running on a cluster (26), then
        learn how to CHANGE it safely once it's live (27)."

    🧭 DECISION GUIDE — where do I start in Part 9?
        | Your situation                                      | Start at |
        | Never touched Kubernetes, unsure you even need it   | 25.1     |
        | Know K8s concepts, need the Docker→K8s noun map     | 25.2     |

        | easypj is already running, need to ship v2          | 27.1     |

        | Pods keep taking traffic before they're actually up | 27.3     |

    [WITHOUT vs WITH KUBERNETES — easypj, single host vs cluster]
        | Question                    | WITHOUT K8s (Docker/Compose)  | WITH K8s (Part 9)              |
        | Where does easypj run?      | one host you picked           | any node the scheduler picks   |
        | Host dies — then what?      | easypj is down                | Pods reschedule to a live node |
        | Traffic grows — then what?  | you manually add containers   | kubectl scale / HPA            |
        | New version ships how?      | docker compose up -d rebuild  | rolling update, 1 Pod at a time|
        | Bad release recovery        | manually redeploy old image   | kubectl rollout undo           |
        | Config/secrets              | .env file on disk             | ConfigMap + Secret objects     |
        | Health awareness            | restart policy only           | readiness + liveness probes    |
