        Part 9 replaces nothing from Parts 1-8 — it hands the SAME image
        to a bigger scheduler. Read 25 for the map, 26 to actually
        deploy, 27 to keep deploying safely.

        Dockerfile ──▶ image ──▶ registry ──▶ Deployment+Service ──▶ rollout
           (Pt.3)       (Pt.3)      (26.2)        (26.3-26.6)          (27.1-27.5)

Chapter 25: Docker → Kubernetes Transition
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Every image, container, network and volume so
    far lived on ONE machine — yours. The moment easypj must survive a
    server dying, or handle more traffic than one box can hold, Docker runs
    out of answers on its own. This chapter draws the exact line: what
    Docker still owns (the image, the Dockerfile, the single-host runtime)
    and what Kubernetes takes over (scheduling, healing, scaling across many
    machines). Problem solved here: "do I throw away Docker to learn K8s?"

    [A] META: Difficulty 🔴 Advanced | Time ~45-60 min | Beyond DCA scope —
        this chapter is the on-ramp to the companion CKA (Certified
        Kubernetes Administrator) guide; nothing here is required to pass
        the Docker Certified Associate exam itself.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — by the end of Chapter 25 you can:
        - State the one-sentence line that separates what Docker still
          owns from what Kubernetes takes over (25.1)
        - Translate any Docker noun (container, image, volume, network,
          compose file) to its Kubernetes equivalent without hesitating (25.2)
        - Walk the 6-step Dockerfile→build→push→Deployment→Service
          journey and label each step Docker-only or Kubernetes-only (25.3)
        - Explain why `kubectl apply` never builds or pushes an image (25.3)
        - Run `kompose convert` on a real compose.yaml and name what it
          gets right and what it can't guess — replicas, limits, probes (25.4)
        - Recognize why `depends_on` has no direct Kubernetes equivalent (25.4)

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: Not a graded DCA domain — Kubernetes concepts sit
        entirely outside the Docker Certified Associate exam blueprint.
        This chapter exists to make the DCA→CKA transition painless, not
        to prep a graded exam question.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 25.1 why leave Docker alone → 25.2 noun-for-noun
        mapping → 25.3 the 6-step deploy journey → 25.4 compose.yaml →
        manifests (kompose).

    25.1 Why Kubernetes After Docker?
         - Docker runs containers on ONE machine
         - Kubernetes runs containers across MANY machines
         - Docker = package your app | Kubernetes = run it at scale
         - The "where" problem: Docker needs you to pick a server; K8s picks for you

         [DOCKER vs KUBERNETES — SINGLE HOST vs CLUSTER]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │              🐳 DOCKER (Single Host)  vs  ☸️ KUBERNETES (Cluster)           │
         │                                                                          │
         │  DOCKER:                        KUBERNETES:                              │
         │  ┌──────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐ │
         │  │   ONE SERVER     │           │         CLUSTER (Many Servers)        │ │
         │  │                  │           │                                      │ │
         │  │  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ │           │  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐│ │
         │  │  │C1│ │C2│ │C3│ │           │  │      🧠 CONTROL PLANE            ││ │
         │  │  └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ │           │  │  API Server | etcd | Scheduler   ││ │
         │  │                  │           │  └──────────────────────────────────┘│ │
         │  │  IF SERVER DIES: │           │                                      │ │
         │  │  💀 Everything   │           │  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐      │ │
         │  │     goes down!   │           │  │ 💪 Node 1  │  │ 💪 Node 2  │      │ │
         │  │                  │           │  │ ┌──┐┌──┐┌──┐│  │ ┌──┐┌──┐┌──┐│      │ │
         │  │  SCALING:        │           │  │ │C1││C3││C5││  │ │C2││C4││C6││      │ │
         │  │  Manual, buy     │           │  │ └──┘└──┘└──┘│  │ └──┘└──┘└──┘│      │ │
         │  │  more servers    │           │  └────────────┘  └────────────┘      │ │
         │  │                  │           │                                      │ │
         │  │  NO auto-healing │           │  IF NODE DIES: Pods move to Node 2 ✅ │ │
         │  │  NO auto-scaling │           │  SCALING: kubectl scale --replicas=10│ │
         │  └──────────────────┘           └──────────────────────────────────────┘ │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [COMPARISON TABLE: Docker vs Kubernetes — 15 Dimensions]
         | Dimension             | Docker (Standalone)   | Kubernetes             |
         | Single Host           | ✅ Yes                | ✅ Yes (Minikube)      |
         | Multi-Host Cluster    | ❌ No                 | ✅ Yes (core feature)  |
         | Auto-Scaling          | ❌ Manual only        | ✅ HPA + VPA built-in  |
         | Self-Healing          | ❌ restart policies   | ✅ Auto-recreates pods |
         | Service Discovery     | ⚠️ Limited (Compose)  | ✅ DNS + CoreDNS       |
         | Load Balancing        | ⚠️ Compose/Manual     | ✅ Built-in Services   |
         | Rolling Updates       | ⚠️ Swarm only         | ✅ Deployment native   |
         | Rollback              | ❌ None               | ✅ kubectl rollout undo|
         | Secret Management     | ⚠️ Swarm secrets      | ✅ Secrets + etcd      |
         | Config Management     | ⚠️ .env files         | ✅ ConfigMaps          |
         | Storage Orchestration | ❌ Manual volumes     | ✅ PV + PVC + CSI      |
         | Namespace Isolation   | ❌ None               | ✅ Namespaces          |
         | RBAC                  | ❌ None               | ✅ Roles + Bindings    |
         | Cloud-Native          | ❌ Not designed for   | ✅ Built for cloud     |
         | Learning Curve        | 🟢 Low                | 🔴 High                |

         🎯 GOAL: State, from memory, the one sentence that separates what
            Docker does from what Kubernetes adds — and point at where the
            single-host diagram above breaks under real traffic.
         [TECH] Docker Engine schedules containers onto exactly the host you
            ran `docker run` on; there is no concept of "another machine"
            inside the engine itself. Kubernetes adds a control plane (API
            server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) that turns MANY
            hosts (nodes) into one schedulable pool — control-plane
            internals: [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
         [ANALOGY] The SINGLE HOST vs CLUSTER diagram above: Docker is one
            kitchen with one chef — if the chef collapses, dinner stops.
            Kubernetes is a restaurant chain with a head office (control
            plane) that reassigns any order to any open kitchen (node).
         🔬 easypj: today `docker run easypj:v1` dies with the laptop. On a
            3-node cluster, the SAME image becomes 3 Pods; killing one node
            just moves its Pods to the survivors (see the table's
            Self-Healing row).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: from the 15-dimension table above, list every
            row Docker marks ❌ or ⚠️ (13 of them), then circle the 2 a
            growing easypj would hit FIRST. Verify: your circled pair is
            Auto-Scaling and Rollback — the two Docker cannot do at all
            without Swarm or K8s.
         📊 SUMMARY: Docker = one host, one daemon; Kubernetes = a cluster
            with a control plane doing the picking for you.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Kubernetes does NOT replace Docker's image format —
            it still runs OCI images your Dockerfiles already build.

    25.2 Concepts Mapping: Docker → Kubernetes
         - Docker Container → Kubernetes Pod
         - Docker Image → Kubernetes Container Image
         - docker-compose.yml → Kubernetes Deployment + Service
         - Docker Network → Kubernetes Network (CNI)
         - Docker Volume → Kubernetes PersistentVolume
         - Docker Compose → Kubernetes + Helm/Kustomize
         [TABLE: Every Docker concept mapped to K8s equivalent]

         🎯 GOAL: Translate any Docker noun to its Kubernetes noun without
            hesitating — this vocabulary swap runs through every later page.
         [TABLE: Docker concept → Kubernetes equivalent — drawn]
            Container          | Pod (1+ containers, one network namespace)
            Image              | Container image (same OCI artifact)
            docker-compose.yml | Deployment + Service (+ Helm chart)
            Docker network     | CNI network (Pod-to-Pod, cluster-wide)
            Docker volume      | PersistentVolume + PersistentVolumeClaim
            docker run         | kubectl apply -f (or run, imperative)
            restart policy     | Pod restartPolicy + Deployment replicas
         [TECH] The mapping is NOT 1:1 everywhere: one Docker container maps
            to a Pod's main container, but a Pod can hold several
            containers sharing localhost and a volume — a shape Docker
            alone cannot express. Sidecar patterns: [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
         [ANALOGY] Relabeling a moving-house inventory: "box" becomes
            "crate", "van" becomes "fleet" — same cargo, new shipping
            company with its own paperwork and bigger trucks.
         🔬 easypj: the postgres_data VOLUME becomes a PersistentVolumeClaim
            bound to a PersistentVolume — same idea (durable disk outside
            the container), different YAML, same Postgres data files.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: take easypj's compose.yaml from Chapter 11 and
            rename each key using this table (django→Deployment,
            postgres_data→PVC, backend network→CNI). Verify: nothing in
            the list has no K8s equivalent — that is the point here.
         [DIAGRAM:flow — compose.yaml splits into 4 K8s objects]
         ┌────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │services:           │───────▶│Deployment  (django Pods, 26.7)             │
         │django, postgres    │───────▶│  replicas: 3, image: easypj:v1             │
         │ports: 8000:8000    │───────▶│Service  (stable :8000 access)              │
         │environment:        │───────▶│ConfigMap+Secret (26.5): DEBUG,             │
         │DEBUG, SECRET_KEY.. │───────▶│  ALLOWED_HOSTS, SECRET_KEY                 │
         │volumes:            │───────▶│PVC: claims postgres_data (17.2)            │
         └────────────────────┘        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         💡 kompose convert (25.4, 29.3) automates roughly this exact split
            from a real compose.yaml — but it cannot invent replica counts,
            resource limits or health probes; those still need the Chapter
            26/27 review a human does by hand before anything ships.

         📊 SUMMARY: same 5 nouns (image, container, network, volume,
            compose file), new names, bigger scope.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "Docker Compose" itself has NO direct K8s object —
            its job splits across Deployment, Service, ConfigMap and PVC.

    25.3 From Dockerfile to Kubernetes Deployment
         - Step 1: Dockerfile (you already have this!)
         - Step 2: docker build + docker push to registry
         - Step 3: Write Kubernetes Deployment YAML
         - Step 4: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
         - Step 5: Write Kubernetes Service YAML
         - Step 6: kubectl apply -f service.yaml

         [COMPLETE WORKFLOW: DOCKERFILE → K8s DEPLOYMENT (6 Steps)]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │          🐳→☸️ DOCKERFILE TO KUBERNETES DEPLOYMENT — FULL JOURNEY           │
         │                                                                          │
         │  STEP 1: Dockerfile           STEP 2: Build + Push                       │
         │  ┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐               │
         │  │ FROM python:3.11 │        │ $ docker build -t        │               │
         │  │ WORKDIR /app     │        │   ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 .│               │
         │  │ COPY req.txt .   │        │ $ docker push            │               │
         │  │ RUN pip install  │        │   ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1  │               │
         │  │ COPY . .         │        └───────────┬──────────────┘               │
         │  │ CMD ["gunicorn"] │                    │                               │
         │  └──────────────────┘                    ▼                               │
         │                                   ┌──────────────┐                      │
         │  STEP 3-4: K8s Deployment         │ 🗄️ Registry   │                      │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────┐     │ ghcr.io/you/  │                      │
         │  │ apiVersion: apps/v1      │     │ easypj:v1     │                      │
         │  │ kind: Deployment         │     └──────┬───────┘                      │
         │  │ metadata:                │            │                               │
         │  │   name: easypj           │            │ STEP 5-6: Deploy              │
         │  │ spec:                    │            ▼                               │
         │  │   replicas: 3            │     ┌──────────────────────────┐          │
         │  │   template:              │     │ $ kubectl apply \        │          │
         │  │     containers:          │     │   -f deployment.yaml     │          │
         │  │     - image: ghcr.io/    │     │ $ kubectl apply \        │          │
         │  │       you/easypj:v1      │     │   -f service.yaml        │          │
         │  │       ports:             │     │ $ kubectl get pods       │          │
         │  │       - containerPort:8000│    │ NAME        READY STATUS │          │
         │  └──────────────────────────┘     │ easypj-xxx  1/1   Running│          │
         │                                   │ easypj-yyy  1/1   Running│          │
         │  STEP 5: K8s Service              │ easypj-zzz  1/1   Running│          │
         │  ┌──────────────────────────┐     └──────────────────────────┘          │
         │  │ apiVersion: v1           │                                            │
         │  │ kind: Service            │     RESULT: easypj running on 3 pods,      │
         │  │ spec:                    │     accessible via Service on port 8000!   │
         │  │   selector:              │                                            │
         │  │     app: easypj          │                                            │
         │  │   ports:                 │                                            │
         │  │   - port: 8000           │                                            │
         │  │     targetPort: 8000     │                                            │
         │  │   type: LoadBalancer     │                                            │
         │  └──────────────────────────┘                                            │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Walk the 6-step journey above end-to-end and name which
            steps are pure Docker and which are pure Kubernetes.
         [TECH] Steps 1-2 (Dockerfile, build, push) are 100% Docker —
            nothing changes from Part 3. Steps 3-6 hand the SAME image to
            a Deployment (desired replica count + Pod template) and a
            Service (stable network identity for those replicas) — kubectl
            reads these YAMLs and drives the API server toward that state.
         [ANALOGY] The journey diagram above is a factory line: stations
            1-2 (Dockerfile, build+push) are the loading dock you already
            run; stations 3-6 hand the crate to a NEW shipping department
            (K8s) deciding how many trucks (replicas) and which docks
            (Service) receive it.
         🔬 easypj: `docker build -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 .` does not
            change at all; only what happens AFTER `docker push` is new —
            a Deployment named easypj requests replicas: 3 of that tag.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: in the diagram's Deployment YAML, find the ONE
            line that is just the Dockerfile's build output (the image:
            field) and the ONE line that never existed in Docker
            (replicas: 3). Verify: the image: line traces straight back
            to the build+push Chapters 4-5 already taught you cold;
            replicas: 3 is the new concept this chapter adds on top.
         📊 SUMMARY: build+push stays Docker; "how many, where, reachable
            how" becomes Kubernetes' job via Deployment + Service YAML.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `kubectl apply` never builds or pushes images — if
            the tag in deployment.yaml was never pushed, every Pod sits in
            ImagePullBackOff forever.

    25.4 docker-compose.yml → Kubernetes Manifests
         - Tool: Kompose (kompose convert)
         - Manual translation: compose services → K8s Deployments
         - compose networks → K8s Services
         - compose volumes → K8s PersistentVolumeClaims
         [CODE: Side-by-side: compose.yaml → deployment.yaml + service.yaml]


         🎯 GOAL: Convert a real easypj compose.yaml into K8s manifests two
            ways — automatic and manual — and know when to trust each.
         [CODE: compose.yaml → K8s, side-by-side core — drawn]
            # compose.yaml (Chapter 11)     # kompose convert output
            services:                       # deployment.yaml
              django:                       #   containers:
                image: easypj:v1            #   - image: easypj:v1
                ports: ["8000:8000"]        #     ports: [{containerPort:8000}]
                depends_on: [postgres]      # service.yaml
                                             #   selector: {app: django}
              postgres:                     # deployment.yaml (2nd) + PVC
                volumes: [pgdata:/var/...]  #   volumeMounts + PVC: pgdata
         [TECH] `kompose convert -f compose.yaml` reads the SAME file
            Chapter 11 built and emits one Deployment + Service per
            service, plus a PVC per named volume — a first draft, not a
            final manifest (guesses replicas: 1, no resource limits, no
            probes).
         [ANALOGY] kompose is a rough translator: it gets the nouns right
            (django, postgres, pgdata) fast, but a human still edits the
            grammar (replicas, health checks, secrets) before it ships.
         🔬 easypj: kompose turns `depends_on: [postgres]` into nothing —
            K8s has no depends_on; Chapter 27's readiness probes replace it.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `kompose convert -f compose.yaml` on your
            easypj file. Verify: count the generated files (one Deployment
            + Service per service, one PVC for pgdata) and confirm the
            postgres depends_on silently disappeared.
         📊 SUMMARY: kompose bootstraps manifests from a file you already
            own; manual translation (Chapter 26) gives production control
            kompose's guesses don't.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: never ship kompose's raw output — no resource
            limits and no health checks means an unbounded, unmonitored Pod.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — what actually changes when the SAME image moves
       from `docker run` to a Kubernetes Pod:
        Both Docker Engine and a Kubernetes node run containers through
        containerd underneath — dockerd talks to it via Docker's own API
        layer, kubelet talks to it directly via the CRI (Container
        Runtime Interface). Neither one reinvents how a container starts:
        both ultimately call runc to create the Linux namespaces + cgroups
        the process runs inside. This is WHY an OCI image built once with
        `docker build` runs unmodified in both worlds — the image format
        never changed, only WHO is asking containerd to run it.

        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ docker run easypj:v1          kubectl apply (Pod easypj-xxx)   │
        │      │                              │ (via CRI)                │
        │      ▼                              ▼                          │
        │ dockerd (Docker API)          kubelet (per-node agent)         │
        │      └──────────────┬───────────────┘                          │
        │                     ▼                                          │
        │               containerd (shared)                              │
        │                     ▼                                          │
        │           runc → namespaces + cgroups                          │
        │                     ▼                                          │
        │          SAME OCI image, SAME running process                  │
        └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        On the Kubernetes side, `kubectl apply` doesn't create the Pod
        directly either: it writes desired state to the API server, which
        persists it in etcd; the scheduler watches for unscheduled Pods
        and assigns a node; THAT node's kubelet then pulls the image and
        asks containerd to run it — the same watch-and-reconcile loop
        that makes a deleted Pod under a Deployment come back within
        seconds.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS:
        - Docker = one host; Kubernetes = many hosts under one control
          plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager).
        - Of the 15 comparison dimensions, Auto-Scaling and Rollback are
          the two Docker cannot do at all without Swarm or Kubernetes.
        - The Docker→K8s noun mapping is not always 1:1 — a Pod can hold
          several containers sharing one network namespace and volumes.
        - "Docker Compose" itself has no single K8s object — its job
          splits across Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, and PVC.
        - Steps 1-2 of the Dockerfile→Deployment journey (build, push)
          stay 100% Docker; steps 3-6 are new Kubernetes concepts.
        - `kubectl apply` never builds or pushes images — ImagePullBackOff
          always traces back to a tag problem, not a cluster bug.
        - `kompose convert` bootstraps manifests fast but guesses
          replicas: 1, no resource limits, no probes — a first draft only.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS:
        - Kubernetes does NOT replace Docker's image format — it still
          runs the exact OCI images your Dockerfiles already build.
        - Never ship kompose's raw output — no resource limits and no
          health checks means an unbounded, unmonitored Pod.
        - `depends_on` silently disappears when kompose converts a
          compose.yaml — Chapter 27's readiness probes replace it.
        - ImagePullBackOff means the tag in your YAML was never pushed
          (or a private registry has no imagePullSecret) — not a K8s bug.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS:
        - Memorize the noun-mapping table cold before touching Chapter
          26's YAML — the vocabulary swap is most of the learning curve.
        - Treat `kompose convert` as a fast first draft, never a final
          manifest — always add limits and probes by hand afterward.
        - When a Pod won't start, check the image tag before questioning
          the cluster.

    🔑 COMMANDS:
        kubectl cluster-info                    # confirms a cluster is reachable
        kubectl config current-context          # confirms kubectl points at the right cluster
        docker build -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1 . # unchanged from Part 3
        docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1       # image must exist in a registry before any Deployment references it
        kompose convert -f compose.yaml         # auto-generates a first-draft Deployment/Service/PVC set
        kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml        # hands the Pod template + replica count to the API server
        kubectl get pods -o wide                # confirms which node each Pod landed on
        kubectl explain deployment.spec         # inline docs for any object's spec fields

    🧪 DRILL (5 min): Run `kompose convert -f compose.yaml` on easypj's
        Chapter 11 file. Count the generated files (should be one
        Deployment + Service per service, plus one PVC for
        postgres_data), then write down the 3 things it did NOT set for

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 25):
        Q1: What's the one-sentence line separating what Docker still
            owns from what Kubernetes adds?
            A: Docker packages and runs a container on one host;
               Kubernetes schedules, heals, and scales containers across
               a cluster of many hosts via a control plane (API server,
               etcd, scheduler, controller-manager).

        Q2: Complete the mapping:
            | Docker              | Kubernetes                          |
            | Container           | ?                                    |
            | docker-compose.yml  | ?                                    |
            | Docker volume       | ?                                    |
            A: Container → Pod; docker-compose.yml → Deployment + Service
               (+ Helm chart); Docker volume → PersistentVolume +
               PersistentVolumeClaim.

        Q3: From the 15-dimension comparison table, which two rows show
            Docker flat-❌ that a growing easypj would hit FIRST?
            A: Auto-Scaling and Rollback.

        Q4: Why can one Kubernetes Pod outgrow "one Docker container"?
            A: A Pod can hold multiple containers sharing one network
               namespace (localhost) and volumes — a shape a single
               Docker container cannot express alone (sidecar pattern).

        Q5: In the Dockerfile→Deployment 6-step journey, which steps are
            pure Docker and which are pure Kubernetes?
                Dockerfile ─▶ build ─▶ push │ Deployment YAML ─▶ apply ─▶ Service YAML ─▶ apply
                └──────── pure Docker ───────┘ └────────── pure Kubernetes ──────────────┘
            A: Steps 1-2 (Dockerfile, docker build + push) stay 100%
               Docker, unchanged from Part 3. Steps 3-6 (write + apply
               Deployment YAML, write + apply Service YAML) are pure
               Kubernetes — kubectl reads the YAML and drives the API
               server toward that state.

        Q6: What error appears if deployment.yaml references a tag that
            was never pushed, and why?
            A: ImagePullBackOff — `kubectl apply` never builds or pushes
               images, it only schedules images already in a registry; if
               the tag doesn't exist there, every Pod trying to pull it
               fails permanently in that state.

        Q7: What does `kompose convert -f compose.yaml` produce from
            easypj's compose file, and what 3 things does it NOT set?
            A: One Deployment + Service per service (django, postgres)
               plus a PVC for postgres_data; it does NOT set real replica
               counts, resource limits, or health probes.

        Q8: Why does `depends_on: [postgres]` disappear when kompose
            converts easypj's compose.yaml, and what replaces it?
            A: Kubernetes has no depends_on concept; Chapter 27's
               readiness probes replace it by controlling when a Pod is
               added to a Service's endpoint list.

        Q9: Compare a Docker volume to its Kubernetes equivalent for
            easypj's postgres_data.
            A: postgres_data as a Docker VOLUME becomes a
               PersistentVolumeClaim bound to a PersistentVolume — same
               idea (durable disk outside the container lifecycle),
               different YAML, same underlying Postgres data files.

        Q10: Using the compose.yaml→K8s flow diagram from 25.2, match
             each key to what it becomes:
             | compose.yaml key           | becomes                      |
             | services: django           | Deployment (Pod template)    |
             | ports: 8000:8000           | Service                      |
             | environment: DEBUG, SECRET_KEY | ConfigMap + Secret       |
             | volumes: postgres_data     | PersistentVolumeClaim        |
             A: As shown in the table above — the compose file's single
                block of YAML fans out into 4 separate K8s objects.

        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ Docker (1 host)  ──noun map──▶  K8s vocabulary  ──6 steps──▶   │
        │                                                  Deployment +  │
        │                                                  Service YAML  │
