Chapter 26: Deploying easypj to Kubernetes
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Chapter 25 mapped nouns and traced one
    journey in the abstract; this chapter runs it for real. Every YAML
    here targets the SAME easypj image from Part 3, deployed onto an
    actual cluster you can reach with kubectl. Problem solved here: "I
    understand Deployments and Services in theory — show me easypj
    actually serving traffic from inside a real K8s cluster."

    [A] META: Difficulty 🔴 Advanced | Time ~60-75 min | Beyond DCA scope —
        hands-on Kubernetes deployment mechanics, the practical half of
        the DCA→CKA bridge.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — by the end of Chapter 26 you can:
        - Verify all 4 prerequisite gates (cluster reachable, correct
          context, registry access, image pushed) before writing YAML (26.1)
        - Build and push a precisely-tagged easypj image, and explain why
          `:latest` is banned in Kubernetes manifests (26.2)
        - Write a Deployment with matching selector/labels and real
          resource requests/limits (26.3)
        - Write a Service and choose ClusterIP vs NodePort vs
          LoadBalancer correctly (26.4)
        - Split easypj's settings into a ConfigMap (non-secret) and a
          Secret, and wire both in via envFrom (26.5)
        - Deploy the full stack in order — namespace → config/secret →
          deployment/service — and verify with port-forward (26.6)
        - Explain why you scale a Deployment, never a bare Pod (26.7)

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: Not a graded DCA domain — hands-on Kubernetes
        deployment mechanics sit outside the DCA blueprint; this chapter
        is direct preparation for the companion CKA guide's Workloads
        domain.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 26.1 prerequisites → 26.2 build/push → 26.3
        Deployment → 26.4 Service → 26.5 ConfigMap/Secret → 26.6 deploy &
        verify → 26.7 Pods vs Deployments/scaling.

    26.1 Prerequisites for K8s Deployment
         - Kubernetes cluster (Minikube, kind, k3s, or cloud)
         - kubectl configured
         - Container registry access
         - Docker image pushed to registry
         [CHECKLIST: 4 prerequisites verified]

         🎯 GOAL: Confirm all 4 prerequisites before writing a single YAML
            line — most "kubectl apply hangs" reports trace back to here.
         [CHECKLIST: before you write any manifest — drawn]
            [ ] a cluster exists — `kubectl cluster-info` returns a URL
            [ ] kubectl context points at it — `kubectl config current-context`
            [ ] you can push to a registry — `docker login ghcr.io` succeeds
            [ ] the easypj image is already pushed — `docker push` completed
         [TECH] `kubectl` reads ~/.kube/config to pick a context — the SAME
            binary can silently point at Minikube, kind, or a production
            cluster depending on which context is current. Cluster
            bootstrap internals (kubeadm, control-plane HA):
            [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
         [ANALOGY] Checking you have the right house key AND the right
            house before knocking — a valid kubectl config for the WRONG
            cluster fails exactly like no config at all, just more
            confusingly.
         🔬 easypj: `docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1` must succeed BEFORE
            any Deployment references that tag — kubectl never builds
            images, it only schedules ones already in a registry.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the 4 checklist commands above in order.
            Verify: all 4 succeed BEFORE you type `kubectl apply` once —
            if step 2 shows the wrong cluster, stop and fix context first.
         📊 SUMMARY: cluster reachable + correct context + image pushed —
            three gates, checked in order, before any YAML runs.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a local Minikube cluster cannot pull an image that
            only exists in your local `docker images` — push it to a
            reachable registry, or `minikube image load` it directly.

    26.2 Building & Pushing the easypj Image
         - docker build -t ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0 .
         - docker login ghcr.io
         - docker push ghcr.io/username/easypj:v1.0
         [TERMINAL: Complete build + push workflow]

         🎯 GOAL: Produce one correctly-tagged, pushed image that 26.3's
            Deployment can reference by exact name.
         [TERMINAL: build + push, drawn]
            $ docker build -t ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0 .
            $ docker login ghcr.io -u you --password-stdin < token.txt
            $ docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0
            $ docker manifest inspect ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0   # confirms it
         [TECH] The tag is the ONLY link between this chapter and the
            Deployment YAML — `image: ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0` must match
            character-for-character, including the registry host. `:latest`
            is banned here: K8s cannot tell "new latest" from "old latest".
         [ANALOGY] Mailing a package: the tag is the exact street address
            on the label. "v1.0" is a house number; "latest" is "somewhere
            on this street" — the carrier (kubelet) needs the number.
         🔬 easypj: reuse Chapter 9.7's multi-stage Dockerfile unchanged —
            only the registry host (ghcr.io/you/) is new; the build itself
            is identical to every prior chapter.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: after pushing, run `docker manifest inspect` on
            the exact tag. Verify: it returns JSON, not a 404 — a 404 here
            is the #1 cause of ImagePullBackOff in the next section.
         📊 SUMMARY: build once, tag precisely, push before any YAML
            references it.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: private registries need an imagePullSecret in the
            cluster — pushing successfully from your laptop does NOT mean
            the cluster can pull; 26.5's Secret is half of that fix.

    26.3 Creating the Kubernetes Deployment
         - apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment
         - metadata: name, labels
         - spec: replicas, selector, template
         - container spec: image, ports, env
         - Resource limits: requests and limits
         [COMPLETE deployment.yaml CODE with annotations]

         🎯 GOAL: Write a Deployment that names the exact image, exposes
            the right port, and never lets one runaway Pod starve the node.
         [CODE: deployment.yaml — drawn, core fields only]
            apiVersion: apps/v1
            kind: Deployment
            metadata: {name: easypj, labels: {app: easypj}}
            spec:
              replicas: 3
              selector: {matchLabels: {app: easypj}}
              template:
                metadata: {labels: {app: easypj}}
                spec:
                  containers:
                  - name: django
                    image: ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0
                    ports: [{containerPort: 8000}]
                    resources:
                      requests: {cpu: "100m", memory: "128Mi"}
                      limits:   {cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi"}
         [TECH] `selector.matchLabels` must equal `template.metadata.labels`
            — this is how the Deployment finds ITS OWN Pods among all Pods
            in the namespace. requests reserve capacity the scheduler
            counts against; limits are a hard ceiling the kubelet enforces.
         [ANALOGY] selector/labels are a name tag, not a leash: the
            Deployment scans the room for Pods wearing "app: easypj" and
            claims them — mismatched labels means it creates orphan Pods
            forever, never recognizing the ones it already made.
         🔬 easypj: gunicorn's own --workers setting (Chapter 6) now works
            ALONGSIDE replicas: 3 — each Pod runs N gunicorn workers,
            times 3 Pods, for the real concurrency ceiling.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`, then
            `kubectl get pods -l app=easypj`. Verify: exactly 3 Pods, all
            Running, all showing image ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0.
         📊 SUMMARY: replicas + matching selector/labels + a container spec
            with real resource requests/limits — the minimum viable
            Deployment.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: skip resources: and one memory-leaking Pod can
            starve every other Pod on its node — this is not optional
            in production.

    26.4 Creating the Kubernetes Service
         - apiVersion: v1, kind: Service
         - spec: selector, ports, type (ClusterIP/NodePort/LoadBalancer)
         - Service type comparison
         [COMPLETE service.yaml CODE with annotations]

         🎯 GOAL: Give the 3 easypj Pods ONE stable address, and pick the
            right Service type for dev vs production.
         [CODE: service.yaml — drawn]
            apiVersion: v1
            kind: Service
            metadata: {name: easypj}
            spec:
              selector: {app: easypj}
              ports: [{port: 8000, targetPort: 8000}]
              type: ClusterIP
         [TABLE: Service type → who can reach it]
            ClusterIP    | inside the cluster only (default, most services)
            NodePort     | cluster + any node IP:30000-32767 (dev/testing)
            LoadBalancer | the public internet, via a cloud LB (production)
         [TECH] A Service is a stable virtual IP + DNS name (easypj.
            default.svc.cluster.local) in front of a Pod IP set that
            changes every time a Pod restarts — kube-proxy keeps the
            mapping current. CNI/kube-proxy internals: [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
         [ANALOGY] Pods are hotel guests reassigned rooms nightly; the
            Service is the FRONT DESK phone number — always the same, no
            matter which room today's guest is actually in.
         🔬 easypj: nginx's old `proxy_pass http://django:8000` (Chapter
            11) becomes `proxy_pass http://easypj:8000` — same pattern,
            the DNS name now resolves to a Service, not a container.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `kubectl apply -f service.yaml`, then `kubectl
            run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- easypj:8000`.
            Verify: it returns HTML even though you never typed a Pod IP.
         📊 SUMMARY: selector finds the Pods, type decides who's allowed to
            call — ClusterIP by default, open up only what needs opening.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a Service's selector uses the SAME label-matching
            rules as a Deployment — a typo silently creates a Service with
            zero endpoints (`kubectl get endpoints easypj` shows empty).

    26.5 ConfigMaps & Secrets for easypj
         - ConfigMap for Django settings (non-sensitive)
         - Secret for SECRET_KEY, DB_PASSWORD
         - Mounting ConfigMap as env vars
         [COMPLETE configmap.yaml + secret.yaml CODE]

         🎯 GOAL: Split easypj's settings into non-secret (ConfigMap) and
            secret (Secret) — never mix SECRET_KEY into a plain YAML again.
         [CODE: configmap.yaml + secret.yaml — drawn]
            apiVersion: v1
            kind: ConfigMap
            metadata: {name: easypj-config}
            data: {DEBUG: "False", ALLOWED_HOSTS: "easypj.example.com"}
            ---
            apiVersion: v1
            kind: Secret
            metadata: {name: easypj-secret}
            type: Opaque
            stringData:
              SECRET_KEY: django-insecure-CHANGE-ME
              DATABASE_URL: postgres://easypj:pg-pass@postgres:5432/easypj_db
         [TECH] A Secret is base64-ENCODED in etcd by default, not
            encrypted — treat it as obscured, not safe from a cluster
            admin. `stringData` lets you write plaintext; K8s encodes it
            on save. Real encryption-at-rest: [KUBERNETES GUIDE].
         [ANALOGY] Directly maps to Chapter 11's .env split: ConfigMap is
            the postcard (DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS), Secret is the sealed
            envelope (SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL) — same two piles, now two
            cluster-native objects instead of one file.
         🔬 easypj: settings.py's `os.environ["SECRET_KEY"]` call does not
            change at all — only WHERE the env var comes from changes,
            via envFrom in the Deployment (26.6).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `kubectl apply -f secret.yaml`, then `kubectl
            get secret easypj-secret -o yaml`. Verify: SECRET_KEY appears
            base64-encoded, not plaintext — `base64 -d` proves it round-trips.
         [TABLE: ConfigMap vs Secret — the exact differences]
         | Aspect          | ConfigMap            | Secret                   |
         | Stored in etcd  | plain text           | base64 (NOT encrypted)   |
         | describe output | shows real values    | masked: <set to key ..>  |
         | get -o yaml     | data: plain text     | data: base64 (needs -d)  |
         | Mutable?        | yes, in place        | yes, in place            |
         | easypj example  | DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS | SECRET_KEY, DATABASE_URL |
         💡 Both objects share one blind spot: a Pod already running with
            envFrom does NOT see an update until it restarts — only a
            volume-mounted ConfigMap/Secret refreshes live (~1 min sync).
            easypj's SECRET_KEY via envFrom needs a rollout restart to rotate.

         📊 SUMMARY: ConfigMap for what's fine to read, Secret for what
            isn't — same env-var split as .env, now cluster objects.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `kubectl apply -f secret.yaml` from a git-committed
            file defeats the point — real production needs a vault/sealed-
            secrets pipeline, not a checked-in YAML.

    26.6 Deploying & Verifying
         - kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
         - kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml, secret.yaml
         - kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml, service.yaml
         - kubectl get pods, svc, deploy
         - kubectl port-forward svc/easypj 8000:8000
         - Open browser, verify easypj is running
         [TERMINAL: Full deploy + verify sequence]

         🎯 GOAL: Go from zero to "easypj answering HTTP requests through
            K8s" using only the 4 YAMLs this chapter built.
         [TERMINAL: full deploy + verify, drawn]
            $ kubectl create namespace easypj
            $ kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml -f secret.yaml -n easypj
            $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml -n easypj
            $ kubectl get pods,svc -n easypj
            $ kubectl port-forward svc/easypj 8000:8000 -n easypj
            $ curl -I http://localhost:8000/jobs/       # HTTP/1.1 200 OK
         [TECH] `envFrom: [{configMapRef: {name: easypj-config}},
            {secretRef: {name: easypj-secret}}]` in the container spec is
            what actually wires 26.5's objects into the Pod's environment —
            without it, ConfigMap/Secret exist but nothing reads them.
         [ANALOGY] port-forward is a temporary phone line straight to one
            Service, bypassing the front desk's real routing — perfect for
            verification, never used for production traffic.
         🔬 easypj: the same `/jobs/` view Chapter 11's nginx served now
            answers through kubectl port-forward → Service → Pod →
            gunicorn — one more hop, same Django code, unmodified.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the six lines above in order. Verify:
            `get pods` shows 3/3 Running BEFORE you port-forward —
            forwarding to a CrashLoopBackOff Pod just times out silently.
         📊 SUMMARY: namespace → config/secret → deployment/service →
            verify — the same order every real rollout follows.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: forgetting `-n easypj` on any command runs it
            against the `default` namespace — objects "disappear" only
            because you're looking in the wrong namespace.

    26.7 Pods vs Deployments — Scaling easypj
         - Single Pod (ephemeral, not recommended)
         - Deployment (manages ReplicaSet, ensures replicas)
         - Scaling: kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5
         - kubectl get pods -w (watch pods come up)
         [DIAGRAM: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods (×5)]


         🎯 GOAL: Explain why you scale the Deployment, never a Pod, and
            trace the object chain that makes `--replicas=5` create Pods.
         [DIAGRAM:architecture — the ownership chain, drawn]
            Deployment easypj (desired: replicas=5)
                    │ creates & owns
                    ▼
            ReplicaSet easypj-7d9f4 (current: 5)
                    │ creates & owns
                    ▼
            Pod  Pod  Pod  Pod  Pod   (each independently schedulable)
         [TECH] A bare Pod has no controller watching it — kill it and it
            stays dead. A Deployment owns a ReplicaSet, which continuously
            reconciles "Pods running" against "replicas: desired"; killing
            a Pod under a Deployment gets it replaced within seconds.
         [ANALOGY] A bare Pod is a single hire with no manager — vanish
            and the seat stays empty. A Deployment is HR policy: "this
            desk always has 5 people" — someone quits, HR (ReplicaSet)
            posts the job again automatically.
         🔬 easypj: `kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5` takes
            easypj from 3 to 5 Pods — Django code untouched, gunicorn
            config untouched, only the REPLICA COUNT changed.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5`,
            then `kubectl delete pod <any-easypj-pod>` and immediately
            `kubectl get pods -w`. Verify: a NEW Pod appears within
            seconds — the ReplicaSet replaced it without you asking twice.
         📊 SUMMARY: never manage Pods directly — scale/manage the
            Deployment; the ReplicaSet is the enforcement layer underneath.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: deleting a Pod created by a ReplicaSet does not
            "clean up" anything — it triggers an immediate replacement,
            the opposite of what a beginner usually expects.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how a Service's virtual IP actually routes traffic:
        A Service's ClusterIP has no process listening on it anywhere —
        it's a virtual address. kube-proxy runs on every node, watches
        the Endpoints object (built automatically from the Service's
        selector matching currently-Ready Pods), and programs iptables
        or IPVS rules that DNAT traffic bound for the ClusterIP straight
        to one of those real Pod IPs. CoreDNS is what resolves
        `easypj.default.svc.cluster.local` to that ClusterIP in the
        first place.

        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ client → DNS lookup "easypj.default.svc.cluster.local"         │
        │              │ (CoreDNS)                                       │
        │              ▼                                                 │
        │      Service ClusterIP (virtual, nothing listens here)         │
        │              │ (kube-proxy iptables/IPVS DNAT rule)            │
        │              ▼                                                 │
        │      one of: Pod-A IP | Pod-B IP | Pod-C IP  (Endpoints)        │
        └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        This is exactly why a failing readiness probe (27.3) removes a
        Pod from rotation with zero code changes anywhere: kube-proxy
        simply stops including that Pod's IP the next time it reprograms
        the DNAT rules.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS:
        - All 4 prerequisite gates (cluster reachable, correct context,
          registry access, image pushed) must pass before any YAML runs.
        - Image tags must be exact and never `:latest` — K8s can't tell
          "new latest" from "old latest".
        - `selector.matchLabels` must equal `template.metadata.labels` or
          the Deployment creates orphan Pods forever.
        - requests reserve scheduler capacity; limits are a kubelet-
          enforced ceiling — skipping them risks one Pod starving a node.
        - ClusterIP (default/internal), NodePort (dev/test), LoadBalancer
          (public/production) — pick the narrowest type that works.
        - ConfigMap = non-secret, Secret = base64-encoded (NOT encrypted)
          — envFrom wires both into the Pod's environment, but a running
          Pod needs a rollout restart to pick up changes.
        - Never scale a bare Pod — scale the Deployment; the ReplicaSet
          is the reconciliation layer that replaces killed Pods.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS:
        - A local cluster (e.g. Minikube) can't pull an image sitting
          only in your local `docker images` — push it to a reachable
          registry or load it directly into the cluster's runtime.
        - Private registries need an imagePullSecret in-cluster; pushing
          successfully from your laptop doesn't mean the cluster can pull.
        - A label typo between a Service's selector and a Pod's labels
          creates a Service with zero endpoints silently — no error.
        - Forgetting `-n <namespace>` runs a command against `default` —
          objects appear "missing" only because you're in the wrong
          namespace.
        - Deleting a Pod owned by a ReplicaSet doesn't clean anything up
          — it triggers an immediate replacement.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS:
        - Run `kubectl get pods,svc -A` when anything "disappears" — it's
          usually a namespace mismatch, not a deleted object.
        - `docker manifest inspect` right after pushing — a 404 there
          predicts ImagePullBackOff before you even apply anything.
        - Check `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` first whenever a Service
          "isn't working" — empty endpoints means the selector is the
          bug, not the network.

    🔑 COMMANDS:
        kubectl cluster-info                                      # confirms a reachable cluster
        kubectl config current-context                            # confirms kubectl points at the right cluster
        docker push ghcr.io/you/easypj:v1.0                        # must succeed before any Deployment references the tag
        kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml -n easypj # deploy both objects into the right namespace
        kubectl get pods -l app=easypj                             # confirm replica count & Running status
        kubectl get endpoints easypj                               # confirm the Service actually found Pods
        kubectl port-forward svc/easypj 8000:8000 -n easypj        # temporary local access, verification only
        kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=5               # scale the Deployment, never a bare Pod

    🧪 DRILL (10 min): Apply easypj's 4 manifests (configmap, secret,
        deployment, service) into a fresh `easypj` namespace in order,
        port-forward, and curl `/jobs/` for a 200. If any step fails,
        name which of the 4 prerequisite gates it violates before
        troubleshooting further.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 26):
        Q1: What are the 4 prerequisite gates that must pass before
            writing any K8s YAML for easypj?
            A: (1) a cluster exists (`kubectl cluster-info`), (2) kubectl
               context points at it (`kubectl config current-context`),
               (3) you can push to a registry (`docker login` succeeds),
               (4) the easypj image is already pushed.

        Q2: Why is tagging an image `:latest` banned in Kubernetes
            manifests?
            A: K8s can't tell "new latest" from "old latest" — the tag is
               the only link between a pushed image and the Deployment's
               `image:` field, so it must be exact and stable (e.g. v1.0).

        Q3: Fill in which Service type reaches which audience:
            | Type         | Reachable by                              |
            | ClusterIP    | ?                                          |
            | NodePort     | ?                                          |
            | LoadBalancer | ?                                          |
            A: ClusterIP → inside the cluster only (default); NodePort →
               cluster + any node IP on 30000-32767 (dev/test);
               LoadBalancer → the public internet via a cloud LB
               (production).

        Q4: Why must `selector.matchLabels` in a Deployment equal
            `template.metadata.labels`?
            A: That's how the Deployment recognizes its OWN Pods among
               all Pods in the namespace — a mismatch means it can never
               find the Pods it already created and keeps creating
               orphans.

        Q5: What's the difference between a Secret and a ConfigMap in
            etcd, and why doesn't that make Secrets "safe"?
            A: Secrets are base64-ENCODED (not encrypted) in etcd by
               default vs ConfigMaps' plain text — base64 is trivially
               reversible, so Secrets should be treated as obscured, not
               safe from a cluster admin without real encryption-at-rest.

        Q6: Trace what happens when a client requests
            easypj.default.svc.cluster.local (26.4's DNS + virtual-IP
            model).
                DNS name ─▶ CoreDNS ─▶ Service ClusterIP ─▶ kube-proxy DNAT ─▶ Pod IP
            A: CoreDNS resolves the name to the Service's ClusterIP;
               kube-proxy's iptables/IPVS rules DNAT that virtual IP to
               one of the Ready Pod IPs in the Service's Endpoints list —
               no client ever addresses a Pod IP directly.

        Q7: Why does a Pod already running with `envFrom` NOT see a
            ConfigMap/Secret update immediately?
            A: envFrom copies values into the Pod's environment at
               container start; only a volume-mounted ConfigMap/Secret
               refreshes live (~1 min sync) — envFrom needs a rollout
               restart to pick up new values.

        Q8: What does `kubectl get endpoints easypj` returning empty
            actually mean, and what's the usual cause?
            A: The Service's selector matched zero Pods — usually a
               label typo between the Service's `selector` and the
               Deployment's Pod template `labels`.

        Q9: What object actually keeps a deleted Pod "coming back" under
            a Deployment, and why does a bare Pod not do this?
            A: The ReplicaSet, which the Deployment creates and owns — it
               continuously reconciles "Pods running" against "replicas:
               desired." A bare Pod has no controller watching it, so
               deleting it leaves the seat empty.

        Q10: In order, what are the 4 deployment steps 26.6 runs, and why
             does that order matter?
             A: (1) create namespace, (2) apply ConfigMap + Secret, (3)
                apply Deployment + Service, (4) verify with `get pods,svc`
                + port-forward — config/secret must exist before the
                Deployment's envFrom can reference them, and Pods must be
                Running before port-forward is meaningful.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 26
        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ namespace → ConfigMap+Secret → Deployment+Service →            │
        │  (26.6)        (26.5)             (26.3+26.4)                  │
        │                                        │                       │
        │                                        ▼                       │
        │                      kubectl get pods,svc → ✅                 │
        │                      port-forward → curl /jobs/ 200            │
        └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        .vs-prose — Chapter 26 turns Chapter 25's abstract noun map into
        4 real YAML files applied in a fixed order: namespace first so
        nothing collides, ConfigMap/Secret next so envFrom has something
        to read, Deployment+Service last so Pods start already knowing
        their settings and immediately have a stable address.
        Verification never trusts "applied without error" — it checks
        `get pods` for Running, `get endpoints` for a non-empty list, and
        a real curl response, because a Service or ConfigMap can silently
        exist while doing nothing.


Chapter 27: Kubernetes Deployment Strategies
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: easypj is now running in K8s — but "running"
    and "safely changeable" are different problems. This chapter covers
    what happens the SECOND time you deploy: shipping v2 without downtime,
    undoing a bad release in seconds, proving a Pod is actually healthy
    before it takes traffic, and keeping dev/staging/prod from sharing one
    fragile YAML. Problem solved here: "the first deploy worked — now how
    do I change anything without breaking production?"

    [A] META: Difficulty 🔴 Advanced | Time ~60-75 min | Beyond DCA scope —
        production Kubernetes operations; this is where the DCA→CKA
        bridge gets closest to real on-call work.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — by the end of Chapter 27 you can:
        - Predict Pod counts of each version at every step of a rolling
          update from maxSurge/maxUnavailable alone (27.1)
        - Undo a bad release with `kubectl rollout undo`, to a specific
          past revision if needed (27.2)
        - Distinguish readinessProbe (Service membership) from
          livenessProbe (Pod restart) and their different consequences (27.3)
        - Run the SAME easypj manifests across dev/staging/prod using
          Namespaces + Kustomize overlays without copy-pasting YAML (27.4)
        - Predict a Pod's QoS class (Guaranteed/Burstable/BestEffort) from
          its requests/limits alone (27.5)
        - Set a namespace-wide ResourceQuota so one team can't starve
          another (27.5)

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: Not a graded DCA domain — rolling updates, probes,
        and QoS are Kubernetes operational concerns entirely outside the
        Docker Certified Associate blueprint; treat this chapter as
        CKA-track depth.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 27.1 rolling updates → 27.2 rollback → 27.3 health
        probes → 27.4 dev/staging/prod (Namespaces + Kustomize) → 27.5
        resource management/QoS.

    27.1 Rolling Updates — Zero Downtime
         - kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=ghcr.io/username/easypj:v2.0
         - kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj
         - How rolling update works: one pod at a time
         - maxSurge and maxUnavailable

         [ROLLING UPDATE VISUALIZED — 5 Pods, Zero Downtime]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                 🔄 ROLLING UPDATE — Step by Step                           │
         │                                                                          │
         │  BEFORE (v1):  ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  5 pods running easypj:v1      │
         │                │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│                                  │
         │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
         │                                                                          │
         │  STEP 1:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  New v2 pod created        │
         │  (maxSurge=1)  │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│  (6 pods total)            │
         │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                             │
         │                                                                          │
         │  STEP 2:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  One v1 terminated             │
         │  (maxUnavail=1)│v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│  (5 pods total)                │
         │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
         │                                                                          │
         │  STEP 3:       ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  New v2 pod (#2)           │
         │                │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v1│ │v2│ │v2│                             │
         │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                             │
         │                                                                          │
         │  ...continues one-by-one until...                                         │
         │                                                                          │
         │  AFTER (v2):   ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐ ┌──┐  All 5 pods running v2!        │
         │                │v2│ │v2│ │v2│ │v2│ │v2│  ZERO DOWNTIME ✅               │
         │                └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘ └──┘                                  │
         │                                                                          │
         │  KEY CONFIG:                                                              │
         │  spec:                                                                    │
         │    strategy:                                                              │
         │      type: RollingUpdate                                                 │
         │      rollingUpdate:                                                       │
         │        maxSurge: 1       # Extra pods allowed during update               │
         │        maxUnavailable: 1 # Pods that can be unavailable during update     │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Predict, from maxSurge/maxUnavailable alone, exactly how
            many Pods of each version exist at every step of the diagram.
         [TECH] `kubectl set image` changes the Pod template inside the
            Deployment; the ReplicaSet controller then creates a NEW
            ReplicaSet (v2) and shrinks the OLD one (v1) in lockstep,
            bounded by maxSurge (extra Pods allowed above replicas) and
            maxUnavailable (Pods allowed missing below replicas).
         [ANALOGY] The step-by-step diagram above is a relay handoff: with
            maxSurge=1 a 6th runner (v2) joins the track BEFORE the 1st
            (v1) steps off — never fewer than 5 runners moving, per
            maxUnavailable=1.
         🔬 easypj: `kubectl set image deployment/easypj
            django=ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0` starts the exact sequence in
            the diagram — 5 Pods stay 5 Pods, never dropping below 4
            Ready with the defaults shown.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run `kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj`
            right after the set image command. Verify: it blocks and
            prints progress until "successfully rolled out" — Ctrl+C
            only stops your terminal's VIEW, not the rollout itself.
         📊 SUMMARY: RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually, bounded by
            maxSurge (over-capacity) and maxUnavailable (under-capacity).
            ⚠️ Gotcha: rolling update is USELESS against a bad image that
            passes startup but fails at runtime under load — pair it with
            27.3's readiness probes or it ships broken Pods as "healthy".

    27.2 Rollback — Undoing a Bad Deploy
         - kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj
         - kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj
         - kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj --to-revision=2
         [TERMINAL: Rollback workflow]

         🎯 GOAL: Undo a bad release in one command, to a specific past
            revision if the immediate-previous one is also broken.
         [TERMINAL: rollback workflow — drawn]
            $ kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj
            #  REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
            #  1         initial v1.0
            #  2         v2.0 (bad)
            $ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj
            $ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj --to-revision=1
         [TECH] Each `kubectl apply`/`set image` that changes the Pod
            template creates a NEW ReplicaSet revision; K8s keeps the
            last N (default 10, via `revisionHistoryLimit`) around so
            undo can re-point the Deployment at an old ReplicaSet.
         [ANALOGY] The same relay from 27.1, run in reverse: `rollout
            undo` reuses the SAME rolling-update machinery, just swapping
            which ReplicaSet scales up and which scales down.
         🔬 easypj: v2.0 shipped a migration that broke `/jobs/` with a
            500 — `kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj` restores v1.0
            Pods with zero downtime, same mechanism as the original deploy.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: deploy a deliberately broken tag, confirm
            `kubectl rollout status` reports failure, then undo it.
            Verify: `kubectl rollout history` still shows both revisions —
            undo adds a new revision, it does not delete history.
         [DIAGRAM:state — easypj: the active pointer moves; ReplicaSets never die]
         ┌───────────────────┐            apply v2.0            ┌───────────────────┐
         │RS rev.1 (v1.0)    │                                  │RS rev.2 (v2.0)    │
         │scale: 3           │─────────────────────────────────▶│scale: 3           │
         │● ACTIVE           │                                  │● ACTIVE (bad)     │
         └───────────────────┘                                  └───────────────────┘
         ┌───────────────────┐           rollout undo           ┌───────────────────┐
         │RS rev.2 (v2.0)    │                                  │RS rev.1 (v1.0)    │
         │scale: 0           │─────────────────────────────────▶│scale: 3           │
         │  idle, kept       │                                  │● ACTIVE again     │
         └───────────────────┘                                  └───────────────────┘
         💡 Neither apply nor undo ever DELETES a ReplicaSet — they only
            edit each one's scale between 0 and the desired count. Undo is
            instant because rev.1's Pod spec was already sitting at scale 0,
            needing no image pull, just a scale-up.

         📊 SUMMARY: rollout history + rollout undo turn a bad release
            into a one-line fix, using the same engine as a forward deploy.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `revisionHistoryLimit` can prune old ReplicaSets —
            you cannot undo to a revision K8s already garbage-collected.

    27.3 Health Checks — Liveness & Readiness Probes
         - Readiness probe: Is the app ready to serve traffic?
         - Liveness probe: Is the app still healthy?
         - Django health check endpoint
         - Probe types: httpGet, tcpSocket, exec
         [CODE: Deployment with liveness and readiness probes]

         🎯 GOAL: Stop K8s from sending traffic to a Pod that is up but
            not READY, and from keeping a Pod alive that is up but stuck.
         [CODE: probes added to 26.3's container spec — drawn]
            containers:
            - name: django
              image: ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0
              readinessProbe:
                httpGet: {path: /healthz/, port: 8000}
                initialDelaySeconds: 5
                periodSeconds: 10
              livenessProbe:
                httpGet: {path: /healthz/, port: 8000}
                initialDelaySeconds: 15
                periodSeconds: 20
         [TECH] readinessProbe controls Service membership — a failing
            readiness check removes the Pod's IP from the Service's
            endpoint list (traffic stops) WITHOUT restarting it.
            livenessProbe controls the Pod's own lifecycle — a failing
            liveness check gets the container KILLED and restarted.
         [ANALOGY] Readiness is a "back of house, not seated yet" sign —
            the front desk stops sending guests, staff keeps working.
            Liveness is a "this employee is unresponsive" alarm — pull
            them out and bring in a replacement.
         🔬 easypj: `GET /healthz/` is a tiny Django view checking DB
            connectivity — during a slow migration it fails readiness
            (correctly hides the Pod) without triggering any restart.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: temporarily make `/healthz/` return 500,
            apply, then `kubectl get endpoints easypj`. Verify: the Pod's
            IP disappears from endpoints while `kubectl get pods` still
            shows it Running — readiness failed, liveness didn't.
         📊 SUMMARY: readinessProbe = "can it serve traffic right now?";
            livenessProbe = "is it stuck and needs a restart?" — different
            questions, different consequences.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: identical liveness and readiness thresholds can
            cause restart storms — a slow-but-recovering Pod gets killed
            by liveness before readiness would have simply hidden it.

    27.4 Environment-Specific Deployments
         - Namespace isolation: dev, staging, prod
         - kubectl create namespace staging
         - kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -n staging
         - Kustomize overlays for env differences
         [CODE: Kustomize structure for dev/staging/prod]

         🎯 GOAL: Run the SAME easypj manifests in dev, staging and prod
            without maintaining three copy-pasted YAML sets.
         [CODE: namespace + Kustomize overlay skeleton — drawn]
            $ kubectl create namespace staging
            $ kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml -n staging
            # kustomize/base/     deployment.yaml, service.yaml,
            #                     kustomization.yaml
            # kustomize/overlays/staging/  kustomization.yaml, patch.yaml
            # kustomize/overlays/prod/     kustomization.yaml, patch.yaml
            $ kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/staging
         [TECH] A Namespace scopes NAMES (two `easypj` Deployments in
            different namespaces never collide); Kustomize scopes FILES —
            a base manifest plus small per-environment patches (replica
            count, resource limits, image tag) merged at apply time.
         [ANALOGY] Namespaces are separate apartments in the same
            building — same address format, no shared furniture.
            Kustomize overlays are one blueprint with sticky notes per
            apartment ("prod: add 2 bedrooms") instead of redrawing the
            whole plan three times.
         🔬 easypj: base/ ships replicas: 1 and DEBUG=True; overlays/prod
            patches replicas: 5 and DEBUG=False — one Deployment source,
            two real behaviors.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: create staging and prod namespaces, then
            `kubectl apply -k` each overlay. Verify: `kubectl get deploy
            -A` shows easypj in BOTH namespaces with DIFFERENT replicas.
         📊 SUMMARY: Namespace = isolation boundary; Kustomize = one base
            + per-env patches, no copy-paste drift between environments.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Namespaces do NOT isolate node resources or network
            by default — that needs ResourceQuota (27.5) and
            NetworkPolicy [KUBERNETES GUIDE].

    27.5 Resource Management in K8s
         - Requests: minimum guaranteed (scheduler uses this)
         - Limits: maximum allowed
         - QoS Classes: Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort
         - ResourceQuota: namespace-level limits
         [CODE: Deployment with resource requests/limits]

         🎯 GOAL: Predict which QoS class a Pod gets from its
            requests/limits alone, and set a namespace-wide guardrail.
         [TABLE: requests vs limits → QoS class]
            requests == limits (both set)     | Guaranteed (evicted last)
            requests < limits (both set)      | Burstable  (evicted 2nd)
            no requests, no limits set at all | BestEffort (evicted first)
         [CODE: ResourceQuota for a namespace — drawn]
            apiVersion: v1
            kind: ResourceQuota
            metadata: {name: easypj-quota, namespace: easypj}
            spec:
              hard: {requests.cpu: "2", requests.memory: 2Gi,
                     limits.cpu: "4", limits.memory: 4Gi}
         [TECH] The scheduler places Pods using requests (guaranteed
            capacity, never oversold); the kubelet enforces limits (hard
            ceiling — CPU throttled, memory over-limit gets the container
            OOMKilled). ResourceQuota caps the SUM across every Pod in a
            namespace, so one team cannot starve another.
         [ANALOGY] requests are a reserved hotel room (always yours);
            limits are the room's maximum occupancy (fire code); a
            ResourceQuota is the whole floor's total occupancy cap shared
            across every room on it.
         🔬 easypj: setting requests==limits on the django container (as
            in 26.3) makes it Guaranteed — the LAST Pod evicted if the
            node runs low, exactly what you want for the web tier.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: apply the ResourceQuota above, then try to
            scale easypj past what it allows. Verify: `kubectl describe
            resourcequota easypj-quota` shows used vs hard, and the
            over-quota Pods sit Pending with a quota-exceeded event.
         📊 SUMMARY: requests reserve, limits cap, QoS class decides
            eviction order, ResourceQuota caps the whole namespace.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a Pod with NO requests/limits (BestEffort) is the
            FIRST killed under node pressure — silence here is not
            safety, it's the worst QoS class by default.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how `resources:` is actually enforced (cgroups):
        A Pod's resources: block isn't a Kubernetes-only concept — the
        kubelet translates it straight into Linux cgroups on the node.
        `limits.cpu` becomes a CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) quota: the
        container gets THROTTLED (paused, not killed) once it exceeds its
        slice in a period — this is why a CPU-limited Pod gets sluggish
        under load instead of dying. `limits.memory` becomes a cgroup
        memory hard cap enforced by the kernel itself: exceed it and the
        kernel's OOM killer ends the container's process immediately —
        the literal mechanism behind "OOMKilled" in `kubectl describe pod`.

        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ Deployment YAML: resources.limits {cpu: 500m, memory: 256Mi}    │
        │            │ kubelet translates on Pod start                   │
        │            ▼                                                   │
        │      Linux cgroup for this container                           │
        │      ├─ cpu quota   → throttle at 500m (no kill)                │
        │      └─ memory cap  → hard limit at 256Mi (OOM kill)            │
        └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        This is also why QoS classes (27.5) matter under real pressure:
        the kubelet's node-level eviction manager reads these SAME cgroup
        numbers to decide who gets killed first when a node runs low on
        memory — BestEffort Pods (no requests/limits at all) have the
        weakest cgroup protection and are evicted before Burstable or
        Guaranteed Pods.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS:
        - RollingUpdate replaces Pods gradually, bounded by maxSurge
          (extra Pods above replicas) and maxUnavailable (Pods allowed
          missing below replicas).
        - Rolling update alone doesn't catch runtime failures under load
          — pair it with readiness probes or it ships broken Pods as
          "healthy".
        - Every image/template change creates a new ReplicaSet revision;
          rollout undo re-points the Deployment at an old one (kept up to
          revisionHistoryLimit).
        - readinessProbe controls Service endpoint membership (no
          restart); livenessProbe controls the Pod's own lifecycle (kills
          + restarts).
        - Identical liveness/readiness thresholds risk restart storms — a
          slow-but-recovering Pod can get killed by liveness before
          readiness would've simply hidden it.
        - Namespace = isolation boundary for names; Kustomize overlays =
          one base manifest + per-environment patches, avoiding
          copy-paste drift.
        - requests reserve scheduler capacity, limits cap actual usage via
          cgroups, QoS class decides node-pressure eviction order, and
          ResourceQuota caps the whole namespace's totals.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS:
        - Rolling update is useless against a bad image that passes
          startup but fails under load — always pair with readiness
          probes.
        - `revisionHistoryLimit` can prune old ReplicaSets — you cannot
          undo to a revision K8s already garbage-collected.
        - Namespaces do NOT isolate node resources or network by default
          — that needs ResourceQuota and NetworkPolicy.
        - A Pod with no requests/limits (BestEffort) is the FIRST killed
          under node pressure — silence here is the worst QoS class, not
          safety.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS:
        - Run `kubectl rollout status` right after a `set image` — it
          blocks until success/failure instead of guessing from `get pods`.
        - Set requests==limits (Guaranteed QoS) on anything you can't
          afford to lose, instead of leaving resources unset.
        - Check `kubectl rollout history` before undoing twice — you
          might already be one revision away from the good one.

    🔑 COMMANDS:
        kubectl set image deployment/easypj django=ghcr.io/you/easypj:v2.0  # triggers a rolling update
        kubectl rollout status deployment/easypj                            # blocks until the rollout finishes or fails
        kubectl rollout history deployment/easypj                           # lists past revisions + change-cause
        kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj                              # reverts to the immediately-previous revision
        kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj --to-revision=1              # reverts to a specific older revision
        kubectl describe pod <pod>                                          # shows OOMKilled / probe failure events
        kubectl create namespace staging                                    # isolates an environment by name
        kubectl apply -k kustomize/overlays/prod                            # applies a base + environment-specific patch

    🧪 DRILL (8 min): Ship a deliberately broken image tag to easypj,
        watch `kubectl rollout status` report failure, then `kubectl
        rollout undo` it — time how long the undo takes and confirm
        `kubectl rollout history` still shows both revisions afterward.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 27):
        Q1: With replicas=5, maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=1, what's the MIN
            and MAX Pod count mid-rollout?
                5 replicas − 1 (maxUnavailable) = 4 min | 5 + 1 (maxSurge) = 6 max
            A: Minimum 4, maximum 6 — the 27.1 diagram never drops below 4
               or exceeds 6 Ready+terminating Pods during the rollout.

        Q2: Why doesn't a rolling update alone protect against a v2 image
            that starts fine but crashes under real traffic?
            A: RollingUpdate only checks that the container process
               started, not that it's actually healthy under load —
               pairing it with a readiness probe (27.3) is what keeps a
               broken Pod out of the Service's endpoints.

        Q3: Fill in the consequence of each probe failing:
            | Probe          | On failure                              |
            | readinessProbe | ?                                       |
            | livenessProbe  | ?                                       |
            A: readinessProbe failing → Pod's IP removed from the
               Service's endpoint list, no restart. livenessProbe failing
               → container killed and restarted.

        Q4: Why can identical liveness and readiness thresholds cause a
            "restart storm"?
            A: A slow-but-recovering Pod that would have simply been
               hidden by a failing readiness check instead gets killed by
               liveness at the same threshold — restarting doesn't fix
               the underlying slowness, so it can repeat.

        Q5: What does `kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj
            --to-revision=1` actually do at the ReplicaSet level?
            A: It scales the rev.1 ReplicaSet back up to the desired
               replica count and scales the currently-active ReplicaSet
               down to 0 — neither ReplicaSet is deleted, only their
               scale changes, which is why undo is near-instant (no image
               pull needed).

        Q6: Why can't you always `rollout undo` to any past revision you
            remember shipping?
            A: `revisionHistoryLimit` (default 10) prunes old
               ReplicaSets — once a revision is garbage-collected, K8s
               has nothing left to scale back up.

        Q7: What's the difference between how a Namespace and a Kustomize
            overlay solve "run easypj in dev/staging/prod"?
            A: A Namespace scopes NAMES (two `easypj` Deployments in
               different namespaces never collide); Kustomize scopes
               FILES (one base manifest + small per-environment patches
               for things like replica count or image tag) — they solve
               different problems and are normally used together.

        Q8: Using the requests-vs-limits table from 27.5, what QoS class
            does a Pod with requests==limits get, and why does that
            matter operationally?
            | requests vs limits  | QoS class  | eviction order |
            | requests == limits  | Guaranteed | last            |
            | requests < limits   | Burstable  | 2nd             |
            | none set            | BestEffort | first           |
            A: Guaranteed — it's evicted LAST under node memory pressure,
               because the kubelet's eviction manager reads the same
               cgroup limits that make Guaranteed Pods the safest to run.

        Q9: What does a namespace-level ResourceQuota actually cap, and
            what happens to a Pod that would exceed it?
            A: It caps the SUM of requests/limits across every Pod in
               that namespace (e.g. total requests.cpu: "2"); a Pod that
               would push the namespace over quota sits Pending with a
               quota-exceeded event instead of being scheduled.

        Q10: Chain together what happens on a node running low on memory
             to a BestEffort Pod vs a Guaranteed Pod.
             A: The kubelet's eviction manager checks QoS class first:
                BestEffort Pods (no requests/limits, weakest cgroup
                protection) are evicted FIRST, Burstable next, Guaranteed
                Pods LAST — the direct operational consequence of the QoS
                table in 27.5.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY — Chapter 27
        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ ship v2 → RollingUpdate (maxSurge/maxUnavail) → probes          │
        │                  │                                 │           │
        │            bad? rollout undo              readiness/liveness   │
        │                  │                                 │           │
        │                  ▼                                 ▼           │
        │         old ReplicaSet scaled up          Service traffic /    │
        │         (instant, no rebuild)              Pod restart gated   │
        │                                                                 │
        │  + Namespace/Kustomize (envs)  + requests/limits/QoS/Quota      │
        └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        .vs-prose — Chapter 27 is the "safely changeable" half of running
        easypj on Kubernetes: rolling updates and rollback handle WHEN
        code changes, readiness/liveness probes handle WHETHER a Pod is
        trusted with traffic or life at all, Namespaces/Kustomize handle
        WHERE (which environment) a manifest applies, and requests/
        limits/QoS/ResourceQuota handle HOW MUCH of the cluster any one
        Pod or namespace is allowed to consume. None of these are Docker
        concepts — they only exist because a cluster, unlike one host,
        has to make these decisions on your behalf.

    [F] PART 9 KEY TAKEAWAYS:
        - The SAME easypj OCI image built in Part 3 runs unmodified on
          Kubernetes — Part 9 changes who schedules/heals/scales it,
          never the image itself.
        - Every Docker noun has a Kubernetes equivalent, but not 1:1:
          "Docker Compose" alone splits into Deployment + Service +
          ConfigMap + Secret + PVC.
        - Deploying for real means 4 gates first (cluster reachable,
          right context, registry access, image pushed), then namespace
          → config/secret → deployment/service, in that order.
        - Kubernetes' scheduling unit is the Pod, managed via a
          Deployment's ReplicaSet — never a bare Pod you create and
          forget.
        - Shipping a change safely needs 3 layers working together:
          rolling update (gradual replacement), readiness/liveness
          probes (traffic/lifecycle gating), and rollback (a one-command
          undo).
        - Namespaces + Kustomize overlays let dev/staging/prod share one
          manifest source instead of drifting copies.
        - requests/limits/QoS/ResourceQuota are what stop one Pod — or
          one team — from starving everyone else on a shared cluster.

    ⚠️ PART 9 GOTCHAS:
        - kompose convert and any auto-generated manifest is a first
          draft only — no real replica counts, no resource limits, no
          health probes.
        - `kubectl apply` never builds or pushes an image —
          ImagePullBackOff always traces back to a tag that was never
          pushed or a private registry with no imagePullSecret.
        - Rolling updates and Namespaces both LOOK like complete safety
          nets but aren't alone — rolling update needs readiness probes,
          Namespaces need ResourceQuota/NetworkPolicy for real isolation.

    ⚡ PART 9 SPEED TIPS:
        - Anchor every new K8s concept to its Chapter 25 Docker
          equivalent first — the vocabulary swap is most of the learning
          curve.
        - When anything seems "broken" in Kubernetes, check
          labels/selectors and namespace scoping before assuming the
          cluster itself is at fault.
