    30.3 Essential Docker Commands for the Exam
         - All docker container, image, volume, network commands
         - docker system commands
         - docker service commands (Swarm)
         - docker stack commands
         - docker secret, config commands
         [COMMAND REFERENCE TABLE: 50+ exam-essential commands]

         🎯 GOAL: Recall command families by their NOUN and pick correct
            flags under time pressure.
         [TECH] The CLI is a grammar (Ch3): docker <noun> <verb> —
            container/image/volume/network/system/service/stack/secret/
            config/node/swarm. The exam exploits near-misses: ps vs
            ps -a, rm vs rmi, save vs export, prune scopes, logs vs
            service logs, inspect on EVERY noun.
         [ANALOGY] Conjugation tables for a language you already speak:
            you know the words; the exam checks the irregular verbs —
            asymmetries like stop (SIGTERM + grace) vs kill (SIGKILL now).
         ⚡ Drill set: docker system df | docker system prune -a |
            docker events --since 1h | docker service ps --no-trunc |
            docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}' <container>
         🔬 easypj: run every family once against the jobpost stack in
            one sitting — list, inspect, prune, stats — so each command
            has a remembered OUTPUT, not just a remembered name.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: from Appendix A, cover the example column and
            write the command for 20 random rows. Verify: ≥18/20 exact,
            flags included — exam questions quote flags verbatim.
         [TABLE: near-miss command pairs — the exam's favorite trap]
         | Verb/flag A | Verb/flag B         | The ONE difference               |
         | ps          | ps -a               | -a also lists STOPPED containers |
         | rm          | rmi                 | container vs image (diff. noun)  |
         | save        | export              | layers+history vs 1 flat layer   |
         | stop        | kill                | SIGTERM+grace vs SIGKILL now      |
         | image prune | image prune -a      | dangling only vs all unused       |
         | logs <ctr>  | service logs easypj | one task vs every task            |
         💡 `docker inspect <id>` breaks the noun-first grammar on purpose:
            given no noun, it auto-detects container vs image vs volume vs
            network by trying each type in turn — the one command tested
            without a matching noun/verb pair.

         📊 SUMMARY: noun-first recall + the classic near-miss pairs =
            most of the command points on the exam.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: prune scopes — docker image prune removes DANGLING
            only; add -a and it removes all UNUSED. The exam loves that
            one word.

    30.4 Dockerfile Writing for the Exam
         - Every instruction you must know
         - Multi-stage builds
         - Best practices that exam graders look for
         [DOCKERFILE TEMPLATE with exam annotations]

         🎯 GOAL: Answer any Dockerfile-instruction question by pointing
            at the layer it creates and the moment it executes.
         [TECH] The exam's Dockerfile axis is build-time vs run-time
            (Ch4): RUN executes at BUILD, CMD/ENTRYPOINT at START; COPY
            vs ADD (ADD = COPY + URL + auto-untar — prefer COPY); EXPOSE
            documents, -p publishes; ARG dies when the build ends, ENV
            persists; exec form vs shell form decides who receives
            SIGTERM. Multi-stage: COPY --from=builder carries artifacts,
            dev toolchains never ship.
         [ANALOGY] A recipe's prep column vs serve column: RUN chops
            (baked into layers); CMD plates the dish when a guest
            (container start) arrives. Multi-stage = prep kitchen and
            serving counter in separate rooms.
         💡 The six ENTRYPOINT/CMD combinations (Ch4's table) ARE an exam
            question — rebuild that table from memory the week before.
         🔬 easypj: the Ch9 production Dockerfile contains every examable
            instruction — recite it line by line and give the WHY of each
            (cache order, non-root USER, exec-form CMD).
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: write a two-stage Python Dockerfile on paper
            in 5 minutes: builder installs into a venv, runtime copies
            it, non-root, exec-form gunicorn. Verify: against Appendix
            D.1 — every deviation is a study item.
         📊 SUMMARY: build vs run time, COPY vs ADD, ENTRYPOINT×CMD, and
            multi-stage mechanics cover nearly all Dockerfile questions.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: "EXPOSE opens the port" is the most common WRONG
            answer on the exam — EXPOSE alone publishes nothing.

    30.5 Docker Compose for the Exam
         - compose.yaml structure
         - Service configuration
         - Networks and volumes in Compose
         - docker compose commands
         [COMPOSE TEMPLATE with exam annotations]

         🎯 GOAL: Answer Compose questions from the file's shape: which
            top-level key, which service key, what default.
         [TECH] compose.yaml = four top-level key groups: services,
            networks, volumes, configs/secrets. Exam picks: named volume
            vs bind mount syntax (short vs long form), depends_on ≠
            "wait until ready", the default per-project user-defined
            bridge (DNS by service name), ports "8000:8000" vs expose,
            override/profiles precedence (Ch12).
         [ANALOGY] The file is an org chart, not a script: services are
            departments, networks the hallways, volumes the archive
            room — questions ask who CONNECTS to whom, not what runs
            first.
         🔬 easypj: the Ch11 full-stack compose file is your flashcard:
            django, postgres (PostgreSQL, as always), redis, nginx —
            every examable key appears in it at least once.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: from memory, write the minimal compose.yaml
            for django + postgres with a named volume and a healthcheck-
            gated depends_on. Verify: docker compose config accepts it —
            it validates without starting anything.
         📊 SUMMARY: know the four top-level keys, the two mount syntax
            forms, and what depends_on does NOT promise.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the exam still shows version: "3.8" headers —
            legacy in modern Compose but valid on the test; don't let it
            rattle you.

    30.6 Docker Swarm for the Exam
         - Swarm initialization and node management
         - Service deployment and scaling
         - Rolling updates and rollbacks
         - Secrets and configs in Swarm
         [SWARM COMMAND REFERENCE TABLE]

         🎯 GOAL: Hit the exam's heaviest domain (Orchestration, 25%)
            with total command of the Swarm lifecycle.
         [TECH] The examable loop: swarm init/join (+ tokens) → node
            ls/update (drain, labels) → service create (replicas,
            publish, secrets, constraints) → scale → update (28.8 flags)
            → rollback (28.9) → stack deploy. Plus the theory spine:
            quorum math (28.7), routing mesh vs host-mode publishing,
            secrets' tmpfs delivery (28.6).
         [ANALOGY] This is the exam's parallel-park: a fixed maneuver
            sequence, practiced until it needs no thought — because a
            quarter of the marks sit on it.
         ⚡ The five most-asked: quorum for N managers, drain a node,
            rotate a join token, publish mode ingress vs host, roll back
            a failed update.
         🔬 easypj: run the ENTIRE loop once on your 3-node lab swarm
            with the jobpost stack — init to rollback in one sitting is
            the single highest-value hour of DCA preparation.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: time that full loop. Verify: under 15 minutes
            without notes, and each command's OUTPUT (not just the
            command) feels familiar when the exam screenshots it.
         📊 SUMMARY: one practiced lifecycle covers a quarter of the
            exam; 28.7-28.10 are the difference between pass and
            near-miss.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: docker service scale easypj=5 and docker service
            update --replicas 5 easypj are BOTH correct — the exam may
            list both; read for "select ALL that apply".

    30.7 Exam Strategy & Tips
         - Time management: 90 minutes, 55 questions
         - Question types: multiple choice, discrete option multiple choice
         - Hands-on vs theory balance
         - Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
         - Recommended practice resources
         [EXAM STRATEGY: 10 tips for success]

         🎯 GOAL: Convert knowledge into points: pacing, flagging, and
            elimination tuned to the DCA's format.
         [TECH] 90 min / 55 Qs = 98s each. Three-pass method: pass 1
            answers everything answerable in <60s and FLAGS the rest
            (~70 min); pass 2 revisits flags (~15 min); pass 3 is a
            sanity sweep (~5 min). Discrete-option MCs: judge each option
            as its own true/false — half-knowledge still harvests points.
            No penalty for wrong answers: never leave blanks.
         [ANALOGY] A buffet with a countdown: sweep the room once taking
            everything easy, THEN queue for the carved roast (the hard,
            flagged questions) — starting with the roast starves you.
         💡 Elimination heuristics that work on the DCA: absolute words
            ("always", "only") are usually wrong; an option naming a
            nonexistent flag is instantly false — your Appendix A drills
            make fakes glow.
         🔬 easypj: translate abstract questions into jobpost concrete:
            "a service's tasks won't schedule" → your 28.10 Pending-
            constraint lab. Recalling the LAB beats recalling the doc.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: one full Appendix H mock, strict 90-minute
            timer, three-pass method. Verify: ≥75% AND fewer than 8 flags
            left after pass 1 — both numbers matter (accuracy AND pace).
         📊 SUMMARY: pace to 98s, three passes, judge options
            independently, answer everything.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: burning 5 minutes on question 3 is how prepared
            candidates fail — the flag button is a skill; practice IT,
            not just content.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — How Discrete-Option Multiple Choice (DOMC) Is Scored
    A classic multiple-choice question has ONE correct option among
    several distractors — picking it earns full credit, picking any
    other earns zero. A DOMC question instead presents a stem with
    several OPTIONS, and each option is judged independently as true or
    false against the stem — functionally several true/false questions
    sharing one prompt. That independence is why "longest answer" or
    "eliminate two, guess between the rest" folklore fails here: an
    option's truth doesn't depend on how plausible the others look, and
    partial knowledge (getting 3 of 4 options right) still harvests
    partial credit rather than zero.

        ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │  CLASSIC MC                       DOMC                          │
        │  Stem: pick the ONE               Stem: judge EACH option       │
        │  correct answer                   true/false, independently      │
        │                                                                   │
        │  ○ Option A                       ☐ Option A   → True/False      │
        │  ○ Option B  (only 1 scored)      ☐ Option B   → True/False      │
        │  ● Option C  ← credit here        ☐ Option C   → True/False      │
        │  ○ Option D                       ☐ Option D   → True/False      │
        │                                    (each judged, each scored)    │
        └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    PROSE RECAP — treat every DOMC option as its own tiny true/false
    question: read it in isolation against the stem, decide, move on —
    don't compare options against each other the way classic multiple
    choice trains you to.

    🔑 COMMANDS
      docker ps -a --format '{{.Names}}: {{.Status}}'    # every container, at a glance
      docker system df                                     # disk usage by object type
      docker inspect <id> --format '{{.State.ExitCode}}'  # why did it die
      docker service ps <svc> --no-trunc                   # full task error text
      docker node ls --filter role=manager                 # quorum health check
      docker swarm join-token manager                       # reprint a join token
      docker service update --rollback <svc>                # manual rollback
      docker image prune -a                                 # reclaim all unused images

         ≥75% AND fewer than 8 flagged questions remaining after pass 1.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 30)

      Q1: You're at month 4 of hands-on Docker with a DCA slot open next
          week. Per 30.1, should you book it?
          A: Docker recommends 6-12 months hands-on; at month 4 the
          honest move is to run 30.1's readiness heuristic (rebuild
          easypj's stack — image, compose, swarm service, secured daemon
          — from empty, without notes) before spending the exam fee.
          Explain: there's no experience gate at registration, so the
          check has to be self-imposed (30.1).

      Q2: You have 20 study hours and self-scored weakness 1-5 per
          domain: Orchestration=2, Images=4, Install=3, Networking=4,
          Security=2, Storage=5. Which two domains get the most hours?
          A:
          | Domain        | Weight | Self-score (lower=weaker) | Priority |
          | Orchestration | 25%    | 2                          | Highest  |
          | Security      | 15%    | 2                          | High     |
          | Installation  | 15%    | 3                          | Medium   |
          | Images        | 20%    | 4                          | Lower    |
          | Networking    | 15%    | 4                          | Lower    |
          | Storage       | 10%    | 5                          | Lowest   |
          Orchestration and Security get the most hours.
          Explain: budget = weight × weakness, not weight alone (30.2).

      Q3: An exam question asks "which command removes an image?" with
          options `docker rm`, `docker rmi`, `docker image rm`, `docker
          container prune`. Which are correct?
          A: `docker rmi` and `docker image rm` (same operation,
          different noun spelling); `docker rm` removes a CONTAINER;
          `docker container prune` removes stopped containers, not images.
          Explain: exactly the near-miss noun trap 30.3 warns about
          (30.3).

      Q4: True or false — "EXPOSE 8000" makes port 8000 reachable from
          the host.
          A: False.
          Explain: EXPOSE is documentation/metadata only; only
          `-p`/`--publish` (or Compose `ports:`) actually maps a host
          port — the exam's most common wrong answer (30.4).

      Q5: `depends_on: [postgres]` is set on django. Does Compose wait
          for postgres to be READY before starting django?
          A: No — by default `depends_on` only waits for the container to
          START, not for the app inside it to be ready; that needs a
          healthcheck-gated `condition: service_healthy`.
          Explain: this exact gap is a favorite DCA trap on Compose
          questions (30.5).

      Q6: Draw the full Swarm command loop you should run in under 15
          minutes without notes.
          A:
             swarm init/join → node ls → service create (replicas,
             publish, secrets) → service scale → service update (28.8
             flags) → service ps → service update --rollback (28.9) →
             stack deploy
          Explain: this loop alone represents Orchestration's 25% —
          rehearsed until each command's OUTPUT, not just syntax, feels
          familiar (30.6).

      Q7: An exam question lists both `docker service scale easypj=5`
          and `docker service update --replicas 5 easypj` and says
          "select all that apply." What do you pick?
          A: Both — functionally identical.
          Explain: DOMC-style questions judge every option
          independently; both being true is valid, not a trick (30.6,
          this chapter's Under the Hood).

      Q8: With 90 minutes and 55 questions, describe the three-pass
          method in one line each.
          A: Pass 1 (~70 min): answer everything solvable under 60s, flag
          the rest. Pass 2 (~15 min): revisit flags. Pass 3 (~5 min): a
          sanity sweep confirming nothing was left blank.
          Explain: pacing to 98s/question only works if the flag button
          is used deliberately (30.7).

      Q9: What THREE things should be true the night before an
          online-proctored exam?
          A: (1) the vendor system check passed on the EXACT machine
          you'll use, (2) government ID matches registration exactly, (3)
          any second monitor is physically unplugged, not just off.
          Explain: logistics failures are free points lost before the
          exam even starts (30.8).

      Q10: Per the 30.9 gap table, which chapter covers Raft quorum math,
           and which covers Docker Content Trust?
           A: Raft quorum math → Chapter 28 (28.7); Docker Content Trust
           → Chapters 20 and 23.
           Explain: the 30.9 table exists because these are commonly
           missed despite being taught earlier — use it as a final audit,
           not a first read (30.9).

PART 11: ADVANCED PRACTICES & PRODUCTION MASTERY                           🔴
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

    THINK BEFORE PART 11:
      What runs where?    → sidecars (cadvisor, inference) ride ALONGSIDE
                            easypj, never inside its container.
      What talks to what? → metrics/logs flow OUT of easypj to Prometheus/
                            Loki; alerts flow BACK to a human, not a container.
      What breaks first?  → your assumption that "it works" — until a
                            dashboard, a postmortem, or a bill proves it.

    [PART 11 INTRO]
    Parts 1-10 got easypj built, tested, secured, and orchestrated — a
    Deployment that starts correctly, scales correctly, and rolls back
    correctly. Part 11 is what happens AFTER that Deployment has been
    live for six months: the difference between a stack that merely
    runs and one a team can actually operate. Four skills unlock, in
    dependency order — seeing a problem before a user reports it
    (Chapter 31), responding to one correctly under pressure (Chapter
    32), controlling what the whole stack costs to keep running
    (Chapter 33), and extending the same Docker mental model to the
    newest workload shape on the platform: local AI (Chapter 34).

    None of this is graded on the DCA exam. All of it is what separates
    "I passed a certification" from "I keep easypj alive in production."

    🧠 ANALOGY: Parts 1-10 taught you to build and fly the plane. Part 11
       is air-traffic control, the black-box recorder, the fuel budget,
       and the newest experimental engine bolted on for testing — none
       of it keeps the plane in the air by itself, but skip all four and
       the plane you built so carefully eventually falls out of the sky
       without warning, or bankrupts the airline keeping it flying.

    │                                                                          │

    │  (metrics, logs,      (triage, chaos drills,     (right-size, image      │
    │   alerts pipeline)     postmortems, runbooks)     cost, build, overhead) │
    │       │                                                                  │

    Read the map as a sentence: "you cannot RESPOND to an incident you

Chapter 31: Observability & Monitoring for easypj
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Every prior chapter answered "is easypj running?"
    with `docker ps` or `kubectl get pods`. Production asks harder questions:
    "is it FAST for real users right now?", "which container is about to
    fall over?", "what changed in the last hour?" — none of which a single
    terminal snapshot can answer at 2 AM. This chapter builds the metrics,
    logs and alerts pipeline that answers them automatically, on top of the
    stdout logging discipline Chapter 6 already forced onto every
    container. Problem solved here: "the site is slow and I have no idea
    why, or since when."

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced/Production · ⏱️ ~90-120 min · production/day-2 depth,
        beyond the graded DCA exam — nothing here is a tested competency,
        everything here is what a real on-call rotation assumes you know.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
        - Explain why `docker stats` cannot be the production monitoring
          story, and name the one container (cAdvisor) that fixes it.
        - Stand up a Prometheus + Grafana stack alongside easypj's
          existing Compose services with zero changes to django, postgres,
          redis, or nginx.
        - Read and write a basic PromQL rate() query against a real metric.
        - Choose the right log driver (json-file / gelf / fluentd) for a
          given shipping requirement, and explain why Chapter 6's stdout-only
          rule is the precondition every one of them depends on.
        - Name the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors,
          saturation) and map each one to a specific easypj/jobpost
          component.
        - Write a ratio-based Prometheus alert rule that survives both a
          traffic spike and a low-traffic outage.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: not graded. The DCA exam stops at running and
        orchestrating containers; it never tests what happens to them a
        week into production. Treat this chapter as the sequel your job
        will actually require once the exam is behind you.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 31.1 builds the metrics SOURCE (cAdvisor) → 31.2
        turns it into a queryable, visual STACK (Prometheus + Grafana) →
        31.3 does the same job for LOGS instead of metrics → 31.4 turns
        both into ALERTS a human actually needs to see.

    31.1 Beyond docker stats — Building a Metrics Pipeline
         - docker stats: live, single-host, single-snapshot, terminal-only
         - No history: close the terminal, the data is gone forever
         - cAdvisor (Container Advisor): Google's per-container metrics
           exporter — reads the SAME cgroup files 6.6's --memory/--cpus
           limits are enforced through, and re-exposes them as /metrics
         - Why this matters past ~10 containers or more than one host

         [DOCKER STATS vs THE METRICS PIPELINE]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │               📉 docker stats — THE ONE-HOST, ONE-SNAPSHOT VIEW          │
         │                                                                          │
         │ $ docker stats --no-stream        → live only, THIS host, THIS second    │
         │ past ~10 containers or >1 host    → no history, no alerts, no chart      │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │                   📊 THE PIPELINE THAT ACTUALLY SCALES                   │
         │                                                                          │
         │ 🐳 easypj-web  easypj-db  redis  nginx   (cgroup stats: CPU/mem/I/O)     │
         │       │ scraped via Docker API + /sys/fs/cgroup                          │
         │       ▼                                                                  │
         │ 📦 cAdvisor:8080/metrics → scraped/15s → 📊 Prometheus TSDB (history)    │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 💡 cAdvisor is the ONLY new piece — Prometheus pulls FROM it; no         │
         │    change to easypj, postgres, redis or nginx themselves.                │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Explain why `docker stats` cannot be the production
            monitoring story, and name the one container that fixes it.
         [TECH] docker stats streams the cgroup counters (6.6) straight to
            your terminal with zero retention — it is a `cat` of live
            state, not a database. cAdvisor reads the same cgroup files
            PLUS the Docker API, converts them into stable time series
            labeled by container name, and serves them as a scrapable
            HTTP endpoint (Prometheus's OpenMetrics text format).
         [ANALOGY] The PIPELINE diagram above: docker stats is looking
            through a single window at a single instant; cAdvisor bolts a
            security camera on that window so someone else (Prometheus)
            can record everything it ever showed.
         🔬 easypj: `docker run -d --name cadvisor -p 8080:8080 -v
            /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro -v /:/rootfs:ro -v
            /sys:/sys:ro gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:v0.49.1` starts watching
            easypj-web, easypj-db, redis and nginx with zero app changes.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the cadvisor command above, then browse
            http://localhost:8080/metrics. Verify: you can find a line
            matching `container_memory_usage_bytes{name="easypj-web"}` —
            that line is what Prometheus will scrape in 31.2.
         📊 SUMMARY: docker stats is a live look; cAdvisor + Prometheus is
            the recorded history that alerting and dashboards need.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: cAdvisor needs read access to the Docker socket and
            the host's /sys and /rootfs — treat that mount with the same
            care as 20.3's socket-mount warning; it sees every container.

    31.2 Prometheus + Grafana via Compose
         - Add prometheus, grafana and cadvisor as services alongside the
           django/postgres/redis/nginx stack from Chapter 10.4
         - prometheus.yml: static scrape_configs pointing at cadvisor and
           django's own /metrics (via django-prometheus)
         - Grafana: reads Prometheus as a data source, renders dashboards
         - A PromQL query and a described dashboard panel, end to end

         [COMPOSE STACK + MONITORING SIDE-CAR]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │            🎼 easypj compose.yaml + THE MONITORING SIDE-CAR              │
         │                                                                          │
         │ django:8000  postgres:5432  redis:6379  nginx:80   (Part 4 stack)        │
         │      │            │              │           │                          │
         │      └────────────┴──────────────┴───────────┘                          │
         │                    │ scraped by                                         │
         │                    ▼                                                    │
         │ 📦 cadvisor:8080 → 📊 prometheus:9090 → 📈 grafana:3000                  │
         │ (per-container      (scrapes cadvisor +   (queries prometheus,           │
         │  cgroup metrics)      django /metrics)      renders dashboards)          │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ Browser → localhost:3000 → Grafana dashboard → PromQL → Prometheus       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CODE: compose.yaml additions — monitoring services]
            services:
              # ...django, postgres, redis, nginx unchanged from 10.4...
              cadvisor:
                image: gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:v0.49.1
                ports: ["8080:8080"]
                volumes:
                  - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
                  - /sys:/sys:ro
                  - /var/lib/docker/:/var/lib/docker:ro
              prometheus:
                image: prom/prometheus:v2.53.0
                volumes: ["./prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro"]
                ports: ["9090:9090"]
                depends_on: [cadvisor]
              grafana:
                image: grafana/grafana:11.1.0
                ports: ["3000:3000"]
                environment: ["GF_SECURITY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=changeme"]
                depends_on: [prometheus]

         [CODE: prometheus.yml — scrape config]
            global:
              scrape_interval: 15s
            scrape_configs:
              - job_name: 'cadvisor'
                static_configs:
                  - targets: ['cadvisor:8080']
              - job_name: 'django'
                static_configs:
                  - targets: ['django:8000']
                metrics_path: /metrics

         🎯 GOAL: Stand up a working metrics + dashboard stack for easypj
            with three new services and no code changes to jobpost.
         [TECH] Compose's service-name DNS (10.4) is what makes this work:
            prometheus.yml says `targets: ['cadvisor:8080']`, not an IP,
            exactly like nginx.conf says `django:8000` in the diagram
            above. Grafana never touches cadvisor directly — it always
            queries Prometheus's stored time series via PromQL.
         [ANALOGY] The diagram's three new boxes are a security desk
            (cadvisor: watches every camera), an archive room (Prometheus:
            records everything the desk reports) and a viewing room
            (Grafana: draws charts from the archive on demand).
         💡 Sample PromQL query — CPU used by the easypj web container:
            `rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{name="easypj-web"}[5m])`
            reads as "average CPU-seconds/second consumed, last 5 minutes."
         💡 Sample dashboard panel: title "easypj Web — CPU & Memory";
            top graph = the PromQL query above (unit: cores, alert
            threshold line at 0.8); bottom graph =
            `container_memory_usage_bytes{name="easypj-web"} / (512*1024*1024)`
            as a percentage gauge, red above 90%.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: `docker compose up -d`, open localhost:3000,
            add Prometheus (http://prometheus:9090) as a data source, paste
            the CPU query into a new panel. Verify: the graph moves when
            you `ab -n 2000 -c 20 http://localhost/jobs/` against easypj.
         📊 SUMMARY: three Compose services turn cgroup numbers into a
            live, queryable, visual dashboard for the exact stack from
            Chapter 4.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: Grafana's default admin/changeme password is a demo
            convenience only — rotate it before this stack ever leaves
            your laptop, the same rule as 20.1's secrets discipline.

    31.3 Centralized Logging — the Loki/ELK Pattern
         - Chapter 2.7 covered log-driver basics (json-file, rotation); this
           section covers SHIPPING logs off the host: gelf and fluentd
         - json-file: local disk only, rotated, never leaves the container
         - gelf: UDP/TCP push to a Graylog-compatible endpoint (e.g. Loki
           via a gelf-to-Loki bridge, or Graylog directly)
         - fluentd: push to a Fluentd/Fluent Bit collector, which routes to
           Loki, Elasticsearch, S3, or all three at once
         - WHY stdout-only logging (Chapter 6's rule) is the precondition: a log
           driver captures a container's stdout/stderr stream — an app
           that writes to its OWN log file instead is invisible to ALL of
           this, driver swap or not

         [DIAGRAM:flow — gunicorn access logs → Loki, numbered ①-⑤]
            ① gunicorn logs access lines to STDOUT (Ch6's rule, not a file)
            ② Docker's log driver captures that stream (per-container)
            ③ driver=fluentd → ships each line to a Fluent Bit collector
            ④ Fluent Bit forwards to Loki, labeled {app="easypj",tier="web"}
            ⑤ Grafana (already in 31.2) queries Loki with LogQL, next to
               the metrics dashboard — logs and metrics, one screen

         [TABLE: log driver comparison — driver | where logs go | best for]
            json-file | local disk, rotated (2.7)   | dev, single host, default
            gelf      | UDP/TCP to Graylog/Loki      | quick push, low setup
            fluentd   | Fluentd/Fluent Bit collector | multi-destination routing
            awslogs   | AWS CloudWatch Logs directly  | ECS/EC2 on AWS
            local     | binary format, disk-capped    | replaces json-file, faster

         🎯 GOAL: Ship easypj's gunicorn access logs to Loki without
            touching a single line of jobpost's code.
         [TECH] The log driver is a daemon-level or per-container setting
            (--log-driver, or daemon.json from 2.7) that intercepts a
            container's stdout/stderr file descriptor — it never reads
            application files. Swapping json-file for fluentd in the
            FLOW diagram above changes step ② only; steps ①, gunicorn's
            own behavior, never move.
         [ANALOGY] Stdout is a single, fixed-position microphone gunicorn
            always talks into (2.7); the log driver is whichever recording
            device is plugged into that microphone today — cassette
            (json-file) or a live radio broadcast (fluentd/gelf). The
            microphone's position never changes, only the recorder.
         🔬 easypj: `docker run --log-driver=fluentd --log-opt
            fluentd-address=localhost:24224 --log-opt tag="easypj.web"
            easypj:v1` — gunicorn's `access_log` output starts arriving in
            Fluent Bit within one request, no gunicorn.conf.py change.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run a local Fluent Bit container listening on
            24224, then start easypj with the fluentd driver above and hit
            /jobs/. Verify: `docker logs easypj-web` now shows NOTHING (the
            driver took the stream) while Fluent Bit's own log shows the
            forwarded access line.
         📊 SUMMARY: json-file for local dev, gelf/fluentd to ship off-box
            — all three work ONLY because easypj logs to stdout (Ch6).
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `docker logs` reads from the LOCAL driver's storage;
            switch to fluentd/gelf and `docker logs` goes silent — that is
            expected, not broken; go read the shipped destination instead.

    31.4 Alerting on What Actually Matters for easypj
         - The four golden signals (Google SRE): latency, traffic, errors,
           saturation — the smallest metric set that catches most outages
         - Applied per tier: django (latency/errors), postgres (saturation:
           connections), redis (saturation: memory), nginx (traffic)
         - A concrete Prometheus alerting rule for /jobs/ error rate

         [TABLE: the four golden signals on the easypj/jobpost stack]
            Signal      | Metric                          | Source
            Latency     | p95 request duration on /jobs/  | django (nginx log)
            Traffic     | requests/sec to nginx            | nginx access log
            Errors      | 5xx rate on /jobs/                | django/nginx logs
            Saturation  | postgres active_connections /max | postgres_exporter
            Saturation  | redis used_memory / maxmemory    | redis_exporter

         [CODE: Prometheus alert rule — high error rate on /jobs/]
            groups:
              - name: easypj-alerts
                rules:
                  - alert: JobsEndpointHighErrorRate
                    expr: |
                      sum(rate(django_http_responses_total_by_status_total
                        {job="django",status=~"5..",view="jobs"}[5m]))
                      /
                      sum(rate(django_http_responses_total_by_status_total
                        {job="django",view="jobs"}[5m])) > 0.05
                    for: 2m
                    labels: {severity: page}
                    annotations:
                      summary: "easypj /jobs/ 5xx rate above 5% for 2m"

         🎯 GOAL: Turn the four golden signals into ONE alert that fires
            before users file a support ticket about /jobs/.
         [TECH] The rule expression divides the 5-minute rate of 5xx
            responses on the jobs view by ALL responses on that view — a
            RATIO, not a raw count, so it stays meaningful whether traffic
            is 10 req/s or 10,000. `for: 2m` requires the breach to persist
            (see the SIGNALS table's Errors row), filtering single blips.
         [ANALOGY] The four signals are a car's dashboard: speed (traffic),
            how hard the engine strains (saturation), the check-engine
            light (errors), and how long the trip is taking (latency) —
            watch only these four gauges and you catch nearly every real
            problem before it strands you.
         🔬 easypj: the SIGNALS table's saturation row is what predicts
            32.1's incident BEFORE it happens — active_connections
            climbing toward postgres's max_connections is the warning
            32.1's cascade ignored.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: load the alert rule into Prometheus, then send
            deliberate 500s (`curl -X POST localhost/jobs/999999/apply/`
            against a job ID that doesn't exist, repeated 20x). Verify: the
            Prometheus /alerts page shows JobsEndpointHighErrorRate move
            from Inactive → Pending → Firing over the 2-minute window.
         📊 SUMMARY: four signals, one metric each, cover latency, traffic,
            errors and saturation across the whole easypj stack.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: alerting on RAW counts instead of ratios pages you
            every traffic spike (Black Friday) and stays silent during a
            LOW-traffic outage (2 requests, both failing) — always ratio.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how `docker stats` and cAdvisor read the SAME data
    Both tools ultimately read the same kernel-maintained accounting
    files under the container's cgroup — `docker stats` calls the
    daemon's `/containers/{id}/stats` API endpoint, which is itself a
    JSON-formatted read of files like `memory.current` and `cpu.stat`
    (cgroup v2, or their v1 equivalents) — the exact files 6.6's
    --memory/--cpus limits are enforced through. cAdvisor does the
    identical read, on a timer, for every container on the host, then
    re-exposes the numbers as Prometheus's OpenMetrics text format
    instead of a one-shot JSON blob.

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ /sys/fs/cgroup/<container>/memory.current, cpu.stat, io.stat  │
         │        │                              │                       │
         │        ▼ (one-shot read)              ▼ (read every N sec)    │
         │  docker stats API call          cAdvisor → /metrics endpoint  │
         │  (dockerd, on demand)            (own process, on a timer)    │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    Neither tool invents new data — they read the SAME kernel accounting;
    the only difference is retention and re-exposure format.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS (Chapter 31)
       ✅ `docker stats` is a live, single-host, zero-retention view —
          use it for right-now debugging, never as a monitoring strategy.
       ✅ cAdvisor is the ONLY new container required to start collecting
          history; it reads the same cgroup data docker stats reads,
          just continuously.
       ✅ Prometheus PULLS metrics from targets on a scrape interval;
          Grafana never talks to cAdvisor directly, only to Prometheus's
          stored time series.
       ✅ Compose's service-name DNS is what lets prometheus.yml say
          `targets: ['cadvisor:8080']` instead of a hardcoded IP.
       ✅ Log shipping (gelf/fluentd) only works because every easypj
          container logs to stdout/stderr — an app writing its own log
          file is invisible to every driver.
       ✅ The four golden signals — latency, traffic, errors, saturation
          — cover nearly every real outage with one metric per tier.
       ✅ Alert on RATIOS, not raw counts, or you page on Black Friday
          traffic and stay silent during a low-traffic outage.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS (Chapter 31)
       - cAdvisor needs the Docker socket plus the host's /sys and
         /rootfs mounted read-only — treat that access like 20.3's
         socket-mount warning; it can see every container on the host.
       - Grafana's default admin/changeme password is a demo convenience,
         not a production credential — rotate it immediately (20.1).
       - Switching a container's log driver to fluentd/gelf makes
         `docker logs` go silent for that container — expected, not
         broken; the stream now goes to the shipped destination instead.
       - Raw-count alert thresholds miss low-traffic outages and mis-fire
         on legitimate traffic spikes — always alert on a ratio.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS (Chapter 31)
       - `docker stats --no-stream` for a single non-scrolling snapshot
         instead of Ctrl+C-ing a live stream mid-debug.
       - Keep Prometheus's `/alerts` page and Grafana's dashboard one
         bookmark apart — most incidents start with one and end in the
         other.
       - Grep a metric name straight off cAdvisor's raw `/metrics` page
         before writing PromQL — confirms exact label spelling (e.g.
         `name="easypj-web"`) instead of guessing.

    🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 31 cheat-card
       docker stats --no-stream                         # one-shot snapshot, no history
       docker run -d --name cadvisor -p 8080:8080 \
         -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro \
         -v /:/rootfs:ro -v /sys:/sys:ro \
         gcr.io/cadvisor/cadvisor:v0.49.1                 # start metrics collection
       curl localhost:8080/metrics | grep easypj-web      # confirm cAdvisor sees it
       docker compose up -d                               # bring up prometheus+grafana too
       docker logs easypj-web                              # only shows LOCAL drivers' data
       docker inspect --format '{{.HostConfig.LogConfig.Type}}' easypj-web  # which driver?

    cadvisor command from 31.1, bring up the Compose monitoring stack
    from 31.2, and paste ONE working PromQL query into a new Grafana
    panel — no notes. Stop the clock the moment the graph moves.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 31)

    Q1: Why can't `docker stats` be the production monitoring solution
        for easypj, even though the numbers it shows are correct?
        A: It is live-only and single-host — close the terminal or
        restart the daemon and the data is gone forever; past ~10
        containers or more than one host there is no history, no
        alerting, and no chart to look back at.
        Explanation: this is exactly the gap 31.1's DOCKER STATS vs THE
        METRICS PIPELINE diagram draws — a snapshot vs a recorded stream.

    Q2 (diagram): What is cAdvisor's actual job, and what does it NOT do?
        A: cAdvisor reads the same cgroup files (plus the Docker API)
        docker stats reads, and re-exposes them as a scrapable /metrics
        HTTP endpoint. It does NOT store history — Prometheus does that
        by scraping cAdvisor on an interval.
             ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
             │ cgroup files → cAdvisor:8080/metrics (no       │
             │ history kept) → scraped every 15s by →         │
             │ Prometheus TSDB (history lives HERE)            │
             └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        Explanation: confusing cAdvisor with a database is the most
        common misunderstanding of this section — it is a re-exposer,
        not a store.

    Q3: In prometheus.yml, why does `targets: ['cadvisor:8080']` work
        without an IP address?
        A: Compose's service-name DNS (10.4) resolves 'cadvisor' to the
        right container automatically — the same mechanism that lets
        nginx.conf say `django:8000`.

    Q4: What does `rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{name=
        "easypj-web"}[5m])` actually compute?
        A: The average CPU-seconds-per-second consumed by the
        easypj-web container over the trailing 5-minute window — a
        smoothed rate, not an instantaneous or cumulative value.

    Q5 (table): Match each log driver to its behavior.
        A:
           Driver     | Behavior
           json-file  | local disk, rotated, the default
           gelf       | UDP/TCP push to a Graylog/Loki-compatible endpoint
           fluentd    | push to a Fluentd/Fluent Bit collector, multi-destination
        Explanation: straight from 31.3's driver-comparison table — each
        row trades "how much setup" for "how far the logs travel."

    Q6: Why is Chapter 6's "log to stdout only" rule a hard
        PRECONDITION for every log driver in 31.3, not just a best
        practice?
        A: A log driver only ever captures a container's stdout/stderr
        file descriptor; an app that writes to its own log file bypasses
        that capture entirely — no driver swap fixes an app that never
        talks to stdout.

    Q7: A teammate switches easypj-web's log driver from json-file to
        fluentd, then reports "docker logs is broken, it shows nothing."
        What's actually happening?
        A: Nothing broken — expected behavior. `docker logs` only reads
        the LOCAL json-file driver's stored data; under fluentd the
        stream is shipped elsewhere. Check the shipped destination
        (Fluent Bit/Loki) instead.

    Q8 (table): List the four golden signals and their easypj-specific
        metric + source.
        A:
           Signal     | Metric                          | Source
           Latency    | p95 request duration on /jobs/   | django (nginx log)
           Traffic    | requests/sec to nginx             | nginx access log
           Errors     | 5xx rate on /jobs/                | django/nginx logs
           Saturation | postgres active_connections/max   | postgres_exporter
           Saturation | redis used_memory/maxmemory       | redis_exporter
        Explanation: one metric per tier is deliberate — the smallest
        set that still catches most real outages (Google SRE's model).

    Q9: Why does the JobsEndpointHighErrorRate rule divide 5xx responses
        by ALL responses instead of alerting on a raw 5xx count?
        A: A ratio stays meaningful regardless of traffic volume; a raw
        count either pages constantly on high-traffic days or stays
        silent during a low-traffic outage where only 2 requests fail
        but both are 5xx.

    Q10: What does `for: 2m` in the alert rule accomplish, and what
        would happen without it?
        A: It requires the error-rate breach to PERSIST for 2 minutes
        before firing, filtering single-request blips. Without it, one
        transient 500 could page someone for a problem that self-
        resolved before anyone even looked.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │        📊 CHAPTER 31 — FROM CGROUP FILE TO A HUMAN GETTING PAGED         │
         │                                                                          │
         │  🐳 easypj-web/db/redis/nginx cgroup stats                              │
         │        │ (31.1) cAdvisor scrapes + re-exposes                            │
         │        ▼                                                                 │
         │  📦 cAdvisor:8080/metrics ──▶ 📊 Prometheus TSDB ──▶ 📈 Grafana (31.2)  │
         │        │                                                                 │
         │        │ (31.3) gunicorn stdout ──▶ log driver ──▶ Loki/Graylog          │
         │        ▼                                                                 │
         │  🚨 (31.4) four golden signals ──▶ ratio-based alert ──▶ on-call paged  │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    .vs-prose — Chapter 31 turns two silent kernel data sources — cgroup
    counters and a stdout stream — into one connected pipeline: cAdvisor
    and Prometheus give that data history and a queryable shape, Grafana
    makes it visible, log drivers ship the text half of the same story
    off-box, and a ratio-based alert on the four golden signals is what
    finally turns all of it into a human being paged BEFORE a user
    complains, closing the loop this chapter opened.



Chapter 32: Incident Response & Production Postmortems
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Chapter 31 gave you eyes; this chapter gives
    you hands. An alert firing at 2 AM is worthless without a rehearsed
    sequence of commands, a way to practice failure BEFORE it is real, and
    a blameless process for making sure the same outage never repeats.
    Every tool used here — docker logs, docker inspect, kubectl describe,
    restart policies, ReplicaSets — was already taught; this chapter is
    the drill that makes reaching for them automatic under pressure.
    Problem solved here: "the alert fired — now what, exactly, do I type?"

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced/Production · ⏱️ ~90-120 min · production/day-2 depth,
        beyond the graded DCA exam — but built entirely from tools the
        DCA blueprint DOES test (docker logs/inspect, kubectl describe,
        restart policies, rollout undo).

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
        - Walk the correct first-responder triage sequence (docker
          logs → docker inspect → kubectl describe → kubectl rollout
          undo) unassisted, on a Pod you've never seen before.
        - Correctly identify exit code 137 + OOMKilled as the kernel's
          verdict, not a guess.
        - Explain the difference between what a restart policy (6.2) and
          a ReplicaSet (26.7) each self-heal, and design a safe chaos
          test that proves it.
        - Write a full Timeline / Impact / 5 Whys / Action Items
          postmortem that stays blameless end to end.
        - Turn a resolved incident into an on-call runbook a teammate can

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: not graded directly — but every tool this chapter
        drills (docker logs, docker inspect, kubectl describe, restart

        this chapter is the pressure-tested version of skills you
        already have.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 32.1 teaches the triage SEQUENCE on a real outage →
        32.2 rehearses failure ON PURPOSE before it's real → 32.3 turns a

        three into a runbook for the NEXT on-call.

    32.1 The Anatomy of a Container Outage
         - A realistic easypj incident: a bad deploy leaks memory, one
           OOMKilled Pod cascades into a full-stack outage
         - First-responder steps, in order, using tools already taught:
           docker logs → docker inspect → kubectl describe → kubectl
           rollout undo (27.2)
         - Reading exit code 137 + OOMKilled correctly (6.6, Appendix F.8)

         [ANATOMY OF AN OOMKilled CASCADE]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │        🔥 ANATOMY OF AN OOMKilled CASCADE — 00:00 TO 00:14               │
         │                                                                          │
         │ 00:00  deploy easypj:v47 (/jobs/search) — no --memory cap set            │
         │ 00:03  search view holds the full queryset in memory per request         │
         │ 00:06  gunicorn worker RSS climbs past the 512Mi node limit              │
         │ 00:07  kubelet OOMKills the worker → Pod restarts                        │
         │ 00:08  readiness probe fails mid-restart → Pod pulled from Service       │
         │ 00:09  remaining 2 Pods absorb 3x traffic → THEY hit the same wall       │
         │ 00:11  3/3 Pods cycling OOMKilled → easypj returns 503 to users          │
         │ 00:14  on-call rolls back to v46 (27.2) → Pods stabilize, 503s stop      │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 🔬 first response: docker logs → docker inspect (OOMKilled?) →           │
         │    kubectl describe pod (Events:) → kubectl rollout undo (27.2)          │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [TERMINAL: the first 90 seconds of triage]
            $ kubectl get pods -n easypj
            NAME              READY   STATUS             RESTARTS
            easypj-7f9-a1b2   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   6
            $ kubectl logs easypj-7f9-a1b2 -n easypj --previous
            MemoryError: unable to allocate 340MB for queryset
            $ kubectl describe pod easypj-7f9-a1b2 -n easypj | grep -A3 Last\ State
            Last State:  Terminated
              Reason:    OOMKilled
              Exit Code: 137
            $ kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj -n easypj

         🎯 GOAL: Reproduce this exact triage sequence, unassisted, in
            under two minutes on a Pod you have never seen before.
         [TECH] The command order is deliberate: `kubectl get pods`
            names the failure MODE (CrashLoopBackOff, RESTARTS count);
            `logs --previous` reads the DEAD container's own output
            (the live one has none yet); `describe` confirms the KERNEL's
            verdict (Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137, per Appendix F.8);
            `rollout undo` is the fastest safe mitigation once root cause
            is a bad deploy, not infrastructure.
         [ANALOGY] The TIMELINE diagram above is a car crash reconstruction:
            each timestamp is a skid mark. You do not redesign the road at
            00:07 — you clear the wreck (rollback) first, investigate
            second (32.3).
         🔬 easypj: the leak is real — an unpaginated `JobPost.objects.
            filter(...)` in the search view materializes every matching row
            before slicing; 26.3's requests/limits caught the SYMPTOM,
            they never fix the QUERY.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: deliberately deploy a view that builds a large
            list in memory, set `--memory 128m` (6.6), hit it with load.
            Verify: you can walk the TERMINAL sequence above from a cold
            start and name Exit Code: 137 as OOMKilled without looking it
            up — Appendix F.8 should already live in your head by now.
         📊 SUMMARY: get pods (mode) → logs --previous (evidence) →
            describe (kernel verdict) → rollout undo (mitigation) — same
            four steps regardless of which service failed.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `kubectl logs` WITHOUT --previous on a restarted Pod
            shows the NEW container's (empty) log, not the crash — the
            single most common wasted minute in a real incident.

    32.2 Chaos Engineering — Practicing Failure on Purpose
         - The idea: kill things ON PURPOSE, in a controlled window, so the
           FIRST time a container dies isn't during a real incident
         - What should happen automatically: restart policies (6.2) for
           standalone containers, ReplicaSet/Deployment self-healing
           (26.7, 28.4) for orchestrated ones
         - A minimal chaos script that kills a random target on an interval

         [THE CHAOS LOOP]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │         🌀 THE CHAOS LOOP — KILL ONE, WATCH THE SYSTEM ANSWER            │
         │                                                                          │
         │ pick a random easypj-web replica or Pod                                  │
         │      │                                                                   │
         │      ▼   docker kill <id>   OR   kubectl delete pod <name>               │
         │      │                                                                   │
         │      ▼   restart policy (6.2) / ReplicaSet (26.7) notices ONE gone       │
         │      │                                                                   │
         │      ▼   new container/Pod scheduled, readiness passes, traffic returns  │
         │      │                                                                   │
         │      ▼   measure: how many seconds was capacity below 100%?              │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 💡 if recovery takes >30s or users see errors, that gap — not the        │
         │    kill itself — is the incident chaos engineering just found for free.  │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CODE: chaos.sh — kill a random easypj Pod every 5 minutes]
            #!/usr/bin/env bash
            set -euo pipefail
            NAMESPACE="easypj"
            while true; do
              victim=$(kubectl get pods -n "$NAMESPACE" -l app=easypj \
                -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}' | tr ' ' '\n' | shuf -n1)
              echo "$(date -Iseconds)  killing pod: $victim"
              kubectl delete pod "$victim" -n "$NAMESPACE" --grace-period=0
              sleep 300
            done

         🎯 GOAL: Prove easypj's self-healing (6.2, 26.7) works BEFORE a
            real deploy tests it for the first time, at the worst moment.
         [TECH] Standalone `docker run --restart unless-stopped` (6.2)
            reacts to a killed CONTAINER; a Kubernetes ReplicaSet reacts
            to a missing POD by reconciling desired-vs-actual replica
            count (26.7) — the chaos script exploits exactly this by
            deleting one unit and timing how fast the controller notices.
         [ANALOGY] The CHAOS LOOP diagram above is a fire drill: you do
            not wait for a real fire to learn the exit route works — you
            trigger the alarm on purpose, on a Tuesday, and time it.
         🔬 easypj: with 3 replicas and readinessProbe from 27.3, killing
            one Pod should show traffic dip to ~67% capacity for a few
            seconds, then return to 100% — never a 503 to a real user.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run chaos.sh above against a 3-replica easypj
            Deployment while `watch kubectl get pods -n easypj` runs in a
            second terminal. Verify: RESTARTS climbs, READY never drops to
            0/3 across all Pods simultaneously, and `curl` against the
            Service never returns anything but 200 during the test.
         📊 SUMMARY: deliberately kill one unit, measure the gap, fix
            whatever the gap reveals — self-healing you have never tested
            is a theory, not a guarantee.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: never point chaos.sh at a namespace with 1 replica —
            you are not testing resilience, you are just causing an outage.

    32.3 Writing a Blameless Postmortem
         - Standard format: Timeline, Impact, Root Cause (5 Whys), Action
           Items — same shape regardless of company or tool
         - "Blameless" means the document names FAILURES OF THE SYSTEM
           (missing memory limit, no query review) never a person
         - Applied end-to-end to the 32.1 OOMKilled scenario

         [CODE: postmortem-2026-07-02-jobs-search-oom.md]
            # Postmortem: /jobs/search 503 outage

            ## Timeline (UTC)
            00:00  easypj:v47 deployed (new /jobs/search endpoint)
            00:07  first Pod OOMKilled (see 32.1 diagram for full timeline)
            00:11  full outage — 3/3 Pods cycling, 503s served
            00:14  on-call rolled back to v46 — service restored

            ## Impact
            - 14 minutes of degraded/down /jobs/search for all users
            - ~1,100 failed requests (503), 0 data loss

            ## Root Cause — 5 Whys
            1. Why did users see 503s?      → all 3 Pods were OOMKilled.
            2. Why were they OOMKilled?     → v47's search view held every
                                              matching JobPost row in memory.
            3. Why unbounded rows?          → `.filter(...)` was never
                                              paginated or `.iterator()`'d.
            4. Why did review miss it?      → no load test against a large
                                              Skills/JobPost fixture set.
            5. Why no load test gate?       → CI (Ch22) checks tests pass,
                                              never checks memory under load.

            ## Action Items
            - [ ] paginate /jobs/search (owner: web team, due: this sprint)
            - [ ] set memory requests/limits on ALL Deployments (26.3)
            - [ ] add a load-test stage to CI before prod deploy (Ch22)
            - [ ] alert on postgres/redis saturation BEFORE next incident (31.4)

         🎯 GOAL: Produce a postmortem for the 32.1 incident that a
            stranger could read and know exactly what changes, and why.
         [TECH] The 5 Whys technique keeps asking "why" against the ANSWER
            to the previous why, not the symptom again — note how question
            4 and 5 move from the CODE bug to the PROCESS gap that let it
            ship; a postmortem stopping at "why 1" fixes nothing structural.
         [ANALOGY] Blameless is an airline crash investigation, not a
            trial: the goal is a checklist change that prevents the NEXT
            crash, never a name in a report — punishing the reporter only
            teaches the next person to hide the next near-miss.
         🔬 easypj: the postmortem above traces one 503 all the way to "no
            load-test CI gate" — that action item, not a scolding email, is
            what actually stops incident #2 from being the same incident.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: write a full postmortem for a DIFFERENT easypj
            incident (e.g., a bad `docker compose down -v` that deleted
            pgdata — see 17.x). Verify: your 5 Whys ends on a PROCESS or
            TOOLING gap, never on a person's name.
         📊 SUMMARY: Timeline, Impact, 5 Whys, Action Items — a postmortem
            that skips any one of the four teaches nothing durable.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: an action item without an OWNER and a DUE DATE is a
            wish, not a fix — it will still be open at the next incident.

    32.4 On-Call Runbooks for easypj
         - A runbook trades "figure it out" for "follow the steps" at 2 AM
         - Format: Symptom → Diagnostic commands → Mitigation → Escalation
         - Ties back to Appendix F's seven troubleshooting categories
           (F.1 container errors, F.2 network, F.3 volume, F.5 daemon, F.7
           Kubernetes) — a runbook is that appendix, pre-filtered per alert

         [CODE: runbook — JobsEndpointHighErrorRate (31.4's alert)]
            SYMPTOM
              Alertmanager: "JobsEndpointHighErrorRate — page"

            DIAGNOSTIC COMMANDS (run in order, stop when one explains it)
              1. kubectl get pods -n easypj
                 → any CrashLoopBackOff or 0/1 READY? go to F.7.
              2. kubectl logs -n easypj -l app=easypj --previous --tail=50
                 → OOMKilled / MemoryError? go to 32.1's triage sequence.
              3. kubectl exec -n easypj deploy/easypj -- \
                   python manage.py dbshell -c "SELECT 1;"
                 → fails? postgres is the problem, go to F.5/F.1 (db).
              4. curl -w "%{http_code}\n" -o /dev/null -s localhost/jobs/
                 → 502/504? nginx→django path is broken, go to F.2.

            MITIGATION
              - Bad deploy confirmed  → kubectl rollout undo deploy/easypj
              - DB saturation (31.4)  → scale down non-critical workers,
                                        raise postgres max_connections temp.
              - Unknown after step 4  → escalate now, do not keep guessing

            ESCALATION
              - No resolution in 15 min → page secondary on-call
              - Data integrity in doubt → page team lead + freeze deploys

         🎯 GOAL: Resolve or correctly escalate the 31.4 alert using ONLY
            the runbook — no live investigation from first principles.
         [TECH] Each diagnostic step is ordered cheapest-and-most-likely
            first (Pod status) to most-specific-last (HTTP path), and each
            one names EXACTLY which Appendix F category to open next —
            the runbook is a routing table into knowledge you already
            wrote, not new knowledge invented under pressure.
         [ANALOGY] A pilot's emergency checklist: nobody re-derives
            aerodynamics mid-flight — they run the printed steps in order,
            because a printed order beats a scared brain's improvisation
            every single time.
         🔬 easypj: step 2 of the runbook is 32.1's ENTIRE first-response
            sequence, condensed into one command — writing the runbook
            IS turning last incident's manual triage into next incident's
            reflex.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: hand this runbook to a teammate who has never
            seen the 32.1 incident and have them "resolve" a simulated
            alert using ONLY the document. Verify: they reach the correct
            mitigation step without asking you a single clarifying
            question — gaps they hit are gaps in the runbook, fix those.
         📊 SUMMARY: Symptom → Diagnostics → Mitigation → Escalation,
            every step pointing at a specific Appendix F category.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a runbook that goes stale (references a removed
            service, an old command) is worse than no runbook — it burns
            the exact 15 minutes escalation was supposed to save.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — what OOMKilled + Exit Code 137 actually means
    When a cgroup's memory usage crosses its configured ceiling (6.6's
    --memory, or a Pod's memory limit underneath), the KERNEL's OOM
    killer — not Docker, not Kubernetes — selects a process inside that
    cgroup and sends it SIGKILL (signal 9). Exit codes above 128 encode
    "killed by signal N-128"; 128+9 = 137 is that SIGKILL, which is why
    "Exit Code: 137" and "Reason: OOMKilled" always appear together in
    `kubectl describe pod` — one is the raw exit status, the other is
    Kubernetes' label for the same kernel event.

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ cgroup memory.max exceeded → kernel OOM killer → SIGKILL       │
         │           │                                          │        │
         │           ▼                                          ▼        │
         │  kubelet observes container death        exit code 137        │
         │           │                                     recorded      │
         │           ▼                                                   │
         │  Reason: OOMKilled  (Kubernetes' label for the SAME event)    │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    Also worth knowing: repeated crashes trigger CrashLoopBackOff, an
    exponential backoff (10s, 20s, 40s... capped at 5 minutes) BEFORE
    Kubernetes retries the container again — that growing delay is why a
    crash-looping Pod takes progressively longer between restarts, not a
    fixed interval.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS (Chapter 32)
       ✅ The triage order is deliberate: get pods (failure MODE) → logs
          --previous (dead container's evidence) → describe (kernel's
          verdict) → rollout undo (fastest safe mitigation) — same four
          steps regardless of which service failed.
       ✅ `kubectl logs` WITHOUT --previous on a restarted Pod shows the
          NEW, empty container's log, not the crash.
       ✅ A restart policy (6.2) heals a single CONTAINER; a ReplicaSet
          (26.7) heals a missing POD by reconciling desired-vs-actual
          count — chaos testing exploits exactly this distinction.
       ✅ Chaos engineering means killing something ON PURPOSE, in a
          controlled window, so the first real failure isn't a surprise.
       ✅ Blameless means naming FAILURES OF THE SYSTEM (a missing memory
          limit, no load-test gate), never a person.
       ✅ 5 Whys must keep asking "why" against the PREVIOUS ANSWER, not
          the original symptom, or it stops at a code bug instead of the
          process gap that let it ship.
       ✅ A runbook (Symptom → Diagnostics → Mitigation → Escalation)
          turns last incident's manual triage into next incident's
          reflex — and a stale one is worse than none.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS (Chapter 32)
       - `kubectl logs` without --previous on a restarted Pod is the
         single most common wasted minute in a real incident.
       - Never point a chaos script at a namespace with only 1 replica —
         that isn't testing resilience, it's just causing an outage.
       - An action item with no owner and no due date is a wish, not a
         fix — it will still be open at the next incident.
       - A runbook referencing a removed service or a stale command
         burns exactly the 15 minutes escalation was supposed to save.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS (Chapter 32)
       - Alias `klp` for `kubectl logs --previous` — it's the step
         everyone forgets under pressure.
       - Keep chaos.sh's sleep interval generous (5 min) on first runs —
         you want time to WATCH the recovery, not just trigger the kill.
       - Draft the postmortem's Timeline section FIRST, straight from
         `kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp` — reconstructing
         it from memory afterward loses minutes that matter.

    🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 32 cheat-card
       kubectl get pods -n easypj                              # failure MODE first
       kubectl logs <pod> -n easypj --previous --tail=50        # dead container's evidence
       kubectl describe pod <pod> -n easypj | grep -A3 "Last State"  # kernel verdict
       kubectl rollout undo deployment/easypj -n easypj         # fastest safe mitigation
       kubectl delete pod <name> -n easypj --grace-period=0     # chaos: kill on purpose
       watch kubectl get pods -n easypj                         # observe recovery live
       kubectl get events -n easypj --sort-by=.lastTimestamp    # postmortem timeline source

    🧪 DRILL (2 min, timed): given only a Pod name in CrashLoopBackOff,
    run the full 32.1 triage sequence and state whether the cause is
    OOMKilled — no notes, no looking up Appendix F.8.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 32)

    Q1: A Pod shows CrashLoopBackOff with RESTARTS climbing. What is the
        correct FIRST command?
        A: `kubectl get pods -n easypj` — it names the failure MODE and
        the restart COUNT before you spend time on slower commands.

    Q2: You run `kubectl logs <pod>` on a just-restarted Pod and see
        nothing useful. What went wrong?
        A: You read the NEW container's (empty) log; the crash evidence
        is in the DEAD container's log. Re-run with `--previous`.

    Q3 (diagram): Walk through what Exit Code 137 + Reason: OOMKilled
        means.
        A: cgroup memory ceiling exceeded → kernel OOM killer sends
        SIGKILL → exit code 137 recorded → kubelet labels it OOMKilled.
             ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
             │ over memory.max → OOM killer → SIGKILL(9) │
             │   → exit 137 → Kubernetes: "OOMKilled"    │
             └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Q4: Why is `kubectl rollout undo` correct in 32.1's scenario, and
        when would it NOT be the right call?
        A: Correct here because the root cause is a bad deploy (v47's
        unbounded query) — rollback removes the bad code immediately. It
        would be wrong if the cause were infrastructure (e.g. a full
        disk) since rollback doesn't fix an environment problem.

    Q5: What's the difference between what a restart policy (6.2) heals
        and what a ReplicaSet (26.7) heals?
        A: A restart policy reacts to a killed CONTAINER on one host; a
        ReplicaSet reacts to a missing POD anywhere in the cluster,
        reconciling desired-vs-actual replica count.

    Q6 (table): Per the CHAOS LOOP diagram, what should happen at each
        step?
        A:
           Step                          | Expected outcome
           kill one Pod                  | one replica goes missing
           ReplicaSet notices             | schedules a replacement
           new Pod ready                  | traffic returns to 100%
           recovery >30s or errors seen   | THAT gap is the real incident
                                          | chaos found for free

    Q7: Why must chaos testing never target a namespace with only 1
        replica?
        A: With 1 replica, killing it just causes a real outage — there
        is no redundancy left to demonstrate resilience against.

    Q8: Why does stopping the postmortem's 5 Whys at "Why 1" fail to
        prevent a repeat incident?
        A: It only restates the symptom (Pods were OOMKilled); the real
        fix comes from following the chain to Why 4 and 5 — no load-test
        fixture, no CI gate for memory under load — which are PROCESS
        fixes, not a one-line code patch.

    Q9: What are the four required sections of a blameless postmortem,
        and what does "blameless" protect against?
        A: Timeline, Impact, Root Cause (5 Whys), Action Items.
        Blameless protects against naming a PERSON in the document —
        punishing a reporter only teaches the next person to hide the
        next near-miss.

    Q10: Why does the JobsEndpointHighErrorRate runbook check
        `kubectl get pods` before checking postgres connectivity?
        A: Pod status is the fastest, cheapest check and rules out the
        most common cause first (a bad deploy); only if that's clean do
        you spend time on slower, more specific checks like a dbshell
        query.
