Chapter 33: Cost & Performance Tuning
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Chapters 26-27 taught requests/limits and
    Chapter 8 taught image optimization as CORRECTNESS and SECURITY
    concerns. Run easypj at real scale and both become MONEY: an
    oversized request wastes a node's capacity every hour it runs; a fat
    image wastes storage, egress and CI minutes on every single build.
    This chapter turns yesterday's best-practice advice into today's
    budget line, with real numbers. Problem solved here: "our Docker bill
    is bigger than expected, and nobody can say exactly why."

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced/Production · ⏱️ ~75-100 min · production/day-2 depth,
        beyond the graded DCA exam — pure cost/performance engineering
        on top of Chapters 8, 22, and 26-27.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
        - Replace a guessed requests/limits configuration (26.3) with
          numbers derived from sampled `kubectl top` data.
        - Translate Chapter 8's image-size optimization into a monthly
          dollar figure across storage, egress, and CI-minutes cost lines.
        - Reshape a multi-stage Dockerfile so BuildKit runs independent
          stages in parallel instead of serially.
        - Decide when Build Cloud (22.5) is worth paying for versus
          running local BuildKit.
        - Design and run a fair bare-metal-vs-containerized benchmark and
          interpret the result correctly.
        - Separate "Docker overhead" from other root causes (a --cpus
          limit, a slow query) when performance looks off.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: not graded — the DCA exam tests that you CAN set
        requests/limits and optimize a Dockerfile; it never tests
        whether the numbers you chose were right. This chapter is the
        measurement discipline the exam assumes you'll eventually add.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 33.1 measures COMPUTE (requests/limits) → 33.2
        prices STORAGE/EGRESS/CI (image size) → 33.3 speeds up the BUILD
        itself (parallel stages) → 33.4 proves what containerization
        actually COSTS in overhead.

    33.1 Right-Sizing Requests & Limits from Real Usage Data
         - 26.3 and 27.5 taught SETTING requests/limits; this section
           teaches MEASURING what to set them TO, from real traffic
         - `kubectl top pod` / `docker stats` sampled over time, not once
         - Right-sizing: requests ≈ typical usage + headroom, limits ≈
           observed peak + margin — never a guess

         [TERMINAL: measuring easypj-web over a real day]
            $ kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers
            POD              NAME     CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
            easypj-7f9-a1b2  django   210m         340Mi
            easypj-7f9-c3d4  django   195m         355Mi
            easypj-7f9-e5f6  django   640m         480Mi   ← traffic spike
            $ kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers \
                --sort-by=memory | head -1     # repeat hourly, log the peak

         [TABLE: 26.3's guessed values vs 33.1's measured values]
            Resource        | Guessed (26.3) | Measured peak | Right-sized
            CPU request     | 250m           | 210m typical   | 200m
            CPU limit       | 1000m          | 640m peak      | 800m
            Memory request  | 256Mi          | 355Mi typical  | 384Mi
            Memory limit    | 512Mi          | 480Mi peak     | 640Mi

         🎯 GOAL: Replace 26.3's guessed requests/limits with numbers
            derived from a week of `kubectl top` samples.
         [TECH] `kubectl top` reads live metrics-server data (instantaneous,
            like docker stats — 31.1's limitation) so it must be SAMPLED
            repeatedly and logged, not read once; requests should sit near
            the observed TYPICAL load (so the scheduler doesn't over-
            reserve nodes) while limits sit above the observed PEAK with
            margin (so legitimate spikes don't get OOMKilled per 6.6/27.5).
         [ANALOGY] The MEASURED TABLE above is packing a suitcase from a
            week of actually worn outfits instead of guessing — 26.3's
            250m/256Mi was a guess before the trip; 33.1's 200m/384Mi is
            what the week actually proved you needed.
         🔬 easypj: the 640m CPU spike row in the TERMINAL example is real
            traffic (a job-alert email blast hitting /jobs/) — set the
            limit UNDER that number and 32.1's OOMKilled cascade recurs on
            every future blast.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: sample `kubectl top pod` for easypj-web every
            hour for one full day, record min/typical/peak. Verify: your
            recommended request sits near typical and your limit sits
            above peak — recompute if either measurement was a fluke.
         📊 SUMMARY: measure with kubectl top over TIME, set requests near
            typical and limits above observed peak — never a guess.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: sampling for one hour catches nothing — right-
            sizing needs a full traffic cycle (usually a week) to see
            both quiet nights and peak-hour spikes.

    33.2 The Real Cost of Image Size at Scale
         - Chapter 8 optimized easypj from 850 MB to 180 MB for SECURITY
           and speed; this section prices that exact same win in dollars
         - Three cost lines: registry storage, egress bandwidth, CI minutes
         - Worked for a team doing 50 image builds/day

         [TABLE: 850 MB vs 180 MB — the same Chapter 8 win, priced]
            Cost line          | 850 MB image        | 180 MB image (Ch8)
            Registry storage   | 850 MB x 200 tags    | 180 MB x 200 tags
                                | kept = 170 GB         | kept = 36 GB
            Egress/pull        | 50 builds/day x 850MB| 50 builds/day x 180MB
                                | = 42.5 GB/day pulled  | = 9 GB/day pulled
            CI minutes         | ~11 min pull (8.1)    | ~2.4 min pull (8.1)
                                | x 50 builds = 550 min | x 50 builds = 120 min
            Monthly CI minutes | ~16,500 min/month     | ~3,600 min/month

         🎯 GOAL: State Chapter 8's optimization win as a monthly dollar
            figure a manager, not just an engineer, will act on.
         [TECH] The three cost lines compound: storage bills per GB-month
            kept across every retained tag; egress bills per GB actually
            transferred (every CI pull, every node pull, every developer
            pull); CI minutes bill per minute of RUNNER time, and pull time
            is runner time even though no build step ran yet. Chapter 8.1's
            "~11 min vs ~2.4 min" pull numbers are the CI-minutes line here.
         [ANALOGY] The COST TABLE above is the airline-baggage analogy from
            8.1, converted to an invoice: every kilo (MB) you stopped
            checking is a fee you stop paying, 50 times a day, forever —
            not once, EVERY build.
         🔬 easypj: at 50 builds/day, the 670 MB Chapter 8 removed is not
            "670 MB smaller," it is ~33.5 GB/day of pulls that never
            happen and roughly 7.2 hours/day of CI runner time reclaimed.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: take YOUR team's real builds/day and registry
            retention policy, plug them into the COST TABLE's formula
            (size x builds/day, size x tags kept). Verify: you can name a
            monthly GB figure and a monthly CI-minutes figure, not just
            "smaller is better."
         📊 SUMMARY: image size is a recurring multiplier — storage x tags
            kept, egress x builds/day, CI minutes x pull time — never a
            one-time number.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: teams that fix image size ONCE and never re-audit
            regress silently as dependencies grow — re-run `docker history`
            (7.6) every quarter, not just at the Chapter 8 rewrite.

    33.3 Build Time Optimization Beyond Caching
         - Chapter 8/22 covered layer caching; this section covers making
           independent build STAGES run in parallel, not just cached
         - BuildKit runs stages with no shared dependency concurrently —
           multi-stage Dockerfiles should be shaped to exploit this
         - `--platform` matrix builds (linux/amd64,linux/arm64) run each
           architecture as its own parallel build graph, not sequentially
         - When 22.5's Build Cloud actually pays for itself vs local CI

         [SERIAL vs PARALLEL MULTI-STAGE BUILDS]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                🏗️ SERIAL vs PARALLEL MULTI-STAGE BUILDS                 │
         │                                                                          │
         │ SERIAL (one lane):                                                       │
         │ deps ─▶ compile ─▶ test ─▶ collectstatic ─▶ final   (4 stages, 1 lane)   │
         │                                                                          │
         │ PARALLEL (BuildKit default — independent stages overlap):                │
         │ deps ─▶ compile ─┐                                                       │
         │ deps ─▶ lint ─────┼─▶ final      (wall-clock = longest lane, not sum)    │
         │ deps ─▶ test ─────┘                                                      │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 💡 parallelism only helps stages that do NOT need each other's           │
         │    output — lint and test run BESIDE compile, never before it.           │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [TABLE: when 22.5 Build Cloud pays for itself]
            Team profile                     | Verdict
            <10 builds/day, 1 local machine  | local BuildKit, Cloud unneeded
            50 builds/day, multi-arch images | Cloud's shared cache wins big
            Many devs rebuilding same deps   | Cloud cache reused across TEAM
            CI runners already fast + cached | Cloud adds cost, not much speed

         🎯 GOAL: Reshape a Dockerfile so independent stages overlap, and
            know when to stop optimizing locally and pay for Build Cloud.
         [TECH] BuildKit builds a DEPENDENCY GRAPH from the Dockerfile, not
            a top-to-bottom script — any two stages that do not COPY
            --from= each other are scheduled concurrently, exactly the
            PARALLEL half of the diagram above. `--platform
            linux/amd64,linux/arm64` doubles the graph into two parallel
            trees; 22.5's Build Cloud adds MORE concurrent workers plus a
            cache shared across the whole team, not just one machine.
         [ANALOGY] The diagram's SERIAL lane is one cook doing every step
            in order; the PARALLEL lanes are three cooks working
            side-by-side who all hand their trays to the same plating
            station (final) — the meal is ready as soon as the SLOWEST
            cook finishes, never the sum of all three.
         🔬 easypj: splitting jobpost's Dockerfile into `deps`, `lint`
            (ruff), and `test` (pytest) stages that all `COPY --from=deps`
            but never from each other lets BuildKit run lint and test
            beside compile — CI wall-clock drops even though total CPU
            work is unchanged.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: split a single-lane Dockerfile's lint/test
            steps into separate stages that both depend only on `deps`,
            then `docker buildx build --progress=plain .`. Verify: the
            build log shows lint's and test's stage numbers interleaved
            in the timestamps, not sequential.
         📊 SUMMARY: cache reuse (Ch8/22) makes REPEAT builds fast;
            parallel stage design makes even a COLD build fast.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a stage that `COPY --from=` an unrelated stage
            "just in case" silently serializes two lanes that could have
            run side by side — audit COPY --from lines when builds feel
            slower than the graph should allow.

    33.4 Benchmarking Container Overhead
         - Does containerizing a Django workload cost real CPU/memory
           versus running it bare-metal? Measure it, don't assume it
         - Reproducible benchmark: same gunicorn command, same hardware,
           container vs host process, same load generator

         [TERMINAL: reproducible overhead benchmark]
            # 1) bare-metal baseline (no Docker at all)
            $ gunicorn easypj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 3 &
            $ wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http://localhost:8000/jobs/
            Requests/sec:  1842.30   Latency p99: 68ms

            # 2) same command, containerized, no limits
            $ docker run -d -p 8000:8000 easypj:v1
            $ wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http://localhost:8000/jobs/
            Requests/sec:  1798.11   Latency p99: 71ms

            # 3) resource usage during the container run
            $ docker stats --no-stream easypj-web
            CPU %: 68.40%   MEM USAGE / LIMIT: 310MiB / 512MiB

         [TABLE: measured containerization overhead]
            Metric          | Bare-metal | Containerized | Overhead
            Requests/sec    | 1842.30    | 1798.11        | ~2.4% lower
            p99 latency     | 68ms       | 71ms           | ~4.4% higher
            Memory (RSS)    | ~290 MiB   | ~310 MiB       | ~7% higher

         🎯 GOAL: Produce a real, repeatable overhead number for easypj
            instead of citing "containers are basically free" from memory.
         [TECH] The comparison MUST hold everything constant except the
            container boundary: same gunicorn --workers, same host, same
            wrk parameters, run back-to-back to cancel out ambient noise.
            The small overhead observed (namespaces + cgroup accounting +
            the bridge network's extra hop) is the real, measurable cost
            of 1.3's isolation — not zero, but small next to a full VM.
         [ANALOGY] The 1.3 VM-vs-container diagram showed containers
            "near-native" CPU overhead as a claim; this section is that
            claim's receipt — the TABLE above is what "near-native"
            measures out to on an actual easypj workload.
         🔬 easypj: a ~2-4% overhead is the price for 1.3's entire benefit
            (portability, isolation, the whole rest of this guide) — worth
            comparing against BEFORE assuming Docker caused a slowdown
            that a slow query or missing index (33.1's real culprit) caused.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the three TERMINAL commands above on your
            own machine, bare-metal then containerized. Verify: your
            overhead lands in a similar small single-digit-percent range —
            a double-digit gap means something else is wrong (bridge
            network MTU, --cpus throttling from 6.6, not "Docker is slow").
         📊 SUMMARY: measured, containerization costs low single-digit
            percent overhead on a Django workload — not free, but rarely
            the real bottleneck.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: benchmarking WITH a --cpus limit set (6.6) measures
            your limit, not Docker's overhead — benchmark unlimited first,
            then re-test with production limits as a SEPARATE number.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — where `kubectl top`'s numbers actually come from
    `kubectl top` is not a new measurement — it queries the Kubernetes
    metrics-server, which polls each kubelet's `/stats/summary`
    endpoint, which is populated by cAdvisor embedded INSIDE the kubelet
    (the same cAdvisor Chapter 31 ran as a standalone container against
    plain Docker). 33.1's "measure, don't guess" numbers and 31.1's
    Prometheus dashboard ultimately trace back to the identical cgroup
    files — `kubectl top` just samples them on demand instead of
    continuously.

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │ cgroup memory.current / cpu.stat (same files as 31.1's cAdvisor)│
         │             │                                                   │
         │             ▼                                                   │
         │  kubelet's embedded cAdvisor → /stats/summary                  │
         │             │                                                   │
         │             ▼                                                   │
         │  metrics-server (cluster-wide aggregator) → kubectl top         │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    This is also why `kubectl top` shares 31.1's core limitation:
    metrics-server keeps only a short in-memory window, so 33.1's
    instruction to sample REPEATEDLY and log the results yourself is not
    a suggestion — long-term history is Prometheus's job (31.2), not
    metrics-server's.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS (Chapter 33)
       ✅ Right-size requests near TYPICAL measured usage and limits
          above measured PEAK with margin — never a guess.
       ✅ `kubectl top` (and docker stats) are instantaneous reads —
          sampling repeatedly over a full traffic cycle (usually a week)
          is what makes the numbers trustworthy.
       ✅ Image size is a recurring multiplier, not a one-time number:
          storage × tags kept, egress × builds/day, CI minutes × pull
          time.
       ✅ Re-audit image size quarterly (`docker history`, 7.6) — teams
          that fix it once regress silently as dependencies grow.
       ✅ BuildKit schedules independent Dockerfile stages CONCURRENTLY
          by default; a stray `COPY --from=` on an unrelated stage
          silently re-serializes two lanes that could run side by side.
       ✅ Build Cloud (22.5) pays for itself with high build volume,
          multi-arch matrices, or many developers sharing one dependency
          cache — not for a single low-volume local setup.
       ✅ A fair overhead benchmark holds everything constant except the
          container boundary, separating Docker's real (small,
          single-digit-percent) overhead from unrelated causes.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS (Chapter 33)
       - Sampling `kubectl top` for only an hour catches nothing —
         right-sizing needs a full traffic cycle to see quiet nights and
         peak-hour spikes.
       - Fixing image size once and never re-auditing lets dependency
         creep regress the win silently — re-check every quarter.
       - `COPY --from=` an unrelated stage "just in case" silently
         serializes two lanes BuildKit could otherwise run in parallel.
       - Benchmarking WITH a --cpus limit already set measures your
         limit, not Docker's real overhead — benchmark unlimited first,
         then re-test with production limits as a separate number.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS (Chapter 33)
       - Run `kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers
         --sort-by=memory` on a schedule instead of manually re-running
         it every hour.
       - `docker buildx build --progress=plain` to actually SEE stage
         timestamps interleave — the default output hides parallelism.
       - Keep a standing `docker history <image> --no-trunc` habit
         before every quarterly image-size review.

    🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 33 cheat-card
       kubectl top pod -n easypj -l app=easypj --containers      # sample usage
       kubectl top pod --containers --sort-by=memory | head -1   # find the peak
       docker history <image> --no-trunc                          # audit layer sizes (7.6)
       docker buildx build --progress=plain .                     # see stage parallelism
       wrk -t4 -c100 -d30s http://localhost:8000/jobs/            # load generator
       docker stats --no-stream easypj-web                        # usage during a benchmark

    🧪 DRILL (15 min): using 33.1's TERMINAL sample numbers (or your own),
    compute a right-sized request/limit pair using the "typical +
    headroom / peak + margin" rule — no guessing allowed.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 33)

    Q1: Why does 33.1 insist on sampling `kubectl top` repeatedly
        instead of reading it once?
        A: Like docker stats, it's an instantaneous reading — one sample
        could catch a quiet moment or a fluke spike. Only repeated
        sampling over a full traffic cycle reveals TYPICAL vs PEAK usage.

    Q2 (table): Using 33.1's measured values, what CPU request/limit
        would you set, and why not the original 26.3 guess?
        A:
           Resource    | Guessed (26.3) | Measured    | Right-sized
           CPU request | 250m           | 210m typical| 200m
           CPU limit   | 1000m          | 640m peak   | 800m
        Explanation: requests sit near typical so the scheduler doesn't
        over-reserve; limits sit above observed peak with margin.

    Q3: Why does setting a memory limit below the 640m CPU spike
        observed in 33.1 risk recreating 32.1's incident?
        A: That spike is real legitimate traffic (a job-alert email
        blast) — a limit set under it OOMKills the container on every
        future occurrence of that same pattern.

    Q4 (diagram): Using the SERIAL vs PARALLEL diagram, why does
        splitting lint/test into their own stages speed up CI wall-clock
        without reducing total CPU work?
        A: BuildKit builds a dependency graph, not a script; independent
        stages with no shared dependency run concurrently, so wall-clock
        equals the longest lane, not the sum — total CPU work is
        unchanged, just spent in parallel.
             ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
             │ deps ─▶ compile ─┐                     │
             │ deps ─▶ lint ─────┼─▶ final             │
             │ deps ─▶ test ─────┘  (longest lane wins)│
             └───────────────────────────────────────┘

    Q5: Give one condition where Build Cloud (22.5) is worth paying for,
        and one where it isn't.
        A: Worth it: 50+ builds/day with multi-arch images, or many devs
        rebuilding the same deps. Not worth it: fewer than 10 builds/day
        on one local machine — local BuildKit is enough.

    Q6: Why does an unrelated `COPY --from=` hurt build time even though
        it looks harmless?
        A: It creates an artificial dependency edge in BuildKit's graph,
        forcing that stage to wait for the unrelated one — serializing
        two lanes that could otherwise run beside each other.

    Q7: Why must the bare-metal and containerized benchmark runs use the
        SAME gunicorn --workers count, host, and load parameters?
        A: To isolate the container boundary as the ONLY variable — any
        other difference would contaminate the measured "overhead"
        number with something unrelated to Docker.

    Q8: The 33.4 table shows ~2-4% lower throughput for the containerized
        run. What causes this overhead?
        A: Namespace and cgroup accounting plus the bridge network's
        extra hop — the real, measurable cost of Chapter 1.3's isolation,
        small next to a full VM.

    Q9: A benchmark shows a DOUBLE-DIGIT percent slowdown under Docker.
        What should you suspect FIRST?
        A: A --cpus throttling limit already applied (6.6), a bridge-
        network MTU issue, or another environmental difference — a
        double-digit gap signals something else is wrong, not "Docker is
        slow."

    Q10: Why re-run `docker history` every quarter instead of trusting
        Chapter 8's original optimization forever?
        A: Dependencies grow over time and image size regresses silently
        — a one-time fix without ongoing audits eventually erodes back
        toward the original bloated size.

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

         │  (33.1) kubectl top, sampled over a week → right-sized requests/limits  │
         │  (33.2) image size × builds/day × tags kept → a monthly dollar figure   │
         │  (33.3) BuildKit DAG → independent stages run in PARALLEL, not serial   │
         │  (33.4) bare-metal vs container, same load → real, small % overhead     │
         │                                                                          │
         │  All four converge on ONE rule: MEASURE, never assume, then price it.   │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    .vs-prose — Chapter 33 replaces four different guesses — a resource
    guess (26.3), an unpriced image-size win (Chapter 8), an unexamined

    percentage that puts Docker's real cost in writing instead of
    folklore.



Chapter 34: Docker & AI Workloads
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    WHY THIS CHAPTER EXISTS: Every workload so far assumed a CPU-bound
    Django process. AI workloads break two assumptions at once: the
    "image" can BE a multi-gigabyte model instead of application code, and
    the container may need a PHYSICAL GPU passed through the isolation
    boundary Chapter 1.3 built on namespaces and cgroups alone. This
    chapter extends easypj with a hypothetical AI sidecar to show both
    changes without abandoning anything already built. Problem solved
    here: "our stack needs a model running next to it — does everything
    I've learned still apply?"

    [A] META: 🔴 Advanced/Emerging · ⏱️ ~75-100 min · production/day-2 depth,
        beyond the graded DCA exam — Docker's newest tooling, ahead of
        any current certification blueprint.

    [C] LEARNING OBJECTIVES — after this chapter you can:
        - Pull and run a local LLM with `docker model pull`/`docker
          model run` and call it through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
        - Explain why a model artifact fits the same OCI pull/cache/
          version model as an application image, despite holding weights
          instead of code.
        - Get a container to see a host GPU with `--gpus`, and verify it
          from inside the container with nvidia-smi.
        - Explain what the nvidia-container-toolkit changes about which
          OCI runtime a container uses.
        - Design a separate Dockerfile and network-only access pattern
          for an ML inference sidecar, without bloating the web tier's
          image.
        - Right-size a GPU-bound container by VRAM footprint instead of a
          guessed fraction, and explain why GPU memory has no throttling
          equivalent to CPU.

    [D] DCA RELEVANCE: not graded — Docker Model Runner and GPU workloads
        are recent platform additions, ahead of any current certification
        blueprint; this chapter previews where the "run a container"
        skillset is headed next.

    [E] SECTION MAP: 34.1 runs a model as a LOCAL SERVICE → 34.2 gives a
        container a HOST GPU → 34.3 wires a real inference SIDECAR into
        easypj's stack → 34.4 right-sizes that sidecar's GPU memory.

    34.1 Docker Model Runner — Running LLMs as Local Services
         - Docker's built-in way to pull and run local LLMs as a service,
           the same mental model as `docker run`, applied to models
         - `docker model pull` / `docker model run` — OCI-distributed model
           artifacts, not application images
         - Exposes an OpenAI-compatible local HTTP endpoint — existing
           OpenAI-client code points at localhost instead of the cloud

         [TERMINAL: pulling and serving a local model]
            $ docker model pull ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M
            Pulling ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M... done (1.9 GB)
            $ docker model run ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M &
            Model server listening on http://localhost:12434/engines/...
            $ curl http://localhost:12434/engines/v1/chat/completions \
                -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
                -d '{"model":"ai/llama3.2","messages":[{"role":"user",
                     "content":"Summarize this job post in one line."}]}'
            {"choices":[{"message":{"content":"Backend Django role..."}}]}

         🎯 GOAL: Run a local LLM as a service and call it exactly like the
            OpenAI API, with zero cloud dependency or API key.
         [TECH] `docker model` treats a quantized model file as an OCI
            artifact — pulled/cached/versioned identically to
            `easypj:v1`, per 1.9's OCI standards, even though the payload
            is model weights, not a filesystem layer of app code. The
            runner serves an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/chat/completions`
            route, so any code written against the OpenAI SDK works by
            changing only the base URL.
         [ANALOGY] The TERMINAL example is `docker pull` / `docker run`
            wearing a model's clothes: same two verbs, same registry
            concept (1.4), the "image" just happens to be weights instead
            of a Python interpreter and Django.
         🔬 easypj: a "summarize this job post" feature can call
            `localhost:12434` in development and a real OpenAI endpoint in
            production — same request shape, per 34.3's sidecar pattern.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: run the TERMINAL commands above and swap the
            prompt for a real JobPost description from your fixtures.
            Verify: the response arrives from `localhost`, and `docker
            model ls` lists the cached model with no re-download on a
            second `docker model run`.
         📊 SUMMARY: `docker model pull/run` brings the exact Docker mental
            model to local LLMs — OCI artifacts, cached pulls, an
            OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: the Model Runner API is NOT authenticated — any
            client that can reach it, including other containers on the
            SAME Docker network, can pull, load, and run models; never
            expose 12434 (or the container-internal DMR endpoint) beyond
            a trusted network boundary.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: quantized models still need real RAM (a 3B-Q4 model
            is ~2 GB resident) — treat it like any other container in
            33.1's right-sizing exercise, it is not free just because it's
            "local."

    34.2 GPU Passthrough with --gpus
         - Prerequisite: NVIDIA driver on the HOST + the
           nvidia-container-toolkit package (registers the "nvidia" OCI
           runtime alongside runc, per 1.9's runtime landscape)
         - `--gpus all` (every GPU visible) vs `--gpus "device=0"` (one
           specific GPU) — same isolation model, one more device class
         - Verifying GPU visibility from INSIDE the container

         [--gpus FLAG — FROM HOST GPU TO CONTAINER PROCESS]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │            🎮 --gpus FLAG — FROM HOST GPU TO CONTAINER PROCESS           │
         │                                                                          │
         │ 🖥️ host: NVIDIA driver + nvidia-container-toolkit installed             │
         │      │                                                                   │
         │      ▼                                                                   │
         │ $ docker run --gpus all easypj-inference:v1        (all GPUs)            │
         │ $ docker run --gpus "device=0" easypj-inference:v1  (GPU 0 only)         │
         │      │                                                                   │
         │      ▼                                                                   │
         │ runtime becomes nvidia (not runc directly) — CUDA libs and               │
         │ /dev/nvidia* devices are injected into the container automatically       │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ $ docker exec easypj-inference nvidia-smi   → GPU listed = success       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         🎯 GOAL: Get a container to see a host GPU and prove it with one
            command, understanding exactly what --gpus changed.
         [TECH] `--gpus` tells dockerd to hand the container to the
            `nvidia` OCI runtime (installed alongside runc per 1.9)
            instead of runc directly; that runtime injects the driver's
            character devices (/dev/nvidia0, /dev/nvidiactl) and CUDA
            userspace libraries into the container's namespace — the same
            namespace isolation from 1.3, just with one more device class
            made visible on purpose.
         [ANALOGY] The diagram above is a hotel giving a room a KEY to the
            gym (`--gpus`) instead of building the room its own gym — the
            room (container) still shares the building's one gym (GPU),
            same as it always shared the building's one kernel (1.3).
         🔬 easypj: 34.3's resume-matching sidecar runs `docker run --gpus
            "device=0" easypj-inference:v1` only if the embedding model
            benefits from GPU acceleration — the web/postgres/redis/nginx
            tier from Chapter 4 never touches this flag at all.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: install nvidia-container-toolkit on a
            GPU-equipped host, then run `docker run --rm --gpus all
            nvidia/cuda:12.5.0-base-ubuntu22.04 nvidia-smi`. Verify: the
            output lists your actual GPU model and driver version, proving
            the passthrough chain end-to-end before touching easypj at all.
         📊 SUMMARY: nvidia-container-toolkit registers a GPU-aware
            runtime; --gpus all/device=N controls which GPUs that runtime
            exposes — same isolation model, one more resource class.
         ⚠️ Gotcha: `--gpus` silently does nothing (no error) on a host
            missing the toolkit — always confirm with `nvidia-smi` INSIDE
            the container, never assume the flag was honored.

    34.3 Containerizing an ML Inference Sidecar for easypj
         - A hypothetical resume-matching service: scores a JobPost against
           an uploaded resume, called by jobpost, never called directly
         - Its own Dockerfile, separate from easypj's — different base
           image, different dependency set, different resource profile
         - Resource considerations distinct from the web tier: CPU-bound
           inference vs I/O-bound Django, no need to scale 1:1 with web Pods

         [THE RESUME-MATCHING SIDECAR NEXT TO easypj]
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │             🧩 THE RESUME-MATCHING SIDECAR NEXT TO easypj                │
         │                                                                          │
         │ 🌐 nginx:80 → django:8000 (easypj/jobpost) → postgres:5432               │
         │                   │                                                      │
         │                   │ POST /api/match  (internal network only)             │
         │                   ▼                                                      │
         │           🧠 inference:9000  (resume-matcher, own Dockerfile)            │
         │           CPU: 2 cores | RAM: 3Gi | no GPU (CPU-only model)              │
         ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
         │ 💡 the web tier stays thin; the heavy model lives in its OWN             │
         │    container so one slow inference call never blocks /jobs/.             │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

         [CODE: inference/Dockerfile — the sidecar's own build]
            FROM python:3.12-slim AS base
            WORKDIR /app
            RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
                  libgomp1 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
            COPY requirements.txt .
            RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
                pip install -r requirements.txt   # sentence-transformers, fastapi
            COPY app/ .
            EXPOSE 9000
            USER 1000:1000
            CMD ["uvicorn", "main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "9000"]

         🎯 GOAL: Add a matching service to the easypj stack that jobpost
            calls over the network, without merging it into django's image.
         [TECH] The sidecar diagram above adds ONE new service to Chapter
            10.4's compose.yaml — `inference:` — reachable only on the
            internal `backend` network (10.4's network isolation), never
            exposed via nginx. Its Dockerfile is intentionally separate
            from easypj's (8.2's base-image choice) because a
            sentence-transformers model needs different, heavier
            dependencies than Django ever will.
         [ANALOGY] The diagram is a restaurant's kitchen line: the grill
            station (django, fast, high-volume) never stops to also run
            the slow sous-vide station (inference) — each has its own
            equipment and its own pace, connected only by an order ticket
            (the POST /api/match call).
         🔬 easypj: jobpost's Skills model gets a `match_score(job, resume)`
            helper that POSTs to `http://inference:9000/match` — if the
            inference container is slow or down, that ONE feature degrades
            gracefully (Skills scoring), /jobs/ itself never notices.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: add the inference service to compose.yaml on
            the `backend` network only, build it, and call it from a shell
            inside the django container with `curl http://inference:9000/
            health`. Verify: the SAME curl fails from your HOST machine
            (no published port) — proof the sidecar is truly internal-only.
         💡 A REAL sidecar calling Docker Model Runner itself (rather than
            easypj's own custom inference service above) would call
            `http://model-runner.docker.internal` from inside a container
            on Docker Desktop — no port needed, unlike 34.1's host-side
            `localhost:12434` (on Docker Engine, use
            `http://172.17.0.1:12434` instead).
         📊 SUMMARY: an AI feature gets its OWN Dockerfile, OWN resource
            profile, and network-only access from django — never bolted
            onto the web tier's image.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: a `pip install sentence-transformers` inside
            easypj's OWN Dockerfile is the anti-pattern this section
            exists to prevent — it fattens 8.1's 180 MB web image with
            weight only the sidecar ever needed.

    34.4 Resource Planning for GPU-Bound Containers
         - Why 33.1's CPU/memory right-sizing math needs a THIRD dimension
           for GPU workloads: GPU memory (VRAM), not just host RAM
         - GPU memory cannot be overcommitted like CPU (no throttling
           equivalent) — it is closer to 6.6's --memory: a hard wall
         - Avoiding GPU memory oversubscription across multiple containers
           sharing one physical GPU

         [TABLE: CPU/RAM right-sizing (33.1) vs GPU right-sizing]
            Dimension        | CPU/RAM (33.1)          | GPU (this section)
            Over-limit result| throttled (CPU) or       | CUDA out-of-memory —
                              | OOMKilled (memory, 6.6)  | the process just crashes
            Shareable?        | yes — CFS time-slices    | only via careful VRAM
                              | many containers on 1 CPU | budgeting per container
            Oversubscription  | safe for CPU (bursty),   | UNSAFE — no swap, no
                              | risky for memory          | throttle, hard crash
            Right-size using  | kubectl top over time    | model's known VRAM
                              |                           | footprint + batch size

         🎯 GOAL: Set a GPU-bound inference container's resource plan so
            it never crashes from VRAM oversubscription under load.
         [TECH] Unlike CPU, which the kernel time-slices fairly (6.6), a
            GPU has no equivalent for VRAM — two containers each assuming
            they own the full 24 GB card will both allocate, and the
            SECOND one's `cudaMalloc` fails outright, crashing that
            process. Requests/limits (26.3/27.5) can request whole GPUs
            via `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` in Kubernetes, but do not sub-divide
            VRAM the way CPU/memory limits sub-divide a core — plan by
            the MODEL's known footprint, not a guessed fraction.
         [ANALOGY] The comparison TABLE above says it plainly: CPU is a
            shared meeting room (everyone gets a turn, 6.6's throttling);
            GPU memory is assigned PARKING SPOTS — once every spot is
            taken, the next car doesn't wait in line, it simply cannot
            park, full stop.
         🔬 easypj: if 34.3's resume-matcher model needs a known 6 GB of
            VRAM per loaded instance, a single 24 GB GPU safely hosts
            THREE replicas with margin — a fourth replica is not
            "throttled," it fails to start.
         🧪 PRACTICE [LAB]: check your model's documented VRAM footprint
            (or measure with `nvidia-smi` while one instance runs), divide
            your GPU's total VRAM by that number, and cap replicas at the
            floor of that division minus one for headroom. Verify: running
            one MORE replica than your calculated cap produces a clean
            CUDA out-of-memory error, not a graceful throttle — confirming
            why the margin matters.
         📊 SUMMARY: GPU VRAM has no throttle and no swap — right-size by
            the model's known footprint, never by a guessed fraction of
            33.1's CPU/RAM playbook.
            ⚠️ Gotcha: `--gpus all` on MULTIPLE containers gives every one
            of them a view of the WHOLE card's memory — Docker does not
            enforce a per-container VRAM limit for you; that discipline is
            entirely on the deployer.

    🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — how ONE registry stores both Django images AND
    model weights
    The OCI Distribution Spec supports ARBITRARY artifact types, not
    just container image layers — a manifest just needs a `mediaType`
    field. A normal image manifest points at gzipped filesystem layers;
    `docker model pull`'s manifest points at a quantized weights file
    instead, but both are pushed/pulled/cached through the exact same
    registry API and content-addressable storage (1.9's OCI standards) —
    the registry doesn't know or care that one "image" is Python +
    Django and the other is a few billion numbers.

         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  OCI Registry (same API for both)                              │
         │    ├─ easypj:v1        manifest → gzipped filesystem layers    │
         │    └─ ai/llama3.2:3B   manifest → quantized weights blob       │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    `--gpus` works on a similar "reuse the existing plumbing" principle:
    the OCI Runtime Spec supports prestart hooks, and nvidia-container-
    toolkit registers one that runs before the container starts,
    injecting /dev/nvidia* devices and CUDA userspace libraries into the
    container's mount namespace — no special-case code in dockerd
    itself, just a runtime swap (runc → nvidia) plus a hook, exactly like
    1.9 described for pluggable runtimes.

    🔑 KEY TAKEAWAYS (Chapter 34)
       ✅ `docker model pull/run` reuses Docker's exact pull/cache/
          version mental model — the payload is weights, not application
          code, but the OCI machinery underneath is identical.
       ✅ The Model Runner serves an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so
          existing OpenAI-SDK code works locally by changing only the
          base URL.
       ✅ `--gpus all` vs `--gpus "device=0"` controls WHICH GPUs are
          exposed; nvidia-container-toolkit is what makes the flag do
          anything at all.
       ✅ Always verify GPU passthrough with `nvidia-smi` INSIDE the
          container — a missing toolkit makes `--gpus` fail silently.
       ✅ An AI feature gets its OWN Dockerfile and its OWN resource
          profile, reachable only over the internal network — never
          merged into the web tier's image.
       ✅ GPU memory (VRAM) has no throttling or swap equivalent —
          oversubscription causes a hard crash, not graceful degradation.
       ✅ Right-size GPU-bound replicas by the MODEL's documented VRAM
          footprint divided into the card's total, with margin — never a
          guessed fraction.

    ⚠️ GOTCHAS (Chapter 34)
       - The Model Runner API is unauthenticated — never expose port
         12434 (or the internal DMR endpoint) beyond a trusted network
         boundary.
       - A quantized model still needs real RAM (a 3B-Q4 model is ~2 GB
         resident) — it is not "free" just because it's local.
       - `--gpus` silently does nothing on a host missing nvidia-
         container-toolkit — always confirm with nvidia-smi inside the
         container.
       - `pip install sentence-transformers` (or any heavy ML dependency)
         directly inside easypj's own Dockerfile is the exact anti-
         pattern 34.3 exists to prevent.
       - `--gpus all` on multiple containers gives EVERY one of them
         visibility into the WHOLE card's memory — Docker enforces no
         per-container VRAM limit.

    ⚡ SPEED TIPS (Chapter 34)
       - `docker model ls` before every `docker model run` — confirms
         the model is already cached and won't trigger a multi-GB
         re-download.
       - Test GPU passthrough with the small `nvidia/cuda:...-base` image
         and `nvidia-smi` BEFORE wiring it into a real inference
         container — isolates a toolkit problem from an app problem.
       - Keep the inference sidecar off nginx entirely (internal network
         only) from the very first Compose draft.

    🔑 COMMANDS — Chapter 34 cheat-card
       docker model pull ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M      # cache a local model (OCI artifact)
       docker model run ai/llama3.2:3B-Q4_K_M &     # serve OpenAI-compatible endpoint
       docker model ls                               # confirm cache, avoid re-pull
       docker run --gpus all <image>                 # expose every host GPU
       docker run --gpus "device=0" <image>          # expose one specific GPU
       docker exec <container> nvidia-smi             # verify GPU visibility INSIDE
       curl http://inference:9000/health              # sidecar reachable only internally

    🧪 DRILL (10 min): on a host with nvidia-container-toolkit installed,
    run `docker run --rm --gpus all nvidia/cuda:12.5.0-base-ubuntu22.04
    nvidia-smi` and confirm your real GPU model appears — do not touch
    easypj's inference sidecar until this passes cleanly.

    🧪 LAB Q&A (Chapter 34)

    Q1: How does `docker model pull` fit the same mental model as
        `docker pull easypj:v1`, despite pulling weights instead of code?
        A: Both are OCI artifacts pulled/cached/versioned through the
        identical registry mechanism — the manifest just points at a
        different payload type (weights vs filesystem layers).

    Q2: Why can existing OpenAI-SDK code call a local Model Runner
        instance with only a one-line change?
        A: The Model Runner serves an OpenAI-compatible
        `/v1/chat/completions` route, so switching the base URL to
        `localhost:12434` is the only required change.

    Q3 (diagram): What does `--gpus` actually change under the hood?
        A: It tells dockerd to hand the container to the nvidia OCI
        runtime instead of runc directly; that runtime injects the
        driver's character devices and CUDA userspace libraries into the
        container's namespace.
             ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
             │ --gpus flag → runtime=nvidia (not runc)      │
             │  → /dev/nvidia* + CUDA libs injected          │
             └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

    Q4: What is the prerequisite for `--gpus` to do anything, and what
        happens if it's missing?
        A: nvidia-container-toolkit must be installed on the host; if
        missing, `--gpus` fails silently with no error — always verify
        with nvidia-smi inside the container.

    Q5: Why does the resume-matching sidecar get its own Dockerfile
        instead of joining easypj's image?
        A: It needs different, heavier dependencies (sentence-
        transformers, fastapi) than Django ever will; bundling them into
        easypj's image would fatten Chapter 8's optimized 180 MB image
        with weight only the sidecar needs.

    Q6 (table): What happens differently when CPU/RAM vs GPU are
        oversubscribed?
        A:
           Dimension  | CPU/RAM result          | GPU result
           Over-limit | throttled or OOMKilled   | CUDA out-of-memory crash
           Shareable  | yes (CFS time-slicing)   | only via manual VRAM budgeting

    Q7: If the resume-matcher needs 6 GB VRAM per instance, how many
        replicas safely fit on a 24 GB GPU, and what happens to the next
        one?
        A: Three replicas fit with margin (18 of 24 GB); a fourth doesn't
        get throttled — it fails to start with a CUDA out-of-memory
        error.

    Q8: Why does `curl http://inference:9000/health` succeed from inside
        django but fail from the host machine?
        A: The inference service is only on the internal `backend`
        network with no published port — proof the sidecar is truly
        internal-only.

    Q9: What is the security gotcha with the Model Runner API?
        A: It is unauthenticated — any client that can reach it,
        including other containers on the same Docker network, can pull,
        load, and run models; never expose port 12434 beyond a trusted
        network boundary.

    Q10: Why can't a GPU-bound container's memory be sub-divided the way
        CPU/memory limits are in Kubernetes?
        A: `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` requests a WHOLE GPU; there's no built-in
        mechanism to sub-divide VRAM the way CPU shares or memory limits
        divide a core — right-sizing must be done by the model's known
        footprint, not a fractional resource request.

    [N] VISUAL SUMMARY
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │      🤖 CHAPTER 34 — THE SAME DOCKER MENTAL MODEL, POINTED AT AI          │
         │                                                                          │
         │  (34.1) docker model pull/run → OCI artifact → OpenAI-compatible API    │
         │  (34.2) --gpus all/device=N → nvidia runtime → CUDA libs in namespace   │
         │  (34.3) inference:9000 sidecar → own Dockerfile → internal network only │
         │  (34.4) VRAM footprint → replica cap → no throttle, no swap, hard wall  │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    .vs-prose — Chapter 34 proves that nothing about Docker's core model
    changes for AI workloads: pull/run still means pull/run even when the
    payload is model weights, --gpus still means "give this container a
    device" the same way volumes give it storage, a sidecar is still just
    a container with its own Dockerfile and network scope, and resource
    planning still means measuring a real footprint — the only new fact
    to internalize is that GPU memory, unlike CPU, has no throttle and no
    swap, so oversubscription fails hard instead of failing gracefully.

    [F] PART 11 KEY TAKEAWAYS
       ✅ Chapter 31 turns silent cgroup counters and a stdout stream
          into a queryable, alertable pipeline (cAdvisor → Prometheus →
          Grafana, plus shipped logs) — the eyes production needs.
       ✅ The four golden signals, alerted on RATIOS not raw counts,
          catch nearly every real easypj outage before a user files a
          ticket.
       ✅ Chapter 32's triage sequence — get pods → logs --previous →
          describe → rollout undo — is the same four steps for every
          incident, rehearsed safely with chaos engineering before it's
          ever needed for real.
       ✅ A blameless postmortem (Timeline/Impact/5 Whys/Action Items)
          and a runbook (Symptom/Diagnostics/Mitigation/Escalation) are
          what stop an incident from becoming a repeat incident.
       ✅ Chapter 33 replaces every guess Parts 1-10 made — resource
          requests, image size's cost, build speed, containerization
          overhead — with a measured number.
       ✅ Image size, once optimized (Chapter 8), is a recurring
          multiplier that must be RE-audited, not fixed once and
          forgotten.
       ✅ Chapter 34 shows Docker's core model — pull, run, isolate,
          right-size — applies unchanged to AI workloads; only GPU
          memory's lack of a throttle/swap equivalent is genuinely new.
       ✅ None of Part 11 is on the graded DCA exam, but all four
          chapters are what keep easypj alive, affordable, and
          recoverable once the exam is behind you.

    ⚠️ PART 11 GOTCHAS
       - Any socket/host mount used for monitoring (cAdvisor's Docker
         socket + /sys + /rootfs) sees every container on the host —
         treat it with 20.3's socket-mount caution, not as a routine
         volume.
       - `kubectl logs` without --previous, and alerting on raw counts
         instead of ratios, are the two most common ways teams waste the
         first minutes of a real incident.
       - Fixing something ONCE — image size, a runbook, a resource limit
         — and never revisiting it lets the underlying problem regress
         silently; Part 11's discipline is recurring, not one-time.
       - Anything exposed for setup convenience (Grafana's admin/
         changeme password, the Model Runner's unauthenticated API, a
         --gpus flag with no toolkit installed to check it) becomes a
         real risk or a silent failure if left unaudited.

    ⚡ PART 11 SPEED TIPS
       - Keep Prometheus's /alerts page, Grafana's dashboard, and the
         on-call runbook one bookmark away from each other — a real
         incident starts in one and ends in another.
       - Sample, don't guess: `kubectl top`/`docker stats` over a full
         traffic cycle beats any resource number pulled from memory.
       - Re-run `docker history` and a chaos drill on a fixed calendar
         cadence (quarterly) — both catch silent regressions long before
         a bill or an outage does.

    A.10 Docker Context Commands (create, ls, use, inspect, rm — manage multiple engines/environments)
         - contexts store endpoint + TLS config under a NAME: docker
           context create prod --docker "host=ssh://deploy@prod-server"
         - beats ad-hoc SSH + DOCKER_HOST exports: named, persistent,
           switchable per command (docker --context prod ps) — no env-var
           leakage between terminals or scripts
         - docker context use switches the DEFAULT target for every
           following command; docker context ls marks the active one (*)

    A.11 docker run — Complete Official Flag Reference
         Full official flag set, grouped by job (builds on the 12-flag
         table in 3.5 — this is the exhaustive reference version).

         Identity, lifecycle & pull policy
            Flag            | Meaning
            --name          | container name
            -h/--hostname   | container hostname
            -l/--label      | metadata key=value
            --annotation    | OCI annotation key=value
            -d/--detach     | run in background, print container ID
            --rm            | auto-remove container on exit
            --restart       | no|always|unless-stopped|on-failure[:N]
                            | (default no)
            --init          | run tiny init as PID 1 (reaps zombies)
            --pull          | always|missing|never (default missing)
            --platform      | target platform, e.g. linux/arm64

         Interactive I/O & signals
            Flag             | Meaning
            -i/--interactive | keep STDIN open
            -t/--tty         | allocate a pseudo-TTY
            -a/--attach      | STDIN, STDOUT or STDERR to attach
            --sig-proxy      | proxy signals to container (default true)
            --stop-signal    | signal docker stop sends to the container
            --stop-timeout   | seconds before SIGKILL on stop
            -q/--quiet       | suppress image-pull output

         Networking
            Flag              | Meaning
            -p/--publish      | [host-ip:]host-port:container-port[/proto]
            -P/--publish-all  | publish all EXPOSEd ports to random ports
            --network         | name|host|none|bridge
            --network-alias   | extra DNS name on a user-defined network
            --ip/--ip6        | fixed container IP on the network
            --dns/--dns-search| custom DNS server / search domain
            --add-host        | extra host:ip entry in /etc/hosts
            --expose          | expose a port without publishing it
            --link            | legacy link to container:alias
            --uts             | host — share host UTS (hostname) namespace

         Environment & filesystem
            Flag             | Meaning
            -e/--env         | KEY=value environment variable
            --env-file       | load env vars from a file
            --entrypoint     | override the image's ENTRYPOINT
            -w/--workdir     | working directory inside the container
            -u/--user        | name|uid[:group|gid] to run as
            -v/--volume      | host:container[:ro|rw]
            --mount          | type=...,target=... verbose volume syntax
            --volumes-from   | reuse volumes from another container
            --volume-driver  | driver for anonymous/named volumes
            --tmpfs          | /path:options tmpfs mount
            --device         | host:container[:rwm] device passthrough

         CPU, memory & resource limits
            Flag                 | Meaning
            --cpus               | CPU count, decimal (e.g. 1.5)
            --cpu-period/-quota  | raw CFS scheduler period/quota
            --cpuset-cpus/-mems  | pin to specific CPUs / NUMA nodes
            -m/--memory          | hard RAM cap, suffix b/k/m/g
            --memory-reservation | soft RAM floor
            --memory-swap        | mem+swap total, or -1 for unlimited
            --memory-swappiness  | 0-100, default -1
            --blkio-weight       | block IO weight, 10-1000
            --pids-limit         | max PIDs, or -1 for unlimited
            --shm-size           | size of /dev/shm
            --ulimit             | type=soft[:hard] resource ulimit

         Security & isolation
            Flag               | Meaning
            --cap-add/-drop    | add/drop one Linux capability
            --privileged       | grant extended (near-host) privileges
            --security-opt     | custom seccomp/AppArmor profile
            --read-only        | mount container root filesystem read-only
            --userns           | host — disable user-namespace remap
            --ipc              | none|private|shareable|container:x|host
            --pid              | container:x|host — share PID namespace
            --cgroupns         | host|private cgroup namespace
            --isolation        | default|process|hyperv container isolation
            --runtime          | alternate OCI runtime for this container
            --oom-kill-disable | exempt container from the OOM killer
            --oom-score-adj    | -1000..1000 OOM-kill preference

         Health checks, GPU, logging & misc
            Flag                    | Meaning
            --health-cmd            | command defining healthy/unhealthy
            --health-interval       | time between checks (default 0s)
            --health-retries        | failures before marked unhealthy
            --health-start-period   | grace period before failures count
                                    | (default 0s)
            --health-start-interval | check interval during start period
                                    | (default 0s)
            --health-timeout        | time before a check itself fails
                                    | (default 0s)
            --no-healthcheck        | disable the image's HEALTHCHECK
            --gpus                  | all, or device=... GPU access
            --log-driver/-opt       | logging driver and its options
            --sysctl                | name=value kernel parameter
            --use-api-socket        | mount the Docker API socket in

         🔬 easypj: `docker run -d --name pg --restart unless-stopped
            --health-cmd "pg_isready -U easypj" --health-interval 10s
            -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16` combines
            lifecycle, health-check and storage flags from four different
            groups above into one production Postgres command.

    A.12 docker network create / docker volume create — Complete Flag Reference
         docker network create
            Flag           | Meaning
            -d/--driver    | bridge|overlay|macvlan... (default bridge)
            --subnet       | CIDR block for the network
            --gateway      | gateway IP within --subnet
            --ip-range     | sub-range of --subnet for allocation
            --ipv4         | enable IPv4 (default true)
            --ipv6         | enable IPv6
            --attachable   | let standalone containers join a swarm/
                           | overlay network
            --internal     | no external (outbound) connectivity
            --ingress      | mark as the swarm ingress network
            --aux-address  | reserve IPs for driver-specific use
            --config-from  | reuse another network's config-only settings
            --config-only  | create a config-only network (no containers)
            --ipam-driver  | custom IPAM driver
            --ipam-opt     | driver-specific IPAM option
            -o/--opt       | driver-specific option
            --label        | metadata key=value
            --scope        | local|swarm network visibility scope

         docker volume create
            Flag              | Meaning
            -d/--driver       | volume driver (default local)
            --label           | metadata key=value
            -o/--opt          | driver-specific option
            --scope           | single|multi (default single)
            --type            | mount|block (default block)
            --availability    | active|pause|drain (default active)
            --sharing         | none|readonly|onewriter|all (default none)
            --secret          | driver secret key=value
            --group           | volume group / consistency-group name
            --limit-bytes     | max capacity to request
            --required-bytes  | min capacity to request
            --topology-preferred/-required | topology placement hints

         ⚠️ --availability, --scope, --secret, --sharing, --group and
            --topology-* target CLUSTER (CSI) volumes — they need API
            1.42+ and Swarm mode, not the plain local driver.

         🔬 easypj: `docker volume create --driver local --label
            project=easypj pgdata` is all a single-host Postgres setup
            needs — the cluster-volume flags above only matter once
            easypj runs under Swarm or a Kubernetes CSI driver.

    A.13 docker exec — Complete Flag Reference
            Flag             | Meaning
            -d/--detach      | run the exec'd command in the background
            --detach-keys    | override the default detach key sequence
            -e/--env         | KEY=value for this exec session only
            --env-file       | load exec-session env vars from a file
            -i/--interactive | keep STDIN open

    A.14 docker build / buildx build — Complete Flag Reference
         Core build inputs
            Flag             | Meaning
            -f/--file        | Dockerfile path (default PATH/Dockerfile)
            -t/--tag         | [registry/]repo[:tag], repeatable
            --build-arg      | KEY=VALUE build-time variable
            --build-context  | name=path, extra named build context
            --target         | build up to a specific Dockerfile stage
            --platform       | target platform(s), e.g. linux/amd64,arm64
            --add-host       | extra host:ip entry during build
            --label          | metadata key=value on the resulting image
            --network        | default|none|host build-time network mode
            --shm-size       | size of /dev/shm during build
            --ulimit         | type=soft[:hard] resource ulimit
            --cgroup-parent  | cgroup parent for build containers

         Cache & output
            Flag              | Meaning
            --no-cache        | ignore all cached layers
            --no-cache-filter | disable cache for named stages only
            --pull            | always attempt to pull a newer base image
            --cache-from      | import cache: registry/local/gha/s3/azblob
            --cache-to        | export cache to the same backend types
            -o/--output       | type=local,dest=path — write build result
            --load            | shorthand for --output=type=docker
            --push            | shorthand for --output=type=registry
            --iidfile         | write the resulting image ID to a file
            --metadata-file   | write build result metadata (JSON) to file
            --progress        | auto|none|plain|quiet|rawjson|tty
            -q/--quiet        | suppress build output, print image ID only

         Supply chain & multi-command
            Flag         | Meaning
            --secret     | id=name[,src=path] build secret
            --ssh        | default, or id[=socket] SSH agent forward
            --allow      | entitlement: network.host, security.insecure
            --annotation | OCI annotation on the image/index
            --attest     | type=sbom,generator=image custom attestation
            --sbom       | shorthand for --attest=type=sbom
            --provenance | shorthand for --attest=type=provenance
            --call       | build|check|outline|targets (default build)
            --check      | shorthand for --call=check

         🔬 easypj: `docker build --target production --build-arg
            DJANGO_ENV=prod --cache-from type=registry,ref=easypj:cache
            -t easypj:v2 .` reuses registry cache and stops at the
            production stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile.

    A.15 docker ps — Complete Reference + All Filter Keys
         Flags
            Flag        | Meaning
            -a/--all    | include stopped containers too
            -f/--filter | key=value filter (see table below)
            --format    | Go template or json output
            -n/--last   | show last N containers (default -1 = all)
            -l/--latest | show only the most recently created container
            --no-trunc  | don't truncate IDs/columns
            -q/--quiet  | print container IDs only
            -s/--size   | show each container's on-disk size

         Filter keys
            Key            | Matches
            id             | container ID (full or prefix)
            name           | container name
            label          | key or key=value label
            exited         | exit code of stopped containers
            status         | created/restarting/running/removing/
                           | paused/exited/dead
            ancestor       | image it was run from
            before/since   | created before/after a given container
            volume         | container using a given volume
            network        | container attached to a given network
            publish/expose | container publishing/exposing a given port
            health         | starting/healthy/unhealthy/none
            is-task        | container is a swarm service task

         🔬 easypj: `docker ps -a --filter status=exited --filter
            ancestor=easypj:v1 --format '{{.Names}}: {{.Status}}'` lists
            every dead easypj:v1 container without the running Postgres
            container cluttering the output.

    A.16 docker search — Find Images on Docker Hub
         Not covered elsewhere in this guide. Queries Docker Hub itself
         (not your local image cache) — useful before committing to a
         base image. Syntax: docker search [OPTIONS] TERM

            Flag         | Meaning
            -f/--filter  | key=value (see filters below)
            --format     | Go template: .Name .Description .StarCount
                         | .IsOfficial
            --limit      | max results returned
            --no-trunc   | don't truncate the description column

            Filter       | Matches
            stars=N      | minimum star count
            is-official  | true|false — official image only
            is-automated | deprecated, ignore

         🔬 easypj: `docker search postgres --filter is-official=true
            --limit 5` shortlists the official postgres image before
            pinning easypj's database base image to a specific tag.

    A.17 docker checkpoint — Experimental Container Freeze/Restore
         Not covered elsewhere in this guide. ⚠️ EXPERIMENTAL and requires
         CRIU 2.0+ installed separately — Docker does not bundle it, so
         most default installs cannot run this today.

            Command                             | Purpose
            docker checkpoint create CONTAINER  | freeze state to disk
              CHECKPOINT [--leave-running]       | (--leave-running keeps
              [--checkpoint-dir]                 | it running afterward)
            docker checkpoint ls CONTAINER       | list saved checkpoints
            docker checkpoint rm CONTAINER CKPT  | delete a checkpoint
            docker start --checkpoint CKPT_ID    | restore a container
              CONTAINER                          | from a checkpoint

         Limitations: needs a recent kernel with seccomp support; -t/--tty
         containers cannot be checkpointed. Treat as a lab curiosity, not
         a production backup strategy for easypj containers.

    A.18 docker system prune — Exact Removal Scope by Flag Combination
         Complements 7.5 — the exact blast radius per flag combination,
         since guessing here has cost real teams real volumes.

            Command                  | Removes
            docker system prune      | stopped containers + unused
                                      | networks + DANGLING images only +
                                      | unused build cache
            docker system prune -a   | same, but ALL unused images (not
                                      | just dangling) — next run re-pulls
            docker system prune      | above, PLUS anonymous volumes not
              --volumes               | used by any container
            docker system prune -a   | maximum blast radius: all unused
              --volumes               | images + anonymous volumes
            -f/--force                | skip the "Are you sure?" prompt
            --filter until=<time>    | only touch things older than <time>
            --filter label=<k>=<v>   | same key = OR; different keys = AND
            --filter label!=<k>=<v>  | exclude matching items by label

         ⚠️ Gotcha: --volumes only removes ANONYMOUS volumes (no --name,
         no compose service reference keeping it alive). easypj's named
         `pgdata` volume survives every combination above — but confirm
         with `docker volume ls` before running -a --volumes on a shared
         host.

    A.19 docker stack deploy — Flags (reference; see Chapter 28.4)

           ignored, not treated as errors
         [TABLE: docker stack deploy — flags]
         | Flag                 | Meaning                                |
         | -c/--compose-file    | path, or "-" for stdin; repeatable to |
         |                      | layer multiple compose files          |
         | -d/--detach          | default true; returns immediately     |
         |                      | instead of waiting for convergence    |
         | --prune              | remove services no longer referenced  |
         | -q/--quiet           | suppress progress output              |
         | --resolve-image      | default always (always/changed/never) |
         |                      | — query registry for image digest and |
         |                      | platform info                         |
         | --with-registry-auth | send registry auth to Swarm agents    |

         - syntax: docker context create [OPTIONS] CONTEXT
         [TABLE: docker context create — flags]
         | Flag          | Meaning                                      |
         | --description | human-readable description for the context   |
         | --docker      | set the docker endpoint: host=<endpoint>     |
         | --from        | create from an existing named context        |
         - examples:
           $ docker context create \
               --docker host=unix:///var/run/docker.sock my-context
           $ docker context create --from existing-context my-context
