Appendix B: Dockerfile Quick Reference — All Instructions
    B.1 Complete instruction list with syntax and examples
    B.2 Dockerfile templates (Python, Node.js, Go, Java, Static HTML)
    B.3 Multi-stage Dockerfile templates
    B.4 Dockerfile for Django (easypj template)
    B.5 .dockerignore templates

    B.6 Modern Dockerfile Features (BuildKit era)
         - here-doc RUN blocks: RUN <<EOF ... EOF — multi-line scripts
           without && chains; one layer, readable
         - COPY --chmod=755 --chown=app:app — ownership/permissions set
           at copy time (no extra RUN chown layer)
         - RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip — persistent
           build caches across builds; --mount=type=secret for build-time
           credentials that never enter any layer
         - parser directives: # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 as line 1 opts
           into the latest Dockerfile frontend features

    B.7 RUN --mount — All 5 Types (Official Reference)
         - RUN --mount attaches a filesystem to that ONE RUN step; unlike
           COPY/ADD, nothing lands in the image unless copied out again —
           built for build-only inputs, caches, and secrets.
         [TABLE: RUN --mount types — type | purpose]
            bind   | mount context/another stage, read-only by default
                   | opts: target, source, from, rw
            cache  | persistent dir for compiler/package-manager caches
                   | opts: id, target, ro, sharing, from, source, mode,
                   |       uid, gid
            tmpfs  | temp in-memory filesystem, scoped to this RUN
                   | opts: target, size
            secret | secure file/env var, exposed only during this RUN
                   | opts: id, target, env, required, mode, uid, gid
            ssh    | forwards SSH agent/keys into this RUN
                   | opts: id, target, required, mode, uid, gid
         - easypj already uses cache and secret (5.7's pip cache and
           pipconf); a bind mount replaces a throwaway COPY for a
           build-only file:
              RUN --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,\
                  target=/tmp/req.txt pip install -r /tmp/req.txt

    B.8 RUN --network and RUN --security Modes
         - two more independent RUN flags — not --mount types — that
           control network and privilege scope for a single RUN step.
         [TABLE: RUN --network | effect]
            default | standard network access (the default)
            none    | no network; loopback only, fully isolated
            host    | shares the host's network stack; requires a
                    | BuildKit allow-entitlement flag
         [TABLE: RUN --security | effect]
            sandbox  | default secure, unprivileged mode
            insecure | elevated/unprivileged-breaking mode; requires a
                     | BuildKit allow-entitlement flag
         - easypj example: RUN --network=none pip install --no-index \
              --find-links=/wheels -r requirements.txt proves the layer
           never reaches PyPI — every wheel came from the local cache.

    B.9 Parser Directives — syntax, escape, check
         - three parser directives exist; ALL must sit before any other
           line (even comments) or Docker silently ignores them.
         [TABLE: directive | purpose]
            # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1  | pins the Dockerfile frontend
                                           | version; unlocks newer syntax
                                           | (e.g. B.6's heredoc RUN blocks)
            # escape=\  (or  # escape=`)  | sets the escape character;
                                           | backtick avoids clashing with
                                           | Windows-style paths
            # check=skip=<name>;error=true| (v1.8.0+) skip one check or
                                           | skip=all; error=true fails
                                           | the build on any check warning
         - easypj's Dockerfile should open with `# syntax=docker/
           dockerfile:1` as line 1 — B.6's heredoc RUN blocks depend on it.

    B.10 Environment Variable Expansion — Full Modifier Reference
         - $var or ${var} expand inside ADD, COPY, ENV, EXPOSE, FROM,
           LABEL, STOPSIGNAL, USER, VOLUME, WORKDIR and ONBUILD. Four
           bash-style modifiers refine the default value:
         [TABLE: modifier | meaning]
            ${var:-word} | word if var is UNSET or EMPTY, else var
            ${var-word}  | word if var is UNSET only (empty string kept)
            ${var:+word} | word if var is SET and non-empty, else empty
            ${var+word}  | word if var is set at all, else empty
         - easypj examples:
              ENV PORT=${PORT:-8000}       # default when PORT unset
              ENV DEBUG=${DJANGO_ENV:+1}   # "1" only if ARG was passed

    B.11 ADD's Git/URL/Checksum Capabilities (vs COPY)
         - ADD does two things COPY cannot: auto-extract local tar
           archives, and accept a remote URL or Git repo URL directly as
           <src> (COPY only takes paths inside the build context).
         [TABLE: ADD-only/extra flag | purpose]
            --keep-git-dir | keeps .git when <src> is a Git repo URL
            --checksum     | verifies a remote file's digest before
                            | adding it; fails the build on mismatch
            --unpack       | controls tar auto-extraction; true by
                            | default for LOCAL tars, false for URLs
            --chmod        | sets perms at add-time (shared with COPY)
            --chown        | sets owner:group at add-time (shared with
                            | COPY)
            --link         | reuses already-built layers (shared with
                            | COPY)
            --exclude      | pattern-based exclusion (shared with COPY)
         - easypj still uses COPY for its own source: local files need no
           extraction or remote fetch, so COPY's narrower behaviour stays
           the safer default (4.2's audit-red-flag warning stands). ADD
           earns its place for a genuine one-off fetch, e.g.:
              ADD --checksum=sha256:<digest> \
                  https://example.com/geoip.mmdb /app/geoip.mmdb
         - Note: heredoc syntax (B.6) isn't RUN-only — CMD, ENTRYPOINT,
           COPY and ADD all accept the same <<EOF ... EOF block form.

Appendix C: docker-compose.yml Quick Reference
    C.1 Complete compose.yaml reference (all keys)
    C.2 compose.yaml templates (Django+Postgres, Django+Postgres+Redis, etc.)
    C.3 compose override templates (dev, staging, prod)
    C.4 Health check templates
    C.5 watch configuration templates

    C.6 Compose File Power Features
         - extension fields: top-level x-* blocks hold reusable chunks
           the parser ignores (x-common-env, x-logging)
         - YAML anchors & aliases: &defaults / <<: *defaults — define
           once, merge into many services; pairs with x-* fields
         - top-level name: key sets the project name inside the file
           itself (replaces relying on the directory name or -p flag)

    C.7 The deploy: Key — Full Reference (Compose-file syntax, Swarm-only)
         deploy: is read by `docker stack deploy` (Swarm mode, Ch28);
         plain `docker compose up` does not act on most of it — the
         CLI-flag versions students actually run day-to-day live in
         28.7-28.10. This is the YAML-file equivalent of those flags.

         - mode: "replicated" (default, N copies) | "global" (one task
           per node) | "replicated-job" | "global-job" (run-to-completion)
         - replicas: <int> — YAML form of `docker service scale`
         - endpoint_mode: "vip" (one virtual IP, load-balanced) | "dnsrr"
           (DNS round-robin to each task's own IP)
         - placement.constraints / placement.preferences — YAML form of
           28.10's --constraint (hard) and --placement-pref (soft)
         - labels: — service metadata; distinct from a service's own
           top-level labels: key

         [TABLE: resources — same sub-keys under limits: & reservations:]
         | Sub-key | Meaning                  | easypj web tier example |
         | cpus    | CPU share, decimal string| limits.cpus: "1.00"     |
         | memory  | RAM, string with unit    | limits.memory: 512M     |
         | pids    | max PIDs in the task     | limits.pids: 100        |
         | devices | GPU/device reservations  | capabilities/driver/count|

         [TABLE: restart_policy — deploy's own restart, not top-level's]
         | Sub-key      | Values / meaning                          |
         | condition    | "none" | "on-failure" | "any" (default)    |
         | delay        | wait between restart attempts, e.g. 5s    |
         | max_attempts | give up after N tries (default: unlimited)|
         | window       | time window used to judge attempt success |

         [TABLE: update_config / rollback_config — mirrored sub-keys]
         | Sub-key           | Values                               |
         | parallelism       | tasks touched per batch              |
         | delay             | pause between batches                |
         | failure_action    | update: continue|rollback|pause      |
         |                   | rollback: continue|pause             |
         | monitor           | how long to judge a new task         |
         | max_failure_ratio | tolerated failure share before acting|
         | order             | stop-first | start-first             |

         easypj cross-ref: 28.8's `--update-failure-action rollback
         --update-order start-first` (CLI) becomes, in a stack file,
         `deploy.update_config: {failure_action: rollback, order:
         start-first}` — same knobs, YAML instead of flags.

    C.8 The build: Key — Full Reference
         - context: / dockerfile: — same two inputs as `docker build`'s
           PATH and -f; dockerfile_inline: writes the Dockerfile inline
           in compose.yaml instead of a separate file
         - args: — build-time ARG values (5.4); labels: — OCI labels
           baked into the built IMAGE, not the running container's
         - target: — build only one stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile,
           same as `docker build --target`
         - platforms: — list form of 5.5's `--platform
           linux/amd64,linux/arm64`; needs a buildx builder
         - cache_from: / cache_to: — YAML form of 5.3's --cache-from;
           e.g. type=registry,ref=... or type=gha for CI caches
         - secrets: / ssh: — YAML form of 5.7's --secret / --ssh
           build-time credentials that never land in an image layer
         - no_cache / pull / privileged / network / shm_size / ulimits —
           one-to-one with their `docker build` flag namesakes
         - provenance / sbom — attestation toggles (bool, or a string
           like "mode=max" / "generator=..."), off by default
         - additional_contexts: — extra named build contexts (as
           NAME=VALUE), usable as `COPY --from=NAME` beyond the base
           context
         - entitlements: — opts BuildKit into extra privileges (e.g.
           network, security.insecure) a build step explicitly requests

         [CODE: easypj's build: key using more than context/dockerfile]
            django:
              build:
                context: .
                target: production
                args:
                  DJANGO_ENV: production
                cache_from:
                  - type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/you/easypj:buildcache
                platforms: ["linux/amd64", "linux/arm64"]

    C.9 Volume Mount Types — the Full List
         [TABLE: the six `type:` values under a long-syntax volumes: entry]
         | type   | Purpose                                         |
         | volume | Docker-managed named volume (postgres_data)     |
         | bind   | Host path mounted straight through (dev source) |
         | tmpfs  | RAM-only, gone when the container stops         |
         | image  | mount another built IMAGE's filesystem (newer)  |
         | npipe  | Windows named pipe (Windows container hosts)    |
         | cluster| Swarm CSI cluster volume, multi-host (newer)    |

         Long syntax is always type: + source: + target: (+ read_only:)
         plus a type-specific sub-block (bind.*, volume.*, tmpfs.*,
         image.*). easypj's postgres_data (11.2) written long-form:
            volumes:
              - type: volume
                source: postgres_data
                target: /var/lib/postgresql/data
         and 11.3's nginx.conf bind mount:
            volumes:
              - type: bind
                source: ./nginx.conf
                target: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
                read_only: true
         image and cluster are the newest two types: image shares a
         built image's filesystem read-only (no extra COPY needed to
         hand static assets to another service); cluster names a CSI
         volume for Swarm's multi-host storage drivers.

    C.10 pull_policy and Other Easily-Missed Attributes
         [TABLE: pull_policy — all 7 values]
         | Value            | Behavior                              |
         | always           | always pull, even if cached locally   |
         | never            | never pull, fail if image is missing  |
         | missing          | pull only if not already cached (dflt)|
         | build            | always build, even if image: is set   |
         | daily            | pull if the cached image is >1 day old|
         | weekly           | pull if cached image is >1 week old   |
         | every_<duration> | pull if cached image older than that  |

         - gpus: short form takes a driver, a count, or the literal
           "all" — the long form's full capabilities/device_ids table
           is 34.2's territory; this is the Compose-file shortcut for
           the same request
         - models: — Compose's hook into 34.1's Docker Model Runner;
           short form names a model, long form sets endpoint_var: /
           model_var: so a service's environment gets the model's
           endpoint URL and name injected instead of hardcoding
           localhost:12434
         - credential_spec: file: or registry: — Windows gMSA
           credentials for a container joining an Active Directory
           domain; unrelated to secrets: despite the similar name

         easypj cross-ref: `pull_policy: build` on the django service
         guarantees `docker compose up` never runs a stale cached
         easypj:v1 image after a Dockerfile change with no new tag.

    F.8 Exit-Code Decoder
         - 0    clean exit — process completed successfully
         - 1    application error — read the app's own logs first
         - 125  docker run ITSELF failed (bad flag, daemon error) — the
                container never started
         - 126  command found but not executable (permissions, not a
                binary)
         - 127  command not found (typo, missing binary, wrong PATH)
         - 137  SIGKILL — OOM kill (check docker inspect
                .State.OOMKilled) or docker kill / stop-timeout expiry
         - 139  SIGSEGV — segfault inside the process (native code, bad
                library)
         - 143  SIGTERM honored — a graceful docker stop

    G.2 Docker acronyms explained

    G.3 Modern & Exam-Critical Terms — Glossary Must-Haves
         - BuildKit — the modern build engine behind docker build
           (parallel stages, cache mounts, build secrets)
         - digest — immutable sha256 identity of an image; tags move,
           digests never do
         - manifest list — one tag serving multiple architectures
           (amd64/arm64); what docker pull resolves on Apple Silicon
         - docker context — named CLI target (local socket, ssh remote);
           see A.10
         - live-restore — daemon.json flag: containers survive dockerd
           restarts
         - routing mesh — Swarm's any-node:port → healthy-task routing
           (ingress network + IPVS)
         - DOCKER-USER chain — the iptables chain reserved for YOUR
           firewall rules, evaluated before Docker's own

Appendix J: 4-Week DCA Study Plan
================================================================================
    A week-by-week study cadence mapping directly onto this guide's own
    Parts and Chapters — the same plan Section 6.7 in the front matter
    points to. Budget ~10-15 hours/week; adjust down if you're already
    comfortable with a given week's domain per your 30.2 self-score.

    J.1 Week 1 — Foundations & Hands-On (Parts 1-2, Ch1-6)
         Goal: own the vocabulary and the CLI grammar cold.
         - Day 1-2: Ch1-3 (the mental model, images/containers/registries,
           install + first container). Drill: 13's LAB Q&A, both chapters.
         - Day 3-5: Ch4-6 (Dockerfile, docker build, docker run &
           lifecycle). Build easypj's own Dockerfile from memory once.
         - Day 6-7: Part 1-2 Key Takeaways review + Appendix A.11-A.15
           (docker run/build flag references) skim.
         Checkpoint: rebuild, tag, and run easypj:v1 from an empty
         checkout, without notes, in under 10 minutes.

    J.2 Week 2 — Images, Compose & Networking (Parts 3-5, Ch7-15)
         Goal: own Image Creation/Mgmt/Registry (20%) and Networking (15%).
         - Day 1-2: Ch7-9 (image management, optimization, the full
           easypj build-and-run walkthrough).
         - Day 3-4: Ch10-12 (Compose fundamentals → easypj's real stack →
           profiles/overrides/scaling).
         - Day 5-7: Ch13-15 (CNM model, easypj's two-network design, host/
           macvlan/overlay + the debugging ladder).
         Checkpoint: stand up easypj's full 4-service Compose stack cold,
         then intentionally break DNS resolution and fix it using only
         the 15.4 debugging ladder.

    J.3 Week 3 — Storage, Security & Shipping (Parts 6-8, Ch16-24)
         Goal: own Storage & Volumes (10%) and Security (15%); build CI/CD
         fluency (not graded, but load-bearing for Domain 2 in practice).
         - Day 1-2: Ch16-18 (volumes/bind mounts/tmpfs, easypj's real
           assignments, overlay2 internals).
         - Day 3-4: Ch19-21 (the security onion, hardening checklist,
           Docker Scout/Bench/Trivy/SBOM).
         - Day 5-7: Ch22-24 (CI/CD pipelines, tagging & promotion —
           graded — testing pyramid).
         Checkpoint: harden easypj to non-root + cap-drop ALL + read-only,
         then run `docker scout quickview` and explain every finding.

    J.4 Week 4 — Orchestration, Bridge & Exam Prep (Parts 9-10, Ch25-30)
         Goal: own Orchestration (25%, the single biggest domain) and
         Installation & Configuration (15%); close every remaining gap.
         - Day 1-2: Ch25-27 (the Docker→Kubernetes bridge — context, not
           exam content, but reinforces the noun model).
         - Day 3-5: Ch28 (Docker Swarm, ALL 10 sections — this is 25% of
           the exam by itself) + Ch29 (Compose portability).
         - Day 6: Ch30 (exam strategy, domain weights, pacing).
         - Day 7: Appendix H full mock exam (100+ questions), timed,
           three-pass method from 30.7; review every miss against 30.9's
           gap table.
         Checkpoint: run the full Swarm lifecycle (init → service create
         → scale → update → rollback) in under 15 minutes, no notes.

    J.5 Exam Week — Final Review
         - Re-run Appendix H questions you missed the first time.
         - Re-read Section 6.2-6.4 (domain weights + coverage audit) once.
         - Confirm exam-day logistics per 30.8 (system check, ID, second
           monitor unplugged) at least 24 hours before your slot.
         - Rest the day before — cramming new material in the final 24
           hours has a worse ROI than a calm, rehearsed test-taker.

Appendix K: DCA Exam Simulator — 15 Practical Tasks
================================================================================
    A scenario-based practice set modeled on the DCA's performance
    expectations, weighted by domain the same way the real exam is
    (Section 6.2). Time yourself: 90 minutes total, all 15 tasks, no
    notes — then check against the Domain 6.4 coverage table to see
    which domain needs another pass.

    K.1  [Orchestration, 25%] Initialize a single-node Swarm, then deploy
         easypj as a service named `easypj-web` with 3 replicas, image
         `easypj:v1`, publishing port 8000.
         Verify: `docker service ls` shows 3/3 replicas running.

    K.2  [Orchestration] Scale `easypj-web` to 5 replicas without editing
         its original service definition, then roll it back to 3.
         Verify: `docker service ps easypj-web` shows the count changing
         both times.

    K.3  [Orchestration] Update `easypj-web` to image `easypj:v2` with
         `--update-parallelism 1 --update-delay 10s
         --update-failure-action rollback`. Simulate a bad tag and
         confirm the automatic rollback fires.
         Verify: `docker service ps easypj-web` shows Shutdown tasks on
         v2 and Running tasks back on v1.

    K.4  [Orchestration] Create a Docker secret named `db_password` from a
         local file and mount it into a new `postgres` service.
         Verify: `docker exec` into the postgres task and confirm
         `/run/secrets/db_password` exists and `docker service inspect`
         never prints its value.

    K.5  [Image Mgmt & Registry, 20%] Build easypj with a multi-stage
         Dockerfile, tag it three ways (git-SHA, semver, and
         semver+SHA combined), and confirm all three share one Image ID.
         Verify: `docker images | grep easypj` shows one ID, three tags.

    K.6  [Image Mgmt & Registry] Promote an image from a `staging` tag to
         a `production` tag by digest, without rebuilding.
         Verify: `docker inspect --format '{{.Id}}'` on both tags returns
         the identical local Image ID.

    K.7  [Image Mgmt & Registry] Run `docker history` on any image you've
         built this session and identify its two heaviest layers.
         Verify: name both layers' originating Dockerfile instruction.

    K.8  [Installation & Config, 15%] Configure a daemon.json with
         `"log-driver": "json-file"`, `"log-opts": {"max-size": "10m",
         "max-file": "3"}`, and `"icc": false`, then restart the daemon.
         Verify: `docker info --format '{{.SecurityOptions}}'` and a log
         rotation check both reflect the change.

    K.9  [Installation & Config] Create a Swarm with 3 managers, verify
         quorum with `docker node ls`, then stop one manager and confirm
         the cluster still accepts writes.
         Verify: `docker service create` still succeeds with 2/3 managers
         reachable.

    K.10 [Networking, 15%] Create two user-defined bridge networks
         (`frontend`, `backend`), attach a `django` container to both and
         a `postgres` container to `backend` only, and prove `django` can
         reach `postgres` by name while a `nginx` container on `frontend`
         alone cannot.
         Verify: three `docker exec ... ping` results matching that
         description exactly.

    K.11 [Networking] Publish a container's port bound only to
         127.0.0.1, then confirm it is unreachable from another machine
         on the LAN but reachable from the host itself.
         Verify: a remote curl fails, a local curl succeeds.

    K.12 [Security, 15%] Take any running container and re-run it with
         `--user 1000:1000 --cap-drop ALL --read-only --tmpfs /tmp`, and
         confirm it still serves traffic.
         Verify: `docker exec ... id` shows a non-root UID, and the app
         responds to a request.

    K.13 [Security] Run `docker scout quickview` (or Trivy) against an
         image and identify whether its Critical/High findings originate
         from the base image or your own added layer.
         Verify: state which layer to fix, based on the base-vs-target
         split.

    K.14 [Storage & Volumes, 10%] Create a named volume, mount it into a
         postgres container, insert data, remove the container, and
         mount the SAME volume into a brand-new postgres container.
         Verify: the data is present in the new container without a
         restore step.

    K.15 [Storage & Volumes] Take a `pg_dump` backup of a running
         database, drop and recreate the database, then restore from the
         dump.
         Verify: a row-count query returns the same number before and
         after the drop/restore cycle.

    K.16  SCORING GUIDE
         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │  Domain              │ Tasks        │ Weight │ Your score /5  │
         │  Orchestration       │ K.1-K.4      │ 25%    │ ___ / 4        │
         │  Image Mgmt/Registry │ K.5-K.7      │ 20%    │ ___ / 3        │
         │  Installation/Config │ K.8-K.9      │ 15%    │ ___ / 2        │
         │  Networking          │ K.10-K.11    │ 15%    │ ___ / 2        │
         │  Security            │ K.12-K.13    │ 15%    │ ___ / 2        │
         │  Storage & Volumes   │ K.14-K.15    │ 10%    │ ___ / 2        │
         └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         Any domain below 80% here is your next study session — cross-
         reference the missed task's chapter citation against Section
         6.3's domain-to-chapter map and re-read that section before
         re-attempting.
